Such matches turn abstract annihilators into usable tests for singular points. Slopes of the defining equations supply standard annihilator members. The zero set of the ideal already traces the singular locus broadly. Rings of dimension one are the natural first case for exact claims.
arxiv-2510-06620:
Shijie Qin examines turbulence through the equations that govern fluid motion. His 2025 paper uses two-dimensional turbulent flow as a test case. He asks a deep question about chaos in the Navier-Stokes equations. Ordinary chaos means a tiny change alters a system's path. Qin studies a stronger form, called ultra-chaos, where even the statistics shift.

To rule out numerical noise as a false cause, he uses a clean simulation method. That method keeps errors so small that they cannot explain the results. He finds that a tiny change in the starting flow leads to huge differences later. The flow's symmetry and its long-run statistics both change. That means small disturbances matter even at the level of averages. The finding helps explain why turbulence is so hard to predict. It also raises a logical puzzle, since real models must ignore some small disturbances.
arxiv-2510-07220:
Wagner and colleagues use a cosmic lens to probe the jet of a blazar, a galaxy firing a beam toward Earth. Their 2025 paper studies PKS 1830-211, whose light a foreground galaxy splits into two images. The team gathered X-ray and gamma-ray data from three space telescopes. They compared a quiet period in 2016 with a flaring one in 2019. A sharpened timing method extracted the lens delay from the gamma-ray record.

The delay came out near twenty-one days, and it stayed fixed across epochs. The brightness ratio between the images also held steady. X-ray output barely changed between the two periods. Gamma rays, in contrast, swung wildly. The combined spectrum fits a model where electrons radiate directly and also bounce infrared light to gamma energies. Stable lens numbers help separate source behavior from lens effects in future studies.
arxiv-2510-07420:
Cavey, Gorsky, Oblomkov, and Turner compute convex bodies that encode the sections of line bundles on nested Hilbert schemes. Their 2025 paper works in algebraic geometry. A Hilbert scheme parametrizes clusters of points on the plane, and nested versions track clusters inside clusters. Line bundles on these spaces carry spaces of sections with rich structure. Earlier work by Haiman described those sections through special ideals in many variables. The authors analyze trailing terms under a monomial order to extract explicit bases for the section spaces from that description.

From those bases, the Newton-Okounkov bodies follow. These convex bodies summarize a bundle's sections the way a shadow summarizes a shape. Computing them turns asymptotic questions about sections into geometry that can be drawn and measured. The nested setting is substantially harder than the classical one, since two point counts interact.
arxiv-2510-07620:
Usman and Lee present DGTEN in this 2025 computer science paper on trust in changing networks. Online systems must judge which users and nodes deserve trust. Those judgments shift over time, and attackers work to distort them. DGTEN is a graph neural network built to score trust while stating its own uncertainty. It also aims to resist attacks such as reputation laundering and sabotage.

The network treats nodes and edges as probability distributions rather than fixed values. It tracks abrupt shifts and smooth trends in trust over time. A defense step down-weights suspicious interactions before they sway the scores. On two signed Bitcoin trust networks, DGTEN beat the best rival method by clear margins. Its gains were largest in cold-start cases, where little history exists for new users. Trust scores guide decisions in finance, social platforms, and device networks.
arxiv-2510-07720:
Liu, Wang, Cui, and Ye wrote this 2025 information retrieval paper on video search. A short text query rarely captures everything a video contains. Systems that match queries to metadata word by word miss that richness. The authors argue that queries should not stand alone. Related queries carry extra shades of meaning that can widen the match. Their framework builds that idea into the search process.

The framework, called Video-Text Cluster, groups related queries into clusters before matching. A Sweeper module then cleans noise out of each cluster. An attention mechanism weighs the cluster's text features against the actual video frames. That keeps retrieval focused on what the video really shows. Across five public datasets, the model beat existing state-of-the-art systems. The results suggest that borrowing meaning from neighboring queries is a cheap way to sharpen video search without new annotations.
arxiv-2510-07820:
Beckey and four coauthors wrote this 2025 quantum information paper on testing whether a quantum state is a product state. A product state has no entanglement across a split. Testers can measure one copy at a time or many copies jointly. The authors ask how many samples each strategy needs. They study two variants: finding any clean split, and checking that every split is clean.

For the first variant, they prove an exponential lower bound for all single-copy algorithms. Joint multi-copy methods are efficient there, so the gap is exponential. That hardness spreads to related entanglement learning tasks. For the second variant, they prove another lower bound separating the strategies. They also give a single-copy local algorithm for the multipartite task that is optimal for two parties. A technical lemma about overlaps of permutation operators drives the proofs.
arxiv-2510-07920:
Li and four coauthors wrote this 2025 paper on a profit mirage in AI trading agents. Language-model traders post dazzling back-tested returns. Once trading moves past the model's training window, those returns collapse. The cause is information leakage baked into the model itself. It has quietly memorized the future it is supposedly predicting. The authors measure that leakage across four dimensions and build tools to fight it.

They release FinLake-Bench, an evaluation suite designed to resist leakage. Their FactFin framework then attacks the cause. Counterfactual perturbations force the agent to learn what drives prices instead of memorizing outcomes. A strategy generator, retrieval, tree search, and a counterfactual simulator form the pipeline. In out-of-sample tests, FactFin beat every baseline on risk-adjusted performance. The authors argue that honest evaluation must assume leakage until proven otherwise. Their work resets expectations for what AI traders really earn.
arxiv-2510-08020:
Duer-Milner and four coauthors wrote this 2025 planetary science paper seeking one mechanism behind the equatorial jets of all four giant planets. Jupiter and Saturn blow strong eastward jets at their equators. Uranus and Neptune blow strong westward ones. Earlier theories explained the two directions with different mechanisms. The shared planetary parameters made that split unsatisfying. The authors instead test convection-driven columnar structures as a single cause.

Their analysis shows the two jet patterns emerge as two stable branches of one solution, a bifurcation. Eastward superrotation and westward subrotation are both stable outcomes of the same dynamics. The branches even share equatorial wave properties and the same leading momentum balance. One mechanism thus covers gas giants and ice giants alike. The result suggests jet formation follows broader rules than planet-by-planet theories assumed. It also gives modelers a unified target when simulating giant planet weather.
arxiv-2510-08120:
Gajcin and five coauthors wrote this 2025 paper extracting readable global policies from language models used as judges of other models' text. Judge models scale evaluation, but their hidden criteria may encode bias. One algorithm generates contrastive, concept-based explanations for individual decisions and verifies each. A second clusters, summarizes, and verifies those local rules into a global policy. The team tested the pipeline on seven harm detection benchmarks.

The extracted policies proved highly faithful to the judge's actual decisions. They also survived robustness checks against perturbations and adversarial attacks. A user study found users understood the judge's policy somewhat better, and perceived usefulness improved significantly. Explanation quality remains limited by the pipeline's own components. Still, the work shows a judge's implicit rules can be surfaced, checked, and debated, which is essential wherever automated judges gatekeep content.
arxiv-2510-08220:
Huang, Fang, Chen, and Wu wrote this 2025 semiconductor physics paper on how electrons move through silicon at cryogenic temperatures, where quantum computer wiring must operate. Using multi-valley Monte Carlo simulations of silicon in the (110) orientation, they found the transport rules change fundamentally when cold. Phonon scattering fades to negligible. Mobility is instead set by a competition: remote Coulomb scattering dominates at low carrier densities, while surface roughness scattering dominates at high densities.

That competition produces a distinct peak in electron mobility at intermediate density. The authors also expose a trade-off with high-permittivity gate oxides such as hafnium oxide. They improve gate control but introduce strong remote phonon scattering that can suppress mobility. Cryogenic transistors run quantum processors' control electronics, so mobility sets real performance limits. The guidance is concrete: choose dielectric and density together, and aim for the mobility peak.
arxiv-2510-08320:
Patryk Lipka-Bartosik and co-authors probe what a reusable quantum helper adds to local operations, in a 2025 arXiv paper. In entanglement theory, two distant parties can transform shared quantum states using local operations and classical messages. Adding a catalyst, a system that helps but stays unchanged, greatly widens what they can do. The open question is how much of that gain comes from the messages alone.

The authors define catalytic local operations, which use a catalyst but no classical communication channel. They compare this class with standard local operations plus classical communication. They also compare it with stochastic versions aided by bounded quantum communication. The classes turn out to be incomparable: each allows transformations the other cannot reach. This shows catalysis and communication are distinct resources, not substitutes for one another.
arxiv-2510-08420:
Rémy Cerda and Alexis Saurin prove a compression property for infinite rewriting systems in a 2025 arXiv paper in logic. Infinitary rewriting handles possibly infinite terms and reduction sequences, modeling programs that run productively forever. Compression says any reduction sequence, however long in ordinal terms, can be shortened. An equivalent sequence of length at most omega, the first infinite ordinal, should always exist.

The authors extend the coinductive presentation of these systems to arbitrary non-wellfounded derivations. They design a generic compression proof that factors out the shared core of earlier arguments. The proof isolates the key property a system must enjoy for compression to hold. Running examples cover first-order rewriting and infinitary lambda calculi, where compression justifies known presentations. A harder application treats cut-elimination in a proof system for linear logic that allows non-wellfounded derivations with fixed points.
arxiv-2510-08520:
Sriram Akella shows that a celebrated toy model of holography fails a three-way entanglement test in a 2025 arXiv paper. Holographic states obey entropy inequalities derived from the Ryu-Takayanagi formula of gravity. Those classic inequalities only involve bipartite entanglement between two regions. A newer GHZ-forbidding inequality uses reflected entropy and tripartite multi-entropy to probe three-way structure.

Akella proves this inequality is either violated or exactly saturated, never strictly satisfied, by stabilizer states. Stabilizer states are a large, tractable class that includes many quantum error-correcting codes. The result therefore shows stabilizer states are not holographic in this stricter sense. As a consequence, tripartite entanglement in the HaPPY code is not holographic. HaPPY is a famous pentagon code often used as a holography toy model. The finding limits how far such toy models mirror real holography.
arxiv-2510-09520:
Ali Javadi-Abhari, Simon Martiel, Alireza Seif, Maika Takita, and Ken Wei report a record in quantum computing in a 2025 arXiv paper. Entanglement links particles so their states must be described together, and faithfully entangling many qubits is a standard benchmark of hardware quality. The test state is the Greenberger-Horne-Zeilinger state, also called a cat state, which is easy to verify but very sensitive to noise.

The team prepared the largest such state to date, spanning 120 superconducting qubits. They combined optimised circuit compilation, error detection with low overhead, and temporary uncomputation, with an automated compiler that maximised error detection under each chip's connectivity and error rates. The measured fidelity was about zero point five six, with a post-selection rate of twenty-eight percent. Several certification methods agreed, and the authors discuss the practical trade-offs among them.
arxiv-2510-09820:
Eleonora Parlanti, Giulia Tozzi, and a large team of co-authors dissect a spiral galaxy seen as it was when the universe was young in a 2025 arXiv paper. The galaxy, known as K20-ID7, sits at redshift about two point two, in the cosmic noon era of peak galaxy assembly. It is a large, star-forming spiral with hints of gas flowing inward.

Combining Webb spectroscopy and imaging with a ground-based instrument, the team resolves the galaxy's stars and gas. They find massive star-forming clumps with low dust obscuration and gas density. The central bulge is modest in mass but heavily dust-obscured, and it likely formed most of its stars in the past while still forming some today. The gas shows near-solar metallicity with enhanced nitrogen relative to oxygen.
arxiv-2510-09920:
Gibson and a large team report a TESS discovery around the star RZ Psc in this 2025 arXiv paper in astronomy. TESS, a space telescope that watches starlight for dips, found transiting exocomets, comets passing in front of the star. The system is only the second known with enough events to measure the size distribution of its comets.

RZ Psc hosts an extreme debris disk, a dense ring of rubble left from planet formation. Counting comets by size lets the team compare this system with Beta Pictoris, the first such system, and with the Solar System. Those comparisons test whether comet populations form in similar ways around other stars. The many detected transits make that size census possible.
arxiv-2510-10020:
Smith, Nathaniel L. Diamant, and Brian L. Trippe frame calibration of generative models as optimization in this 2025 arXiv paper on machine learning. Generative models are often miscalibrated: class probabilities and other statistics of their samples drift away from the values users want. Fixing the drift without wrecking the model is the problem.

The authors pose calibration as a constrained optimization problem. They seek the closest model, measured by Kullback-Leibler divergence, that satisfies the calibration constraints. Closeness matters because a heavy-handed fix could distort everything else the model does well. The framework turns calibration from ad hoc patching into a principled adjustment, with the trade-off between accuracy and fidelity stated in the objective itself.
arxiv-2510-10220:
Keskin, Mehmet Yaşar, and K. Kurt study constant-roll inflation in a modified gravity theory in this 2025 arXiv paper in cosmology. Inflation is the rapid early expansion of the universe. The authors work in f(R, phi, X) gravity, where the gravitational action depends on curvature, a scalar field, and its kinetic energy.

Under a constant-roll condition, which fixes how fast the field's velocity changes, they use a generalized potential raised to a power. They derive formulas for the spectral index, which describes the pattern of primordial fluctuations, and the tensor-to-scalar ratio, which compares gravitational waves to density waves. The dynamics turn out to be governed mainly by the power parameter and the potential's shape, a testable simplification.
arxiv-2510-11120:
When two lead nuclei pass very close without touching, the intense light from one can strike the other and create particles. Vendulka Humlová reports new ALICE Collaboration measurements of one such process in this 2025 arXiv paper. The team studied incoherent production of J/psi mesons, bound states of a charm quark and an antiquark, in lead-lead collisions, a channel sensitive to how gluons fluctuate inside nuclei.

The collisions ran at a nucleon-nucleon energy of 5.02 TeV, and the analysis sorts events by photon-nucleus energy and by momentum transfer, which reflects the size scale being probed. At small momentum transfer, the production rate rises as the photon energy grows. At larger momentum transfer, that growth is suppressed compared with the trend at low transfer. The authors note that this is the first study of incoherent photoproduction at the LHC mapped against both variables together.
arxiv-2510-11220:
Rayleigh-Bénard convection, fluid heated from below and cooled from above, is a classic test case for turbulence simulation. Shijie Qin, Kun Xu, and Shijun Liao simulate its two-dimensional form in this 2025 arXiv fluid dynamics paper. They solve the Navier-Stokes equations by direct numerical simulation in double precision, varying only the time-step size used by the solver.

They find two kinds of final flow, one vortical and one zonal, with completely different statistics. As the time-step shrinks to very small values, the two flow types alternate frequently, suggesting each type's time-steps are densely distributed. Because time-step size is tied to numerical noise, the result means stochastic numerical noise hugely influences the final flow and its statistics. That clashes with the Navier-Stokes model's own assumption that small disturbances are negligible, a logic paradox the authors say needs more investigation.
arxiv-2510-11420:
Programs for quantum computers mix quantum operations with ordinary classical logic, including decisions made mid-computation from fresh measurements, and compilers need a representation that captures both. Mark Koch and a large team introduce HUGR in this 2025 arXiv quantum computing paper. HUGR, the Hierarchical Unified Graph Representation, is an intermediate representation designed for mixed quantum-classical programs and the tooling that compiles them.

The design stresses expressivity and extensibility, aiming to cover near-term and future quantum devices and new programming abstractions as they appear. Its graph structure is machine-friendly and supports pattern-matching compilation techniques, while an MLIR-inspired design lets tools reason at several levels of abstraction and lower smoothly between them. Safety is built in through strict static typing and linear quantum types, so compilation tools can be built quickly without fear of breaking programs. A full specification and a reference implementation are open-source.
arxiv-2510-11520:
Outdoor navigation remains risky for people who are blind or have low vision, and AI assistants trained on ordinary image datasets rarely learn the hazards and landmarks that matter to them. Kedi Ying and co-authors build a dataset aimed at that gap in this 2025 arXiv computer vision paper. Their mmWalk dataset is simulated and combines multi-view sensing with accessibility-oriented features for safe outdoor walking.

The dataset holds 120 manually controlled walking trajectories in scenarios, with 62,000 synchronized frames and over 559,000 panoramic images across color, depth, and semantic channels, including corner cases and accessibility landmarks. A companion benchmark, mmWalkVQA, adds over 69,000 visual question-answer triplets in nine categories for safe walking assistance. State-of-the-art vision-language models, tested zero-shot and few-shot, struggled with its risk assessment and navigation tasks. A model fine-tuned on mmWalk, validated on real-world datasets, performed effectively, showing the dataset's value.
arxiv-2510-11620:
Long chains of thought make models smarter and more fragile: one bad planning step derails everything after it. Siheng Xiong, Ali Payani, and Faramarz Fekri dissect where the derailments start in this 2025 arXiv machine learning paper. Analyzing raw traces, they trace most errors to planning steps, not the execution that follows.

Their framework, Multi-Path Plan Aggregation, interrupts single-pass reasoning at intervals to generate several candidate plans and aggregate them into a refined plan, via a lightweight LoRA module. For training, they introduce online Step-DPO, a process-level preference method using twisted sequential Monte Carlo to supply step-by-step supervision. Across math, science, and logic benchmarks, the method beat both a DeepSeek-R1 distillation baseline and outcome-reward reinforcement learning. It used only ten percent of the supervised data and five percent of the preference pairs.
arxiv-2510-11820:
Anna R. Barth and nine co-authors show how sound can steer the thickness of dense slurries. Many suspensions, mixes of particles in liquid, thicken suddenly when sheared, a headache for mixing and pumping. Gentle acoustic vibration can soften that thickening in real time. Their 2025 arXiv paper gives the first measured account of the effect, which smart-material designers need for full control.

The team probed suspensions under acoustic perturbation and folded the results into a universal scaling picture. In that picture, viscosity follows one master function that crosses between two critical points: frictionless jamming and frictional shear jamming. The sound's effect can be captured as an effective repulsion pushing particles apart. Its strength comes out roughly equal to the acoustic energy density in the liquid. With that rule, the framework predicts a suspension's viscosity under new sound settings without fresh measurements. The authors show such predictions directly.
arxiv-2510-11920:
Omkar Dhungel and seven co-authors show a gentle way to probe superconductors with diamond dust. Nitrogen-vacancy centers are atomic defects in diamond whose fluorescence reports the local magnetic field. Sprinkling nanodiamonds on a superconductor lets teams sense its magnetism by light, with no microwaves and almost no disturbance. Their 2025 arXiv paper tests the approach on thin films of YBCO, a famous high-temperature superconductor.

Working at very low fields, with wiggles of about one millitesla, the team watched the Meissner effect, the superconductor's expulsion of magnetic field, through cross-relaxation field sensing. From the glow's changes they extracted two key numbers: the transition temperature where superconductivity switches on, and the penetration field where magnetism first breaks in. The method tolerates rough surfaces, which many sensing techniques cannot. It suits studies of flux vortices in samples with complex shapes.
arxiv-2510-12020:
Ivan R. Vasquez and A. Oliveros stress-test a modified theory of gravity against the universe's whole biography. In f(Q) gravity, Einstein's theory is rebuilt around nonmetricity, the failure of rulers to keep length under transport. Their 2025 arXiv paper chooses an exponential form for the modification and studies it with dynamical systems methods, which reduce the cosmic equations to an autonomous flow with equilibrium points.

Because the exponential spawns transcendental equations, the critical points are located by careful approximation and then tested for stability in terms of the model parameters. The model passes the basic historical audition: it exhibits the three main domination epochs, radiation, matter, and dark energy. The authors then switch on a linear interaction between dark matter and dark energy. The coupling shifts the equilibrium structure and leaves a nontrivial mark on the late-time de Sitter attractor, the universe's final resting state.
arxiv-2510-12220:
Bai and co-authors introduce Hierarchical Koopman Diffusion, a framework for fast image generation with a readable process, in a 2025 arXiv paper. Diffusion models produce high quality images but sample slowly because they denoise step by step. One step methods are fast yet hide the intermediate stages that make diffusion editable and controllable.

The method rests on Koopman operator theory, which lifts nonlinear dynamics into a space where they evolve linearly. In that lifted space the diffusion trajectory has a closed form solution, so sampling takes one step while intermediate states stay open to manual changes. A layered design splits the dynamics across spatial resolutions, with separate Koopman subspaces handling coarse and fine detail. Experiments show competitive one step generation quality. Studying the operators' spectra also gives a principled way to read and steer the generative process.
arxiv-2510-12620:
Mayer and a large team simulate the birth of a star with radiation and magnetic fields in a moving mesh code, in a 2025 arXiv astrophysics paper. In the run, a jet launches itself. They implemented radiative transfer with flux limited diffusion in the AREPO code. Splitting the radiation terms into explicit and implicit parts keeps the timestep practical. The scheme passed standard tests for radiation diffusion, gas coupling, and radiative shocks, and works with local timestepping.

As a demonstration they collapse a one solar mass molecular cloud core down to the second Larson core, the embryonic star. A fast jet erupts self consistently from the second core, nested inside a slower magnetic outflow from the first core. Magnetic fields amplify enormously in the second core, which is ringed by a small disk. They present the run as proof their method handles the multiscale, high resolution physics of protostar formation.
arxiv-2510-13220:
He and colleagues make AI agents improve themselves at test time in this 2025 arXiv paper. Agents typically cannot learn complex skills on the fly, behaving like clever but clueless interns in new environments. To measure that gap, the authors introduce a benchmark where an agent plays the same text adventure game across consecutive episodes. The agent must improve between attempts. In this setup, reflection, memory, and reinforcement learning baselines all struggle.

Their framework, EvoTest, evolves the entire agentic system after every episode without any fine-tuning or gradients. An actor agent plays, while an evolver agent studies the episode transcript and rewrites the configuration. It revises the prompt, logs effective state-action choices into memory, tunes hyperparameters, and learns tool-use routines. EvoTest consistently raised performance, beating reflection and memory baselines and even online fine-tuning methods, and it was the only approach to win any of the games outright.
arxiv-2510-13920:
Ye Yuan, Mohammad Amin Shabani, and Siqi Liu tackle query-focused table summarization, where a system must describe spreadsheet-like data in plain sentences that answer a user question. Their 2025 arXiv paper argues that older table-to-text models need costly retraining, while prompting large language models with whole tables wastes tokens and exposes private data.

They propose FACTS, an agentic workflow that builds reusable templates offline, before any question arrives. Each template pairs an executable SQL query, which pulls the needed numbers, with a text template that turns results into a summary. Because templates serve many tables with the same layout, summarization stays fast, and only table schemas go to the language model, protecting the data itself. On standard benchmarks, FACTS consistently beat the baseline methods tested.
arxiv-2510-14020:
Rohan Shenoy offers an elementary proof of the discrete renewal theorem, a classic result about processes that restart after random waiting times, in this 2025 arXiv note. Renewal processes model anything from machine repairs to arrivals separated by gaps, and the theorem describes the long-run rate at which events occur when the gaps between them are bounded.

Shenoy deliberately avoids the standard heavy machinery: no Markov chain theory, no complex analysis, and no generating functions, only elementary real analysis. He introduces the one-dimensional discrete renewal process through a board game example, making the setup concrete before proving the theorem in the common special case where interevent times are bounded. The note also supplies background and history on the Erdős-Feller-Pollard theorem, the celebrated earlier result in the same line. Readers see where the discrete renewal theorem sits in the development of probability theory.
arxiv-2510-14220:
Dibert and a large collaboration describe how they calibrated the SPT-SLIM mapping instrument against the sky during its first deployment on the South Pole Telescope, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Before its measurements of faint spectral lines can be trusted, the detectors' responsivity, how strongly they answer to sky brightness, must be pinned down under observing conditions.

During two weeks of on-sky operation in the 2024-2025 austral summer, the team measured detector response as the telescope changed elevation, which changes the atmospheric load. They combined those data with atmospheric opacity readings from a site radiometer, simulated South Pole atmospheric spectra, and laboratory-measured detector responses. From these they modeled each detector's responsivity to sky loading. They used the model to calibrate observations of the Moon and cross-checked the result against the Moon's brightness temperature as it varies with phase, validating the calibration chain end to end.
arxiv-2510-14520:
Tenyo Takahashi settles an open problem in modal logic by showing that a property of logics can be decided algorithmically, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Modal logics extend logic with operators for necessity and possibility, and most questions about them, beyond consistency and exceptions, are undecidable: no algorithm can answer them in general.

The property at stake is being a union-splitting in the lattice of all normal modal logics, a notion about how a logic sits among its extensions. Takahashi provides a semantic characterization of union-splittings in terms of finite modal algebras. This converts an infinitary question into a finite check and thereby proves decidability. It answers a problem posed in 2007. Clarifying the connection further, the paper shows that in this lattice, having a decidable axiomatization problem and being a decidable formula are themselves decidable properties. This resolves another long-standing question from 1997 for this setting.
arxiv-2510-14720:
Moretti, Loreau, and Benzaquen model, in a 2025 arXiv paper, the global race between rising food demand and the forests and soils that farming consumes. A larger, wealthier population wants more food, especially meat. Meeting that demand expands and intensifies agriculture, which drives deforestation and degrades ecosystems. The damage then feeds back on yields, raising future land needs.

Their spatially explicit model links demand paths to crop and livestock production and land conversion, and it reproduces the joint trends seen since 1960. Comparing scenarios yields three lessons. Supply-side fixes alone, such as organic conversion or lower livestock density, often backfire: they trigger compensatory land expansion that erases the ecological gains. Demand-side change, especially eating less meat, relieves both expansion and intensification pressure consistently. Only substantial demand cuts, around forty percent of the projected excess by 2100, increased forest area and reduced degradation at the same time.
arxiv-2510-15320:
Yunlu Wang, Yunlong Xiao, Pengcheng Hong, and Ronggang Ping set up a future test of fundamental symmetries in the decays of a charmed baryon. Their 2025 arXiv paper studies parity and charge-parity symmetries, whose breaking helps explain why the universe holds more matter than antimatter. The focus is the three-body decay of the Xi_c baryon into a Xi baryon plus two pions.

Working with the helicity formalism, which tracks particle spins through the decay, the team derives the complete angular distribution formula for the decay and its secondary steps. They fold in the effects of polarized electron and positron beams, since the planned Super Tau-Charm Facility would collide such beams. The paper then evaluates how sensitively the asymmetry decay parameters could be measured under different data volumes and beam polarization choices. The authors present the results as a theoretical framework to guide that future experiment's symmetry program.
arxiv-2510-15620:
On-device assistants rank texts with cross-encoders, but scoring every candidate fully is slow and memory-hungry. Jiahao Zhou and colleagues from Shanghai Jiao Tong University and Huawei address this in a 2025 arXiv paper. Their insight is that only relative order matters for top-K selection, not exact scores for each candidate. Rankings also settle early, in middle layers, which opens the door to pruning candidates sooner. Their system Grating prunes clusters of candidates progressively while bounding memory through sliding windows.

On rerankers up to eight billion parameters, Grating cuts latency by up to eighty-nine percent. Peak memory falls by up to ninety-five percent in microbenchmarks, with no precision loss. Three real on-device applications show smaller but still clear gains.
arxiv-2510-15720:
Reinforcement learning agents can act unsafely while learning, which blocks real-world deployment. Edwin Hamel-De le Court, Gaspard Ohlmann, and Francesco Belardinelli propose a safety method in this 2025 arXiv paper. Their algorithm, ProSh, adds a risk budget to the state of a cost-constrained learning problem. A learned cost critic estimates danger, and a shield filters the agent's action distribution. The shield keeps every sampled action safe in expectation, without needing a model of the environment.

The authors prove an upper bound on expected cost that holds throughout training. The bound depends only on the backup critic's accuracy. Under mild assumptions, experiments confirm safety even during the training phase itself.
arxiv-2510-16220:
Djamel Eddine Boukhari, working alone, teaches a computer to judge facial beauty by pairing two very different neural architectures. Predicting human aesthetic ratings is hard because judgments depend on whole-face structure, while convolutional networks mostly see local patches and vision transformers, which see globally, pay a quadratic computational cost.

His ensemble, VM-BeautyNet, fuses a vision transformer, strong on global structure and symmetry, with a Mamba state-space model that scans features and textures with only linear cost. On the SCUT-FBP5500 benchmark the pair reaches a Pearson correlation above 0.92 with human scores, with low average errors, setting a new best. Heat-map visualizations confirm the two backbones attend to complementary cues, giving the prediction an interpretable basis.
arxiv-2510-16420:
Adam Husted Kjelstrøm, Andreas Pavlogiannis, and Jaco van de Pol ask a hard question in a 2025 paper. Given a quantum circuit, can a computer find the smallest circuit that does the same job? A circuit is a set of steps that act on quantum bits. The team counts cost by gate count or depth, for four kinds of gates.

They prove the task is hard for a class called co-NQP, a high bar in computing. That puts it past the usual layers of hard tasks, unless those layers collapse. The proof holds for any gate set that can build two key gates exactly. The result tells builders not to expect a fast exact shortcut tool.
arxiv-2510-16520:
Mordehai Milgrom, the sole author, sorts claims about MOND gravity in a 2025 paper. MOND is a view that tweaks gravity at very low pull, as a rival to dark matter. No full base theory of MOND exists yet. Milgrom splits claims into primary ones, from the core tenets alone, and secondary ones, which need more. He homes in on the deep-MOND limit, where pull is low in all spots.

He shows how some primary claims flow from the core tenets. Even deep-limit claims need the full tenet set, he argues. That is because all MOND forms must meet Newton's laws at high pull. A fast shift between the two zones ties the deep zone down. The split helps tests aim at the core idea itself.
arxiv-2510-16820:
Thomas Dooms and Ward Gauderis, a two-author team, use bilinear autoencoders to pull polynomial structure out of neural network representations. Sparse autoencoders are a standard lens for finding readable features inside a model, but what a feature means depends on the inputs that trigger it. Polynomials can be studied on their own, with no input needed.

Their autoencoders split representations into quadratic polynomials, which can describe shapes from flat concepts to curved manifolds. The pair discusses upgrades that rank the pieces by importance, group them into clusters, and keep activations sparse. They present the work as a first step toward hidden features that stay nonlinear yet open to direct algebraic analysis.
arxiv-2510-17020:
Reuben R. W. Wang and John L. Bohn compare collisions in ultracold dipolar gases in a 2025 paper. Ultracold gases are clouds of atoms cooled near absolute zero. Their molecules pull on each other through dipolar forces. Collisions govern how such a gas moves and settles.

The key quantity is the elastic scattering cross section. It measures how strongly two molecules deflect each other. Experimenters can partly control it with applied fields. The authors place three collision settings side by side. They cover bare point dipoles and two shielding schemes. One scheme uses steady electric fields, the other microwaves. Microwave shielding also includes the effect of elliptical polarization. The comparison highlights which features survive across all settings.
arxiv-2510-17320:
Physicists who calculate how gravity behaves at the smallest scales need reliable rules for the particles involved, including ghost particles used in the maths. Boris Latosh, writing alone, presents version four of FeynGrav, a software package that supplies those Feynman rules for gravity models. The update fixes two main gaps and adds smaller changes meant to make daily use smoother.

Latosh gives a fuller treatment of the BRST formalism, a bookkeeping scheme for gauge theories, covering both general relativity and quadratic gravity with a finite set of ghost and graviton rules. The package also adds rules for a newer set of variables that write the gravity action in polynomial form. Small quality of life changes round out the release.
arxiv-2510-17420:
Simple models of money swapping between two people at a time reproduce the uneven wealth patterns seen in real economies. Suchismita Banerjee, writing alone, extends those models so that several people trade at once inside a closed system where total money stays fixed. Multi party trades are common in real markets, yet the classic two person models cannot capture them.

Banerjee finds that as the number of people in each trade grows, the long run wealth pattern shifts smoothly from a steep exponential shape toward an almost even spread. Two standard inequality measures fall steadily as group size rises. The effect also differs from the known levelling caused by saving habits, suggesting group trading itself is a distinct levelling force.
arxiv-2510-17520:
Canran Xiao, with Chuangxin Zhao and two co-authors, attacks rare label neglect in a 2025 arXiv paper. Many tagging tasks assign several labels to each item, but a few common labels dominate training. Rare labels then get ignored, even though they often matter most in practice. The authors recast the task as a cooperative game, meaning players who gain by working toward one shared score.

In their design, parts of the label set go to different players. Players earn bonus rewards for rare labels and for disagreeing with each other. These bonuses push learning toward the neglected tags without hand set class weights. Tests on standard and very large datasets showed clear gains on rare labels. Separate checks confirmed the players split the work.
arxiv-2510-17720:
Nanda Kumar Rengarajan, with Jun Yan and Chun Wang, improves named entity recognition under scarce labels in a 2025 arXiv paper. Named entity recognition finds names of people, places, and organizations in text. It normally needs large amounts of hand labeled data, which is costly to produce. Zero shot and instruction tuned models often miss domain specific entities.

Their framework, called PANER, pairs a simpler instruction template with a paraphrase trick. The template uses the long context windows of recent large models. The trick rewrites the text around each entity while keeping the entity itself fixed. That expands training data without breaking meaning. On standard few shot tests, the method averaged an F1 score of about 80. Paraphrasing alone added up to seventeen points.
arxiv-2510-17820:
Markus Meister argues that retina science now has a standard model. The retina is the light-sensing tissue at the back of the eye. Its neural circuits turn light patterns into signals for the brain. Meister says one simple circuit model now explains many early vision effects.

The same model, with different settings, yields many distinct computations. Meister lays out the model and what it explains. He also asks what conditions let such a unifying model emerge here. Few areas of systems neuroscience have reached this state. The model now serves as a baseline for future retina research.
arxiv-2510-18220:
Ho Yin Ng and Emily S C Ching model how heat spreads in a turbulent fluid trapped between two vertical walls at different temperatures. Vertical convection of this kind drives flows in rooms, tanks, and geophysical settings. Their model lets the eddy thermal diffusivity vary with position instead of fixing one number for the whole layer.

From it they derive the average temperature profile in closed form. Two universal scaling curves describe the near-wall and central regions across heating strengths and fluid types. Both match direct simulation data well. Fluid dynamicists get a compact theory for a profile that usually needs heavy computation.
arxiv-2510-18420:
Abdullah Ajasa, with Mubarak Badamasi Aremu and Ali Nasir, reviews control methods for permanent magnet synchronous motors, a compact and efficient motor type used in demanding drives. These motors behave in nonlinear ways, and loads and settings shift during use, so speed control stays hard. Sliding-mode control is a trusted answer, but recent years brought many adaptive, fractional, and intelligent variants, leaving the literature scattered.

The review sorts more than two hundred studies from 2020 to 2025 by control order, surface design, disturbance handling, tuning method, and use of intelligent tools. Clear trends appear: classic switching control is giving way to smoother adaptive and data-driven hybrids that cut vibration while staying robust. Gaps remain in hardware testing, energy use measurement, and tuning in real time, which the authors flag for future work.
arxiv-2510-18820:
Reilly Milburn and her seven co-authors search for gas escaping from three young planets, watching for a hydrogen-alpha transit signal as each planet crosses its star. Escaping atmospheres help explain gaps in the known planet population, and young planets, where loss is still strong, are the best places to catch the process. The team used high-resolution spectrographs on three telescopes, checking their method against calmer stellar lines.

Two planets, aged about four hundred and forty-five million years, showed no transit signal, with tight upper limits. The youngest, at seventeen million years, showed excess absorption of about three and a half percent, timed with the transit, narrow, and shifted in velocity, all pointing to the planet. The authors stress caution: the star's own hydrogen line varied by a similar amount, and the signal was shorter than the light transit, so the detection is probable and requires confirmation.
arxiv-2510-19220:
Xiaoqing Lan and five co-authors improve detection of space objects in geostationary orbit from optical images, where targets are faint, star backgrounds are busy, and interference is common. Missing a dim object or raising false alarms both matter for tracking the crowded belt above the equator.

A wavelet method sharpens target features and suppresses noise in single frames, then a multi-frame scheme completes trajectories by matching detections across time with a global assignment algorithm. Filtering for time consistency and stepwise refinement cleans the tracks further. Tests on a public dataset show the pipeline handles gaps and false detections well.
arxiv-2510-19320:
P Chakraborty and five co-authors use pion-kaon femtoscopy to probe how particles are emitted in relativistic heavy-ion collisions. Differences in emission between pions and kaons reveal the role of the hadronic stage, when the hot droplet of deconfined matter cools and particles keep interacting before flying free.

Two models at the same collision energy are compared: one follows every stage through the hadronic phase, while the other converts matter to hadrons suddenly and skips later interactions. Sorting pairs by transverse velocity heightens sensitivity to those interactions. The comparison shows what femtoscopy measurements can teach about the final cooling stage.
arxiv-2510-19420:
Chengcan Wu and four co-authors propose a dynamic defense for multi-agent language model systems against corrupted agents. In such systems, one adversarial agent can inject misleading claims that spread from agent to agent, quietly poisoning the group's final answer, while older graph-based defenses assume a fixed communication structure.

Their method models communication as a signed directed graph without cycles and pushes each agent's contribution backward from the final decision, exposing who actually drove a bad outcome. Malicious agents can then be identified and isolated. Experiments support the approach for keeping collaborative agent teams trustworthy.
arxiv-2510-19620:
Patrick Becker and Fabian Frank study how small the quota in multiwinner voting can be while still guaranteeing proportional representation. Standard fairness rules, justified representation and its extended version, assume a fixed quota such as Hare or Droop. The authors instead let the quota shrink to fit each election instance, measured by a parameter alpha.

They show all commonly studied voting rules can fall short of the optimal quota by a specific additive gap. Computing the best alpha for a given election turns out to be NP-complete. To make the idea usable, they give an integer programming method for finding committees meeting the shrunken quota, with positive results for elections where voters or candidates fall along a line.
arxiv-2510-19920:
Douglas Stanford and Cynthia Yan propose a fix for a divergence that plagues the gravitational sum over topologies in three dimensions. Hyperbolic three-manifolds have volumes that accumulate at limit points, which are cusped manifolds, making the sum over geometries diverge. Their proposal is to renormalize by including the cusped manifold itself as a counterterm.

The move reinterprets the zeta-function regularization that Maloney and Witten used for a sum over black hole geometries. For pure supergravity, cusps with even spin structure play the same canceling role. Cusps with odd spin structure are not needed against any divergence, the authors note, but they earn their place by making an index nonzero, a small fact with structural consequences.
arxiv-2510-20020:
Luise Ge, Gregory Kehne, and Yevgeniy Vorobeychik give the first study of distortion in voting when voter utilities are linear functions of candidate features. Distortion measures how much welfare a voting rule can lose by using rankings instead of true utilities. Here each candidate is a vector, and a voter value is a weighted sum of its entries.

The team proves bounds for both deterministic and randomized rules that depend only on the dimension of the candidate space, not on how many candidates or voters there are. They also give fast instance-optimal algorithms for cutting distortion on a given election. Tests use recommendation data and opinion surveys with language model embeddings.
arxiv-2510-20320:
Hanbing Fang and Yu Li prove a sole-form claim for tangent flows at tube-shaped points in Ricci flow. Such points form as the flow nears a break. The pair set a Lojasiewicz-type bound for the W-entropy at a marked point. The bound needs the shape near that point to sit close to a stock tube form, or a share of one.

With that bound in hand, the bent Ricci flow near the point must run to the tube form in a fixed gauge. It can not drift from one tube flow to the next at the first break time. The claim firms up past sole-form marks for this class of breaks in shape flow work.
arxiv-2510-20420:
Vladimir M. Shevlyuga, Yulia A. Vorontsova, and Tatiana V. Pavlova study how phosphorus tribromide molecules adsorb and break apart on a silicon surface, using scanning tunneling microscopy and density functional theory. At room temperature the molecule dissociates completely into phosphorus and bromine atoms on the Si(100) surface. In most cases the fragments are seen spread across three neighboring silicon dimers in the microscope images.

The calculations confirm that full dissociation at room temperature is expected, matching the observations. After the sample is heated to four hundred degrees, phosphorus becomes incorporated into the silicon, shown by silicon atoms ejected onto the surface. The authors note the findings matter for placing individual phosphorus atoms into silicon through a halogen mask.
arxiv-2510-20820:
Gordon Guocheng Qian leads thirteen co-authors on CanvasComposer, a system for making personalized group photos that keep several real people recognizable in one shared scene. Earlier generators often lose or blend identities when more than one reference face appears.

Borrowing from pro editing software, the system places each person as a separate cutout layer on a shared canvas, so overlap never erases reference detail. A pruning step keeps only tokens from visible regions, and training with mixed source references teaches the model to blend lighting and style instead of pasting. Wide tests show coherent scenes with strong identity keeping, ahead of leading rivals for multi person generation.
arxiv-2510-21020:
Konstantinos Christopher Tsiolis leads two co-authors on phase transitions in stochastic gradient learning of single index models, where labels depend on a nonlinear function of one hidden direction. Sample complexity is classically set by the information exponent of that link function.

Repeated gradient steps on one sample with varied learning rates were known to beat that limit down to a smaller generative exponent, but only within a learning rate window. Outside the window the picture changes, and learning rate itself induces phase transitions between regimes. Mapping those transitions clarifies when clever step schedules help and when they cannot rescue a hard target function.
arxiv-2510-21120:
Alec Helbling leads five co-authors on SafetyPairs, a framework that generates counterfactual image pairs differing only in the features that flip a safety label. Knowing what exactly makes an image unsafe is hard, since a small gesture or symbol can change everything while data sets give only coarse labels.

Image editing tools create matched pairs where one version is benign and the other violates a stated policy, isolating the decisive features. Such pairs can train and audit safety classifiers on the true drivers of harm rather than correlations. Finer safety data supports moderation systems that explain and defend their calls.
arxiv-2510-21420:
Isabella Masina and Mariano Quiros ask where new physics should enter if the forces of the Standard Model are to merge into one at high energy. Inside the known model, two of the force strengths already meet at a very high partial unification scale. Full meeting needs corrections from whatever lies beyond.

They build a simple general parametrization of those corrections. Whenever the corrections to the two non-Abelian forces come out equal or nearly so, the full meeting point stays at or near the partial one. Teasing the scales apart takes clearly unequal corrections. The scheme is tested on low-energy and split supersymmetry. It is also tested on desert models with nothing new in between. String-inspired cases include one striking option. It puts unification near one hundred TeV with a low string scale.
arxiv-2510-21520:
Omer Moussa and Mariya Toneva fine-tune speech language models on brain data so the models predict human brain responses to spoken language more faithfully. Earlier brain-alignment work trained a separate fit for each person and starved on small per-person data sets, which blocked both new-person predictions and group-level science.

Their brain-tuning trains one model to predict scanner responses from many participants at once. The tuned models still align well with each individual brain, yet they also generalize. Predicting a new person's brain data needs about five times less scanning, overall alignment rises by up to half, and the models transfer to unseen data sets. As a bonus, the brain-tuned models also improve on meaning-based language tasks, hinting that pooled brain training yields more general representations of meaning.
arxiv-2510-21620:
Markus Exner and six co-authors create and measure butterfly molecules, fragile pairs in which a ground-state rubidium atom clings to a partner whose outer electron orbits enormously far away. The bond forms when that Rydberg electron scatters off the nearby atom in a P-wave pattern, giving the molecule its winged name and shape.

A three-photon excitation scheme assembles the molecules in an ultracold rubidium gas, gently mixing in the needed atomic states. The measured binding energies, giant electric dipole moments of thousands of Debye, and lifetimes all match theory closely. Two long-lived vibrational levels sit just below the parent atomic threshold. The team frames the result as a founding step toward making ultracold negative ions and heavy ion-pair systems in the laboratory.
arxiv-2510-22120:
Maksim Kosmakov builds a bridge between two descriptions of the same random motion. On one side sit families of Brownian paths forced never to cross, whose positions at any fixed moment obey a classical law tied to multiple orthogonal polynomials. On the other side sit random matrix ensembles, whose eigenvalues mimic those positions but usually only for the simplest starting arrangements.

Kosmakov constructs a unitarily invariant Hermitian matrix ensemble whose eigenvalue law at any fixed time matches the non-intersecting bridge law exactly, even when several paths start or end at the same point. Exact consequences follow, including a path-level version of the ensemble, a compact single-integral formula for its partition function, and fixed-time identities for its resolvent. A comparison with the Gaussian external-field ensemble shows the two agree on spectra but differ in angular behavior.
arxiv-2510-22520:
Learning from graphs, where data points link to each other, often relies on random walks that wander node to node. Michael Ito, Danai Koutra, and Jenna Wiens note in 2025 that those walks can miss much of a graph under real sampling limits, weakening what a neural network can learn.

Their random search neural networks use searches that visit every node by design. In sparse graphs, only a modest number of searches are needed to cover all edges. Paired with general sequence models, the networks can approximate any suitable graph function. Tests on molecular and protein tasks beat walk based rivals, sometimes using far fewer sampled sequences.
arxiv-2510-22820:
Alexander Chernov, writing alone in 2025, studies additive actions on toric varieties. A toric variety is a geometric space built from fans of cones. An additive action moves points by a group of translations. Induced actions extend to the full projective space. Projective space adds points at infinity.

Such actions match pairs of an algebra and a subspace. Chernov focuses on toric cases, mainly surfaces. For linearly normal toric varieties, the algebra is monomial. Monomial means built from single term polynomials. The subspace is spanned by variables. He also describes pairs for toric surfaces. Those surfaces sit in low dimensional projective spaces.
arxiv-2510-22920:
Spencer H Bryngelson tackles a costly math problem in the study of bubbly flows, where gas bubbles of many sizes move in a liquid. Models need average values from the full spread of bubble sizes. Those averages change over time before they settle, and that early phase matters for real machines.

Computing the averages is slow because the sums swing up and down fast. Bryngelson offers a faster integration method that cuts the work at each point in a simulation. Engineers who model bubbly flows can use the approach to run larger cases without losing the time-changing detail they need.
arxiv-2510-23220:
V D Pipwala and five co-authors test Type-II Cepheid stars as distance markers for other galaxies, using the Andromeda galaxy M31 as a benchmark. Several standard candles anchor the cosmic distance scale, but Type-II Cepheids have rarely been put to work despite their promise. Ordinary least squares fitting is sensitive to outliers and treats uncertainties poorly.

The team instead uses a Bayesian robust regression model to fit the Cepheid data for M31. A cleaner distance from this independent candle would cross-check the scale built on other stars. The project argues this overlooked class deserves a regular place in distance work.
arxiv-2510-23320:
Máté Gedeon and Péter Mihajlik built LibriConvo, a simulated speech dataset for systems that tell speakers apart and turn speech into text. The corpus is built from read-aloud book speech, reshaped into dialogues that sound like real talk. Their 2025 pipeline builds on an earlier speaker-aware simulation method and adds careful timing control.

To keep the talk natural, they took timing patterns from real phone calls and squeezed long pauses. They grouped clips by book, so nearby lines stay on topic. They also picked room echoes that fit the scene. The set holds more than 240 hours in 1,496 dialogues with 830 speakers, split so no speaker appears twice. In tests, one modern system cut speaker labeling errors to about eleven percent, far below the older pipeline. A tuned speech model reached word error rates near seven percent, beating a large general model used untuned.
arxiv-2510-23720:
Xiang Li and three co-authors argue that chiral gapped states of matter are, in a precise sense, universally non-topological. Their starting point is an operator version of the Li-Haldane conjecture, which links the entanglement Hamiltonian of a disk region to edge physics. Studying regions with sharp corners, they extract universal facts about corner entanglement.

The corner results rest on conditions that can be checked locally on the wavefunction. The authors define a number that measures how robust the corner entanglement is, and show it blocks the existence of a gapped boundary. A practical reward follows. From any wavefunction in such a phase they can build a gapped Hamiltonian. They conjecture it sits closer to the renormalization group fixed point than the original. The analysis reveals a conformal geometry in bulk entanglement, invisible to topological field theory, and explains a formula for the chiral central charge.
arxiv-2510-23820:
Shahab Jahanbazi and two co-authors design task scheduling for Internet of Things devices that run on harvested energy, with no battery at all. Such devices sip power from their surroundings, so energy arrives in fits and starts while deadlines stay hard. In these jobs, a chain of sensing, computing, and transmitting must finish inside every reporting cycle.

The authors frame the problem as a Markov decision process with long-term average reward, tracking capacitor voltage, task order, allowed start windows, and safe-running rules. Their reward favors completing the chain while punishing risky low-energy starts. They prove the process is unichain and that the best stationary policy has a threshold shape, yielding a simple scheduler. A second model with correlated, Markov-style energy arrivals extends the idea under conditions. The threshold scheduler beat baselines on completion rate, power failures, and delay, especially when energy was scarce.
arxiv-2510-23920:
Grant Hopkins and three co-authors tackle a measurement problem that appears across marketing, genomics, ecology, and policy: estimating ratios of category means when the data were sampled preferentially. Both the units observed and the categories they fall into can be skewed by the sampling process, which distorts naive averages. Earlier results leaned on parametric forms or strong shape restrictions.

The authors show the ratios can be identified under a mild independence assumption, or with a category constraint such as a fixed reference category. Their target quantities, adjusted or not for covariates, need no parametric assumptions and read plainly. They build an efficient, doubly robust estimator around targeted minimum loss, and it performs well even with many rarely seen categories. Simulations back the theory, and an application picks out bacteria whose abundance differs between diarrhea cases and controls.
arxiv-2510-24120:
Ziyu Liu and six co-authors tackle the high cost of graph based retrieval for question answering with large language models. Graph methods build a knowledge graph from text chunks, which helps with multi step reasoning in fields like biomedicine and law. But making the graph takes many model calls to pull out entities and links, so costs grow fast at scale.

Their method, G2ConS, first picks the most useful chunks and builds a concept graph without model calls. A careful study showed some words, called concepts, and their documents matter far more than others. By focusing on those, the method cuts construction cost while keeping retrieval strong for multi step questions.
arxiv-2510-24420:
Éric Fusy builds a tree model for five connected planar triangulations, working alone. He studies triangulations of a pentagon with no separating triangle or quadrangle, called 5c-triangulations, a family closely tied to 5-connected planar triangulations. Such highly connected maps are hard to count and generate directly.

Fusy proves these triangulations correspond one to one with five regular plane trees obeying a simple local rule at inner edges. The bijection yields explicit generating functions for rooted cases, in the same algebraic extension as a known result by Gao, Wanless, and Wormald. It also gives efficient uniform random generation and compact encoding methods for these maps.
arxiv-2510-24520:
Tanmoy Mondal and Pinaki Majumdar, two authors, map electron flow in a magnet lattice. The Heisenberg-Kondo lattice couples moving electrons to local spins. Spins also link to their neighbors, and electrons hop between sites. The pair chart how resistance changes with heat, density, and coupling. Their lattice is two-dimensional, with twenty sites on each side.

Spin patterns come from Langevin dynamics, a noise-driven simulation method. Conductivity is computed from exact energy states by the Kubo formula. At high density or weak coupling, resistance just climbs with heat. At very low density and strong coupling, electrons trap themselves. An electron polarizes nearby spins and digs its own trap. Resistance then peaks near the magnetic transition, a clear sign. The pair also find a shared curve for the plain scattering regime.
arxiv-2510-24720:
Meisam J Seikavandi and seven co-authors build a way to read feelings from gaze in face to face scenes. Their frame joins eye track runs with Big Five trait scores and cues from the clip shown. The goal is to guess both the feeling a viewer saw and the one they felt.

Seventy three adults watched speech clips while their gaze was logged, then gave trait and feeling scores. Nets that used the full gaze run plus traits and clip cues beat old base lines. Clip cues helped most for seen feelings, while traits helped most for felt ones. The split shows why feeling reads need more than the face alone.
arxiv-2510-24920:
Elizabeth Lin and seven co-authors report a March 2025 meet of firms and state staff on safe software supply chains. Such chains give much worth, but a weak link can let in an attack that hits near all web users. Hacks on these chains have grown fast in the past few years.

Four hosts from a state backed safe chain hub ran the meet, with eighteen guests from seventeen groups. Goals were to swap field tales on what works and what hurts in guard of these chains. The report sums what guests shared on real use, gaps, and needs. It is a field view for both shops and rule makers.
arxiv-2510-25620:
Francesca Benini led four co-authors on lubricant additives. Paolo Restuccia, Sophie Loehle, and Quentin Arnoux helped. Maria Clelia Righi closes the five-author team. Their 2025 paper studies phosphorus-based anti-wear additives. Additive results depends on adsorption at metal interfaces. Three additives are investigated on iron and hematite.

Octyl acid phosphate, dibutyl hydrogen phosphite, and amine phosphate were studied. Ab initio calculations and steel tests were mixed. Amine phosphate showed strongest adsorption on iron surfaces. Dibutyl phosphite joined, while octyl phosphate interacted weaker. Under tribological settings, dibutyl phosphite dissociated more readily. Dibutyl phosphite formed stable deposits on surfaces. Amine phosphate showed poor retention in readings.
arxiv-2510-25820:
Vanessa Figueiredo and David Elumeze explore whether tight prompt rules improve dialogue for game characters run by a large language model. These characters, called NPCs, are the figures a player meets who are not controlled by a person. The team test their ideas in The Interview, a voice based detective game that runs on GPT-4o, a commercial language model.

A small study with ten players compared high and low constraint prompts and found no clear gain in player experience. The authors then rebuilt the prompt as a hybrid scaffold and tested it with a model as judge. Structure helped the quest giver stay stable, but suspect characters lost some spark and believability.
arxiv-2510-26020:
Feijie Wu leads seven co-authors in a training method for language model agents that solve tasks by calling external tools. Such agents mix reasoning in words with tool calls, but training from final success alone leaves a credit problem: which step helped or hurt is unclear. Their method, PORTool, builds a rewarded rollout tree where attempts share a common start before branching, so alternative steps can be compared in the same context.

Each step gets an importance score, dominated by whether its descendants can reach a correct final answer, plus a bonus for well formed, successful tool calls. Policy updates then favor efficient, useful steps. The approach aims for stronger tool use from only outcome level supervision.
arxiv-2510-26220:
J. Philidet and K. Belkacem develop a new particle based code to model churned heat driven flow inside stars more in a realistic way. Stellar evolution models treat heat driven flow crudely, most of all near the boundary between heat flow and radiating zones. The interplay of heat driven flow with tones also limits how well seismic tones can be predicted for low mass stars. Those tones are the tones a star rings with.

Their framework tracks one point stats of heat driven flow with Lagrangian chance density function methods, where a Fokker Planck equation governs the spread of particle carried churned traits. A Monte Carlo build represents the flow with many notional particles that interact through a mean flow estimated from the particles themselves. The scheme is akin to smoothed particle fluid flow theory. Benchmark cases validate the code.
arxiv-2510-26320:
Syed M. Arslan, Syed Shahmir, Noureldin Mohammad, Saif Al-Kuwari, and Muataz Alhussein survey twin field quantum key distribution, a method for sharing secret keys over very long distances. Standard quantum key distribution suffers a rate distance limit and needs trusted repeaters to go farther. In the twin field design, both parties send phase encoded weak coherent pulses to an untrusted central node, where single photon interference does the work.

That interference lets the secret key rate scale with the square root of channel transmittance, which enables record distances in principle. The survey covers the original protocol and its key rate derivation, major variants such as phase matching and sending or not sending designs, security proofs from asymptotic to finite key settings. It also covers experimental milestones and deployment challenges.
arxiv-2510-27020:
Yana Wei leads six co-authors in teaching vision systems to learn human-object interactions step by step. Detecting who is doing what to which object is easy in a fixed world, but real settings keep adding new interactions. Stepwise learning risks catastrophic forgetting, meaning old skills vanish as new ones arrive, plus drift in known interactions and unseen combinations.

Their framework learns objects and relations separately, without storing old examples. Two distillation losses, which pass lessons from an older model to a newer one, keep relation features stable across combinations that share a relation. On two standard datasets it beats prior methods on forgetting, drift, and unseen combinations. Code is released for follow-up work.
arxiv-2510-27120:
Yongxin Chen, Tryphon Georgiou, and Michele Pavon recast gradient descent as an optimal control problem. Gradient flows describe systems that slide downhill on an energy or loss surface, a core picture in optimization and physics. The authors show continuous-time gradient descent in flat space is exactly an optimal controlled evolution for a suitable action cost, with a matching result for the stochastic version.

They extend the view to flows over probability distributions, where entropy drives movement in Wasserstein space, the geometry of distributions under transport cost. Over product spaces with two coupled distributions, steepest descent splits into two control velocities with equal and opposite fluxes. Links to the classic JKO scheme and Schrodinger bridges suggest uses from sampling theory to coordinating communicating microrobot swarms.
arxiv-2510-27220:
Yow-Ming Robin Hu, Elena A. Ostrovskaya, and Eliezer Estrecho study a strange trembling motion in this 2025 physics paper. The motion is called zitterbewegung, a rapid jitter of a wave packet, a small bundle of waves. It was first known for fast electrons. The trio asks how the jitter works in open systems, ones that gain or lose energy.

They work out equations for the motion by hand. In open systems, they find, the spin-like traits of the packet act in new ways. Extra push terms appear that closed systems never show. They also find a new term in the packet's speed, tied to a measure of the space's shape. The work uses exciton-polaritons, half-light, half-matter particles in solids, as its test case.
arxiv-2510-27320:
Jia-Ning Chen, Zong-Kuan Guo, and Liang-Bi Wu compute the ringing tones of a rotating black hole with quantum corrections. Those tones, called quasinormal modes, are the fading vibrations a disturbed black hole emits, now heard in gravitational wave ringdowns. The team studies scalar perturbations with a hyperboloidal framework that turns the spectrum problem into a two-dimensional eigenvalue problem solved by a pseudo-spectral method.

With spectra in hand, they build a parameter estimation pipeline for gravitational wave data using informative priors drawn from the inspiral-merger phase mass and spin distributions. Priors consistently tighten estimates of the quantum correction parameter, and inferred spin begins to differ from the standard Kerr model. The authors frame results as methodological, opening a path to testing quantum gravity deviations by spectroscopy.
arxiv-2510-27620:
Khaled Kassem and five co-authors report a way to see through thick, shifting scatter in 2025. Tissue and other dense matter scramble light into speckle, a grainy pattern that shifts fast. Classic methods that map the scrambling need the pattern to stay still, so they fail when the medium moves.

Their method uses links in speckle brightness at two close colors to build a hologram in software. No phase, which is the timing of light waves, needs to stay stable, and short shots freeze the motion. Tests show sharp images through both still and moving scatter. The approach could aid medical scans and remote sensing in messy settings.
arxiv-2511-00220:
Pouya Ghari, Simone Sciabola, and Ye Wang address a common flaw in tuning large pre-trained models: one reward score rarely captures all that matters. A text model may need to be clear, safe, and on topic at once. A drug model faces a similar mix of goals. Tuning on one score alone can distort the rest.

Their method cycles through several rewards in turn, fine-tuning the model on each one in repeated rounds. The approach extends leading reinforcement learning methods, and the team backs it with theory. Tests on text, biological sequences, and small molecules beat strong baselines, which suggests the cycling helps balance competing goals.
arxiv-2511-00320:
M G Masteghin and six co-authors map the full damage left by focused ion beams, fine tools used to cut and build at the nanoscale. Most checks measure only the beam's bright core, where most ions land. The faint tail matters for precise jobs like placing impurities in a chip, yet it is usually missed. The team uses an advanced electron microscopy method that records diffraction at every scan point.

By comparing patterns from known exposures with spots dosed by a gallium beam, they detect damage at extremely low levels. A noise-based score proved more sensitive and robust than standard dark-field imaging. The fuller profile helps users judge beam performance beyond simple sharpness and tailor settings for delicate work.
arxiv-2511-00520:
Hòa Bùi and Alberto De Marchi speed up cutting plane methods, a classic way to solve nonlinear discrete optimization without relaxing whole-number decisions into fractions. The methods are powerful in theory but erratic in practice. Recent work showed that building cuts at projections of infeasible points onto the feasible set helps greatly, and the authors ask whether cuts at feasible points near the optimum help even more.

Their hybrid pairs the global guarantees of cutting planes with the local search of projected gradient methods, which scout promising regions and supply tighter cuts. The focus is binary problems with convex, differentiable goals, where projections reduce to mixed-integer linear programs. Experiments across solver setups confirm better solutions found faster. The framework extends naturally to wider discrete domains.
arxiv-2511-00620:
Autumn Toney-Wails and Ryan Wails test whether a language model's confidence means what probability says it should. Certainty is often read from token logits, with probabilities and entropy standing in for trust. In gambling-like scenarios with known odds, though, a well-behaved model's token probabilities should track the theoretical distribution of outcomes, a stricter demand than mere accuracy.

The authors probe GPT-4.1 and DeepSeek-Chat with ten probability prompts, such as rolling a six-sided die, with and without fairness cues. Both models answered every scenario validly and perfectly. Yet their token-level probabilities and entropy values consistently diverged from the theoretical distributions. Certainty signals, the study warns, should not be confused with calibrated probability in high-stakes decision support.
arxiv-2511-01020:
Ana Bokulic and Filip Pozar construct the first noncommutative corrections to a broad class of theories where electromagnetism is nonlinear. Noncommutative geometry deforms spacetime so that positions fail to commute, and the deformation here is applied through a Drinfeld twist, with the effects passed into the matter sector by the Seiberg-Witten map.

Two sources of nonlinearity now interact: the one already present in nonlinear electrodynamics, and the one from the noncommutative deformation. Starting from a static, symmetric dyonic black hole with spherical shape, carrying both electric and magnetic charge, they solve the equations of motion order by order in the deformation parameter. Corrections to the metric and the gauge potential are then computed for several leading nonlinear theories.
arxiv-2511-01120: Carla Mariana da Silva Pinheiro studies multiplicative statistics in a unitary random matrix ensemble whose probability measure carries a deformation controlled by a parameter. Earlier work on such deformations handled a bounded or decaying parameter. This paper extends the results to a growing parameter, kept under a controlled rate. It derives the asymptotic expansion of the statistics. It also shows that the underlying statistics relate to the study of the lower tail of the KPZ equation, a central model of random growth.
arxiv-2511-01220:
David Sommers and colleagues introduce SQDMetal, an open source workflow to model the electromagnetic behavior of superconducting quantum circuits. Such tools matter greatly when designing quantum devices, but the standard tools are mostly commercial, and open parallel alternatives have been scarce.

SQDMetal is a Python interface that links Qiskit Metal for design, Gmsh for meshing, Palace for large parallel runs, and ParaView to view the results. Mesh studies show strong agreement with two leading paid packages on eigenmode and capacitance numbers. Models of resonators and transmon qubits match experiments well. Extras include getting Hamiltonians by the energy participation ratio method, kinetic inductance effects, and full 3D device geometry.
arxiv-2511-01420:
Christoph Lenzen tackles gradient clock synchronization, the problem of keeping neighboring clocks in a large network close to each other even when no two clocks in the network agree exactly. Earlier theory gave tight bounds, but those bounds rest on pessimistic assumptions: worst-case measurement errors guaranteed for the whole life of the system, and oscillators always drifting at their worst rate.

Lenzen builds a gentler model that asks only that measurement and frequency errors stay stable over short periods. In that model he re-analyzes existing methods and beats the established lower bound on local skew, sometimes dramatically.
