The method works backward from the distribution's cumulative function, again and again, and reads the values at the interval's right endpoint, giving a sequence of numbers that captures the whole law.

That sequence turns out to be a scaled moment sequence of the mirrored random variable, which ties it to classical moment theory and makes its basic content clear. Zimmerman maps which sequences can arise, and shows the map from probability measures to primitive sequences matches the two spaces exactly. Fixing the first few terms of the sequence yields sharp bounds on quantities of all measures sharing them.
arxiv-2605-08120:
Paolo Proia, Mauro Sbragaglia, and Giacomo Falcucci simulate how to melt phase change materials faster. These materials store and release heat as they melt and freeze, and a solid block is often heated from one boundary with metal fins reaching inside. The team runs three-dimensional simulations with buoyancy in the melt.

Comparing finless, single-fin, and multi-fin cells at equal heating power, they confirm that fins speed melting. A single fin turns out to be suboptimal, because several fins exploit the spaces between them and melt the material more evenly. Spacing matters too: fins placed too close overlap in effect and waste their advantage.
arxiv-2605-09120:
Haven Kim and Julian McAuley release Reddit2Deezer, a dataset for research on music recommendation through conversation. The field has faced a trade-off: real dialogues are scarce and small, while made-up dialogues scale easily but feel artificial because they were never naturally spoken.

The resource grows out of about one hundred ninety thousand real Reddit threads paired with their closing comments. Each mentioned track links to a Deezer identifier, which unlocks audio previews and facts like genre, popularity, and tempo. Two versions are offered, one raw and one paraphrased for long-term sharing. Human checks confirmed the dialogue quality, the correctness of the track links, and the faithfulness of the paraphrases.
arxiv-2605-09220:
Cueto and a colleague study optimal control in a nonlocal function space framework with two parameters: a horizon parameter delta and a fractional parameter s between 0 and 1. Constraints take the form of minimising an energy density. The study focuses on two cases: a well posed case with convex energy from the nonlocal p-Laplacian, and a broader poly quasiconvex energy with possibly non unique minimisers. The study ends by analysing how local problems are approximated two ways: taking s to 1, or delta to 0.

The authors set up groups of truncated nonlocal gradient based control problems, with states minimising a nonlocal energy density and controls from an admissible class. They also study how solutions converge when either parameter nears its local limit, approximating solutions to PDE based local problems. The work gives a rigorous localisation picture for nonlocal control, bridging nonlocal and classical local models.
arxiv-2605-09620:
Faruqi and eight colleagues present MiXR, an extended reality system for composing 3D models by harvesting shapes from real objects. Generative 3D tools make models from text or images. But they give users little control over spatial structure. Re prompting often loses desired traits. MiXR lets users cut segments from captured objects, such as a donut arc for a handle, and place them directly in 3D space to set the design's structure. Generative AI then blends a coherent model from that layout.

In a controlled study with 12 participants, MiXR users rated their designs closer to target. They felt more in control. They reported lower mental workload than with a generative composition baseline. The hybrid workflow splits intent from polish. Users set spatial structure in plain terms. The model handles geometric finish. That split suits design tasks where exact relationships are hard to put in words alone.
arxiv-2605-09920:
Wen and three colleagues proposed VIGOR, a verifier-free reinforcement-learning reward built only from the policy model itself. Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards needs gold labels or domain verifiers, which limits scaling to new tasks. VIGOR samples a group of completions per prompt and rewards outputs with smaller gradient norms of teacher-forced negative log-likelihood under current parameters.

Smaller gradient norms suggest a completion aligns better with the current policy, giving an intrinsic preference signal. A square-root-of-T scaling corrects the length bias of averaged token gradients, and group-wise rank shaping steadies reward scales. On math reasoning benchmarks, VIGOR beat the RLIF baseline and transferred to code when trained only on math. On Qwen2.5-7B-Base post-trained on MATH, it gained 3.31 points in math accuracy and 1.91 points in code accuracy over that baseline.
arxiv-2605-10020:
Wongso and six colleagues built TrajDLM, a topology-aware block diffusion text model for trip making. True-to-life synthetic GPS trips matter for transport, urban planning, and what-if tests, since privacy concerns limit access to real travel data. Current models trade speed against road network shape. Free-space methods run fast but ignore the road network. Topology-aware methods rely on slow look-back search.

TrajDLM models trips as chains of single road segments. It joins a block core for fast cleanup, road-aware codes from a road network encoder, and road-limited sampling for linked, true-to-life trips. Across three city-scale sets, it scored well on fine-grained local match scores while running up to 2.8 times faster than prior work. It also showed strong zero-shot transfer across domains, plus unseen transport modes.
arxiv-2605-10220:
Zhang, writing alone, argues stellar age compression reshapes the thick-disk story. The thick disk's formation timescale is debated in Galactic study. The age-metallicity relation, formation timescale and gradients read as rapid bursty formation. But stellar ages are never seen, so inferred ages may carry compression.

Using the same sample and matching with two age scales, spectroscopic astroNN and asteroseismic APOKASC-3 ages, the paper checks marks. Under seismic anchoring, rapid-formation signals weaken. The age-metallicity slope flattens from about minus three to minus two per dex. Formation timescale widens from about three to about three and a half gigayears, and formation age shifts from about nine to six. Reverse tests show added noise only broadens ages and cannot match it. A squeezing map with lambda below one matches a narrower spread, a steeper link and rapid-formation-like marks.
arxiv-2605-10320:
Tsz Hin Hui and three colleagues propose a new way to build order parameters, the quantities that distinguish phases of matter. Topological phases are usually characterized by non-local invariants, but the authors extract generic patterns from the dominant Fock states of many-body ground states instead. Their 2026 paper shows that these real-space order parameters classify phases more finely than standard tools.

In the extended Su-Schrieffer-Heeger model, the standard winding number cannot fully separate all phases. The new order parameters reveal a hidden sub-structure, with each topological sector splitting into two distinct phases. Beyond marking phase boundaries, they measure the depth of a phase and stay robust at transitions in disordered systems. The framework also gives a practical finite-size diagnostic for the Berezinskii-Kosterlitz-Thouless transition in the interacting spin-1/2 XXZ model, and it applies broadly across quantum many-body systems.
arxiv-2605-10420:
Diego Manso Anda and Pierre A. Haas study invasion waves in microbial communities where bacteria switch phenotypes. Clonal bacterial groups split into types, including a persister type resilient to rivalry. Their 2026 paper models two competing species in space. One switches, both by chance and in response to its rival, to that dormant state. The authors ask how that switching shapes travelling waves of invasion.

Combining analytic and numeric results, the authors find a surprising asymmetry. That switching does not change the speed of the rivals' wave into the switching group. Conversely, switching can quicken the wave by which that group invades its rivals. Bacterial persistence, the results suggest, can be an offensive rather than defensive survival strategy, surprising given persisters' usual reputation as a defensive refuge.
arxiv-2605-10620:
Stefano Vignolo and three colleagues treat the Dirac field as an effective spinorial fluid. They use the polar decomposition of the Dirac field for that picture. They then build a 1-plus-1-plus-2 covariant formalism without tetrad fields and Clifford matrices. Their 2026 paper asks when a self-gravitating Dirac field can sit inside locally rotationally symmetric space-times. The types covered are I, II, and III.

To meet symmetry needs, the authors extend previous work. They assume the velocity and spin fields lie in planes set at each point by generators of time-like and space-like congruences. Those generators underlie the 1-plus-1-plus-2 decomposition. They present analytical and numerical solutions showing how the proposed framework applies. The covariant formalism avoids specific coordinate systems and yields a picture tied to measurable variables.
arxiv-2605-10820:
Moksh Jain and six colleagues present MaD Physics, a benchmark that tests whether AI agents can do science under measurement budgets. Real discovery trades measurement quality against quantity, yet existing agent benchmarks either quiz static knowledge or let agents experiment without limits.

The benchmark offers three environments built on distinct physical laws, including altered laws that block answers memorized from training. Agents spend a budget on measurements, then must infer the law and predict future states. Two skills get scored: inferring models from data and planning measurements wisely. Builders of scientific agents get a test that mirrors the resource squeeze of real labs.
arxiv-2605-11120:
Raktim Bhattacharya inverts sensor design for large space-time systems: given an error budget but uncertain or missing sensor models, build the measurement odds that enforce the budget. Old design places sensors first and guesses states second, and demands valid forward models per sensing type.

Among candidate result beliefs meeting a set error bound against a desired target, the framework selects the one closest to the prior in Kullback-Leibler divergence, yielding a maximum-entropy result belief. The induced likelihood follows as the Radon-Nikodym derivative. The method covers Wasserstein, maximum-mean-discrepancy, f-divergence, moment, and hybrid error measures, with discrete particle-level plans, solver cost, and a closed-form symmetric exponential-tilt answer. Sensor builders get design from error budgets alone.
arxiv-2605-11220:
Carson Dudley and Reiden Magdaleno test whether prediction markets beat simple baselines for infectious disease forecasting. Markets like Polymarket and Kalshi pool collective judgment in real time and rival experts in elections and finance. But market players are self-selected and usually have no epidemiological training.

The team studies Polymarket forecasts from 2025 and 2026 for weekly cumulative influenza hospitalizations in the US, which has the expert-curated CDC FluSight ensemble, and monthly measles cases, which does not. Markets rival low-performing individual FluSight models but lose to the ensemble. Even the best market-ensemble mix puts zero weight on markets. For measles, markets lose to simple statistical baselines. Forecasters get a caution: market wisdom does not transfer to disease dynamics.
arxiv-2605-11820: Akiyoshi Tsuchiya proves a conjecture on Gorenstein simplices. Their h-star polynomials take the form 1 plus powers of t. Earlier work with Hibi and Yoshida had classified such simplices only when v is prime or a product of two primes. They guessed the count of unimodular equivalence classes depends only on v's divisor lattice. Tsuchiya gives a constructive classification for general v. Classes are parametrized by strict divisor chains plus recursive combinatorial data, and an explicit counting formula follows.
arxiv-2605-12020: Armen Sargsyan and three colleagues observe seven magnet-driven jumps of the cesium 6S to 7P line at 456 nm. These jumps, barred at zero field, matched theory from Zeeman math. In fields from 0.2 to 3 kG they beat standard jump strengths, with shifts reaching about 17 GHz near 3 kG. These traits suit optical frequency standards and field sensors with sub-micron detail in the blue.
arxiv-2605-12320: Luca Parolari and four colleagues learn polyp pictures from colonoscopy videos with noisy self-training, issued in 2026. Guided contrastive learning needs correct good and bad pairs, but linking tracklets of the same polyp across a video costs expert effort. The authors derive self-taught links from the stepwise workflow of procedures, then handle their noise with a noise-aware loss. Tests across polyp finding, matching, sizing, and tissue sorting show the method beats prior rivals. It matches or exceeds recent base models, with a light encoder trained on just 27 videos.
arxiv-2605-12420: Sahu and Pabari model dust shed by main-belt asteroids as it drifts toward the inner planets. Their N-body simulations include solar gravity, planetary pulls, radiation pressure, Poynting-Robertson drag and solar wind. They measure dust flows to Mars, Venus and Mercury, inputs needed for ablation on the first two and impacts on the third, and derive impact speed distributions. The calibrated fluxes match established models closely for all three planets, and close-encounter speeds track the dust population's orbital elements.
arxiv-2605-12620: Singhi and six colleagues make embodied agents more reliable by checking actions before taking them. Multimodal language models bring strong vision-language reasoning to embodied tasks, yet stay brittle on out-of-distribution scenes. Their VeGAS framework samples an ensemble of candidate actions at test time and uses a generative verifier to pick the most reliable one, without changing the underlying policy. Crucially, an off-the-shelf model used as verifier gives no gain, motivating a data synthesis strategy driven by language models to train a better verifier.
arxiv-2605-12720: Ram and Ramdas prove that optimal sequential tests yield log-optimal e-processes, completing a two-way story. It was known that thresholding an e-process yields every level-alpha sequential test, and log-optimal e-processes yield optimal sequential tests. The converse was open: whether optimal tests can be aggregated into log-optimal e-processes. The team proves they can, using WAIT e-processes: weighted sums of stopping-time indicators that start at zero, are nondecreasing and increase only at stopping times.
arxiv-2605-12920: Dongre and Hakkani-Tür ask whether talking actually helps embodied agents that share a household task but see only part of the world. They extend the PARTNR benchmark with a dialogue channel so two agents can compare notes while working. Dialogue cuts action clashes by 40 to 83 percentage points, yet task success falls versus silent teamwork. New measures of world-model alignment show the gap between seeming coordination and genuine shared understanding.
arxiv-2605-13320: Thomas Kloster and Fred Espen Benth carry out the first strict study of electricity price volatility across day-ahead prices in Germany, Norway and Spain. Treating observed prices as local averages of a hidden price process, they build estimators of weekly integrated variance. Their method copes with mean reversion in prices and with smoothing effects in the estimated variance. Their decomposition shows each zone has quite different drivers of volatility. Apparent leverage effects, where falls move volatility more than rises, vanish once suitable state variables are taken into account.
arxiv-2605-14120: Rahman proposes Mini-JEPAs, a fleet of small sensor-specialized foundation models for hydrologic questions. Geospatial foundation models pack multispectral observations into dense embeddings for environmental reasoning in plain language. One planetary-scale model handles broad mapping well but blurs specialized water signals, and such generalist models are often pricey, gated and compute-hungry. A routing agent instead consults five 22-million-parameter Mini-JEPAs, each tuned to one sensor stream, from Sentinel optical and radar data to thermal, phenology and topography-soil stacks.
arxiv-2605-14320: Alshahrani develops an adaptive-metric method for outer approximation in bounded convex vector optimization, for multi-goal problems. The metric used to measure progress changes from step to step, while error is still judged in a fixed Euclidean norm. He proves a faster convergence rate known only for the standard norm extends to every fixed inner-product norm. Cut directions also spread out when the upper image has a strictly convex, bounded-curvature boundary. Tests on three problems confirm the rate, in fewer steps where fronts curve enough.
arxiv-2605-14620: Wei, Li, Zhao, He, Li, Yao, Lu, Peng, Wang, Im and Yang develop LA-BHH, a bandit hyper-heuristic that is landscape-aware for choosing visiting orders in drone inspection routing. It uses 2-opt, swap, relocate, plus Or-opt moves as its arms. It builds context from landscape descriptors and live search state. It refreshes a LinUCB controller from improvement rewards. On forty-five generated routing instances it is claimed to beat rival hyper-heuristics and nearest-neighbour construction.
arxiv-2605-14720: McWade and Farhang investigate oscillator phase noise in OTFS systems. They analyse phase-noise interference and derive signal-to-interference-plus-noise expressions for free-running oscillators and continuous- and discrete-time phase-locked loops. Inter-Doppler interference is shown to be severe, and methods that correct only the common phase error cannot fix it. A joint channel and phase-noise estimator based on Wiener filtering is proposed, with gains up to eight decibels claimed.
arxiv-2605-14920: Jianping Li and eight colleagues built a drone that explores unknown places with a spinning laser scanner, called LiDAR, that turns on its own. Their FU-MPC controller steers the scanner along the planned flight trajectory, weighing new ground to map against the risk of losing track of position. A global planner first groups frontier boundaries into viewpoints and orders them by travel cost. Trials in complex scenes beat fixed scanning patterns on both coverage speed and steady localization.
arxiv-2605-15020: Evelyn Smith and four colleagues test whether property tax assessment must trade accuracy against fairness. Systematic errors now burden owners of cheaper homes disproportionately, making the tax regressive. Across 26 million sales in 95 percent of United States counties, accuracy and fairness move together under current practice. Adding property features usually improves both, and folding in public Census data, a feasible reform in most counties, lifts both well above the status quo.
arxiv-2605-15120: Sining Ang and three others present CLOVER, a planner for end-to-end autonomous driving that closes the gap between imitation training and rule-based evaluation. Imitating one logged path can still break safety, feasibility, or comfort rules, while farther options may score well. CLOVER makes diverse candidate trajectories and scores them with forecast planning-metric sub-scores. Evaluator-filtered pseudo-expert trajectories widen breadth, and conservative closed-loop self-distillation refines both generator and scorer.
arxiv-2605-15220: Michael Y. Hu and four others argue that data mixing is an online decision recurring across all of language-model training, not a one-phase problem. Old methods serve one phase, need proxy models, or assume fixed domains. Their OP-Mix algorithm mocks candidate mixtures by interpolating low-rank adapters trained on the current model, grounding search in actual learning shifts without other proxies. Across pretraining, ongoing mid-training, and ongoing instruction tuning, OP-Mix finds near-optimal mixtures at a fraction of rival compute.
arxiv-2605-15320: Thuan Hoang Nguyen and five others offer FFAvatar, a feed-forward framework rebuilding animatable 3D Gaussian head avatars from a few unposed portraits in seconds. Multi-View Query-Former fuses source images into a standard Gaussian representation, moved by FLAME parameters guessed straight from pixels without offline pulling. A three-stage curriculum moves from pretraining on over one million identities, through multi-view fine-tuning on 360-degree captures, to extra personalization within 500 steps. Face keeping and motion faith set a new standard.
arxiv-2605-15520: Xian Gao, Bo Hui, Min-Te Sun, and Wei-Shinn Ku show that credit for data in shared training can be gamed. One player can puff up its own measured credit while keeping overall skill. Their attack slips in small fake batches tuned by latent search, playing on patchy label spread and tester quirks. It lifts the foe's credit and reorders credit for honest players, with no loss of accuracy and no trip of shape-based guards. Credit itself is thus a fresh attack front.
arxiv-2605-16020: Białas and three colleagues address a training headache for neural-network samplers in Monte Carlo simulation. Blank-slate models must relearn physical symmetries from scratch, which slows them near phase transitions. Starting from a prior probability distribution instead, their method eases training for the Ising model and a spin glass. It also helps simulate larger discrete spin systems.
arxiv-2605-16420: Bompai and four others rebuild missing frames in top-down drone video of autonomous surface vehicles via trajectory-guided diffusion. Raw GPS logs plus a single reference frame feed a pretrained diffusion model with no domain fine-tuning. GPS coordinates map into image space, yielding motion cues that condition the SG-I2V model. SG-I2V yields the most natural-looking frames, the most realistic motion magnitude, and the strongest GPS trajectory adherence. Trajectory-guided diffusion thus works for maritime video reconstruction under low-texture, small-object conditions.
arxiv-2605-16520: Yi, Pan, Shi and Qu analyze sampling-based optimization, which solves nonconvex problems without gradients, through the lens of smoothing. They recast such methods as gradient descent on a smoothed objective, akin to noise-conditioned score ascent in diffusion models. Smoothing widens the locally convex region around the global minimizer but introduces an optimality gap, a coverage-optimality trade-off. Their annealed algorithm, DIDA, provably reaches the global optimum and beats other gradient-free methods in tests.
arxiv-2605-16620: Turkoglu, Sethuraman and Fekri introduce SCOUT, a framework for learning causal graphs that may contain cycles, from soft interventions whose targets are unknown. Most earlier methods assume acyclicity, Gaussian noise, or known targets, all of which fail in real systems. SCOUT maximizes data likelihood with two normalizing-flow designs, contractive residual flows and neural spline flows, and beats leading methods on graph recovery and target recovery in synthetic and real tests.
arxiv-2605-16820: Preiner, Niemetz and Barrett present a decision procedure for the SMT theory of extensional constant arrays. The SMT theory of extensional arrays gives read and write operators with extensionality, but cannot briefly express arrays initialized with a default value. Existing procedures for constant arrays cover only infinite domains, and solvers support only a fragment for finite domains. Their procedure supports arbitrary domains, presented as an abstract calculus with refutational and satisfiability soundness. In the Bitwuzla solver, it is evaluated on diverse benchmarks and use cases.
arxiv-2605-16920: Siriwardana's team analyses fluid antenna systems whose elements slide along a track with spatial correlation. Exact distributions are intractable, so they build a level-crossing-rate method giving near-exact approximations and tight bounds for the best spot. For one fluid antenna they characterise signal-to-noise, signal-to-interference, and combined ratios under Rayleigh and Ricean fading, then extend it to two receiver layouts with maximum-ratio combining. They find tail odds grow with track length, and one wavelength of movement cuts outage a thousandfold.
arxiv-2605-17320: Huang and colleagues present TClone, a system that lets computer-use agents fork live graphical workspaces the way code branches fork. A workspace can be snapshotted, branched into isolated copies, rolled back, or selectively merged, with fast branching kept apart from durable checkpointing. In end-to-end agent tests it cuts total task latency sharply against both KVM and CRIU, making safe speculative execution practical.
arxiv-2605-17620: Finck and colleagues present SynVA, a toolkit for vessel mesh generation and consistent aneurysm making. Brain aneurysms grow without warning and may rupture, causing stroke and bleeding, yet research is limited by scarce labeled data. SynVA combines flow-matching methods for healthy vessel meshes with learning-based aneurysm generation from existing vessel shapes. A rule-based model built only on body principles and statistical priors enables large dataset generation. The team releases 50,000 labeled mesh samples for vision tasks such as segmentation, and tests show realistic vessel shapes and plausible aneurysms.
arxiv-2605-17720: Nicholas Sica and Baris Taskin build chip-scale rotary traveling-wave oscillators, arranged as bricks, to lock oscillator-based Ising machines into step at a multiple of their working frequency. On-chip locking signals are hard to keep stable because manufacturing spread disturbs their phase, so the team tests their bricks under process, voltage, and temperature variation. Their bricks hold a steady 2.31 GHz locking signal and keep 93% to 97% accuracy on a 324-node max-cut problem, where ring-oscillator rivals fail to lock at all.
arxiv-2605-18020: M Yashwanth and four colleagues present FedUCA, a federated learning method that treats the server as a planner lifting global results by keeping clients in the group. Rational clients may quit when teamwork gains fall short of local value floors, which harms the global model and can kill training. FedUCA keeps clients in by making participation pay, so the global model improves. Tests on standard datasets show far more clients staying and a better global model.
arxiv-2605-18320: Yifei Chen's 2026 paper presents ISEP, widening the feasible action set in offline reinforcement learning without breaking safety. Strict constraints usually keep policies near the behaviour policy, blocking better actions just outside its support. ISEP interpolates a value function between logged data and policy samples, densifying high-reward regions while bounding value error. The widened support creates a multimodal landscape where plain deterministic averaging collapses to invalid actions. ISEP answers with stochastic action choice, alternating conservative cloning and optimistic expansion signals, realized as ISEP-FM with conditional flow matching.
arxiv-2605-18820: Hongyu Gu and Jingwen Fu show how training can discover superposition reasoning, where a whole reasoning frontier is carried in parallel instead of unrolled step by step. Earlier work hand-built such a frontier for graph reachability, leaving open whether training could find it past symmetric saddle points. They isolate two ingredients: a Möbius attractor holding the equal-weight frontier among its optima, and cascade supervision, which keeps gradients alive across depth. Plain end-to-end supervision stalls, while their recipe matches predicted final-step scores closely in tests.
arxiv-2605-18920: Wei Chen and eight colleagues improve generative recommendation by using synergy between data types rather than merely aligning them. Current systems produce item codes and fuse signals from each type, but they miss traits that no single type reveals alone. Their SynGR model rewards links across types during generation and curbs leaning on dominant types. It thus captures item meaning beyond shared or single-type signals, and tests on three benchmarks show it beating prior methods.
arxiv-2605-19020: Rahul Anand and four colleagues test vision base models for open set iris spoof checks. Five models face three shift tests: unseen trick tools, unseen sets, and infrared to plain light transfer. Models move well across like sets but fail on unseen trick tools and fall hard across light. Low rank tuning helps some cross set cases yet deepens trick and light failure, so closed set scores prove no open safety.
arxiv-2605-19220: Tiejin Chen and three colleagues argue that uncertainty scoring for large language models is miscast as a safety check. Most current methods only measure how consistent a model's own answers are, not whether they are true. That leaves them blind to confident hallucinations: stable but wrong answers that score as certain. They name three ills: touchy settings, a loop mistaking stability for truth, and proxy scores with no ground truth. They urge a shift to outside checks, native uncertainty design, and scoring tied to objective truth.
arxiv-2605-19320: Mingxuan Cui and colleagues attack a stubborn flaw in text-to-image models: rendered words often come out garbled. Earlier fixes bolt on special modules or alter encoders, complicating use across base models. Their TextAlign leaves the generator untouched and instead trains it with a layered reward, judging errors at whole-image, word, and letter levels and turning defect calls into one preference signal. On two leading generators it lifts text accuracy on optical character checks without harming general image quality.
arxiv-2605-19420: Yun and Chen replace single-point waypoints in robot navigation with a dual-heatmap scheme. Fixed waypoints collapse spatial uncertainty and often aim at unreachable object centers, causing failures. Their vision-language framework predicts one heatmap of reachable regions and a second for facing direction, forming a potential field that local planners can follow. A synthetic data pipeline and simulation benchmark support the design, and tests across Jetbot, H1 and Aliengo robots show far better placement of goals in free space.
arxiv-2605-19820: Miñarro and Herranz extend quantum geometry to include many body group swings. Quantum geometry tracks wave change in k space, and recent work recasts it in terms of ground state dipole swings driven by band to band mixing. The team dresses carriers and response points on the fly with group modes and focuses on Berry curvature. Group parts can be told apart from bare band ones through uneven channels in energy losing bounce spectra. Side swings and non local time couplings make this moving curvature.
arxiv-2605-20120: Gabriel Rongyang Lau examines an Aristotle API proof attempt in Lean 4 for the Grasshopper problem from IMO 2009. The artifact states a generalised theorem and proves four helper lemmas for a maximality and adjacent-swap exchange strategy. Yet the main theorem is closed directly by one unresolved sorry. The Aristotle summary names the missing counting step, showing at least n distinct forbidden values, but the Lean source never encodes it separately. Local proof search thus succeeds while global combinatorial bookkeeping stays unresolved.
arxiv-2605-20220: Silvia Licciardi and three co-workers apply scientific methods to music philology in a structural analysis of Rossini settings of the Metastasio arietta Mi lagnerò tacendo. A musical score gives performance instructions and sometimes implicit hints of the composer's aims, while variants and revisions complicate study. Through computational analysis with parsing, data mining and graph theory, they explore melodic, harmonic and textual choices in one Rossini setting. The results are a significant unicum, laying groundwork for systematic philological study and for generative models investigating the creative process.
arxiv-2605-20420: Li and 30 co-workers automate stacking of two-dimensional van der Waals layers for twistronic devices. Hand stacking is slow and imprecise, blocking study of emergent phases in stacked layers with a twist. Their robotic system follows the dry-transfer protocol for exfoliated sheets and learns from stacking metadata via reinforcement learning. As a demo it fabricates twisted bilayer graphene and shows its unconventional superconductivity near the magic angle.
arxiv-2605-20520: Sayash Kapoor and seventeen colleagues argue that fixed tests misjudge leading AI systems. Such tests reward tasks that are easy to specify, grade by machine, and run cheaply. The paper backs a second kind of test instead: long, messy, real-world jobs judged in small numbers by people. As a trial, an agent built and published a simple iPhone app with only one avoidable human fix.
arxiv-2605-20920: V. Ribeiro and Yves Laprie test speech articulation synthesis with articulatory phoneme recognition. Machine learning advances and speech-motion datasets now let vocal tract synthesis be conditioned on phonetic sequences, a key step. Yet quality scoring lacks a clear meaning. Ranking machine-made models is tricky due to own taste, and this adds special knowledge of vocal tract anatomy and sound. Their proposal uses phoneme recognition as a proxy, on the idea that spotting from motion traits better captures nuances like correct places of speech.
arxiv-2605-21020: Ziang Liu, Zheyu Wu, and Bruno Clerckx design beamforming and direction estimation for MIMO radar aided by a microwave linear analog computer, MiLAC. MIMO radar offers waveform diversity and large spatial degrees of freedom, making it attractive for high-resolution sensing, a sharp eye. Scaling to massive arrays improves sensing but raises hardware cost, power use, and digital processing load. The microwave linear analog computer, MiLAC, tackles those challenges by shifting linear operations from the numeric domain to the analog domain, with promising benefits shown for communications, a prior use.
arxiv-2605-21120: Bing-Dong Wan, Jun-Hao Zhang, Yan Zhang, and Ming-Yang Yuan work out masses for four-quark states with a rare quantum label. They use sum rules from quantum chromodynamics, the theory of the strong force. Hidden-bottom states land near eleven gigaelectronvolts, and hidden-charm states near four and a half. The bottom case is most stable, but the authors warn that linked currents need not mean four distinct particles, and they list decay routes for Belle II, LHCb, and BESIII searches.
arxiv-2605-21420: Shreyas Vinaya Sathyanarayana and co-authors present HiRes, an inspectable precedent memory for reaction condition recommendation. Chemists need both accurate predictions and the precedents justifying them. HiRes combines a graph encoder, cross-attention, multi-stream fusion, and a retrieval layer. It reaches top-one scores of zero point nine two nine for catalyst, zero point five three four for solvent, and zero point five three zero for reagent.
arxiv-2605-21620: Sidhant Misra and co-authors set out general revenue adequacy conditions for energy transport networks. Wholesale electricity trade rests on optimization, yet power grid and gas pipeline equations are often non-convex, so pricing guarantees are hard to generalize. Their formal setting covers nonlinear physical network flows, and they verify the result for DC and AC power flow plus steady-state gas flow in pipelines.
arxiv-2605-21920: Zhongyi Zhang and Yixin Cao study minimum sum set cover, where vertices are picked one by one and each edge pays the spot of its first covering vertex. For graphs this becomes minimum sum vertex cover, and a solution pairs a cover set with an ordering of its vertices. The authors tighten the upper bound on a key directed parameter, improving Liu and co-authors, and build graphs nearly matching it. They also show the problem is tractable in the fixed-parameter sense on bounded-rank hypergraphs.
arxiv-2605-22020: Yuke Li and co-authors present ForeSplat, an optimization-aware foresight method for feed-forward 3D Gaussian Splatting. Fast single-pass reconstruction models struggle to match per-scene optimization quality, largely for lack of large-scale 3D annotations, and standard feed-forward training targets only zero-step rendering error. ForeSplat trains an initialization that anticipates later refinement, so fewer refinement steps reach higher peak quality. Across TinySplat, Pi3X, and a distilled edge variant, ForeSplat-trained starts beat their vanilla counterparts, even fully converged ones.
arxiv-2605-22220: Junsu Kim and co-authors propose demultiplexing orbital angular momentum light from a single intensity profile. OAM modes enable multi-channel division with performance scaling linearly in mode count, yet splitting each superposition state is complex. Spatial-domain methods need gratings and apertures that can cut efficiency and accuracy. Their method restores orthogonality of OAM pair states under one intensity profile, with no extra receiver-side optical structure. Simulation results under various conditions test the approach.
arxiv-2605-22620: Joarder and team propose a multi RLIF framework: an answer cluster reward and a finish self-trust reward. Reinforcement learning (RLVR) lifts LLM thought, but needs outside help. Reinforcement learning from inner feedback (RLIF) is a choice that grows well, using model signals. Older RLIF methods rely on a single reward, leading to hacking and crashes. GDPO scaling cuts gaps. KL penalty hits low tokens, keeping search and blocking late crashes. Across math and code benchmarks, the method lifts stability, nearing supervised RLVR methods.
arxiv-2605-22720: Kryshtal tests nine model setups from four providers on 90 multi turn conflict scenarios. The scenarios cover false equivalence over documented atrocities, genocide denial and missed ethnic slurs. Failure rates run from 6 percent to 47 percent, making model choice a safety decision. When users pressed for balance where international courts had already assigned responsibility, five of nine setups failed 80 to 100 percent of the time. Kryshtal releases the framework for this domain and urges adding it to alignment test portfolios.
arxiv-2605-22820: Heredia and Roncel propose the Integrable Context-Dependent Demand Network, a neural model that learns retail demand as a smooth function of prices and context. Because demand is learned in log form, price elasticities, the sensitivity of demand to price changes, fall out exactly from the learned surface. Across three retail datasets it predicted comparably to rivals while giving clean, economically sensible own-price and cross-price responses.
arxiv-2605-23020: Korsky improves the Buffon discrepancy problem, which asks how closely a one-dimensional set of size L in a convex body can match Crofton-predicted line-intersection counts. Steinerberger proved an upper bound of order L to the one-third via a Steinhaus longimeter build. Using a star-discrepancy theorem of Aistleitner, Bilyk, and Nikolov, Korsky builds full-chord sets with discrepancy of order log L to the three-halves for every fixed compact convex body with piecewise smooth boundary. In the disk he proves a log L lower bound.
arxiv-2605-23120: Ishizuka asks whether the reduction from permutation equivalence of complementary dual codes to isomorphism extends to a nondegenerate symmetric bilinear form M. He defines what it takes for M to yield a reduction. He proves that for length at least three and field size, this holds when M is permutation invariant. The reduction then goes beyond LCD codes to codes with 1D hull. These are codes whose hull is spanned by a vector having nonzero coordinate sum. He counts these codes exactly and gives a polynomial time reduction algorithm.
arxiv-2605-23220: Guo and six coauthors present WMAttack, an automated attack-search framework for world-model agents. Weak hand-tuned attacks overstate robustness. WMAttack searches attack families, budgets, steps, restarts, plus allocation rules. Self-Correcting Attack Search refines proposals using reward, action, runtime, and rollout feedback. Representation-Guided Attack Retrieval reuses past configurations from similar tasks. On Atari and DeepMind Control, WMAttack finds stronger attacks. It lifts reward dip from 0 point 497 to 1 point 034 on DreamerV3 Atari and from 0 point 319 to 0 point 682 on DeepMind Control.
arxiv-2605-23320: Li and nine coauthors propose the Ventilator Decision Support System (VDSS). It is a human-in-the-loop multi-agent setup joining modular choice parts through contract-driven set links, giving tracked proof for review. VDSS performs online taste tuning with a local bandit, tuning doctor tastes from the final picked choice at each tuning cycle to guide later tips. Past ICU path replay with expert review shows higher tip yes rate and fewer talk rounds to reach a good plan.
arxiv-2605-23420: Kostiuk and colleagues measure social norm alignment, the agreement between answers to a social dilemma, in free-form conversation rather than multiple-choice tests. Their framework matches solutions pairwise, covering model-to-human, model-to-model, and human-to-human pairs, with two metrics for stated and explicit agreement. They build 3000 Danish dilemmas judged by three panelists as cultural reference points. Rankings stay consistent across models, and agreement runs higher for neighbor disputes and shared living than for other dilemma types.
arxiv-2605-23520: Ruschel and colleagues build a framework for how a net of oscillators picks shared frequencies and settles into stable patterns through delay plasticity. Their adaptive axonal delays copy a brain trick: activity-dependent myelination tunes signal speeds and thus the lags between cells. They show frequency picking and sudden, explosive relaxation swings in delay-coupled phase oscillators, both on brain wiring data and on fully coupled ring nets.
arxiv-2605-23820: Zaman and Garimella measure privacy leakage in anonymized conversational AI logs, using complete ChatGPT histories donated by over 1,000 users in Brazil, India, Nigeria, and Pakistan. On explicit disclosure, 34.5 percent of user messages contain personal information across a twenty-category taxonomy. On this filtered cohort, an off-the-shelf model still recovers each user's age, gender, and country at weighted F1 of 0.84, 0.90, and 0.88, with the median user identified from the first 5 percent of their conversation history.
arxiv-2605-23920: Belotti and three colleagues ask whether tasks meant to measure real human effort still do so now that language models can do them cheaply. Across eight classic effort tasks and 23 models from three providers, most tasks fell to accurate, near-free automation, with only a few holding out. Newer generations did better, and mid-tier models closed fast on the leaders, while promised cash rewards changed nothing. The authors warn that unsupervised scores may now show model skill rather than genuine effort.
arxiv-2605-24020: Nguyen's dissertation advances vision-language intelligence across captions, visual dialog, and interactive instruction following. For captions, GRIT merges grid and region cues through a DETR-based detector, trains end to end, and beats prior methods on scores and speed. For dialog, LTMI, a light-weight transformer for many inputs, matches a standard transformer version with under one-tenth of its weights on VisDial. For instruction following on ALFRED, a two-stage setup first decodes orders without visual context, then fuses visual cues, reaching an unseen success rate of 8.37 percent.
arxiv-2605-24120: Bao and James point out a link between two quantum jobs: a code's power to fix errors and its power to sense a parameter. Their example ties an absorption-emission code to a sensor state for arbitrary state rotation, showing that error-correcting capacity tracks sensing ability. The authors hope a unified view will let sensor designers borrow tricks from error correction. That would turn code ideas into sharper quantum sensors rather than treating the two fields as separate crafts.
arxiv-2605-24420: Doan, Gu, and Alouani show that batch norm lifts memory of odd samples and leak risks. Batch norm is widely used for faster, calmer training, but its leak effects were new. Across datasets and designs, it lifts memory of odd ones, seen through out-of-spread memory, per-sample pull, and member attacks. That extra memory turns straight into leak weakness, with batch-norm models far more open to member attacks. A gear-level look at the backward pass shows it lifts margin growth for odd samples.
arxiv-2605-24520: Muhammad Muneeb and David B. Ascher present AnnotateMissense, a 2026 framework that annotates and benchmarks predictions of whether single-letter protein changes cause disease. It merges population, conservation, transcript, and protein-language-model evidence into one genome-wide resource. Benchmarked on 132,714 ClinVar-labeled variants, its full 303-feature XGBoost model reached a mean MCC of 0.9411 with near-perfect ROC-AUC. The final model then scored more than ninety million variants across the human genome.
arxiv-2605-24620: Kristin Kirchner and others analyze Monte Carlo estimation for Banach-space-valued random variables. In practice, computation uses finite subspaces of growing dimension. Their error analysis tracks how Rademacher constants depend on subspace dimension, yielding novel complexity results for single-level and multilevel means and injective moments of any order. In favorable cases the error-versus-work bounds shed that link. For Lebesgue variables, the convergence rate follows the integrability alone. The analysis exposes how sampling error trades against approximation gaps, and number tests confirm the bounds.
arxiv-2605-24820: Wen-Shi Tang and co-authors test four magnetic braking models in cataclysmic variables, where standard forecasts clash with observations. Other models have been discussed for neutron star binaries but never tested in these variables. Both the Convection And Rotation Boosted model and the tau-boosted model prove too strong, failing to match the period gap spot, so they suit these variables poorly. The saturated, boosted, and disrupted model matches some parts better than standard braking but worsens other mismatches. Convective turnover timescale choices strongly affect non-standard models.
arxiv-2605-25020: Abdurrahim Yilmaz and colleagues test a small language model run locally, keeping data private, for mining long pemphigus follow-up records. Thirty patients gave 541 visit notes, 89,336 words in all, with 56 items marked by two dermatologists. The local model, Qwen3 4B Thinking 2507, retrieved items at 82.25 percent mean accuracy across 1,680 tasks. Doctors rated its visit summaries highly on quality, accuracy, and use, preferring them in 53.3 percent of cases. The authors suggest such models can support clinical decisions with proper human checks.
arxiv-2605-25220: Aviral Chharia and Fernando De la Torre learn 3D Gaussian head avatars from randomly sampled 2D images alone. They use no multi-view data, 3D supervision, or intermediate view synthesis. Their MVCHead model enforces multi-view consistency in the 3D representation while regressing Gaussians. A hierarchical state space block refines Gaussians from coarse to fine. An SE(3) multi-view critic judges whether self-renders come from one underlying configuration. The result leads on perceptual quality, texture, and geometric consistency, and the team releases FaceGS-10K.
arxiv-2605-25420: Khalid Yusuf Dahir measures a safety gap between English and Somali in models, where Somali rarely gets tests. His SomaliBench benchmark pairs 100 harmful-intent prompts across languages, verified by a native author, and tests four models alike. Refusal gaps run 0.40 to 0.93 across models, all significant, meaning Somali prompts face refusal far less often. For three models the main Somali failure is unclear output, not fluent harmful compliance. A judge model classified responses, with a native spot-check in agreement, while raw generations stay unreleased since some may be harmful.
arxiv-2605-25620: Fu and colleagues ask what a world model should remember when an agent must plan from vision alone. Frozen visual embeddings carry rich detail but also much a task does not need. Pixel-trained latents, by contrast, lack semantic structure. Their TC-WM shrinks high-dimensional visual embeddings into a small latent space and aligns part of it with the agent's physical state. It rebuilds embeddings to keep useful visual structure. Tests show better modeling and more precise control than leading rivals.
arxiv-2605-25720: Aichmüller, Hesse and Geffner tackle combinatorial generalization in reinforcement learning through classical planning. In sparse-reward domains, real-time search fails, and planning methods often need expert demos, hindsight relabeling, or goal-state random walks. Their self-improving weighted A-star framework pairs a relational graph neural network heuristic with search. Search data update the heuristic by Q-learning. The resulting heuristics serve as general policies, solving new instances without search and transferring zero-shot from small Blocksworld instances to 488-block problems.
arxiv-2605-25820: Yuan, Zhao and Meng tackle parallel reading in diffusion-based multimodal models, where each step commits masked tokens at once. Confidence-based ranking puts spots alone, missing shared visual grounding. The team introduces the Visual Redundancy Index and Visual-Redundancy-Controlled Decoding, favoring complementary spots via token-to-image attention. Across benchmarks it cuts overlap with modest runtime overhead. It gains up to about 19 percent on M3CoT and 7 percent on MMBench over confidence-based reading.
arxiv-2605-26020: Aiken, Ross, Shvydkoy and Xue study complex multiplication points on the boundary of the classic fundamental domain for SL2(Z). Duke showed such points spread evenly across the domain as discriminants tend to minus infinity. The authors prove the boundary points also spread evenly along the boundary. They further pin down exactly when every CM point of a given discriminant lies on the boundary. Along the way, they classify, under an assumption, all negative discriminants whose class group has small exponent. The work links point distribution to algebraic structure.
arxiv-2605-26620: Lukas Ellinger and three others introduce Granuscore, a yardstick for how fine or coarse wording is, needing no reference text. Older gauges mostly count surface detail or sentence specificity. Granuscore instead reads structure in a layered embedding space, recovering known orderings on a test set and tracking shifts across discourse settings. It also explains wiggles in specificity beyond sentence length. On four question-answering sets, it exposes steady gaps between questions, gold answers, and model replies.
arxiv-2605-26720: Chong and three colleagues probe how self-evolving language-model agents turn feedback into plans when generating CUDA kernels, the programs that run fast computations on graphics processors. Their CUDAnalyst layer freezes trajectories and injects feedback selectively, allowing clean attribution of each planning choice to its feedback sources. Explicit planning helps only when feedback is aligned, effective plans emerge from structured combinations of feedback, and strong models' plans partly transfer to weaker ones.
arxiv-2605-27220: Hussain and Nielbo study retrieval in a live question-answering system on the Danish National Encyclopedia. Synthetic queries suggest over 90 percent of queries need language-model augmentation for high coverage, but under the live deferral policy only 27.8% of real queries do. The authors call this gap the Coverage Illusion: the need for augmentation shows only after searching, so pre-search routing cannot fix it. Their cheapest-first cascade escalates only when a step returns nothing, lifting quality, cutting latency by about a third, and serving most real queries without augmentation.
arxiv-2605-27520: Vasudev Mittal and Geraint Lewis test the cosmic dipole with the Ellis and Baldwin method across multiple flux cuts. Splitting the catalog into disjoint flux bins and fitting the dipole jointly beats the traditional single-cut approach for non-power-law luminosity functions. The method works best where the luminosity function shape changes most, promising decisive results for upcoming surveys.
arxiv-2605-27820: Liu and colleagues benchmark tool-using agents from the wearer's viewpoint, with tasks grounded in first-person video across five daily settings. EgoBench couples seeing, multi-step tool use, and live user interaction, judged by strict process and outcome checks. Even the best of eight video models succeeded only about a third of the time.
arxiv-2605-28020: Wang and colleagues wake task behavior in frozen pretrained models with no extra training. Their Energy-Based Decoding steers text with a light reward model tied to the base model's own habits. It raised one base model's instruction scores steeply and cut another's math wait sharply, giving a fairer read of raw pretrained skill.
arxiv-2605-28120: Chen and colleagues make legal AI reasoning open to checking by sorting law into a layered graph and splitting the job three ways. In LegalGraphRAG, one agent hunts for proof, a second checks it against source texts, and a third judges from checked proof alone. The setup beat older graph-retrieval rivals on sound, trusty legal analysis.
arxiv-2605-28220: Robin Coutelier, Thomas Hader, and Laura Kovács refine SAT solving with graph backtracking, which follows the implication graph instead of coarse decision levels. Weighted by a user-chosen function, it unassigns the lightest literals on conflict and generalizes both chronological and non-chronological backtracking. In their NapSAT solver it cut literal propagations and improved runtime.
arxiv-2605-28320: Mazen Alamir and Sacha Clavel find short, plain piece-wise polynomial rules in factory time series with many raw inputs. They build on an older hidden-rule method, turning hidden polynomials into plain pieces. On six-axis and four-axis robot arms in tests, the short rules beat deep nets on fresh contexts.
arxiv-2605-28420: Yasser Taha, Grégoire Montavon, and Nils Körber propose Conveyance, a loss for settings where classes relate to each other in structured ways. Standard losses treat classes as symmetric and miss those links, above all under structured noise. Conveyance encodes graph-like class links without joint spreads or hand-tuned utility tables, growing two margins over distinct class splits. It matches or beats rivals built for one task on hierarchical classification, ordinal regression, and multiple-instance learning, giving one unified approach.
arxiv-2605-28520: Yang Zhang and four colleagues forecast market impact of financial events with GS-Fuse, joining text and prices. Existing models fuse the two streams symmetrically, missing when event text truly adds value beyond price history. GS-Fuse opens toward event text only when it adds value, guided by Granger causality, and aligns event representations and fine textual cues with future price paths at several levels. As a plug-and-play adapter over language and time-series models, it beats rivals across assets and horizons.
arxiv-2605-28620: Pierre Albin, Markus Banagl, and Paolo Piazza compare analytic and topological Gysin maps in Part 2 of their study of smooth atlas stratified spaces. A bordism-like description of K-homology due to Jakob, close to the geometric K-homology of Baum and Douglas, plays a central role. The authors prove this description equivalent to the analytic K-homology of Kasparov, using Thom's transversality theorem to describe Gysin maps compatibly with Jakob's definition. The result links the analytic maps from Part 1 with the topological maps of the second author.
arxiv-2605-28720: F. Ritort coins heatomics, the science of entropy production in cells at cell and molecule scales. Cells hold a nonequilibrium steady state by consuming energy and shedding heat, and heat loss tracks the entropy production rate, a universal cellular signal. Matter sheds one watt per kilogram, conserved across scales at ten thousand times the Sun's density, yet near the universe's average. This power sets the bar for generating negentropy, which sustains order, and the Variance Sum Rule extracts entropy production from probe fluctuations and state equations.
arxiv-2605-28920: Gabriel Loaiza-Ganem and colleagues extend conformal risk control to generative models with a framework called Conf-Gen. Conformal prediction gives formal uncertainty guarantees for supervised learning. Image and language generators fall outside its usual scope, so Conf-Gen adapts the method while easing its assumptions. The framework joins past attempts to apply conformal ideas to language models and opens new uses. These include guarantees on non-memorized images, enough clarifying questions from a chat system, and correct agent output.
arxiv-2605-29020: Aarushi Bhargava, Gaurav Gardi, and Metin Sitti show ultrasound-driven bubbles can penetrate dense fibrin networks in chronic blood clots. Oscillating bubbles carve three-dimensional paths that let nanobead markers infiltrate up to 200 micrometers deep. One bubble's radial stress sits far below fiber fracture strength. Instead, thousands of repeated loadings below fracture strength accumulate damage and soften the network until it yields. At low force the network softens then resists further damage, while at higher force it keeps softening. The physics follows viscoplastic bubble-fibrin mechanics.
arxiv-2605-29220: Leonidas Zimianitis and colleagues built RIPPLE, a tool that recasts microscopy annotation as sparse correction. A user clicks a starting point, the tool proposes a full track, and the user steps in only where the track drifts. They tested it on five hard microscopy sets, four of jellyfish motion and one of fast-moving sperm landmarks. RIPPLE matched the quality of full manual annotation while cutting manual clicks by three to twenty-five times across the sets. It can thus supply the gold-standard data that future trackers need.
arxiv-2605-29520: Lorenzo Vito Dal Zovo studies finite-time transition probabilities for the open-boundary totally asymmetric simple exclusion process. Most theory treats the steady state, but he counts transition sequences between configurations and equates them with standard Young tableaux of recent non-classical shapes. That extends the periodic-boundary cylindric-tableaux correspondence to the open case. He then builds tableau-like objects allowing repeated cells under the diagram's partial order. Their counts go into exponential generating functions, and transition entries become signed sums of those functions.
arxiv-2605-29720: Zhichao Chen and five colleagues offer a quick gauge of how good a face recognition dataset can be, with no full training run. Their Intrinsic Quality score joins a neighbour-agreement check on shared identity labels with a rank-based gauge of embedding spread and variety. Light proxy models or small data slices suffice, so teams can spot weak or messy sets before paying for heavy training. The paper sets out a test plan for clean, noisy, and mixed sets to check whether the score forecasts later skill.
arxiv-2605-29820: Kun Wang develops an adaptive method to certify a prepared state's match to a target stabilizer state. An earlier result gave the best worst-case lower bound from one fixed generator gauge, but gauge choice can leave wide ambiguity. For one gauge, Wang derives the matching optimal upper bound. He then turns gauge choice into an adaptive design problem with exact endpoint linear programs and witness elimination. The scheme tightens monotonically, recovers exactly once all nontrivial stabilizers are covered, and proves full coverage necessary in the worst case.
arxiv-2605-29920: Daniil Shlenskii and four colleagues train one-step generative models from a symmetry in flow matching. When the two end distributions match, the drift field dies at the middle time, and its size gives a sound gap measure, the Midpoint Divergence. Randomly flipped blends stretch the gap past the midpoint, and symmetric random blends widen it further. A variational form of the widened gap yields a workable training goal for a one-step maker. The resulting Midpoint Generative Models stand level with rival one-step methods on firmer theory.
arxiv-2605-30020: T. Huertas-Roldán and nine colleagues report 20 weak, still-unidentified molecular lines from the carbon-rich planetary nebula IC 418, seen at three radio bands with two telescopes. None matches known molecules, known radio lines or instrument flaws. The spacings fit neither simple linear molecules nor symmetric tops, though a repeated doublet pattern appears. Estimated spin values point to carriers of 4 to 13 atoms, and the authors favour bent carbon molecules shed by processed grains, ruling out buckyball relatives.
arxiv-2605-30120: Lixuan Guo and five colleagues replace clustering with sparse coding in costly multi-vector retrieval. Leading systems tame billion-scale token vectors with dimension reduction and K-means, paying in indexing delay and lost meaning. Their Single-stage Sparse Retrieval method projects token embeddings through a sparse autoencoder into a highly sparse code, then uses inverted indexing with no clustering step. On BEIR it cuts indexing time fifteenfold against ColBERTv2 and halves retrieval latency, while improving retrieval quality.
arxiv-2605-30220: Yiran Wang and Guido Montúfar present TriSearch, a reinforcement learning method for optimizing objectives over polytope triangulations via bistellar flips. Feasible flips are encoded by supporting circuits and local subtriangulations, letting a policy rank them from local features. The interface works across dimensions, traversing the flip graph without enumerating the full space. In three and four dimensions, TriSearch generalizes zero-shot from small cases to larger polytopes. It tops metric objectives in 3D and finds more distinct Fine, Regular, Star triangulations in 4D than current samplers.
arxiv-2605-30520: Yuan, Abanto-Leon, and Hollick plan schedules for wireless sensor-actuator nets that run multi-rate control in factories. Their plan offers four tactics: two-phase scheduling for sure links, a least-laxity-first rule that keeps queues short on tight-storage gear, opportunistic packet bundling, and repeat scheduling. Tests show bundling lifting schedulability by up to nearly double and cutting run time, while repeat scheduling slashes run time and link and storage costs sharply. The plan beats prior methods in lifelike factory tests.
arxiv-2605-30720: Malla's 2026 study introduces the Kalimati Vegetable Price Index, a composite of 135 daily commodities from Kathmandu over ten years. The index creates a stable broad signal, cutting single-crop noise. From 64 features, fourteen models were tested. The models span statistical, tree-based, deep learning, hybrid, and transformer designs, across horizons of 7 to 90 days. Tree-based ensembles proved most robust, while statistical models and transformers struggled with noise. A momentum-corrected stacking ensemble performed best at 90 days, with low percentage error and most variance explained.
arxiv-2605-31120: Binglun Wang and colleagues teach a simulated swimmer from just one example motion. Swimming resists shortcut modelling, since water presses and flows over the whole body at once. The team therefore compresses body-water forces into a compact code that a fast graphics-card solver can train on. The resulting policy handles new goals, water densities, currents and all four racing strokes, beating rival methods with a 63.9 percent success rate on unseen tests.
arxiv-2605-31220: Kyriakou, Ulmer and Titov ask whether multilingual language models carry confidence signals that transfer across languages. Most confidence work studies English only. Many methods degrade or need retraining in other languages. A lightweight linear probe trained on one language predicts answer correctness from middle-layer representations in unseen languages, with no target-language supervision. Confidence signals cluster in middle layers, the authors find, suggesting a shared confidence subspace across languages.
arxiv-2605-31420: Mirzoyan and Avagyan extend a U-Net VAE galaxy sorting framework to a larger JWST sample spanning redshift 0.5 to 4. They focus on massive systems with stellar masses above 10 billion solar masses. Their cleaning and sorting pipeline analyses 1,380 galaxies to identify disk-like shapes across cosmic time. Their sorter finds 382 disk-like galaxies; some show fuzzy features in line with current deep-learning limits. Disk-like forms persist over many redshifts and stellar masses, hinting massive disks were more common in the early universe than once assumed.
arxiv-2606-00320:
Chen, Shen, Deng, and Lei build a live guard for tail risk with no fixed data rules. Tail risk weights the worst losses in a run. Old guards lean on calm data or plain means. Live data can drift or shift by plan, which breaks those crutches.

Their frame joins three strands of math in one loop. Fit-free tail checks meet online learning in the mix. A known split form for tail risk, from Rockafellar and Uryasev, seeds the step rules. Proof shows the kept tail risk nears the mark in the long run. The gap from a scant run stays small and firm. Tests span fund risk work and harm cuts for big chat models.
arxiv-2606-00720:
Wu and Öz study rival trading bots on fast blockchains in this 2026 paper. Bots hunt arbitrage, where the same asset trades at two prices at once. Some bots search off-chain and send one set trade. Others spam the chain with repeat tries and let the chain itself find the chance.

The pair build a model of how block order rules, fee floors, and shocks shape this contest. They test it on cyclic arbitrage data from the Base chain, from June 2025 to February 2026. A trace-level tool sorts trades by bot style, and the labels match clear gaps in how trades run. In their sample, the spam style is just 23 percent of activity but makes 95 percent of spam. After Base changed its setup, fee income shifted toward trades that worked. Spam bots paid higher fees and ate a smaller share of block space.
arxiv-2606-00820:
Hao and co-authors pull apart why AI agents change their minds in debate in this 2026 paper. Multi-agent debate is often judged by how much answers shift or agree. But a shift alone cannot show that peers helped. The team runs five GPT-4o agents on hard MMLU-Pro questions where they first disagree.

Three setups are matched: self-reflection alone, peer stances only, and full peer reasoning. Even with no peers, 37 percent of agent-question pairs flip. Among pairs stable under that control, 29.3 percent adopt a peer answer once stances are shown. Those adoptions mix fixes, new errors, and swaps between wrong answers. Full reasoning lifts each agent's own score but adds no extra group gain over self-reflection. It also burns 57 percent more tokens. A neutral nudge cuts both harmful and helpful adoption, with no clear accuracy gain. The claim: convergence is a murky signal of value.
arxiv-2606-00920:
Zhou and co-authors measure how far re-running a code benchmark can sharpen its scores in this 2026 paper. A benchmark score wobbles for two reasons. Decoding is random, and the problem set is finite. They test 16 models on 99 recent LeetCode-style problems, with two prompts and five runs each. The design gives 15,840 judged runs in all.

The pooled intervals that repeat-run habits invite are wrong both ways, they find. Such an interval is about twice too narrow for new problems and twice too wide for the fixed set. With sound clustering, 12 of 15 neighbor pairs on the leaderboard cannot be told apart. A variance ceiling caps what repeats can buy: at best, intervals shrink by 23 percent. For the median model the cap is 14 percent. Two to three runs suffice to learn the parts that matter, they conclude. More runs mostly burn compute.
arxiv-2606-01120:
Sun and co-authors diagnose how AI verifiers weigh their own knowledge against fetched proof in this 2026 paper. In retrieval based fact checking, a model judges a claim against evidence. Its built in knowledge may lean one way before the evidence lands. That lean can clash with the context. No testbed measured how verifiers settle such clashes.

Their testbed, PAVE, sorts a verifier into four states by its prior: right or wrong, confident or not. It then watches two skills. Does the verifier hold a right prior against misleading proof? Does it drop a wrong prior when sound proof arrives? Across seven models, arbitration is unreliable and varies a lot by model, they find. Their fix is a light test time method based on Jensen-Shannon divergence. It lifts factual reliability with no change to the model, and holds up across model families.
arxiv-2606-01520:
Shokri asks when learned models transfer across unlike domains. One latent predictive design could serve many settings. A driving scene, a robot workspace, and an order book all qualify. The parts for one domain exist and are validated. What is not known is when transfer works, and by how much. TERRA gives that question a formal treatment. Each domain is a controlled Markov process on a latent grid.

Any setup splits into thin adapters and a shared core. The core is meant to stay invariant across domains. A cross-domain map is scored by bisimulation discrepancy. Gromov-Wasserstein distance serves domains with no shared coordinates. A transfer bound separates source error from structural mismatch. The claim is stated in falsifiable form.
arxiv-2606-01620:
Xu and co-authors generate streamable talking portrait videos in real time. Video diffusion models make vivid portraits but cost too much compute. Interactive uses need streaming, not offline rendering. Their framework conditions on speech audio and reference images. A causal video VAE performs deep latent compression. Reference images guide the VAE as extra inputs. The network can then focus on dynamic information. Static appearance needs less capacity under that design. A residual auto-encoding extension sharpens space-time causality handling.

The generator is a Rectified Flow Transformer. It produces video latents block by block, autoregressively. Speeds beat baseline models by a significant margin. Quality matches or beats large models on realism and vividness. Comprehensive experiments back those claims.
arxiv-2606-01820:
Venturini and co-authors build a tool to mark speech errors in fine detail. Such marks aid study of child speech and clinic work. Hand marking is slow and needs expert skill. It is hard to scale to large sets of speech records. Their TalkTag tool uses a tuned chat model for the task.

TalkTag marks errors in the CHAT style used by experts. It was built with very scarce training data. Child story speech served as the base case. Tests show the marks are quite precise, the authors report. The tool also flags spots where speech is truly unclear. It offers a scalable stand-in for hand marking.
arxiv-2606-01920:
Li and co-authors rethink how distilled data sets are built from diffusion models. Distillation condenses large data sets into compact synthetic ones. Diffusion methods use pretrained generative priors for realism. Most still follow a rigid generate-and-use plan. A fixed per-class budget is set in advance.

Generation and final allocation stay tightly coupled there. That can waste budget on redundant samples. Or it can leave classes with weak examples. Their Pool-Select-Refine plan works in two stages. First, an over-complete candidate pool is generated. A compact subset is then selected under the budget. Refinement polishes the chosen samples afterward. The design makes allocation an explicit choice.
arxiv-2606-02020:
Xu and co-authors chart how entropy evolves during chain-of-thought reasoning. Reasoning traces show a consistent two-phase structure. An uncertainty region of exploration comes first. It shifts sharply into a confidence region. Convergence marks that second phase of the trace.

The confidence region holds two key properties. Answers there become highly accurate and stable. Models also generate many unneeded tokens there. They keep writing long after reaching the right answer. Early exit can exploit both properties at once. It stops computation safely when returns diminish. Test-time scaling can prioritize converged trajectories instead. Detection is cast as sequential change-point detection. The framing is the first of its kind here.
arxiv-2606-02120:
Han and co-authors detect mistakes in first-person video with two cooperating models. The task is to tell if a user acts incorrectly. Egocentric video shows the action from the wearer's view. Long-tailed errors make the task hard to learn. Rare mistakes are the ones models miss most.

Their UE-MCM method pairs a small and a large model branch. The large branch judges fine-grained action correctness. The small branch checks coarse video context as well. It spots actions that look right locally but break the workflow. A CLIP-based video encoder powers the small branch. Diffusion contrastive reconstruction enhances that encoder first. Understanding guides the collaboration between branches. Tests target long-tailed mistake detection performance.
arxiv-2606-02620: Sanford explores a classic question with a twist. How well can irrational numbers be approached by fractions? Here the denominators are not free. Only denominators from a chosen subset of the natural numbers are allowed. A specific notion of density for such subsets is introduced. With that tool in hand, Sanford proves a restricted analog of a theorem of Dirichlet. The classic result sets a floor for how good such fractions can be. The note shows how much of that guarantee survives when the choice of denominators is cut down.
arxiv-2606-02720:
Bolamperti and co-authors study a cluster of young, metal-poor galaxies seen through a gravitational lens. The Cosmic Archipelago is an ensemble of galaxies at redshift near 6.14. The cluster MACSJ0416 lenses them strongly. JWST and VLT data combine in a joint spectrophotometric analysis. One member, CA4, gets close attention. It is UV-faint, compact, and magnified by a factor of 3.73.

CA4 holds just 4.3 million solar masses in stars. It forms stars at 0.46 solar masses per year. Its metal content is about 2 percent of the Sun's. It produces ionizing photons efficiently. Large shares of its Lyman-alpha and Lyman-continuum light escape. Five more systems at the same redshift are confirmed. All are young and metal-poor. The group forms a strong overdensity in a small volume. Such faint galaxies may have driven cosmic reionization. The Archipelago serves as a rare lab for early galaxy groups.
arxiv-2606-02920:
Di Gennaro, Shevchenko, and Yang tackle the cost of making a language model forget selected training data. Unlearning should mimic a model that never saw those examples. It should do so without full retraining and without losing general skill. Past methods train for a fixed budget, then pick a checkpoint by testing many saved copies.

Their method, MASC, corrects itself by a margin rule during training. For each text to forget, it shrinks the logit gap between the true next token and its top rivals. Training stops once that gap is small across enough token positions. No downstream evaluation is needed. On the TOFU and MUSE benchmarks, MASC matched rival forget-retain trade-offs at a fraction of the compute cost. The authors also note a scaling pattern. As model size grew, forget quality held steady while retained utility rose, for MASC and for a rival method alike.
arxiv-2606-03120:
Banerjee, Yadav, Chellappa, and Roy improve 3D Gaussian Splatting, a way to render new views of a scene. Plain pixel losses check only total error. They let training shift error across frequency scales, which blurs fine detail. The flaw bites hardest when few views are on hand to guide the fit.

Their method, KC-3DGS, adds wavelet-domain checks based on the stats of natural images. One loss aligns wavelet coefficients at many scales, so lost detail is fined. A second loss pushes rendered images to match the heavy-tailed frequency stats of true images. A third term fines cross-band overlap, which aids frequency focus. Tests span five datasets, from indoor scenes to hard outdoor ones. On the hardest outdoor set, one perception score rose by about nine percent, and standard scores rose too. With just 12 training images, quality rose while looks stayed strong.
arxiv-2606-03320:
Aivazidis bounds how many subgroups an abelian p-group can have. The count depends on the group's type, coded by a partition. Column heights of the partition's Ferrers diagram set the main exponent. Each term takes the floor of the squared column height over four. The leading coefficient counts central choices in blocks of columns with odd height, and the constants are sharp on homocyclic blocks.

The proof starts from Delsarte's formula. Blocks are split by column height. Each homocyclic block is bounded by successive Durfee squares. Three applications follow. One is a comparison theorem for p-groups whose nilpotency class is below p. One gives diagonal summatory bounds with the shape held fixed. One gives leading terms at fixed rank for finite abelian p-groups. The work gives algebraists a sharp count where past bounds were loose. It shows how the shape of a partition drives the subgroup total.
arxiv-2606-03420:
Shankar and co-authors present PHAF, a fast way to build lifelike hand avatars for one person. It needs just two photos of the hand. One shows the back of the hand, the other the palm. Older methods rely on slow optimization to reach similar quality. That slowness blocks live use on small edge devices.

PHAF aligns a hand mesh with semantic guidance from the photos. It then pulls out dense texture detail to transfer onto the mesh. A view-based inpainting network smooths and fills the texture. The result renders well from new viewpoints. A parametric hand model drives accurate finger poses and motion. Tests show visual quality on par with prior methods. Yet texture creation runs about 30 times faster. That speed makes the avatars fit for live AR and VR use. Graphics engines already in wide use can host them directly.
arxiv-2606-03520:
Ai and co-authors solve a finite palette problem tied to Turán densities of hypergraphs. The setup starts with a self-converse tournament on at least two vertices. How many admissible triples can an m-color palette hold? The palette must avoid two special palettes linked to the tournament. The answer ties the count to a degree-square Turán number for digraphs.

A prefix-majorization lemma for convex out-degree moments does key work. Applied to directed cycles, it gives an exact value for the directed triangle case. That value yields a sharp palette endpoint of one third minus a small term. Combined with known palette theorems, it builds finite 3-graphs whose uniform densities approach one third.
