The extremal palettes are described, and an edit-distance stability result is proved. One third is thus an accumulation point of such densities. Extremal combinatorics readers get sharp values plus structure.
arxiv-2606-03620:
Wang and co-authors add physics guidance to self-distilled policy optimization for language models. In self-distillation, a model learns from its own outputs given privileged information. Fixed step sizes are risky in that setting. Teacher corrections help on some batches and mislead on others. Uniform trust can destabilize training late in the run.

Their method, PGPO, draws on viscous-fluid dynamics formalized as a stochastic differential equation. An information-modulated step-size multiplier sets trust per update. The multiplier comes from a mutual-information estimate between student predictions and teacher feedback. It preserves the weak-approximation guarantees of standard SGD. Overhead per step is negligible. On Science-QA, PGPO beats self-distillation in three of four domains. Gains reach 4.5 points. It also stays stable where the baseline collapses late in training.
arxiv-2606-03720:
Nobre and co-authors tackle missing neutron cross-section data for unstable fission products. Such data serve nonproliferation, forensics, fuel assay, and reactor design. Astrophysics needs them too. Libraries cover isotopes near stability well. Far from stability, theory is often the only source. Simplified model assumptions leave the error on predictions unquantified.

The team discusses ways to close the gap. Machine learning, better reaction models, and fresh experimental data can jointly constrain parameters. The long-term goal is evaluated files for top-produced fission nuclei. Those files would go to the ENDF/B library for a future release. Early results compare the usual simplified approach with a more realistic one. The realistic version accounts for nuclear deformation. Nuclear data evaluators get a path toward quantified off-stability data.
arxiv-2606-03920:
Yu and co-authors benchmark visual state tracking in multimodal video models with VSTAT. Watching a video means tracking entities, states, and events over time. Single frames never suffice for that skill. Current model evaluations barely test it. VSTAT holds 834 clips from synthetic and real-world video. Its 1,500 questions need continuous perception across the whole stream.

State-of-the-art models score far below humans on the set. They sit only modestly above answer-prior baselines. Thinking traces are compared against the video to locate the failure. Models reason and track correctly in text form. They fail at seeing the events they must track. Recent agentic approaches, video agents and coding agents alike, do not fix the gap. Perception, not reasoning, is the bottleneck the benchmark exposes. Video model teams get a diagnostic target for the next round of work.
arxiv-2606-04020:
Cheng, Jin, and Chang present SpliceBind, a graph neural network for drug prospects. Splice-driven resistance affects up to 40 percent of patients on targeted kinase drugs. Standard tools judge one structure at a time. They cannot compare forms made by splicing. SpliceBind judges binding pocket druggability across isoforms instead.

On 229 kinase pockets, it reached an AUROC of 0.703. Held-out families gave a stronger 0.761 score. It also beat the P2Rank baseline on the main test set. A study of six known variants split resistance into two tiers. Shape changes from deletions or pocket breaks are structurally visible. Allosteric routes stay invisible to any pocket-based tool. Learned embeddings still caught one affinity case that geometry missed.
arxiv-2606-04120:
Kai Zhang leads a large team introducing SaliMory in 2026, a memory system for conversational agents meant to act as lifelong companions. Such agents must remember user facts, tastes, and ongoing context across every chat, but stuffing raw history into the prompt degrades reasoning.

SaliMory trains one language model to run a structured memory with stages for filtering, consolidation, and recall, each with its own reward signal so credit for success lands on the right stage. The framework cut failures blamed on memory by a third. It beat the prior state of the art by over ten percent in end-to-end accuracy and more than doubled the rate of responses judged well personalized.
arxiv-2606-04220:
Kargi Chauhan warns in 2026 that AI scientist systems risk scaling a flaw already in the record. The flaw is publication bias: positive results get published, null results get shelved. Automated systems trained on that record inherit the skew.

Worse, they can amplify it. A system that mines the literature for leads will mostly find positive claims. It may then dress weak findings as solid ones, a kind of evidence laundering. Chauhan formalizes the risk and puts rough numbers on the distortion. Proposed remedies include null-result databases, mandatory disclosure of failed runs, and retraction-aware training data. The paper is a caution, not a ban. It urges builders to fix the record's bias before automating on top of it.
arxiv-2606-04720:
Vuong and colleagues screen a family of atom-thin Janus materials that could split water with sunlight while also serving spintronics, in a 2026 arXiv materials paper. Janus monolayers have different atoms on their two faces, which creates Rashba spin splitting.

Swapping the chalcogen tunes the Rashba effect: the sulfur and selenium versions show moderate splitting near the conduction band, while the tellurium version shows giant splitting near both band edges. Band gaps of 1.21, 1.27, and 0.76 electron volts are favorable for photocatalysis, and all three align their band edges suitably for overall water splitting, with predicted solar-to-hydrogen efficiencies of about 22, 26, and 30 percent respectively. The authors propose these monolayers as promising candidates for spintronic devices and high-performance photocatalytic water splitting.
arxiv-2606-05320:
K. S. Babu, Sai Charan Chandrasekar, Sudip Jana, and Sudip Manna connect high-quality axions to flavor hierarchies and to gravitational waves in this 2026 arXiv paper. Axions solve the strong CP problem, but Planck-scale effects can spoil the symmetry behind them, the axion quality problem. Gauged flavor symmetries explain why quark and lepton masses span orders of magnitude through the Froggatt-Nielsen mechanism.

The authors show the flavor symmetry can shield the Peccei-Quinn symmetry, producing a high-quality flavored axion with unit domain wall number. Such a construction predicts two signatures. The first is flavor-changing neutral currents, visible in rare kaon decays into a pion plus an axion. The second is a gravitational wave background sourced by the evolution and decay of cosmic string networks. Axionic strings can radiate axions to account for the dark matter abundance, tying flavor physics to a gravitational wave probe.
arxiv-2606-05420:
Gianluca Guidi and colleagues measure the electricity use and carbon emissions of United States hyperscale data centers in this 2026 arXiv paper. The rapid spread of these large facilities, driven by artificial intelligence adoption, has raised concerns about the industry's environmental footprint, but facility-level numbers have been scarce.

Across different assumptions about how fully each facility is loaded, the centers consumed roughly 68 to 99 terawatt-hours of electricity. They were associated with about 37 to 54 million metric tons of carbon dioxide emissions over that year. Under the scenario, their demand equaled 1.8 percent of United States electricity consumption, with roughly 54 percent of the attributed generation coming from fossil fuels. Their electricity-weighted average carbon intensity was about 545 grams of carbon dioxide per kilowatt-hour, roughly 48 percent above the national grid average of 370 for the period.
arxiv-2606-05520:
Jorge Guccione, Juan Guccione, and Valqui classify algebraic extensions in a 2026 arXiv paper on pure math. Their objects are linear cycle sets, structures tied to solutions of the Yang-Baxter equation. An extension glues one such structure onto another in all possible ways. Counting those gluings is a basic problem in the field. The authors take the simplest base case, a trivial cycle set, and an abelian group as the glued part.

Both parts are assumed to be finite cyclic p-groups, with a small extra case handled for the prime two. Under those limits the team lists every possible extension in explicit form. The list is complete and can be computed directly. They also work out two invariants, the socle and the center, for each structure on the list. The study was funded by a research grant from a Peruvian university.
arxiv-2606-05920:
Xin Wang and a large team argue that code agents should be graded on vague requests and second chances in a 2026 arXiv paper. Real web users rarely write full specifications up front. Requirements surface as they react to a first draft. Asuka-Bench simulates that loop: a code agent builds, a UI agent tests the live site, and a user model turns failures into feedback for the next round.

Fifty web tasks carry seven hundred eighty-four criteria and over two thousand expected outcomes. Eight language models ran under two agent frameworks. Weighted pass rates spread across a thirty-eight-point range. Models also differed sharply in repairing flaws once feedback arrived. Even the strongest model finished only about half the projects after three rounds. Underspecification plus iteration, the authors conclude, exposes gaps that one-shot benchmarks hide. The benchmark stays far from saturated.
arxiv-2606-06320:
Gizem Yüce, Giorgos Nikolaou, and Nicolas Flammarion sharpen machine unlearning in this 2026 arXiv paper. Unlearning removes targeted knowledge from a trained language model while keeping its general skill. Not every token in a passage marked for forgetting matters equally, though. Some carry the secret, and others are filler the model should keep. Earlier methods guessed token importance with helper models or hand built rules.

Their insight defines importance through conflict. A token is specific to forgetting when training to forget it does not fight the goal of retaining everything else. Their method, ATWU, learns a small scorer over hidden states that weighs tokens during unlearning, alternating with updates to the model itself. On the TOFU and RWKU benchmarks it achieved the best forget and retain trade offs, beating sample level methods and heuristic weighting. Its learned scores also matched human marked forget spans closely.
arxiv-2606-06920:
Tiny language models fit on phones and edge devices, but tuning them is treacherous. Nair and Tao document that trap in this 2026 arXiv paper. They benchmarked five models under one billion parameters on math reasoning. Full fine tuning, retraining every weight, often made small models worse.

Below three hundred million parameters, full tuning dropped accuracy under the untuned baseline. The authors call this negative transfer, a form of catastrophic forgetting. Lightweight methods that tune only a small added part stayed stable. Two such methods split the wins by task type. DoRA led on hard grade school word problems. LoRA led on pattern matching tasks. Even simple few shot prompting beat full tuning on the smallest model. Their advice is blunt: default to the light methods for small aligned models. Avoid full tuning below five hundred million parameters.
arxiv-2606-07320:
De Zayas and Rojas prove a negative result about a relativistic wave equation in this 2026 arXiv paper: some equations have no closed-form solution. They study a scalar particle governed by the Klein-Gordon equation inside a smooth potential shaped by an alpha-attractor function, a form borrowed from cosmology. The question is whether solutions can be written using elementary operations and special functions, the class mathematicians call Liouvillian solutions.

Using Picard-Vessiot theory, which analyzes differential equations through their symmetry groups, the authors show the Galois group is the full special linear group. That group is not solvable, which rules out Liouvillian solutions. They go further, using a transcendence theorem to show no rational change of variables can recast the equation into a standard solvable form. The conclusion is that this case sits outside the landscape of exactly solvable relativistic quantum systems, so numerical methods are unavoidable there.
arxiv-2606-07720:
Farhan and Chaudhary give language models a persistent memory for silent reasoning in this 2026 arXiv paper. The starting point is CoCoNuT, a method where a model reasons in continuous internal states instead of written words, exploring several paths at once. The authors identify a flaw they call the concept bottleneck: each new reasoning pass overwrites earlier hidden states, so facts computed early are lost as problems deepen.

Their fix, AGCLR, adds a gated concept stream that survives across all reasoning passes. Three learned gates decide what to write into memory, what to read back, and what to forget. The motivation is stark: on the HotpotQA question benchmark, plain CoCoNuT scored about ten percent exact match, no better than ordinary written chain-of-thought. With the memory stream added, performance improved consistently across maths, question-answering, and logic benchmarks built on GPT-2, and the advantage grew as reasoning depth increased.
arxiv-2606-07920:
Yaguang Yang, Qiang Le, and Isaac E. Weintraub of the Air Force Research Laboratory combine learning with classical optimisation for robot path planning, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Planning a route around obstacles is nonlinear and non-convex, and the two standard toolkits fail in opposite ways. A trained learning agent reacts in real time but its path need not be shortest. Optimisation finds excellent paths but needs accurate models and heavy computation.

The hybrid pairs the agent with an arc-search interior-point method, a refinement algorithm that follows curved search paths through the feasible region. The learning component supplies fast, feasible candidate routes; the interior-point machinery then polishes them toward optimality under the model. The aim is the agent's speed with the path quality of optimal control. The work comes from the Air Force Research Laboratory's Control Science Center.
arxiv-2606-08220:
An, Ge, Gong, and Zhang propose that clouds of particles around spinning black holes can amplify gravitational waves, in this 2026 arXiv paper. A rotating black hole can grow a cloud of ultralight bosons, particles far lighter than an electron, through superradiance, an effect that drains rotational energy into the cloud. The authors compare the system to a gravitational atom and ask whether passing gravitational waves, ripples in spacetime, can trigger stimulated emission, the process that makes lasers and masers work.

They work out the selection rules, which state which transitions are allowed, and the threshold conditions an incoming wave must meet for amplification to occur. The emission rate depends sharply on the boson mass, and for favored mass ranges the amplified signals could grow several orders of magnitude stronger than spontaneous emission alone. That boost would bridge the sensitivity gap between ground-based interferometers and pulsar timing arrays.
arxiv-2606-08420:
Gatidis, Langlotz, and Bluethgen teach a vision-language model the anatomy of chest X-rays, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Vision-language models pretrained on large image-text collections understand images globally. But they do not explicitly encode fine-grained anatomy, which limits spatially precise tasks such as segmentation. CheXanatomy integrates explicit anatomy knowledge into a pretrained model through autoregressive token-space supervision. The model learns to generate anatomical segmentation masks by next-token prediction, the same mechanism it uses for words.

To obtain supervision at scale, the authors synthesize chest radiographs from computed tomography volumes and forward-project the CT labels to create masks. The approach is evaluated on synthetic and real images against a standard U-Net baseline.
arxiv-2606-08920:
Zhang and colleagues present PolyBuild, a method that draws building outlines directly from aerial and satellite images, in this 2026 arXiv paper. The usual route labels pixels first, then cleans the result through several post-processing steps, which is slow and error-prone. PolyBuild skips that chain and outputs polygons in one pass. Its first module detects each building and sketches an initial contour from center features of four sub-regions.

A second module then refines the outline. It mixes image features from a convolutional network with the contour's positional information inside a Transformer decoder, capturing local detail and global shape. Starting from four sub-region centers, rather than one center point, gives the network richer contour information. On 3 building datasets, including the WHU aerial and WHU-Mix benchmarks, PolyBuild beat state-of-the-art mask-based and contour-based methods.
arxiv-2606-09120:
Chen and colleagues teach a consensus protocol to tune itself, using reinforcement learning instead of hand-set knobs, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Byzantine fault tolerant protocols let replicas agree on a transaction order despite some being malicious. Modern designs mix leader-based voting with DAG-based data spreading and expose many parameters. Static, heuristic settings degrade badly when workloads shift or networks vary.

AutoPilot monitors conditions and adjusts parameters online. Learning is decentralized, so polluted data from one learner cannot steer the system. Built on Autobahn, a state-of-the-art protocol, AutoPilot converged to the best configuration under change. It cut end-to-end latency by 49.8 percent versus the default. It beat random configuration exploration by 73.3 percent, showing the gains come from learned steering, not luck. The work points toward self-driving protocols that adapt continuously instead of being tuned once and left to drift.
arxiv-2606-09320:
Sudhir Pujahari and Punya Plaban Satpathy ask how much of a shape's sound is needed to pin down its spectrum in this 2026 arXiv paper. The spectrum of a Riemannian manifold is the list of vibration frequencies of its Laplace-Beltrami operator, analogous to the notes an instrument can play. Two manifolds are called nearly isospectral when their spectra agree except for finitely many entries.

The authors prove that for compact locally symmetric manifolds, near isospectrality already forces full isospectrality. First they settle the case where both manifolds share the same universal cover, the simpler space that wraps around them. Then, using heat-kernel invariants, quantities extracted from how heat spreads on the manifold, they show the universal covers themselves must coincide. The result extends across compact quotients of irreducible symmetric spaces of noncompact type. Within these classes, late agreement forces full agreement.
arxiv-2606-09620:
Jan Kamm and his co-authors present a planner that choreographs hundreds of floating robots on water in this 2026 arXiv paper. Show designers sketch a few key poses, and the tool must fill in safe paths between them. The hard part is contact: each robot must dodge all others, and that web of checks grows fast with fleet size.

Their pipeline first builds a graph of which robots can clash. It then splits the fleet into small clusters that act on each other. Each cluster is solved on its own, in parallel, with fixes for the ways splits can go wrong. Tests ran fleets of up to five hundred robots. One real show path, near two and a half thousand steps long, was planned in just over one second. The system has run live shows: twenty-four craft on Lake Zürich, and a display at the Venice Biennale.
arxiv-2606-10020:
McAlpine and his team build a Bayesian digital twin of the nearby universe's large-scale structure, in a 2026 arXiv paper on cosmology. Their Manticore-Deep reconstruction infers the primordial initial conditions of a huge comoving volume and evolves them forward under gravity. Five galaxy redshift surveys, including SDSS and BOSS, are constrained jointly in one hierarchical Bayesian framework using the BORG algorithm. A tiled inference strategy makes the computation feasible at about four megaparsec resolution.

The posterior ensemble of density and velocity fields reproduces the observed structure causally, with starting points that fit the standard cosmological model. Late-time outputs match the expected matter power spectrum, bispectrum, and halo mass function on tested scales. Two independent checks against data not used in the fit, including cross-correlation with the Planck cosmic microwave background lensing map, validate its fidelity. The volume extends more than tenfold beyond the companion local analysis.
arxiv-2606-10120:
Asiful Arefeen and colleagues build a decision-support system that recommends meals to keep blood sugar in range, in a 2026 arXiv paper on health informatics. Postprandial hyperglycemia, the glucose spike after eating, is a key risk factor for metabolic disorders, yet dietary guidance is often static and hard to personalize. MetaPlate instead generates personalized meal recommendations guided by counterfactual explanations, which show what small change would alter an outcome.

The system combines glucose monitor readings, wearable signals, and meal inputs to model pre-meal context. A machine learning model predicts post-meal glucose response with an error of about sixteen milligrams per deciliter in the reported tests. A counterfactual optimization module then adjusts meal composition, shifting macronutrient amounts, to hold glucose at or below a target level. A retrieval-augmented language model layer turns the result into human-readable recommendations and explanations that users can follow.
arxiv-2606-10320:
Rabelo and his team review what academia and industry each say about communication skills for software engineers, in a 2026 arXiv paper on software engineering training. Communication is now widely seen as key in the field. Yet discussion remains split across academic papers and gray literature such as blogs, talks, and industry reports, limiting shared grasp of how it is valued, taught, and applied.

The review finds strong overlap between academic and gray sources in treating communication as a core skill for software engineers. Differences appear in emphasis: scholars focus more on concepts and hard evidence, while gray literature stresses practical effects and new industry habits. By mapping both sources together, the authors give teachers and employers a fuller picture of which communication skills matter, from teamwork and client talk to writing and remote work. They also show where teaching still lags behind the hopes voiced by working engineers.
arxiv-2606-10420:
Kubo works out the strongest magnetic field a clean superconductor can withstand before its shielded state collapses, in a 2026 arXiv paper on superconductors. The superheating field is the stability limit of the Meissner state, in which a superconductor expels magnetic flux. It sets the ultimate gradient for superconducting accelerator cavities made of niobium.

For a niobium-like material at a fifth of its critical temperature, he obtains a superheating field near two hundred ninety millitesla. That is far higher than naive stretching of the near-critical-temperature Ginzburg-Landau result would give. For a TESLA-shaped niobium cavity, that equals a built-in stability limit of about sixty-seven megavolts per meter of accelerating gradient. The result matters for next-generation particle machines. Their cavity designs chase gradients that only make sense if the material limit, now computed more soundly at low temperature, permits them.
arxiv-2606-10520:
Wang and co-authors unify two styles of model compression in this 2026 arXiv paper, again targeting two-bit large language models. Post-training quantization shrinks a trained model without retraining. Scalar quantization rounds each weight alone: fast, but at two bits its accuracy can fall by more than thirty percent on some tasks. Vector quantization groups weights into a codebook and preserves far more, at extra cost. UniSVQ bridges them by writing codewords as an affine transform of integer lattices.

Because dequantization becomes a simple affine step, the model keeps a structure nearly as plain as scalar quantization while reaching accuracy comparable to vector methods. A block-wise fine-tuning stage reduces reconstruction error. Across model families and zero-shot benchmarks, UniSVQ beats the best scalar methods, adding only twenty extra parameters per weight matrix. Against vector quantization it matches accuracy with far fewer extra parameters and higher throughput.
arxiv-2606-10620:
Wu and Huang test whether image generators understand time in this 2026 arXiv paper, introducing the ImageTime benchmark. A model that truly models the visual world should keep identities, objects, and causal order stable as a scene changes, which storyboarding demands. Earlier tests mostly grade single images or full videos. ImageTime asks for one image holding four ordered key states of an action: initial, onset, transition, and final. Each scenario is decomposed into stage predicates and forbidden causal violations, then scored by a vision-language judge.

The benchmark covers twenty-two domains and 375 action concepts in 750 cases. Across eight systems, the strongest, GPT Image 2 and Nano Banana 2, still fail on causal preconditions, intermediate-state visibility, and quantity conservation. Weaker systems often cannot even produce the four-panel layout. Polished synthesis, the authors conclude, does not imply reliable temporal construction.
arxiv-2606-10820:
Tang and colleagues speed up language model serving in this 2026 arXiv paper. Standard models generate one token per forward pass, which makes high-load batch serving slow. K-Forcing distills a trained model into a push-forward map: random noise goes in, and a block of several future tokens comes out in one pass, modeled jointly rather than one by one.

Training uses progressive self-forcing, widening the block while the student learns to match the teacher's output distribution. At four tokens per pass, K-Forcing serves text about 2.4 to 3.5 times faster across batch sizes on LM1B and OpenWebText, with modest quality loss. A quality gap to the teacher remains at larger blocks.
arxiv-2606-11120:
Kang and Narasimhan rethink how to grade a football pass in a 2026 arXiv paper. A pass is usually scored by what actually happened, one outcome. Their method, Monte Carlo Pass Search, asks what could have happened. For each observed pass it infers the kick parameters. Then it samples many counterfactual executions and options, playing each forward. The pass is judged by a distribution of value, not one result.

The work builds on the first public high-fidelity tracking data with 3D ball trajectories, from Germany's Bundesliga. A learned world model, adapted from a trajectory generator built for autonomous driving, rolls each candidate forward until the next ball interaction. Training used only seven matches, yet the generator gave strong best-of-twenty forecasting accuracy against baselines. Two execution-surplus scores separate players who beat their passes' difficulty from players who simply choose high-value options.
arxiv-2606-11220:
Liu and three co-authors introduce LifeSentence in a 2026 arXiv paper, forecasting human life outcomes from panel data. Conventional statistics predict life trajectories poorly, discarding event sequence. Transformers keep the sequence but demand huge training sets that panels rarely have. LifeSentence writes each life event as a structured natural-language record and instruction-tunes a pretrained language model.

Trained on about sixty-five thousand people from the German Socio-Economic Panel, the model beat classical and deep learning baselines in an eighteen-task evaluation. Joint event-and-timing prediction improved threefold over the best baseline. Given event sets with timestamps stripped, it rebuilt chronological order with 91.2 percent Kendall's tau agreement. Without explicit supervision it recovered known patterns of social stratification, the education premium, the gender wage gap, and the motherhood penalty. A natural-language interface lets researchers pose counterfactual questions linking early-life histories to late-life endpoints.
arxiv-2606-11320:
Cormier and five co-authors build models to make diagrams accessible in a 2026 arXiv paper, with support from Canada's NSERC. Node-link diagrams are boxes and arrows representing graphs, concept relationships, and flowcharts. They are hard to access non-visually. Assistive interfaces exist, but they need a machine-readable representation of the diagram, while diagrams are usually published as plain bitmap images.

The team presents a set of related compact deep learning models for semantic segmentation of node-link diagrams, labeling each pixel by its diagram role. On a large synthetic dataset of such diagrams, the models show excellent quantitative and qualitative performance. They reach per-pixel accuracy over 93 percent. The authors frame segmentation as the missing front end. Once a bitmap diagram is segmented into nodes, edges, and labels, non-visual interfaces can work from published images rather than source files that rarely exist.
arxiv-2606-11520:
Luo and co-authors from the University of Electronic Science and Technology of China and SenseTime Research synthesize training data for operating-system agents in a 2026 arXiv paper. Capable OS agents need data capturing clear user intents, multi-turn delegation, and grounded tool execution, properties missing from existing datasets. Their ISE paradigm, Intent, Simulate, Execute, addresses the gaps in three stages.

Stage one constructs about fifty thousand structured intents on a four-part framework of persona, domain, task, and complexity, yielding 43,956 unique intents after dedup. Stage two drives multi-turn interaction through a role-locked user simulator grounded in actual execution outcomes, producing 23,132 complete trajectories. Stage three executes every tool call in a live, isolated OS workspace, giving authentic failure and recovery dynamics. Fine-tuning on the resulting ISETrace lifts ClawEval pass rates from 19.3 to 37.7 on Qwen3-8B, beating a GPT-4o reference and a much larger base model.
arxiv-2606-11720:
Runlong Yu attacks a famous open problem in fluid mathematics in this 2026 arXiv paper. The three-dimensional Navier-Stokes equations govern fluid motion, and whether their solutions can blow up in finite time is a million-dollar question. One-component regularity asks whether controlling a single velocity component suffices to guarantee smoothness. Yu proves a conditional reduction theorem.

Starting from a scale-invariant bound and smallness of the critical vertical component, he compares the true solution with a strict two-and-a-half-dimensional shadow class. The comparison happens in a quotient space adapted to pressure behaviour. The error term from coarse graining is absorbed as a positive covariance stress into a buffer. Under seven explicitly listed structural inputs, he derives a lower bound on the regularity radius at the origin. Yu is candid: this is not an unconditional resolution, only a reduction to a finite-mode obstruction.
arxiv-2606-11820:
Daniel Dadush, László A Végh and Giacomo Zambelli solve linear programs exactly through an oracle in this 2026 arXiv paper. A linear program optimises a linear objective over a polyhedron. In the oracle model the polyhedron is not listed explicitly; an algorithm can only ask a separation oracle whether a point is feasible.

Their algorithm returns exact primal and dual solutions using a number of oracle calls that grows quadratically with dimension times a logarithmic factor. The bounds depend on a geometric condition number of the constraint system, not on the objective, and need no prior knowledge of that number. For rational data this yields a polynomial-time method. The algorithm is black-box: it needs only an approximate solver subroutine, with cutting plane methods achieving the stated times. A general framework extracts exact dual certificates from approximate ones, strengthening classical rounding results.
arxiv-2606-11920:
Ritabrata Das proves a comparison theorem for symmetry groups over different number systems in this 2026 arXiv paper. Kazhdan's classical result says that for a reductive group, two sufficiently close local fields have isomorphic Hecke algebras, so their representation theories correspond. Das extends this to metaplectic groups, covering groups that wrap the original group several times, here the n-fold cover of the special linear group.

The fields are non-archimedean local fields, such as the p-adic numbers, whose residue characteristic avoids dividing n, and both contain all n-th roots of unity. The covering complicates everything: representations of the cover are genuinely different objects, and the algebra isomorphism must respect the covering structure. Establishing the Kazhdan isomorphism here means the theories of metaplectic groups over close fields can be transferred between each other. Such transfers underpin comparisons in the Langlands programme, linking representations and number theory.
arxiv-2606-12020:
Hui Li and six colleagues partially undo quantum information loss on an optical table in this 2026 arXiv paper. Open quantum systems leak information to their environment through decoherence and dissipation, and the lost information cannot be fully recovered. The Petz recovery map is a construction from theory guaranteeing almost optimal partial recovery. Despite wide use in theory, the map had seen only a handful of experiments, each under one fixed noise model.

This team implemented it for a broad family of photonic qubit channels with tunable decoherence and dissipation. Their striking trick is tabletop reversibility: for a good range of reference states, the recovery uses the very same devices as the forward noisy evolution. Quantum state tomography verified the recovery even when inputs deviate from the ideal reference. The results show Petz recovery can be realised resource-efficiently, giving experimenters a practical tool for mitigating information loss.
arxiv-2606-12120:
Pratik Jawanpuria and Bamdev Mishra bring curved-space geometry to a workhorse matching problem, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Optimal transport finds the cheapest way to move mass between distributions, but exact solvers scale quadratically as data grows. Low-rank versions shrink the plan into small factors, yet current methods use flat first-order steps needing careful tuning. The authors treat factored matchings as curved surfaces inside the space of tables.

On these surfaces they build Riemannian geometry, the math of curved spaces, with a Fisher-Rao ruler for distances. The framework covers plain transport, shape-matching variants, and unbalanced cases where mass may appear or vanish. For unbalanced problems, every operation becomes a closed-form rescaling with no inner loops. Each step costs time linear in dataset size. For convex costs, a rank-sufficiency certificate with a gap bound confirms global optimality. Their solvers converge faster than rivals across sizes.
arxiv-2606-12520:
Kim and co-authors find that the sprawling world of crystals secretly lives on a low, curved map, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Chemistry got a periodic table; materials science never did, because crystals vary in too many ways at once. The team applies nonlinear maps that squash many descriptors onto a curved surface, using the Inorganic Crystal Structure Database. A few descriptor mixes capture most of the spread in material traits.

The map sorts itself. Untold, it separates superconductors from ordinary materials and splits superconductor families along lines that cut across chemical likeness. Position on the map also tracks critical temperature, where superconductivity switches on, across families. Forecasts of that temperature follow from geometry alone, with no knowledge of the pairing mechanism behind it. Hidden order in decades of data thus steers quantum behavior. Discovery can hunt by map coordinates, probing empty regions, instead of wandering the full descriptor space.
arxiv-2606-12920:
Goginava proves a summable endpoint criterion for the almost-everywhere convergence of rectangular Fourier sums on the multidimensional torus, in this 2026 arXiv paper. In several variables, Fourier series can be summed over growing boxes, and convergence in the Pringsheim sense needs every side of the box to grow. Unlike the 1-D Carleson-Hunt theory, continuity alone does not force convergence, so smoothness demands, stated through moduli of continuity, are vital.

Zhizhiashvili's theory gave sufficient conditions slightly above a critical logarithmic scale, leaving the endpoint open. Goginava's criterion works exactly at that critical scale for all dimensions d at least 2 and all exponents p between 1 and 2, with a summable secondary weight at the iterated-logarithmic level. The result answers the Zhizhiashvili-Marcinkiewicz problem for p strictly between 1 and 2, and sharpens the classical sufficient conditions at p equals 1 and p equals 2.
arxiv-2606-13520:
Bates and colleagues present AsInst in this 2026 arXiv paper, a language for reasoning about distributed programs whose steps run out of order. Choreographies describe the communication pattern of a distributed system as a single global program. Futures-based implementations let later steps start before earlier ones finish, improving latency and throughput. But actual behaviour depends on resources: communication delay, computation time, failures, and recovery. Existing formal models say which executions are possible, not how likely they are or how long they take.

AsInst is a probabilistic, resource-aware semantics for asynchronous choreographies with out-of-order execution. Programs are interpreted as temporal Bayesian networks that model both the values produced at runtime and the times they become available. The authors prove this central semantics correctly captures a corresponding futures-style network semantics. With timing and probability inside the model, designers can ask quantitative questions about protocol designs before deploying them.
arxiv-2606-13620:
Jost studies a measurement trade-off in the modelling of lipid metabolism in this 2026 arXiv paper. Lipids, the fats central to cell membranes and energy storage, are tracked with mass spectrometry, which destroys the sample it measures. A recently proposed strategy attaches multiple labels to lipid molecules, extracting time-course data from a single destructive measurement. Each extra label multiplies the model's computing cost, creating a basic tension between information content and analysis cost. Jost asks how many labels a model should include.

Using synthetic data from a five-label experiment, he measures how using fewer labels affects parameter accuracy, path recovery, and computing time. Using three of the five labels emerges as a practical balance between lab feasibility, inferential power, and tractability. An application to triglyceride cycling in liver cells shows the reduced model still recovers the biology. The lesson generalises to other label-based metabolic studies.
arxiv-2606-14620:
Asaria, Salomone, and Gandhi measure how a diffusion language model actually writes text in a 2026 arXiv paper. Diffusion models are marketed as parallel decoders that produce many tokens at once, unlike autoregressive models writing left to right. The team instrumented DiffusionGemma, a twenty-six-billion-parameter open model, recording which positions its sampler commits, when, and with what confidence.

Across a probe suite of six hundred eighty-six prompts in six regimes, decoding was neither parallel nor block-sequential. A partial left-to-right bias appeared, weak token by token and stronger when viewed coarsely, so the apparent block size was an artifact of the measuring scale. Tokens committed in large simultaneous batches in a short late burst, and structured JSON came out in nearly arbitrary order. Commit confidence tracked correctness on math reasoning but carried no signal on factual recall.
arxiv-2606-14820:
Yuxuan Chen and co-authors test whether audio models truly encode sound direction cues in a 2026 arXiv paper. Spatial audio models score well on localization tasks. But high scores may not mean the model uses the tiny timing gaps between the two ears. Those gaps, called interaural phase, help humans locate sound. The team built a hearing-based benchmark from the binaural masking level difference. That is the boost a tone gets when the two ears hear it out of phase.

They tested nine frozen audio models of three kinds. Four one-ear control models scored zero, as expected. Two general two-ear models showed almost no phase sense. Dedicated spatial models did much better, though below the ceiling. Careful ablations showed the general models lean on interference textures, not true phase math. Speech success came from broad loudness envelopes.
arxiv-2606-14920:
Hamilton and co-authors study the emotions policing student AI use in a 2026 arXiv paper. Computing students now use AI tools widely. Norms around that use are unsettled. The authors ask how shame and guilt shape whether students show or hide their use. They read these emotions as social signals that regulate behavior.

Nineteen computing students were interviewed. Students described hiding their AI use and disclosing it only selectively. They shamed themselves, their peers, and even faculty for using AI. Shame and guilt coexisted with continued use rather than stopping it. That pairing bred cycles of reduced agency and moral tension. Students felt their AI use clashed with identities as competent, hardworking, or ethical. Some used addiction language for their habits. The authors urge classroom practices that support open discussion and responsible use.
arxiv-2606-15420:
Che and coauthor introduce Constitutional Value Potentials in a 2026 machine learning paper, a way to read a language model's internal priorities. A constitution lists the values a model should follow, but behavior alone cannot show which value wins when two collide, say helpfulness against harmlessness. The authors learn, for each value, a scalar potential from the model's hidden state, trained on an independent judge's verdict about which value the model's answer preserved.

The difference between two potentials forms a priority margin, and a monitor built on it predicts constitution violations on held-out conflicts with high accuracy across three model sizes. The signal appears as the answer begins, early enough to flag attacks that merely reword a request. Pushing activations along a value direction also shifts the model's judged trade-offs the intended way. Internal margins like these give safety teams a gauge that output checks alone cannot provide.
arxiv-2606-15520:
Ericson revisits his own 1986 Icon software package in 2026, rebuilding its Euclidean domain algorithms as a formalization in the Lean 4 proof assistant. The original package, a New York University technical report, implemented procedures from Lipson's algebra catalog over integers, rationals, modular rings, polynomials, and power series. Icon lacked typeclasses, so the package faked generic arithmetic with a custom runtime dispatch trick.

The port separates proved mathematics, computable mirrors for testing, and formatting that reproduces the 1986 benchmark output line for line. All fourteen application algorithms from the report are defined and typecheck with no sorry placeholders left. Only some results, chiefly integer gcd and the extended Euclidean algorithm, carry machine-checked proofs in Mathlib. The rest are regression-trusted, meaning they are checked against the old output rather than proved. Ericson states that boundary plainly, and lists the coherence proofs still owed between the proved and computable layers.
arxiv-2606-15820:
Villié and colleagues model coherent structures in flow through a narrowed vessel in 2026, asking how far linear theory explains a transitional turbulent flow. Behind a stenosis, wall shear stress swings drive disease progression and plaque rupture risk. Working from a large-eddy simulation at Reynolds number 4000, the team applies stability and resolvent analysis.

Global stability analysis finds an unstable, sinuous stationary mode tied to Coanda-type wall attachment, dominant at low frequencies. At intermediate frequencies a second growth region appears in the shear layer, with axisymmetric fluctuations strongest, contrary to lower-Reynolds studies. The optimal resolvent response aligns strongly with the leading SPOD mode. Exploiting the low-rank structure, they reconstruct turbulent kinetic energy and wall stress from that one mode. Behind the stenosis, axisymmetric fluctuations dominate the wall stress, with one mode capturing over half of it. Linear mechanisms, it turns out, organise much of this complex flow.
arxiv-2606-16220:
Tursun and colleagues survey spectral lines in 2026 from W33, one of the richest molecular line sources in the galaxy. At 2.4 kiloparsecs away, this star-forming region suits centimeter line searches. The team scans the 18 to 26 gigahertz range, the 1.3 centimeter band.

The survey identifies 44 radio recombination lines and 24 molecular lines, excluding the main ammonia isotopolog. The recombination lines come from ionized gas in W33 Main. Intensity ratios between line pairs match expectations under local thermodynamic equilibrium. The helium-to-hydrogen share is 10.7 percent, plus or minus 1.8, consistent with expectations. Helium lines nevertheless show broader widths than hydrogen, by a few kilometers per second. That gap hints the two gases have slightly different spatial distributions. These lines belong to nine species, including methanol and cyanoacetylene.
arxiv-2606-16720:
Böttger and colleagues measure how web tracking moved into the first party in a 2026 privacy study. Blocking third-party trackers once worked well, so trackers shifted their code into the visited site's own context or onto its server. Those first-party and server-side methods hide data flows from the usual browser tools, and their true scale was unclear.

The team built a provider-independent detection method and scanned top websites at large scale. More than half of the analyzed sites now use first-party or server-side tracking techniques. Grouping scripts by similarity and mapping their links shows a dense ecosystem dominated by major vendors, with Google at the center. Standard filter lists prove largely ineffective against this style of tracking. The authors propose new filter rules aimed at first-party requests, and those rules block substantially more tracking requests than traditional lists in their tests.
arxiv-2606-16820:
Liang and colleagues develop an algorithm for a hard class of optimization problems in a 2026 paper. The problems ask for the best decision while some variables must satisfy complementarity, meaning pairs of quantities where at least one must be zero, inside second-order cones. Standard optimality theory breaks down at every feasible point of such problems, so off-the-shelf solvers lack guarantees.

The authors adapt the augmented Lagrangian method, which handles constraints through penalty terms folded into the objective and is prized for matrix-free implementation. They tailor it to the cone complementarity setting and prove what it delivers. When penalty parameters or the augmented function stay bounded, the iterates converge to feasible points. Under an added nondegeneracy condition, they converge to K-stationary points, a basic optimality notion for this problem class. Numerical tests, including high-dimensional cases, show the method works in practice.
arxiv-2606-17120:
Ersoy and Wiesner explain grokking as escape from a trap in a 2026 paper on neural network training. Grokking is the sudden jump to good generalization long after a network seems stuck overfitting. Why the delay, and why so abrupt?

Deep networks undergo first-order phase transitions as weight-decay strength varies, each unlocking a new feature. Below a critical strength, metastable states coexist, separated by energy barriers. A trapped model sits in a low-accuracy state until gradient noise knocks it over the barrier. In deep linear networks, engineered trapping reproduces grokking-like delays across two orders of magnitude in escape time. Escape times obey Arrhenius scaling, the classic physics law for noise-activated barrier crossing. The number of metastable states matches the number of learnable features. Evidence suggests the same mechanism runs in nonlinear networks, tying a machine learning mystery to established statistical physics.
arxiv-2606-17220:
Tao and colleagues present a 2026 arXiv paper on legal case retrieval. A retrieval system must find past cases that match a dispute's facts and statutes. Dense neural methods have improved, yet the lexical method BM25 stays a strong baseline. Legal language rewards precise word matching, which suits BM25 well.

Instead of replacing BM25, the authors let a language-model agent improve its queries. The agent writes rewriting rules, tests rule sets, and drops rules that fail. No model parameters are trained in the process. On the Chinese LeCaRD-v2 benchmark, the method beat baselines that did not evolve. Those baselines included human-designed rules and greedy rule selection, with the largest gains under a high-capacity core model.
arxiv-2606-17320:
Andreev and colleagues, reporting for the NA64 experiment at CERN, present a 2026 arXiv paper setting tighter limits on a hypothetical new particle, a Z prime boson tied to the baryon-minus-lepton symmetry. Such extensions of the Standard Model link the origin of neutrino masses to possible dark matter candidates. The boson would couple directly to ordinary fermions and could be made when an electron beam strikes a fixed target in the experiment.

The analysis uses the full electron-beam data set gathered from 2016 to 2022, roughly three times the statistics of earlier NA64 work. A resonant production channel boosts sensitivity in one part of the mass range the team probes. For the unbroken symmetry case, the new bounds beat those from dedicated neutrino-scattering experiments at sub-GeV masses. Limits for scenarios where the boson decays invisibly into dark matter are also derived.
arxiv-2606-17420:
Zhang and colleagues present a 2026 arXiv paper on harmonising tau PET brain scans across sites, tracers, and scanners for Alzheimer's disease research. Such scans track disease progression, but site effects add non-biological shifts that inflate biomarker variance and can masquerade as biology. The danger grows when the source and target cohorts differ in subgroup mix, since careless harmonisation can erase real signal tied to tau status while chasing scanner differences between the sites.

Their model learns a direct stochastic transport between source and target distributions, guided by entropy-regularised optimal transport rather than a noise prior. A subgroup-aware reweighting, built from a Feynman-Kac scheme, keeps the transport biologically consistent without changing the solver. A spherical network works vertex by vertex on cortical surface maps. Against three rival methods, alignment, subgroup matching, and disease classification all improved.
arxiv-2606-17920:
Aprile and colleagues in the XENONnT collaboration report precision measurements of two lead isotopes' beta decays, in a 2026 paper. XENONnT is a dark matter detector filled with liquid xenon, and radon calibration data let the team watch lead-212 and lead-214 nuclei decay inside it. Knowing exactly how often each isotope decays straight to its ground state matters for modeling the detector's background.

The measurements describe the calibration data accurately with their models. For lead-212 they confirm the literature branching ratios and cut the uncertainty on the ground-state share by a factor of three. The lead-214 ground-state value also agrees well with prior results. Beyond the numbers, the study shows that quiet, low-background xenon detectors double as fine tools for precision nuclear physics.
arxiv-2606-18020:
Alfonsi and colleagues solve exactly how particles cluster on a tiny ring at equilibrium, in a 2026 statistical physics paper. Their model is a one-dimensional lattice gas wrapped into a ring, a stand-in for molecules binding along small circular substrates. Neighbors can attract, making binding cooperative, or repel, making it anticooperative, and the ring exchanges particles with a reservoir.

From exact correlation functions the authors derive finite-size formulas for mean occupancy, the number of domain walls, and the number of clusters of each size, plus two forms of the cluster-size distribution. The results expose strong finite-size and parity effects, sharpest near half filling in small rings. To reach larger lattices without enumerating every microstate, they add a combinatorial scheme that sorts configurations by cluster counts and sizes, shrinking the state space that must be handled.
arxiv-2606-18120:
Rashidi shows that a routine templating choice silently decides how exposed a language model app is to forged chat roles, in a 2026 security paper. Many apps build prompts with Handlebars, the default template format in Microsoft Semantic Kernel. Its double-brace form escapes HTML in inserted values, while the triple-brace form inserts them raw, a choice documented as being about web safety alone.

The catch is what escaping actually rewrites. It neutralizes role delimiters built from angle brackets. It leaves delimiters built from square brackets, colons, or Markdown hashes fully intact. So three of seven common chat formats stay exposed either way. Nearly six thousand trials across four commercial models confirm the mechanism. The oldest model tested obeyed hijack instructions in almost all raw trials. Escaping helped only where the delimiter was angle-based and the model had room to refuse.
arxiv-2606-18520:
Gokhale and colleagues study how small a geometric embedding can be while encoding the ancestor structure of a hierarchy, in a 2026 theoretical computer science paper. Embeddings power modern retrieval, and for tree-like data relevance means reachability in a directed graph, but guarantees for such embeddings degraded on deep hierarchies, sometimes needing as many dimensions as nodes.

They prove that any directed tree admits a reachability embedding in three dimensions, whatever its size or depth. For graphs of treewidth t, they construct embeddings whose dimension grows only modestly with the graph. They complement these with lower bounds showing that general directed graphs really can require dimension as large as their size, and that their treewidth bound is nearly tight. Bounds based on the number of cross edges round out the picture. Tests confirm the embeddings achieve much smaller dimensions than earlier guaranteed methods at high recall.
arxiv-2606-18920:
Fukshansky and colleagues survey structured lattices in 2026. A lattice is a regular grid of points in space, and structured ones are built from number fields and like ideas. Well-rounded lattices get close focus. They link to dense sphere packing and to old conjectures by Minkowski and Woods. The survey starts with basic theory and moves to new builds with extra symmetry.

Later parts turn to uses in secure codes and in wireless links. The authors review learning-with-errors problems in plain, ring, and polynomial forms. They note where results on one form carry to another, and where hardness is still in doubt. Open tasks include near-best packings in high dimensions and the hardness of short-vector problems. The point is clear. Added structure can bring speed and small size, but it must be checked with care so that security does not suffer.
arxiv-2606-19220:
Magalhães and colleagues introduce XGBoost-Forget in 2026, a machine unlearning method for the XGBoost model on network intrusion data. Unlearning removes specific data points from a trained model without full retraining, a need driven by privacy and data correction duties. Most unlearning research targets deep learning on images. Intrusion detection instead relies on tabular data, where gradient-boosted trees like XGBoost are a workhorse and unlearning tools are scarce.

The approach is evaluated on two tabular intrusion datasets covering internet-of-things and general network traffic. Metrics cover predictive performance, unlearning speed, and forgetting quality. XGBoost-Forget keeps performance close to the original model while unlearning far faster than retraining from scratch. That balance matters for security operations, where a poisoned or withdrawn record must be removed quickly without degrading detection. The work shows practical unlearning is feasible for the tabular models that security teams actually deploy daily.
arxiv-2606-19520:
Bertrand Travacca releases ev-flow in 2026, an open tool that builds fake but realistic electric vehicle charging records. Grid planners need large sets of single-vehicle charging profiles to test future demand. Real charging logs are scarce and private, and older generators lean on non-U.S. travel surveys.

ev-flow grounds its output in 2017 National Household Travel Survey records and regional sales mixes for eight U.S. regions. A nine-stage pipeline turns survey days into year-long travel calendars for matched donor drivers. Winter cold adds an energy uplift, and plug-in start times follow a published sixteen-part Gaussian mixture model. A state-of-charge ledger tracks each battery, with a gasoline range term for plug-in hybrids. Every run repeats exactly from one master seed. Checks on the Bay Area profile pass eleven tests, with all gaps explained from past studies.
arxiv-2606-19820:
John Bamberg and Jake Rigg extend the clique adjacency polynomial to all finite graphs in 2026. A clique is a set of vertices joined pairwise; the clique number caps its size. Soicher's polynomial bounded clique numbers for edge-regular graphs alone.

Key parameters are rewritten through average vertex degree and average edge degree over candidate cliques. A generalised bound follows, plus a clique existence polynomial that drops an auxiliary variable. Computation becomes easier as a result. Classical spectral and linear programming bounds from Delsarte, Hoffman, and Haemers set the bar. The generalised method beats those bounds for several graph families. Infinite families from projective geometry show gains over the Delsarte bound in particular. Feasible parameter region techniques make the method practical for messy, unstructured graphs too.
arxiv-2606-19920:
Hunter Kuperman, Minchan Jung, Rahul Ghosh, and Evangelos Theodorou present Deep Coordinator in 2026, a learned tuner for distributed robot solvers. Distributed optimization scales well for multi-agent problems, yet solvers such as ADMM-DDP need hand-tuned penalty settings for each new task. Deep Coordinator unrolls a fixed number of solver rounds into a network that adjusts those penalties while solving, reacting to how the optimizer is performing.

Training such a tuner with labels can collapse to useless outputs, so the team trains it without supervision instead. On simulated fleets of cars and quadrotors, trajectories match the quality of conventional solvers while running six to nine times faster. The speedups persist on systems up to eight times larger than those seen in training. Learned self-tuning could make distributed planning practical for robot fleets that change size and task.
arxiv-2606-20520:
Jun He and Deying Yu design a broker that keeps the power to change production systems out of autonomous agents' hands. Their 2026 paper argues that agents which reason in non-deterministic ways should not directly mutate cloud, deployment, and data systems. Access control says who an agent is; assurance layers vouch for proposed actions; neither enforces anything at the moment of change.

The Sovereign Execution Broker sits at that moment. It takes certificates from a Sovereign Assurance Boundary and checks that each requested change matches the certified contract, its validity window, and its policy and revocation epochs. Agents propose; the broker alone disposes, and only within the bounds on the certificate. Control planes for agents gain a hard gate, so a hallucinating agent cannot improvise its way into production.
arxiv-2606-20620:
Arina Oberoi develops a viscosity framework for stable image reconstruction in a solo 2026 paper rooted in scale-space theory. Viscosity solutions are a weak form of solution for equations that may not have smooth answers. Comparison rules yield uniqueness and contraction in the supremum norm, meaning the largest error cannot grow.

Oberoi then motivates a hybrid method: a learned inverse map followed by diffusion, a smoothing step guided by the equation. That diffusion step is non-expansive, which supports stability. On a scan task classifying mesothelioma, a cancer linked to asbestos, the method reaches a score of 0.875 with little change across training runs. A baseline swings from 0.49 to 0.80 with no clear pattern. The contrast matches the steady role the theory predicts
arxiv-2606-21020:
Geon Choi and seven colleagues introduce CheXpercept in 2026, a benchmark for expert-level lesion perception in chest X-rays by vision-language models. Model evaluation for chest imaging has mostly tested disease presence alone. That does not verify whether a model sees lesions as a radiologist does. Their benchmark mirrors a radiologist's workflow in sequence: coarse detection, fine contour work, and attribute extraction.

The dataset is built by a semi-automated pipeline with review by six medical experts. It holds over ten thousand question items from thousands of chest X-rays. Seven critical lung and heart lesions are covered. Fourteen general and medical models are benchmarked. Models do adequately only at the coarse level. Accuracy falls sharply on deeper visual tasks. Benchmarks that test perception depth can expose clinical risk that a single disease label hides, because treatment depends on where and what a lesion is.
arxiv-2606-21420:
Malhotra and ten colleagues present a catalogue in 2026 of stars that emit at the hydrogen-alpha line, mined from the Gaia space mission's low-resolution spectra. Gaia's third data release offers spectra for over 219 million sources, and H-alpha emission flags active and unusual stars. The team measured the line's equivalent width for every source and kept 556,100 candidates showing an emission-like feature.

Most candidates proved false: ninety-five percent are cool M-type stars whose molecular bands fake an emission peak. A semi-supervised classifier plus manual labeling removed the impostors, leaving 28,394 genuine emitters. Be-like stars dominate, with active M dwarfs, Herbig stars, quasars, Wolf-Rayet stars, and cataclysmic variables also present. Widths and classifications agree with higher-resolution studies, and ground-based follow-up supports the catalogue.
arxiv-2606-21720:
Theophilus Ansah-Narh, Nia Imara, Benedicta Woode, and Emmanuel Proven Adzri treat a radio telescope's beam as a signal-processing problem in 2026. Ghana's 32-meter GRAO antenna suffers residual sidelobes, structural diffraction, and cross-polarization leakage that limit high-dynamic-range and polarization-sensitive observing. Their fix reframes beam shaping as finite-impulse-response filtering, using the match between angular displacement and spatial frequency.

Classical FIR design methods, window-based and Parks-McClellan, are adapted to run directly on simulated electromagnetic Jones fields. Applied to GRAO's 5 GHz beam model, the filtering cuts near-in sidelobe ripple, smooths the beam, and pushes cross-polar leakage below minus 30 dB at boresight. Calibration stability and polarimetric precision improve with it. The method needs no hardware changes and extends to other single dishes and phased arrays, as a digital complement to optical tuning.
arxiv-2606-22120:
Ayaz and colleagues tackle, in 2026, the inverse problem of measuring surface elastic parameters in soft solids. Surface tension and surface shear stiffness shape behaviour at small scales there, but resist direct measurement. Bulk behaviour and nonlinearity tangle the signal, so older identification methods built on idealized boundary conditions perform poorly. The authors replace the formula-based forward model with a data-driven model trained on finite element simulations under realistic constraints.

A neural network learns the force-displacement response of a cylindrical specimen across wide ranges of surface tension and shear modulus. A genetic algorithm then searches that surrogate for the set matching a given response, including responses corrupted with five percent noise. Across all tested sets, identified values erred by less than eight percent. Repeated noisy trials produced narrow confidence intervals, showing robustness. The framework offers an efficient alternative for realistic lab setups.
arxiv-2606-22220:
Wang and colleagues introduce MultiMem in 2026, the first metric for measuring memorization in multimodal contrastive learning. These models learn by aligning data across modalities such as text, image, video, and audio. Such memorization helps on rare samples but also retains noise and outliers, hurting results on new data.

Through careful analysis with MultiMem, the authors rank what drives memorization. Cross-modal semantic misalignment matters most among the factors studied. Text is the dominant modality driving it, followed by video, then image, then audio. Targeted tweaks across all modalities reduce it, as the new metric shows. They also improve model performance. The work gives the field its first framework for measuring and reducing harmful data retention in such models.
arxiv-2606-22620:
Kaibalyapati Mishra studies the wage effects of India's college expansion in this 2026 economics paper. The post-liberalisation expansion was meant to widen degree access for historically excluded groups, above all Scheduled Caste and Scheduled Tribe workers. Mishra asks whether those workers benefited, or paid for the expansion instead.

The study merges eight rounds of national employment surveys from 1987 to 2011. It adds a district-level measure of expansion intensity across ninety-one districts in six states. The return to a degree stays large throughout. Yet for post-2004 graduates in high-expansion districts, the premium erodes. Non-SC/ST graduates earn about nine percent less than peers in low-expansion districts. SC/ST graduates face a further penalty of about a third. That caste gap is absent before the expansion and emerges only afterwards. Mishra reads this as credential devaluation hurting the disadvantaged most, and flags the design's limits.
arxiv-2606-23020:
Gentian Zavalani settles one case of the Bojanov-Naidenov problem in a 2026 approximation theory paper. The problem asks which bounded polynomial of a given degree can have the largest derivatives on an interval. Chebyshev polynomials, a famous oscillating family, are the usual extremal suspects. Zavalani studies quartics, polynomials of degree at most four, and their second derivatives. The candidate champion is the fourth Chebyshev polynomial, scaled to stay within one in absolute value on the interval from minus one to one.

Zavalani proves a tail estimate comparing the second derivative of any such quartic against the champion's. The estimate implies the champion wins for every increasing convex measure of derivative size. When the measure is strictly increasing, equality holds only for the champion or its negative. The proof stays elementary and finite. Interpolation at five special points reduces everything to checking thirty-two sign patterns.
arxiv-2606-23120:
Shichang Meng and colleagues adapt time-series models to new domains without touching the source data in a 2026 machine learning paper. Source-free adaptation starts from a trained model and unlabeled target data only. Time signals drift in two ways. Their patterns shift over time, and their frequency makeup shifts too, a spectral change earlier methods mostly ignored. The team's method, SAFA, aligns both the time behavior and the spectrum of target signals with what the source model expects.

Meng and colleagues first model the source domain at several scales, capturing time links and frequency traits together. A trainable module then adjusts phase and amplitude for target signals in the frequency domain, nudging them toward the source distribution. Experiments on several benchmark datasets show the method adapts effectively and robustly across settings.
arxiv-2606-23220:
Mateo Cámara and colleagues build a landmark database of the English lexicon by synthesizing speech in a 2026 paper. Acoustic landmark theory views speech as organized around sharp acoustic events caused by gestures of the vocal tract, like closures and releases of the mouth. Studying those landmarks has been held back by a lack of large, cleanly labeled datasets. The team flips the problem. Instead of labeling recorded speech, they generate speech from landmark patterns via the Pink Trombone, a physical vocal tract synthesizer.

Cámara and colleagues render the English lexicon in two adult voice setups, one male and one female. Because they control the gestures directly, landmark labels land at the exact times of the physical events. Over two hundred thousand synthesized words carry time-aligned annotations. The corpus supports lexicon-wide statistics on landmark patterns and training of automatic landmark detectors.
arxiv-2606-23320:
Anton Baychkov, Markus Brill, and Markus Utke mix voting rules for participatory budgeting in a 2026 social choice paper. Participatory budgeting lets citizens vote on which public projects get funded from a fixed pot. Single rules chase single goals: a greedy rule maximizes total welfare, while the Method of Equal Shares pursues proportional representation. Real decisions often want both goals at once. Inspired by mixed-member parliamentary systems, the authors define mixed rules. Two or more rules run in sequence, each spending a set fraction of the budget.

Baychkov and colleagues build a theoretical framework for such mixtures and adapt existing rules to it. They focus on adjusting the Equal Shares stage to repair representation imbalances left by earlier rules. One adjustment provably improves on a natural proportionality baseline. Extensive tests on real elections complement the theory.
arxiv-2606-23420:
Bruno Machado and colleagues give flow matching robot policies a smarter starting point in a 2026 paper. Flow matching has become a standard way to clone behavior for robot manipulation. The policy learns to turn a simple source distribution into real actions. Standard versions always start from the same fixed Gaussian source. Robot action spaces are fragmented and uneven, though, so that blind start forces the model to learn tangled fields. Their framework, LAFM, replaces the single source with a library of learned priors. A latent action model reads the scene and picks the prior that fits.

Machado and colleagues report clear gains from the informed start. Task success rose by about twenty-three percent in real-world robot deployments. On the LIBERO-90 benchmark it rose by about ten percent. The method also beat massively pretrained rivals in their comparisons.
arxiv-2606-23620:
Das, Jaikumar, Karekkat, and Mandal model neutron stars that have soaked up dark matter while staying hot inside, in a 2026 paper on astrophysics. Neutron stars are the dense remnants of dead massive stars, and they can capture dark matter particles as they move through the galaxy. Earlier work on cold stars found that gathered dark matter raises the central density. This study asks whether the effect survives in a hot star.

The team builds an equation of state, the rule linking pressure and density, with matching temperature and dark matter profiles for heavy fermionic dark matter. The density enhancement proves robust, though visible effects need a fairly massive star. Heat and dark matter push the star's properties in opposite directions. Their contest sets where conformality, a sign of matter behaving scale freely, begins near the core.
arxiv-2606-23720:
Hipler, Leucker, and Rodler unify two monitoring tasks, detecting failures and finding their causes, inside one specification language, in a 2026 paper on formal methods. Runtime verification watches a running system for deviations from its specified behavior. Model based diagnosis then works out which components must be faulty to explain those deviations. Used separately, the two steps lose information and timing, because diagnosis starts after monitoring without its full record.

The framework builds both parts on Lola, a stream based language that transforms input streams into output streams through equations. System descriptions become special streams that implicitly represent all possible diagnoses for the observed behavior. Constraints maintained in Lola combine with a satisfiability solver plus standard diagnosis algorithms, yielding minimal diagnoses while the system runs. A multi instant theory extends the method to faults that persist over time, and the approach handles reasoning under uncertainty.
arxiv-2606-23820:
Yang and colleagues explain how a sulfur bearing molecule recently spotted in cool giant exoplanets gets made, in a 2026 paper on exoplanet atmospheres. Webb observations have found carbon disulfide in several temperate gas giants, but the chemistry behind it was unclear. The team takes TOI-6894 b, where the molecule was reported, as a test case. Photochemical models follow how starlight driven reactions build and destroy the molecule.

The models show carbon disulfide forming through coupled heat driven and light driven chemistry. Methane supplies the carbon and hydrogen sulfide the sulfur. Its abundance peaks in temperate to warm atmospheres, around five hundred to seven hundred kelvin, fading for colder and hotter planets. That matches the reported detections and non detections.
arxiv-2606-23920:
Soiffer, Squires, Guan, Hartford, and Ravikumar argue that a popular hope for generative AI fails badly for standard diffusion models. The hope is composing new outputs by combining conditions never seen together. Their 2026 paper treats machine learning. The task trains a model on some condition combinations and asks for others, such as the joint effect of two drugs tested only separately. Math at the distribution level says the target can be built by combining the sources geometrically. The authors conjecture that no inference time technique can do this efficiently in certain well motivated settings.

Theory guided arguments and experiments on synthetic and realistic data support the conjecture. Correction methods cut one kind of error, yet score error hits far harder when the target lies outside the training combinations. Small score errors tolerable in distribution become ruinous out of it. The task needs a different approach, not better inference patches.
arxiv-2606-24220:
Nersisyan builds links inside four-dimensional spaces that are split one way yet stay joined smoothly. Mazur manifolds are contractible four-dimensional building blocks. They anchor the study of exotic smooth structures: shapes that look plain yet are smoothly strange. Writing alone in 2026, Nersisyan explores links, sets of surfaces, inside such manifolds and simple ambient spaces.

Non-split two-component links are constructed inside the four-sphere, their components cannot be pulled apart smoothly. Moved into connected sums of complex projective planes, the links become split topologically. Yet they remain non-split smoothly, a gap only dimension four makes possible. Results include exotic pairs of simply connected, definite four-manifolds with boundary, and exotic embeddings of various Mazur manifolds inside the four-sphere. Nersisyan's constructions add concrete, Kirby-calculus-friendly examples to a field where exotic effects are often proved to exist without ever being drawn.
arxiv-2606-24320:
Clark and colleagues at Zyphra present ZONOS2, a text-to-speech model built for naturalness, prosody, and voice cloning fidelity. The 2026 technical report scales its predecessor sharply. An eight-billion-parameter mixture-of-experts backbone keeps only a fraction of parameters active per token. That improves latency and throughput. Training data expands from hundreds of thousands of hours to several million hours, through a new processing pipeline.

Simplified post-training and conditioning recipes are credited for gains in naturalness and cloning fidelity. Evaluation covers synthesis quality, speaker similarity, and word error rate. It also covers ZTTS1-Eval, a new benchmark released alongside the model. ZONOS2 holds its own against state-of-the-art systems, while keeping good streaming latency. Zyphra releases the weights and inference code under an Apache 2.0 licence.
arxiv-2606-24420: This paper builds a multi-signal confidence engine for LLM-based document field extraction, beyond logprobs. The building builds. Their engine is multi-signal confidence. The extraction is LLM-based document field. It is AI. The building is beyond logprobs.
arxiv-2606-24520:
Yan Gao, Luxian Yang, and Jinsong Zeng classify a family of fractals from complex dynamics. Their objects are the Julia sets of McMullen maps. A Julia set records which starting points stay bounded when a formula is applied again and again. In this family the sets take carpet, necklace, and cluster shapes. The authors ask when two such sets can be reshaped into each other by a quasisymmetric map, one with controlled distortion.

Gao and colleagues settle the question for the postcritically finite maps, those whose critical points end in repeating cycles. They give a complete quasisymmetric classification of these sets. They also prove each set has only the symmetries forced by the map itself. Its symmetry group is exactly the finite dihedral group those symmetries generate. The result proves rigidity for every topological class in the family. It also gives the first rigid examples known in each class.
arxiv-2606-24820:
Hovhannes Tamoyan and four colleagues present SHERLOC, a framework that helps code repair agents find faults before editing. Language model agents solving repository level tasks spend about half their interaction budget just locating the bug. Existing localisation tools are graded as file retrieval, returning locations without the diagnostic context that a repair agent needs. SHERLOC pairs a reasoning model with compact repository tools and a self recovery mechanism.

The name expands to Structured Hypothesis driven Exploration and Reasoning for Localization. On SWE-Bench Lite it reaches 84 percent top one localisation accuracy. On SWE-Bench Verified its top one recall is about 81 percent. At roughly thirty billion parameters it matches or beats rival agentic methods.
