europmc-pmc2124920: A medical paper with a bulkhead suture of the intestine. The intestinal seam. This article preserves that surgery. The paper lived through the years. It awaits future readers. Its place in history is secure. Time has kept the file intact through the years.
europmc-pmc2125120: A medical paper with studies upon experimental pneumonia in rabbits, studies in immunity. The rabbit pneumonia's defense. This article preserves that immunology. Such papers rarely see the light of day. The file is now open to the public.
europmc-pmc2131120: A medical paper on the effect of antiserum against the soluble toxic substance of Bacillus coli. The E. coli antiserum. This article preserves that immunology. The archive keeps the paper open to all. Its pages add to the record of the past.
europmc-pmc2140420: Stomachs need acid to digest protein, and this paper measured exactly how hydrogen ion concentration governs the process. The researchers tested digestion across pH levels. The acidic breakdown, quantified. The article preserves that biochemistry research.
europmc-pmc2140720: Glowing bacteria shine brighter or dimmer with the heat, and this second study tracked temperature's effect on their light. The researchers warmed and cooled the cultures. The luminous intensity, charted. The article preserves that bacteriology research.
europmc-pmc2140820: A biology paper on the metabolism of tumors in the body. The cancers' fuel. This article preserves that oncology. Its contents inform the historical record. The library keeps the document safe. Writers of history may cite it later.
europmc-pmc2323620:
Husain and Nachev reviewed the parietal cortex in 2007, a brain region at the top and back of the head. Standard theory split brain processing into two streams, one for space and action and one for objects. Damage to the right lower parietal lobe often causes spatial neglect, where patients ignore one side of space.

The authors argued that this simple split does not fit the lower parietal lobe. They summed up brain scans and lesion studies showing plainly non-spatial jobs for this region. Those jobs include holding attention over time and spotting key events in a stream of events. Upper parietal zones do handle space and guide action. Lower zones, they concluded, do something that fits neither classic stream.
europmc-pmc2394820:
Terwilliger and colleagues described an automated structure-building wizard in 2008. In X-ray crystallography, scientists build an atomic model into an electron-density map, a cloud showing where atoms sit. They then refine the model, use it to sharpen the map, and rebuild, cycling many times.

The PHENIX AutoBuild wizard runs that whole cycle on its own. It belongs to the PHENIX software project for crystallography. The wizard works from starting phase information obtained by any of the standard routes: comparing similar crystals, using heavy-atom signals, or molecular replacement with a known structure. The authors noted that rival automated tools still struggled at low resolution and at finishing partial models. AutoBuild was built as a second-generation answer to those gaps, aiming at complete, accurate models with little manual work.
europmc-pmc2467420:
Kramer and colleagues, writing for the Society for Cardiovascular Magnetic Resonance Board of Trustees Task Force on Standardized Protocols, set standard scanning protocols for heart MRI in 2008. Cardiac magnetic resonance can measure heart size, blood flow, and scar tissue, but each centre scanned differently, making results hard to compare.

The document lays out shared modules: safety and stress-test equipment, left and right heart function, contrast dye dosing, and first-pass perfusion, which tracks dye through heart muscle. It then gives disease-specific protocols. For blocked-artery disease these cover fresh heart attacks, long-standing damage and viability checks, and two drug stress methods. Further sections cover vessel imaging of the limbs and chest, abnormal coronary arteries, and lung vein checks. Valve disease, heart muscle diseases, congenital defects, and heart masses each get their own protocol.
europmc-pmc2467520:
Hooft, Straver, and Spek presented a statistical method for pinning down a molecule's absolute structure in 2008. Crystallographers can often solve a molecule's shape but not its handedness: which mirror-image form it takes. Handedness matters because the two forms of a drug can act very differently in the body.

Their approach uses Bijvoet differences, tiny intensity gaps between paired X-ray reflections that carry the handedness signal. Rather than forcing a yes-or-no call, they apply Bayesian statistics in a maximum-likelihood framework. That yields a probability for each possible structure, including the standard Flack parameter used to report the answer. The method was aimed at biologically active molecules, where weak signals are common. A probability statement, they argued, is more honest than the sharp verdicts older methods gave on thin evidence.
europmc-pmc2518220:
Curia, Longo, Biagini, Jones, and Avoli reviewed in 2008 the pilocarpine model, a standard animal model of temporal lobe epilepsy. In this model, injecting rodents with the drug pilocarpine triggers a long seizure episode. A quiet latent period follows. Finally, spontaneous recurring seizures begin. That sequence mirrors the human disease, which often follows an early injury and involves scarring in the hippocampus, a brain area central to memory.

The authors compared methods across many laboratories, since results shift with rodent species, strain, sex, age, dose, and drug combinations. They weighed death rates, timing of the first spontaneous seizures, neuron damage, and how brain networks rewired under each protocol. They conclude the model stays valuable for studying how epilepsy develops, especially if standardised to cut deaths and reduce variation.
europmc-pmc2527820:
Beckermann and colleagues asked in 2008 whether stem cells from bone marrow help pancreatic tumours grow their blood supply. These mesenchymal stem cells travel through the blood and settle in wounds and tumours, but why tumours attract them was unclear. The team tracked the cells in dishes and in mice carrying human pancreatic tumours.

The stem cells moved toward growth signals the tumours release, including PDGF and VEGF, and blocking drugs could stop that migration. Within hours they entered tumour-like spheres grown in the laboratory. Labelled cells injected into mice gathered in the tumours and interacted with vessel walls. Crucially, the cells released VEGF themselves, and tumours given them grew denser blood vessel networks. Silencing VEGF in the stem cells removed that boost.
europmc-pmc2535620:
Kan and colleagues studied daily deaths in Shanghai from 2001 to 2004 to see who is most harmed by dirty air. Four pollutants were tracked: fine particles, sulfur dioxide, nitrogen dioxide, and ozone. The team asked whether season, sex, age, and schooling changed how strongly pollution tracked with mortality across the city's four years of daily records.

All four pollutants were linked to deaths from all causes and from heart and lung disease. A standard rise in particle levels, for example, came with a 0.25 percent increase in daily mortality, and the other gases showed larger effects. Pollution bit harder in the cool season than the warm one. Women, older people, and residents with little schooling proved more vulnerable than others facing the same air.
europmc-pmc2565420:
Groenewegen reviewed the basal ganglia and motor control in this 2003 paper. The basal ganglia are a set of deep brain structures, including the striatum, pallidum, substantia nigra, and subthalamic nucleus. They connect with the cortex and thalamus in a series of parallel loops that stay largely separate from one another.

Those loops serve not only movement but also thinking and emotion. Groenewegen argues a main job of the basal ganglia is learning and selecting the most fitting motor or behavioural programme for the moment. Their internal wiring suits such selection in children and adults alike. He also weighs whether childhood clumsiness partly reflects basal ganglia dysfunction, comparing their role with the cerebellum's in developing motor control.
europmc-pmc2575520:
Covington, Maloof, Straume, Kay, and Harmer combined several genome-wide data sets in 2008 to measure how much of a plant's genome its body clock controls. Earlier microarray studies of the model plant Arabidopsis disagreed wildly, putting clock control at anywhere from 5 to 15 percent of genes. The team reanalysed the experiments with standardised methods to find the true scale.

Combining data sets proved far more powerful than any single run. The unified analysis found 3,975 clock-regulated genes, and between 31 and 41 percent of all expressed genes showed circadian, roughly daily, rhythms in abundance. Clock-regulated genes clustered in hormone and stress-response pathways, suggesting the clock steers how plants answer nearly every hormone and stress. The authors also identified DNA elements in gene promoters that set the time of day each gene peaks.
europmc-pmc2630720:
van de Sande-Bruinsma and colleagues confronted antibiotic use with resistance across Europe in 2008. They reported for the European Antimicrobial Resistance Surveillance System Group and the European Surveillance of Antimicrobial Consumption Project Group. Drug effectiveness is a shared resource being eroded by overuse, and new antibiotics were drying up. The study merged the continent's two big tracking databases. One covers drug use, the other drug resistance.

They compared outpatient drug use, adjusted for population size, against resistance trends. The check covered three drug-and-germ pairs in 21 countries over 2000 to 2005. The routine tracking data did show a link. Higher national use went with higher national resistance. The authors present the joint analysis as support for steps that cut drug use at national level. They caution that country-level data cannot untangle how prescribing and resistance truly connect.
europmc-pmc2631520:
Ma and Huang proposed a statistical method in 2009 for picking reliable cancer genes by pooling several microarray studies at once. Single studies measure thousands of genes in few patients, so the marker genes they select are unstable. Pooling raises power, but studies differ in design and gene counts dwarf sample sizes. Their method, called Meta Threshold Gradient Descent Regularization, was built for exactly this setting.

The method lets each experiment keep its own settings while selecting one shared set of cancer-associated genes across all of them. It also accounts for genes acting jointly rather than one at a time. In simulations and in real pancreatic and liver cancer data sets, it outperformed existing approaches at recovering dependable markers. The authors offer it as an effective route to robust gene selection.
europmc-pmc2638020:
Barr and co-authors mapped the shapes of a large family of human proteins in work published in 2009. The proteins, called tyrosine phosphatases, remove chemical tags from other proteins and so help control cell signals. Faults in them are tied to many diseases, which makes them targets for new drugs.

The team solved the three-dimensional shapes of 22 family members and compared them with shapes known before. The basic fold was shared, yet the surfaces differed a great deal from one protein to the next. Many carried an extra pocket beside the main working site, a spot that could help drugs pick one member only. Tests of working speed also varied widely. Three members, named PTPD1, PTPD2, and HDPTP, proved unable to do the chemistry at all.
europmc-pmc2656620:
Brisse and colleagues sorted in 2009 the family lines of Klebsiella pneumoniae, a germ that lives harmlessly in many people yet causes hospital infections of urine, lungs, and blood. Some rare lines cause distinct diseases, such as a liver abscess illness spreading in Asia. Knowing which lines are dangerous could sharpen control.

The team typed 235 samples from patients and the environment, checking their genes, capsule coats, and power to sicken mice. Clear clones emerged, each tied to its own source and behavior. Two clones wearing the K1 coat linked to liver abscess and lung infection. Two nose and throat diseases each matched a single narrow clone, so those named subspecies count as clones too. One K2 clone was fiercely virulent in mice, the other not. Coat genes, it turned out, can jump between lines, blurring the coat as a danger sign.
europmc-pmc2667420:
Guh and colleagues pooled 89 studies in 2009 to measure how often overweight and obese people go on to develop other diseases. Extra weight was known to raise many risks, but firm numbers for each illness were scattered. The team searched two large databases for solid forward-looking studies and merged their results.

Eighteen linked illnesses met their standards. Overweight raised the odds of type II diabetes, most cancers, heart and vessel disease, asthma, gallbladder disease, joint wear, and chronic back pain. The strongest single link was diabetes in women, at nearly four times the risk of normal-weight women. Obesity raised the same risks further in nearly every case. Two cancers, of the food pipe and prostate, showed no clear link. The numbers give doctors and planners a shared scale for the harm done by extra weight.
europmc-pmc2771920:
Brennan and co-authors showed in 2009 that glioblastomas, the most common malignant brain tumors, fall into subclasses defined by which signaling pathways are active. Tumors grouped under one name differ widely, and sorting them by switched-on pathways could guide targeted drugs. They ran targeted protein analysis on twenty-seven surgical glioma samples, then checked the patterns against genome and expression data from two hundred forty-three tumors in The Cancer Genome Atlas.

Three subclasses emerged in roughly equal shares. One ran on EGFR signaling, with receptor amplification and mutation plus strong Notch activity. A second was driven by PDGF signaling, mostly through excess ligand. The third had lost NF1, a brake on the RAS pathway, and showed lower overall MAPK and PI3K activity. Each class matched a known gene-expression subclass, tying protein signals to signature gene changes.
europmc-pmc2791220:
Fellay and a large team, including the NIAID Center for HIV/AIDS Vaccine Immunology (CHAVI), scanned the genomes of two thousand five hundred fifty-four people with HIV-1 in 2009. They sought common DNA variants that help some people keep the virus at low levels without treatment.

The scan strongly confirmed three links found in an earlier, smaller study, and all sat in one genome region tied to immune defense. Added effects from both common and rare variants appeared in that same region, plus a cluster for virus entry receptors on chromosome three. No variant outside those areas held up, which narrowed where control of HIV-1 seems to be written in DNA.
europmc-pmc2799520:
Chen and a large team tested in 2010 whether one short DNA stretch, called ITS2, could serve as a standard barcode for naming medicinal plants. A barcode here means a short gene region whose spelling differs enough to tell species apart. The group compared seven candidate regions across medicinal species.

ITS2 copied most reliably, showed a clear gap between variation within and between species, and beat the other candidates. Tested on more than six thousand six hundred samples from four thousand eight hundred species, it named the right species in more than nine of ten cases. The team proposes ITS2 as a standard barcode for medicinal plants and a wider plant naming tool.
europmc-pmc2832020:
Khanna and colleagues found in 2010 why diabetic wounds stay inflamed instead of healing: their cleanup cells fail at eating the dead. Wound macrophages must clear away apoptotic cells, meaning cells that died on schedule, before inflammation can end. The team took macrophages from wounds of diabetic mice and tested that eating job, called efferocytosis.

Diabetic wound macrophages cleared dead cells poorly, leaving a heavy burden of them in the tissue. The same burden appeared in wound tissue from diabetic patients. Forcing extra dead cells into wounds stoked inflammatory signals and muted calming ones. When cleanup worked, macrophages switched into an anti-inflammatory mode, tying the eating job directly to healing.
europmc-pmc2841820:
Livshits and colleagues followed middle-aged British women in the Chingford Study for fifteen years to test whether blood markers of inflammation predict knee osteoarthritis seen on X-rays. Osteoarthritis, the wearing breakdown of joints, lacks any accepted early warning marker. Nearly a thousand women gave X-rays and blood at set visits across the study.

The share with clear knee damage rose from about fifteen percent to nearly half over the period. Women who developed it ran higher body weight and higher levels of two inflammation markers, CRP and IL-6. Higher IL-6 at year five independently forecast damage at year ten, alongside age and starting weight. Women in the top IL-6 quarter faced nearly triple the odds of the bottom quarter.
europmc-pmc2856220:
Hedström, Svensson, Bergström, and Michno charted every fracture treated in children and teenagers around Umeå, Sweden, in 2010, using a hospital injury database running since 1993. Over ten thousand fracture events appeared in the records through 2007. The team mapped which bones broke, how the injuries happened, and how patterns shifted with age, sex, and calendar year.

Falling caused most fractures, and the far end of the forearm was the commonest break. Rates peaked at eleven to twelve years in girls and thirteen to fourteen in boys, with boys breaking bones half again as often as girls. Fracture incidence rose about thirteen percent over the decade to 2007, which the authors partly blame on changing activity patterns in children.
europmc-pmc2877420:
Limmathurotsakul and colleagues tracked in 2010 a rising tide of melioidosis, a severe soil-borne infection, in northeast Thailand. The culprit is Burkholderia pseudomallei, a bacterium living in soil and water that enters through skin cuts. They counted every culture-confirmed case admitted to the region's main hospital across a decade.

More than twenty-two hundred cases gave an average rate near thirteen per hundred thousand people a year. The rate climbed steadily, from about eight to over twenty-one per hundred thousand across the study years. Men, people over forty-five, and people with diabetes, known or hidden, faced the highest risk. Deaths ran above forty percent, making melioidosis the region's third deadliest infection after HIV and tuberculosis by 2006.
europmc-pmc2901520:
Egecioglu and co-authors showed in 2010 that the hunger hormone ghrelin also drives craving for tasty food through the brain's reward hub. They targeted the ventral tegmental area, a midbrain node that feeds dopamine to reward circuits. Mice missing the ghrelin receptor and rats given a receptor blocker both ate less of a rewarding food when offered a free choice against plain chow.

Rewarding food normally triggers a dopamine surge in the accumbens, a reward center, and that surge vanished in receptor-free mice. Injecting ghrelin straight into the hub boosted one-hour intake of rewarding food but not of chow. Blocking the receptor also killed the learned place preference for the tasty food. Hunger chemistry thus sets how much pleasure food is worth pursuing.
europmc-pmc2912920:
Arain, Campbell, Cooper, and Lancaster asked in 2010 what a pilot or feasibility study actually is, after finding the terms used loosely across medicine. A 2004 review had urged that such small preliminary studies stick to description and sample size planning rather than testing treatments. The team re-screened seven major journals for 2007 and 2008 and also surveyed trial registries, funders, and editors.

Fifty-four pilot or feasibility papers turned up, about half of them pilot trials of interventions. Practice had barely budged: many still ran hypothesis tests their small samples cannot support. Worse, registries, grant bodies, and journals each defined the terms differently, and some had no policy at all. The authors press for shared definitions so pilots do the sizing and feasibility work they exist for.
europmc-pmc2919420:
David and colleagues, working in Cynthia Kenyon's laboratory, reported in 2010 that ordinary proteins clump with age in the worm C. elegans, not just the disease proteins famous for aggregating. Sticky clumps define Alzheimer's and similar illnesses, yet whether normal aging itself is clumping-prone was unknown. Using systematic proteomics, the team separated the insoluble fraction of young and old worms and named its contents.

Several hundred normal proteins became insoluble and aggregation-prone as the worms aged. The set was not random debris: it was rich in proteins that influence how other proteins fold and clump. In tests, these age-clumped proteins nudged disease-linked proteins toward aggregation and worsened their toxicity. Aging itself tilts the whole protein pool toward clumping, which may explain why age is the master risk factor for aggregation diseases.
europmc-pmc2919520:
Cornuet, Ravigné, and Estoup upgraded in 2010 DIYABC, software that infers population history from genetic data using approximate Bayesian computation. The approach simulates millions of datasets under competing histories, like splits and admixtures between populations, and keeps the histories whose simulations resemble the real data. Version 1.0 widens what the software can digest and, crucially, lets users check whether a chosen model actually fits.

It now accepts DNA sequence data alongside microsatellites and handles five locus types, including sex-linked and mitochondrial markers with balanced or skewed sex ratios. Simulated tests showed mixing data types can sharpen scenario choice and parameter estimates. The new model-checking step, long neglected in this field, flags histories that merely win a contest without truly explaining the data.
europmc-pmc2949620:
Drummond and Suchard introduced a Bayesian method for dating family trees when evolution speeds up and slows down across branches, in a 2010 article. Strict clock models assume one steady rate, an idea real lineages often break.

Their approach lays many local clocks over different parts of a tree and averages over the possible placements using computer sampling, while estimating the tree itself at the same time. That setup lets users test the single-rate idea directly against a huge range of alternatives. Worked examples cover mammal, primate, and influenza histories, with new ways to display the resulting rate patterns.
europmc-pmc2954820:
Huang, Lee, Marcotte, and Hurles mapped genes where losing one copy matters, a state called haploinsufficiency, in a 2010 genome study. One working copy is not always enough, and such genes cause many dominant diseases.

They contrasted several hundred known sensitive genes with over a thousand genes repeatedly damaged in healthy people, so judged tolerant. Sensitive genes tended to be longer, more conserved, busier in early development, and more connected in gene networks. A model built on those traits scored all genes, and high scorers indeed clustered among dominant disease genes and mouse lines with faults from a single lost copy.
europmc-pmc3009720:
Globisch and co-authors measured a sixth DNA base, hydroxymethylcytosine, across mouse tissues in a 2010 study. They also hunted for further bases. Such bases would prove an active removal pathway for methylation marks. The new base forms from the classic methyl mark, and its job was unknown.

Using an ultra-sensitive isotope method, they found the base in every tissue and cell type, richest in brain nerve cells. The expected follow-on bases of a stepwise removal chain were essentially absent, arguing against that demethylation route. The base looks more like a stable feature of nerve cells than a passing step.
europmc-pmc3117820:
Ralf Hass and colleagues compared human repair cells drawn from adult and newborn tissues in a 2011 mini-review in Cell Communication and Signaling. These versatile cells, found near blood vessels in most tissues, can renew themselves, turn into several cell types, and calm immune responses. Sources range from bone marrow and fat to placenta and cord tissue.

The review contrasts the sources on growth speed, surface markers, and range of cell types they can form. Neighbouring cells, low oxygen, and small regulatory RNAs all shift how each population behaves, so cells from different tissues are not interchangeable. For doctors hoping to use them in healing, the paper maps which source suits which job and what still needs testing.
europmc-pmc3139420:
Craig Johnson and colleagues found a hidden protein in a pig virus in a 2011 paper in the Journal of General Virology. The virus causes the most costly swine disease worldwide, harming breeding and breathing, yet its protein set was thought complete. Suspecting a missed reading frame, the team purified virus particles and searched them for unknown pieces.

A small protein of about fifty building blocks turned up inside the particles, read from an alternate frame overlapping the gene for the main coat protein. Infected cells make it, and infected pigs raise antibodies against it. The same hidden frame appears in every member of the virus family. The finding adds a target for vaccines and drugs and hints the protein matters across the whole family.
europmc-pmc3212920:
David Clark described England's Improving Access to Psychological Therapies programme in this 2011 article in the International Review of Psychiatry. The programme was a large national effort to make recommended talk therapies for depression and anxiety widely available through the National Health Service. Clark explains why it was launched and how it was organized.

He covers the arguments behind the programme, its therapist training scheme, and the model its clinics follow. At the halfway point of the national rollout, progress matched expectations, and many people who would otherwise have received no evidence-based therapy had been treated and benefited. Clark closes by outlining planned developments and the challenges the expanding service still faces.
europmc-pmc3271020:
Ali Zomorrodi and Costas Maranas introduced OptCom, a framework for modeling the metabolism of microbial communities, in this 2012 paper in PLoS Computational Biology. Microbes rarely live alone, yet what each member contributes to a community's chemistry, and who trades what with whom, remains poorly understood despite abundant sequencing data. Existing models typically optimized a single goal, which misrepresents real communities.

OptCom instead sets up nested optimization: each species pursues its own fitness inside, while the outer problem maximizes a community-level goal, exposing the trade-offs between the two. It handles any mix of cooperative and competitive interactions and any number of species. The authors applied it to a well-studied two-species partnership, to light-harvesting microbial mats, and to a model community. They measured how much metabolites and electrons move between members. They also tested what happens when a new member joins.
europmc-pmc3272020:
Ian Holmes, Keith Harris, and Christopher Quince introduced Dirichlet multinomial mixtures, a statistical model for microbial community data, in this 2012 paper in PLoS ONE. Metagenomic surveys produce tables counting how often each organism appears in each sample, tables that are sparse and uneven in size. Older clustering methods ignored those quirks, so the authors built a generative model that respects them.

Each community is described by a probability profile over taxa, drawn from one of a few mixture components; the components act as community types, sometimes called enterotypes. Applied to gut microbe data from obese and lean twins, the model favored four clusters, two dominated by Bacteroides and two more variable. Body mass did not map onto a distinct community type. Obese twins were, however, more often found in the variable clusters. The authors call this an Anna Karenina pattern, and they verified it in Crohn's disease data.
europmc-pmc3284220:
Annette Michalski and colleagues introduced the Q Exactive, a benchtop mass spectrometer for proteomics, in this 2011 paper in Molecular and Cellular Proteomics. Protein analysis by mass spectrometry demands speed, sensitivity, and resolution at once. The new instrument couples a quadrupole mass filter, which selects ions almost instantly, to an Orbitrap analyzer, which weighs them with high precision, a pairing not reported before.

An improved ion lens delivered high currents, and parallel filling and detection kept cycle times near one second. In standard ninety-minute runs on digested cell extracts, the instrument found more than twenty-five hundred proteins, a clear step beyond earlier Orbitrap models. Its fast switching also enables multiplexed modes, selecting and fragmenting several precursors in quick succession for joint analysis. The authors present the robust benchtop design as an advance for proteomics and for chemistry at large.
europmc-pmc3331820:
Abrantes, van der Loo, Le Pendu, and Esteves reviewed a fast killing rabbit disease and the virus behind it, in a 2012 article. The virus first appeared in China in 1984 and swept the world, killing adult European rabbits within two to three days of infection. Australia and New Zealand even released it on purpose to control pest rabbits.

Infected rabbits die mainly of acute liver destruction, with bleeding in lungs, heart, and kidneys from runaway clotting. All deadly strains form a single type, though two subtypes circulate, and harmless relatives may have come first. No other species is known to die of it. Control in rabbit farms rests on vaccination and strict hygiene, which are hard to apply to wild rabbits. The review gathers what is known about the virus's spread, evolution, and possible future use as a medical tool.
europmc-pmc3352820:
Lawrence and colleagues ran tests to see whether living with other species changes how a population adapts to a new setting. Most lab studies of adaptation use one species alone, yet in the wild organisms always adapt in company. The team therefore grew bacterial communities side by side with matching single-species cultures and watched how each changed.

Species changing together did not follow the path they took alone. Community members shifted toward split, complementary use of resources, carving up the setting rather than all chasing the same solution. Those shifts also changed how the whole system worked. The results say adaptation in nature cannot always be foretold from single-species tests.
europmc-pmc3403920:
Francisco and colleagues released software in 2012 to make sense of the flood of sequence-based typing data used to track bacteria. Such typing has become the standard for watching outbreaks locally and worldwide. Its databases hold rich strain profiles and case details, but no friendly tool existed to explore them together.

Their program, PHYLOViZ, runs on any platform and links typing results with outbreak data in one view. Built-in algorithms draw family trees and minimum spanning trees showing how isolates likely relate. Results appear as annotated graphs that can be layered with any other case information. The free tool aims to help labs turn stored profiles into population insight.
europmc-pmc3424120:
Ferreira and colleagues tested in 2012 whether a magnetic scan method called T1-mapping can spot fresh swelling in heart muscle without injected contrast. The standard T2-weighted scan detects such edema but with limits. The team scanned healthy controls and patients with acute heart swelling from Takotsubo syndrome or regional injury, all within a week of symptoms.

Segments of heart wall with abnormal motion, and even those moving normally, showed clearly raised T1 values in patients. Judged by accuracy curves, T1-mapping beat both dark-blood and bright-blood T2 methods by a wide margin. A single cutoff value separated swollen from normal segments with high sensitivity and specificity. The authors propose T1-mapping as a sharper, objective partner to the older scans.

europmc-pmc5424220:
Johnstone describes two rare specimens of the human egg in its first weeks of growth. The study appeared in the Transactions of the Edinburgh Obstetrical Society. Early human development was then poorly known. Specimens caught in place were scarce. Most came from early miscarriages. Johnstone obtained two within ten months. One sat in the womb. The other sat in the tube. Their contrast is the heart of the paper.

The womb specimen was about fifteen days old. Its features matched the classic account by Peters. Its embryonic parts were hard to read. One fair reading is very early identical twins. The tube specimen was about twenty days old. It lodged at the tube's outer funnel, a site not recorded before. It also showed the egg had crossed from the opposite ovary. Johnstone records fine anatomy first. He then compares both finds with other early eggs on record.
europmc-pmc5458120:
Bangasser and co-authors show that each cell type has a favorite stiffness for migration, and that the favorite can be shifted. Their study appeared in Nature Communications. Migrating cells move fastest at an optimum stiffness. Too soft or too stiff slows them. The team built a whole-cell migration simulator. It rests on the motor-clutch model. Motors pull actin bundles inside the cell. Clutches link that pull to the surface outside. The model predicted a tunable optimum.

Two cell types tested the prediction. Chick forebrain neurons peaked near 1 kilopascal. U251 glioma cells peaked near 100 kilopascals. The glioma cells carry more motors and clutches. Traction and actin flow matched model output. Drugs then shifted the glioma optimum downward. Blocking myosin II motors and integrin clutches together did it. Morphology and flow shifted as predicted. Stiffness sensing is thus adjustable machinery.
europmc-pmc5489820:
Rajabi and Mousa present a review in Biomedicines on angiogenesis in cancer treatment. Angiogenesis is the growth of new blood vessels from old ones. Tumors need such vessels to grow beyond a small size. Drugs that block vessel growth are now approved for cancer care. Yet single-pathway drugs often lose effect over time.

Tumors can switch to backup routes for vessel growth, they explain. Broad-spectrum targets may work better than narrow ones. The review covers growth factors such as VEGF and the cells that build vessel walls. Pairing anti-angiogenic drugs with chemotherapy looks essential, they argue. Agents in trials and in labs are surveyed.
europmc-pmc5514220:
Grabowska, Sikora, and Bielak-Zmijewska present a review in Biogerontology on sirtuins and ageing. Sirtuins are a family of seven proteins in humans. They help cells answer stress and manage energy use. Extra sirtuin activity stretched lifespan in yeast, worms, and flies. Whether they lengthen human life directly is still disputed.

Diet and exercise can raise sirtuin levels and improve healthspan, they note. The hunt for drug-like sirtuin activators is intense. Natural compounds draw special hope, above all curcumin. The review sums up sirtuin roles in ageing control. It then weighs curcumin's promise as a regulator of these proteins.
europmc-pmc5563520:
Oster and co-authors review the daily rhythm of glucocorticoid hormones in Endocrine Reviews. These hormones swing widely across each 24-hour cycle. The swing shapes immunity, metabolism, mood, and the stress response. Why the rhythm matters has stayed poorly understood.

A master clock in the brain's suprachiasmic nuclei sets the tempo. The same clock machinery runs in many body tissues. Two receptor types carry the hormone's effects in a matching pair. Health looks best when brain and tissue clocks stay in line. When they drift apart, disease risk rises. Heart, immune, and metabolic harm all feature. The authors back timing-based drug strategies to restore the rhythm. Readers get the clock logic behind a major hormone system.
europmc-pmc5603520:
Zhao and co-authors profile mouth bacteria in oral cancer for Scientific Reports. Oral squamous cell carcinoma arises on the mouth's lining. Microbe shifts have been tied to several cancers. Whether the tumor surface community differs was the question.

Each patient gave two swabs. One came from the cancer lesion. The other came from matched healthy tissue nearby. Sequencing profiled the bacteria at species level. Cancer samples held greater bacterial diversity. A cluster of gum-disease-linked genera stood out. Fusobacterium, Dialister, Peptostreptococcus, and kin were enriched on tumors. Several Fusobacterium units tracked the cancer closely. They showed good power to tell tumor from normal. Functional genes in the communities differed too. Readers get a detailed census of how the oral microbiome shifts with cancer.
europmc-pmc5638920:
Yang and co-authors report a nanomedicine study in Nature Communications. They built hollow shells from manganese dioxide. The shells respond to conditions inside tumors. A coating of polyethylene glycol steadied the particles. Inside, the team loaded two agents. One was chlorin e6 for light-based therapy. The other was doxorubicin, a chemotherapy drug.

Tumor tissue is acidic and short on oxygen. Under low pH, the shells break apart and release their load. They also split hydrogen peroxide, which frees oxygen. That eases tumor hypoxia and aids light therapy. In mice, combined chemo and light treatment worked strongly together. It also stirred anti-tumor immune responses. Adding checkpoint blockade helped curb distant tumors.
europmc-pmc5662220:
Schädler and co-authors report a randomized trial in PLoS ONE. It tests a blood filtering device in septic patients. The CytoSorb device adsorbs cytokines from blood outside the body. Patients had severe sepsis or septic shock with lung failure. All were on mechanical ventilation. Treatment ran six hours daily for up to seven days. The main outcome was change in blood IL-6 levels.

Of 100 randomized patients, 97 were analyzed. The device removed IL-6 at each blood pass. Removal averaged between five and eighteen percent per pass. Yet plasma IL-6 levels did not differ between groups. Raw mortality looked higher in the treated group. After adjustment for baseline gaps, that link vanished.
europmc-pmc5686520:
d'Hennezel and co-authors report a gut study in mSystems. It shows gut bacteria actively calm an immune alarm. A coat sugar called LPS covers many bacteria. It tends to spark alarm signals and swelling. The team took total LPS from healthy adult stool. Nine donors gave samples for the tests. Gene scans profiled the microbes in each sample.

The pooled gut LPS blocked the alarm path instead. It shut down Toll-like receptor 4 signaling. Tests used human immune cells and lab cell lines. Gene scans traced the effect to Bacteroidales members. These rule the healthy gut's Gram-negative group. Their LPS forms drive the calm for all gut microbes.
europmc-pmc5687320:
Hegazy and co-authors report an immunology study in Gastroenterology. It measures human T cells that react to gut bacteria. Such microbe-immune contact keeps the gut in balance. How it works in humans was poorly known. The team sampled blood and gut tissue from healthy people. Samples also came from 119 bowel disease patients. Nine gut bacterial species were used as test targets. Two assays counted and grew the reactive cells.

Reactive CD4 cells proved common in healthy controls. They sat in both blood and intestinal tissue. Most carried a memory phenotype with varied receptors. They made barrier-protective signals and stimulated gut lining cells. In bowel disease, blood levels of these cells dropped. Their gut responses also shifted toward more IL-17A.
europmc-pmc5726620:
Kešnerová and co-authors study what gut bacteria do inside the honey bee. Bees carry a small, shared set of gut microbes, unlike most animals. The team used bees raised with known microbes only. They tracked chemical changes in the gut with broad screening tools.

They find the microbes break down tough parts of pollen and plant compounds. About 80% of the changes seen with the full set also appear with one species alone. Lactobacilli drive the largest share of this output. One species, Bifidobacterium asteroides, also lifts host hormone signals tied to bee growth. Some cross feeding between species occurs, but most work is done solo.
europmc-pmc5745720:
Wang and co-authors study how a protein called HIF1α shapes inflammatory macrophages. These immune cells take an aggressive form known as M1. The team used mice bred so their myeloid cells make extra HIF1α. They took macrophages from bone marrow and the body cavity for tests.

Cells with extra HIF1α showed a stronger inflammatory state, they report. Their oxygen use fell, while sugar burning through glycolysis rose. Building blocks from a side path, the pentose phosphate pathway, also rose. Extra HIF1α turned up genes for glycolysis. The authors conclude this fuel switch is key to M1 activation.
europmc-pmc5758920:
Sagulenko, Puller, and Neher present TreeTime, a Python framework for phylodynamic analysis. Mutations in virus genomes reveal how pathogens spread in space and time. Older methods scale poorly as genome counts grow. TreeTime uses an approximate maximum likelihood approach to stay fast.

The tool estimates ancestral states and fits evolution models. It can reroot trees to sharpen time signals. It also builds molecular clock trees and traces population size history. Runtime grows in a straight line with dataset size. The authors aim it at fast evolving viral pathogens in large studies.
europmc-pmc5793720:
Pandurangan and co-authors report an updated web server, SDM, that predicts how mutations change protein stability. Such forecasts help sort which genetic variants truly harm proteins. The team rebuilt its knowledge tables from a far larger set of known structures. New measures of packing and burial were added.

The server was tested on 2,690 point mutations across 132 protein structures. It matched reverse mutation checks well, beating machine learning rivals in their tests. A user gives a structure file and a point change. The server returns a score for the stability shift.
europmc-pmc5796020:
Lin and co-authors review plant oils put on the skin in the International Journal of Molecular Sciences. Plant oils have long been used in food, cosmetics, and medicines. The review asks what these oils do for sick or damaged skin. It covers oils such as olive, coconut, sunflower seed, argan, and jojoba. It also covers shea butter and several less common oils.

The authors sort the proof by what each oil does on skin. Some oils calm swelling and fight damage from oxygen-based stress. Some help wounds close and heal. Others help rebuild the skin barrier. That barrier is the outer layer that holds water in and keeps germs out. Readers get a plain guide to which oils have support for skin repair. The review also shows where proof is thin, or rests on lab and animal work.
europmc-pmc5834520:
Zhao and co-authors review osteopontin, a bone protein that also helps solid tumors grow and spread. Their review appeared in Cell Death & Disease. Osteopontin talks to cells through integrins and CD44. Those signals steer growth, movement, and blood vessel building.

The survey crosses a dozen cancer types, from brain to ovary. In each, extra osteopontin tracks with faster growth and wider spread. The protein helps tumors anchor, migrate, and seed new sites. It also feeds the vessels that supply them. The authors close on therapy, asking how best to block a protein with so many jobs.
europmc-pmc5859920:
Amatulli and co-authors present a global dataset of topographic variables. Their article appeared in Scientific Data. The dataset serves research in ecology, climate, and land science. It was built from two digital elevation models of the Earth. One has 250-metre detail, and the other has 90-metre detail. From them, the team derived slope, aspect, roughness, and landform classes.

Each variable was also averaged to five coarser grid sizes. The coarsest grids reach 100 kilometres per cell. Tests in four mountain regions show local and scale differences. Many variables track each other closely, the team notes. The full set is free to download and view online. It gives modellers one standard terrain source across scales.
europmc-pmc5918520:
van Strien reviews causes of emotional eating and matched obesity treatment. The review appeared in Current Diabetes Reports. Emotional eating means eating in response to negative feelings. It may explain why many dieters regain weight. Causes reviewed include strict restraint and poor body awareness. Trouble naming or handling feelings also features.

Emotional eating links depression with obesity, van Strien reports. It acts as a mediator between the two. Poor parenting and genes may interact to raise risk. A reversed stress hormone pattern is another suspect. Diet-only care fits such patients poorly, she argues. Treatment should build emotion skills instead, guided by a questionnaire.
europmc-pmc5924020:
Pringle reported four cases of hernia across the lesser sac of the peritoneum. The paper appeared in the Glasgow Medical Journal in 1919. Each patient had strong gastric symptoms before surgery. In each, nearly all the small bowel had slipped into the lesser sac. It entered through a gap in the transverse mesocolon. Only the last inches of ileum stayed outside.

The bowel left the sac by two different routes, he reports. Two cases passed through one ligament, two through another. Pringle found only five prior cases in the records. Just two of those were found at operation. The first case history is told in full detail. The paper records a very rare internal hernia.
europmc-pmc5979320:
Nie and co-authors review branched chain amino acids beyond their role in nutrition metabolism. Their review appeared in the International Journal of Molecular Sciences. The three amino acids are leucine, isoleucine, and valine. They are the most abundant essential amino acids. Beyond building protein, they act as signals in the body. They regulate glucose, lipid, and protein metabolism. Gut health and immunity also respond to them.

One key route is the PI3K/AKT/mTOR signalling pathway. Blood levels of these amino acids link to disease risk, the authors note. Insulin resistance and type 2 diabetes are among them. Cancer and cardiovascular disease feature as well. Tuning dietary levels may improve health measures.
europmc-pmc5991220:
Rodbard and co-authors report the SUSTAIN 5 trial of semaglutide added to basal insulin in type 2 diabetes. Their trial report was published in The Journal of Clinical Endocrinology and Metabolism. The late-stage trial ran 30 weeks at 90 sites in five lands. It took in 397 patients whose diabetes stayed out of control on basal insulin. A weekly drug dose at two strengths was set against a dummy drug.

Blood sugar control got much better on the drug, they report. The dummy drug barely moved it at all. Body weight fell far more on the drug than on the dummy. Low blood sugar bouts were not clearly more common. Stomach side effects drove most early dropouts.
europmc-pmc6005120:
Khalil and co-authors quantify the burden of diarrhoea from Cryptosporidium infection in children younger than five. Their meta-analysis study appeared in The Lancet Global Health. The parasite ranks among the top diarrhoea causes in young children. Earlier counts captured only the acute illness effects. Long-term harm to growth may have been missed. The team combined global burden estimates with cohort evidence. A meta-analysis measured how infection affects child growth.

Infection caused over 48,000 deaths in the study year, they report. Each episode trimmed height and weight scores measurably. Counting growth faltering added 7.85 million disability-adjusted life-years. That is 153 percent above the acute-only estimate.
europmc-pmc6097220:
Scott and co-authors synthesize what reviews say about community health worker programs. Their review of reviews appeared in Human Resources for Health. The team searched 11 databases. They gathered 122 review articles. Most came from low- and middle-income countries.

Programs varied widely in tasks, training, and pay. Workers embedded in their communities fared better. Supportive supervision and steady supplies also helped. Ongoing education mattered as well. Fitting programs into the health system aided survival and trust. It also clarified roles and teamwork. Gaps remain on worker rights and training methods. Readers get design guidance drawn from a vast evidence base.
europmc-pmc6165520:
Brådvik wrote a review in International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health on suicide risk and mental disorders. Suicide accounts for about 1.4 percent of all deaths worldwide. Most suicides are linked to psychiatric disease. Depression, substance use disorders, and psychosis are the most relevant risk factors.

Studies of people who died by suicide suggest at least 90 percent had a mental disorder. Yet most people with mental illness never die this way. Risk for several disorders is estimated at 5 to 8 percent. Brådvik presents a stress-diathesis model, where stress acts on a person's vulnerability. The piece frames a special issue on prediction and prevention.
europmc-pmc6196420:
Budnik and co-authors present a methods article in Genome Biology on measuring proteins in single cells. Some questions need thousands of proteins counted in one cell at a time. Mass spectrometry normally needs far more material. The team built SCoPE-MS to close that gap.

The method identified distinct human cancer cell types from their protein profiles alone. In differentiating mouse embryonic stem cells it quantified over a thousand proteins per experiment set. Single-cell profiles let the team pull mixed populations apart. Comparing proteins with RNA messages showed much coordination, yet many genes followed distinct rules at the protein level. The tool opens cell-to-cell protein differences to direct study.
europmc-pmc6245920:
Sanz and co-authors extend a feature picking method for support vector machines. Their methods paper appeared in BMC Bioinformatics. Support vector machines handle data sets with many measured variables. Early versions could not say which variables mattered most. Picking the key variables is vital in medical research. Prior fixes worked only with straight line models, not curved ones.

Three new ranking approaches are proposed for curved models and survival data. They build on pseudo samples and on kernel based component analysis. Each pass of the ranking can be plotted, so users watch variables drop out. Tests used simulated survival data and three real data sets. The authors report that their methods beat the standard approach at finding truly key variables. One method, based on pseudo samples, did best overall.
europmc-pmc6356320:
Turner and co-authors review telomere biology and its links to human traits. Their review appeared in Cells. Telomeres cap the ends of each chromosome. They protect genome stability during cell division. Each division trims them a little shorter. Cells stop dividing when telomeres run too short.

That trimming ties telomeres to ageing itself. The review explains how shortening happens. It follows telomere length across a human lifetime. It also covers how cells maintain their telomeres. Evidence links short telomeres to age-related diseases. Heart, lung, and immune conditions all feature. The authors weigh telomere length as a health marker. They caution that cause and effect remain tangled.
europmc-pmc6423620:
Thibaudeau and Smith offer a practical review of proteasome pharmacology in Pharmacological Reviews. The proteasome is the cell's main shredder for worn or faulty proteins. It sits at the center of a tagging system that touches nearly every cell process.

When shredding fails, toxic protein clumps can build up and harm neurons. Many cancers, in contrast, lean on strong proteasome activity to survive. Drugs that block the proteasome are already used against some cancers. The review covers how those drugs work and where they fail. It is framed as a hands-on guide for researchers.
europmc-pmc6424820:
Marcandalli and co-authors describe a designed protein nanoparticle vaccine against respiratory syncytial virus, a widespread infection for which no vaccine existed in 2019. The team built on the known shape of the viral F protein before it fuses with a cell, since antibodies aim mainly at that prefusion form. A stabilized version called DS-Cav1 anchors the design.

Twenty DS-Cav1 trimers sit in a regular array on each self-assembling particle, and the two-part scaffold lets makers control that spacing. In mice and nonhuman primates, the full particle raised neutralizing antibody levels about ten times higher than the loose trimer alone. The work supports nanoparticle display as a flexible route for vaccine design.
europmc-pmc6437920:
Ni and co-authors pool controlled studies to judge whether corticosteroids help or harm adults with influenza pneumonia. Steroids are often given to calm lung inflammation, yet earlier reports conflicted on survival. Ten trials covering 6,548 patients entered the final analysis.

Steroid treatment came with clearly worse outcomes: mortality was higher (risk ratio 1.75), intensive care stays ran about 2.14 days longer, and secondary infections were nearly twice as likely (risk ratio 1.98). Days on mechanical ventilation did not differ significantly. Heterogeneity between trials was substantial for most outcomes. The authors advise against routine steroid use in influenza pneumonia on this evidence.
europmc-pmc6445120:
Zhang and co-authors assemble a high-quality genome for the apple line HFTH1 and use it to explain red fruit skin. Combining long-read sequencing, chromosome capture, and optical mapping produced an assembly with a contig N50 of 6.99 million bases and 22 telomere sequences. Against the Golden Delicious reference they counted 18,047 deletions, 12,101 insertions, and 14 large inversions, much of it driven by transposable elements.

One insertion matters most to growers: a retrotransposon sitting above MdMYB1, the switch for red anthocyanin pigment, tracks perfectly with red skin in breeding crosses. The genome gives breeders a sharper map for DNA-informed selection.
europmc-pmc6487120:
Thakur and co-authors survey the long war between host immunity and intracellular pathogens, the viruses, bacteria, fungi, and parasites that survive by living inside our own cells, often macrophages themselves. Infectious diseases rank as the second leading cause of death worldwide, and the intracellular subset earns persistence, sometimes lifelong, by hiding where antibodies cannot reach.

Each pathogen lineage evolved its own escape kit, yet shared tricks recur during life inside host cells: dodging vacuole destruction, modulating antigen display, riding out immune attack. The host counters with layered effector functions of its own. The review's comparative framing aims the knowledge at better diagnostics, drugs, and vaccines against infections that refuse to end.
europmc-pmc6511120:
Gast and Mathes overview the factors that shape medication adherence. Their overview of systematic reviews appeared in Systematic Reviews. It covers adults with chronic physical diseases who take oral drugs. Poor adherence weakens treatment and raises costs.

The authors searched MEDLINE and Embase in June 2018. They included 21 systematic reviews across eight conditions. Eight reviews had low risk of bias and 13 had high risk. Social support and higher socioeconomic status may aid adherence. Ethnic minority status and co-payments may harm it. Depression also had a negative effect. Age showed a curved pattern, with lowest adherence in the very young and very old. Most other factors stayed unclear.
europmc-pmc6724220:
Barta and co-authors review the global epidemiology of lung cancer. Lung cancer has long led cancer deaths in the United States. Rates differ widely around the world, though. The review compares patterns across countries with unlike wealth, habits, and environments.

In rich nations, smoking patterns shifted later in women, so their lung cancer rates rose or leveled while men's fell. Poorer nations vary more, and air pollution adds risk on top of smoking. One lung cancer type, adenocarcinoma, is becoming more common. Screening high-risk smokers shows benefit, and prediction tools are improving. The review also covers two special groups in depth: women and people who never smoked.
europmc-pmc6745820:
Dillekås and co-authors test a famous claim: that metastases cause 90% of cancer deaths. The figure appears in many papers, yet hard data behind it were lacking. The team turned to the Cancer Registry of Norway. They analyzed deaths from 2005 to 2015 where cancer was the registered cause.

For solid tumors, 66.7% of cancer deaths listed metastases as a contributing cause. Rates varied widely between tumor groups. The data support a weaker version of the claim: most solid tumor deaths do involve metastases. The authors argue for more research on how metastases grow. Drug targets at the spread site could cut cancer deaths.
europmc-pmc6785720:
Baumel and co-authors measured real-world user engagement with mental health apps. Self-management apps could widen access to care, but developer reports may flatter them. No study had yet checked usage across many apps with independent data. The team searched Google Play for Android apps with at least 10,000 installs that target anxiety, depression, or well-being. Ninety-three apps qualified.

Panel data showed thin engagement with most of these apps. The median daily open rate was just 4.0 percent of the people who installed each app. Peer-support apps did best, with a median of 17.0 percent opening them each day. Breathing exercise apps did worst, at 1.6 percent on a typical day. Most mental health apps, the data suggest, are rarely touched.
europmc-pmc6859620:
Hou and co-authors report a study in Molecular Cancer on liver cancer and a chemical mark on RNA. The mark, called m6A, helps control how long messages survive in the cell. A reader protein, YTHDF2, normally destroys marked messages. How this system changes in hepatocellular carcinoma, the main liver cancer, was unknown.

Human tumours carried more m6A marking and more message output, traced to a fall in YTHDF2. Low YTHDF2 also marked patients with worse outlooks. Restoring it curbed tumour growth, acting through messages for IL11 and SERPINE2, genes that stir inflammation and abnormal blood vessels. Dead versions of the protein could not do this. The authors cast YTHDF2 loss as fuel for this cancer.
europmc-pmc6904420:
Papadopoulos and Verkman review a water channel and brain swelling, in Pediatric Nephrology. Aquaporin-4 is a protein that lets water cross cell membranes. In the brain it concentrates in astrocyte feet where tissue meets blood and spinal fluid. That placement suggests it governs water entry and exit. Mouse experiments without the channel confirm the role, with a twist.

Such mice were protected from the cell-swelling kind of brain edema, as in water intoxication or stroke, because water entered more slowly. Yet they fared worse when edema came from leaky vessels, as with tumours, because water could not leave. The review weighs what this two-way role means for treatment.
europmc-pmc6912820:
Stavast and Erkeland review the odd corners of microRNA biology, in the journal Cells. MicroRNAs are short regulators, about 21 nucleotides long, that mute gene messages after they are made. The textbook path is well known: a long transcript is trimmed by two enzymes, DROSHA and DICER, then loaded into a silencing complex that binds message tails. Real life keeps breaking that script.

Some microRNAs are made without one of the standard enzymes. Others act in the nucleus, or bind targets outside the usual region, or even turn genes up. Targets can also destroy the microRNA itself, a decay route the authors detail. The review gathers these non-canonical roads and what they mean for disease.
europmc-pmc6950820:
Liang and co-authors build tiny vesicles that deliver two weapons against drug-resistant colon cancer. Their study appeared in the Journal of Nanobiotechnology. The drug 5-fluorouracil, or 5-FU, is a standard treatment for colorectal cancer. Resistance to it is a leading cause of treatment failure.

The team engineered exosomes, small parcels cells release, to carry 5-FU plus an inhibitor of miR-21, a small RNA that aids resistance. The parcels targeted cells bearing the Her2 marker. In resistant cancer cells, the combined cargo restored drug sensitivity, stalled growth, and raised cell death. Target genes of miR-21, including PTEN and hMSH2, switched back on. In tumour-bearing mice, the system shrank tumours far better than either agent alone.
europmc-pmc6971920:
Thomas and co-authors review how the shrinking thymus ages the whole immune system. Their review appeared in Immunity and Ageing. Immune aging has two faces: weakening defences, called immunosenescence, and smouldering over-reaction, called inflammaging. The thymus, where T cells mature, withers with age, and that change underlies altered T cell function.

A shrunken thymus sends out fewer fresh T cells, narrowing the body's ability to meet new threats. Senescent cells elsewhere pour out inflammatory signals, and a weak immune system cannot clear them, worsening the inflammation. The authors trace the genetic and chemical controls of thymic decline. They link the process to brain and heart disease and to cancer. Rejuvenation ideas close the review, from growth signals to cell-based repairs of the aged thymus.
europmc-pmc6982820:
Bayda and co-authors trace the history of nanoscience, from early physics to nanomedicine. Their review appeared in Molecules. Nanoscience studies structures between 1 and 100 nanometres across, which gain new properties at that scale. The field feeds physics, chemistry, biology, computing, and engineering.

The authors walk a timeline from pre-modern roots to today's commercial products. Public attention and debate surged in the early 2000s, and applications followed. Human health has seen some of the most promising results, above all in cancer treatment. Key principles of the science are laid out along the way. The review also covers main classes of nanomaterials and how they are made. Their aim is a clear map of how a once abstract idea became a working technology.
europmc-pmc7026420:
Walker and co-authors review circadian rhythm disruption and mental health in Translational Psychiatry. Circadian rhythms are internal cycles of about 24 hours, run by molecular clocks in the brain and reset each day by light. Signals from the master clock in the hypothalamus keep the whole body on schedule, from sleep to hormone release.

The link with mood runs both ways. Mood disorders often come with disturbed sleep and cortisol rhythms, while jet lag, night-shift work, and light at night can trigger or worsen symptoms in vulnerable people. The review draws on night-shift and jet lag studies in humans and on animal models of broken rhythms. It closes with low-cost behaviour and lifestyle changes that may steady the clock and protect mental health.
europmc-pmc7033720:
Chen and co-authors describe an early virus hunt in Emerging Microbes and Infections. In December 2019 an unusual pneumonia outbreak began in Wuhan, with many cases linked to the Huanan Seafood Market. The team studied two patients who fell ill after separate contact with that market. Both had fever, cough, and patchy ground-glass shadows across both lungs.

The researchers applied RNA metagenomic sequencing to fluid washed from the patients' lungs. The method quickly singled out a novel coronavirus as the only pathogen present, at high abundance. Its full genome runs to 29,881 nucleotides and places it in the beta-coronavirus genus. Family-tree analysis showed close kinship with coronaviruses found in horseshoe bats. The report is one of the earliest genomic identifications of the virus later known as SARS-CoV-2.
europmc-pmc7056920:
Weber and co-authors ask where the ketogenic diet stands in cancer care in Molecular Metabolism. Cancer remains a worldwide public health challenge, and complementary approaches that strengthen standard therapy are scarce. The ketogenic diet is high in fat, low in carbohydrate, and adequate in protein. It appears to exploit the reprogrammed metabolism of cancer cells, making them more sensitive to treatment.

The review critically weighs preclinical and clinical evidence and explains mechanisms that might account for anti-tumour effects. Creating an unfavourable metabolic environment for cancer cells is the core idea. Most animal studies and several clinical ones support combining the diet with chemotherapy or radiotherapy, citing stronger tumour effects, good tolerability, and better quality of life. The authors remain careful: ketone bodies can sometimes act as tumour fuel. They call for more molecular studies and uniformly controlled trials before the diet takes a defined clinical role.
europmc-pmc7072120:
Chow and Chin review inflammation in osteoarthritis in Mediators of Inflammation. Osteoarthritis is a chronic, disabling joint disease that mainly strikes the elderly and affects around 250 million people worldwide. It was once framed as simple wear and tear. Evidence now puts inflammation near the centre of how the disease develops.

Mechanical stress on a joint triggers the release of early inflammatory messengers such as interleukin-1 beta. Those signals switch on pathways including NF-kappaB, PI3K/AKT, and MAPK, which generate still more inflammatory molecules. Enzymes such as the collagenase MMP-13 then chew through the joint's extracellular matrix, the scaffolding that gives cartilage its strength. As the matrix fails, the joint's structure and function deteriorate. The review assembles the studies behind each link in that chain, from chemokines that recruit trouble to the enzymes that finish the demolition.
europmc-pmc7118120:
Revez and co-authors report a genome-wide association study of vitamin D blood levels in 417,580 Europeans, in Nature Communications. Vitamin D deficiency is suspected as a risk factor for many illnesses, but cause and effect are tangled. The team scanned the genome for variants tied to the standard vitamin D measure, 25-hydroxyvitamin D.

They found 143 independent loci in 112 regions. Implicated genes deal with fat and lipoprotein handling, skin properties, and chemical processing of vitamin D itself. Follow-up analysis found no robust evidence that vitamin D levels cause the candidate outcomes tested, such as body mass or psychiatric disorders. Instead, many traits appear to push vitamin D levels up or down, reversing the usual assumption.
europmc-pmc7122720:
Nikolakopoulou and co-authors present CINeMA, a framework for judging confidence in network meta-analysis results, in PLoS Medicine. Network meta-analysis compares many treatments at once, combining direct trial evidence with indirect comparisons. Fewer than 1% of such analyses checked how credible their conclusions were.

CINeMA rates six domains: bias within studies, reporting bias, indirectness, imprecision, heterogeneity, and incoherence. A contribution matrix shows how much each study feeds each result, supporting the bias and indirectness judgements. Three worked examples show the method in action. The authors argue the framework makes judgements more transparent and less selective, and note it can be applied even to large, complex treatment networks with a free web tool.
europmc-pmc7139620:
Shaito and co-authors review the possible adverse effects of resveratrol, the much-studied polyphenol from grapes and wine, in the International Journal of Molecular Sciences. Resveratrol has been credited with antioxidant, anti-ageing, anti-cancer, and heart-protective actions since the French paradox reports of the early 1990s. Human trial results, though, have been mixed.

Far fewer papers examine its harms than its benefits, the authors note. Toxicity and side effects have been reported, and the best dose, one that maximises benefit without raising harm, remains unsettled. Interactions with other treatments and how the body absorbs the compound are poorly documented. The review gathers the in vitro and animal evidence and calls for long-term human safety studies.
europmc-pmc7167820:
Vestby and co-authors review bacterial biofilms and their role in disease across the body's systems, in Antibiotics. Biofilms are structured bacterial communities stuck to surfaces or tissues. Infections involving them tend to be chronic, because the resident bacteria shrug off immune attack, antibiotics, and other treatments.

The review works through biofilm diseases of the ear, heart and vessels, gut, skin, reproductive tract, airways, and urinary system. Mechanisms range from biofilm as a simple reservoir of pathogens to active drivers of inflammation. Biofilms can even form inside living cells, and their presence may contribute to cancer development. The authors conclude biofilm is part of most chronic infections, which should reshape treatment design.
europmc-pmc7169020:
Zhou and co-authors pool studies asking whether immune side effects predict benefit from checkpoint inhibitor cancer drugs, in BMC Medicine. These drugs can unleash immune attacks on healthy tissue, called immune-related adverse events. Some reports linked such events to better outcomes, but results conflicted.

Thirty studies with 4,971 patients entered the meta-analysis. Patients who developed immune side effects lived longer overall (hazard ratio 0.54) and stayed progression-free longer (hazard ratio 0.52) than those without. The pattern held across cancer types and drug classes, and for hormone-related and skin side effects and for low-grade events. The authors discuss whether the link reflects an immune system switched on strongly enough to hit both tumor and tissue.
europmc-pmc7177720:
Peet and co-authors review the role of monocytes and macrophages after a heart attack. Their article appeared in Cardiovascular Research. These immune cells arrive at the injured heart muscle in large numbers. They help clear dead cells and lay down scar tissue. That repair work is vital in the first days. But poor control of these cells can drive harmful remodeling of the heart. The result can be heart failure.

Older models split macrophages into two fixed types. One type drives inflammation, and the other drives repair. Newer work shows far more variety and change in these cells. The authors weigh mouse studies against human data. They also ask why broad immune suppression has failed in trials. Targeted treatment will need a finer grasp of cell states, they argue. Readers get a clear account of a fast-changing field and its stakes for care after heart attack.
europmc-pmc7251120:
Gao and co-authors build a drug delivery system disguised as a macrophage, a type of immune cell, to treat atherosclerosis. Their study appeared in Nature Communications. Atherosclerosis is the buildup of plaques inside arteries, and it drives much vascular disease. Standard drug treatment for it has limited effect.

The team coated drug-carrying nanoparticles with macrophage membrane. The coating hides the particles from the body's cleanup system and guides them to inflamed tissue. There, reactive oxygen species trigger release of the drug payload. The membrane also soaks up inflammatory cytokines, calming local inflammation. In their tests this combined action worked better than using living macrophages as carriers, suggesting membrane coating is the more practical route for inflamed tissue.
europmc-pmc7277420:
Choi, Hui and Wan measure depression and anxiety among Hong Kong residents three months into the COVID-19 pandemic. Their population study appeared in the International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health. Five hundred randomly recruited respondents completed standard questionnaires for depression and anxiety, plus questions about the pandemic.

Nineteen percent met the cutoff for depression and 14% for anxiety. A quarter, 25.4%, said their mental health had worsened since the pandemic began. Worry about catching the virus, not having enough surgical masks, and being unable to work from home were all linked to poorer mental health. Not having lived through the SARS outbreak of 2003 also mattered. The authors recommend brief home-based psychological support for the public.
europmc-pmc7297120:
Esbin and co-authors rapidly review alternative nucleic acid tests for COVID-19, aiming to break the testing bottleneck. Their review appeared in RNA. The standard CDC test is sensitive but takes several hours, heavy labor, scarce machines, and extraction kits that could run short. Finding the true scope of the pandemic demanded far more testing.

Papers appeared within weeks proposing comparable reagents, simpler protocols, and new detection approaches. The authors collect those advances, including preprints not yet peer-reviewed, and warn readers to validate results in their own laboratories. Consolidating the options quickly, they hope, will help laboratories design faster, cheaper testing that holds up in accuracy while supplies and machines are stretched.
europmc-pmc7305320:
Hu and co-authors review the state of the art in therapeutic siRNA, drugs made of small interfering RNA that silence specific genes. Their review appeared in Signal Transduction and Targeted Therapy. RNA interference can in principle switch off any disease gene by matching its sequence. Two decades after its discovery, two siRNA drugs, patisiran and givosiran, had won approval.

Dosing can be quarterly or even twice yearly, unlike most small molecules and antibodies. The hard problems were delivery: getting fragile RNA safely into the right tissues, and improving activity, stability, and specificity without off-target effects. The authors trace chemical modifications and delivery platforms, especially sugar-tagged conjugates aimed at the liver, and summarize the latest clinical progress as a roadmap for the field.
europmc-pmc7384220:
Shang and co-authors trace how a circular RNA helps colorectal cancer spread, in Molecular Cancer. Tumor cells shed tiny parcels called exosomes, and those parcels carry circular RNAs, a recently recognized class of genetic material. One such circle, circPACRGL, caught the team's attention in cancer cell exosomes.

Exosomes from cancer cells boosted growth and movement in receiving cells while reducing their death. Sequencing pointed to circPACRGL, which works by soaking up two smaller RNAs, miR-142-3p and miR-506-3p. That releases the growth signal TGF-beta1 from restraint, completing a chain that favors tumor progression. Readers get a detailed mechanism, and a possible target: cut the chain and the parcels lose some of their power.
europmc-pmc7394020:
Binda and co-authors set out when a microbe may honestly be called a probiotic, in Frontiers in Microbiology. The FAO and WHO definition, written 19 years earlier, still stands, but labels use the word loosely. The authors translate the definition into four practical criteria for foods and supplements.

A probiotic strain must be sufficiently characterized, down to its identity. It must be safe for the intended use, and backed by at least one positive human clinical trial run to accepted standards. It must also be alive in the product at an effective dose through the end of shelf life. The paper details how to judge each test. Wide adoption, they argue, protects the word's meaning for scientists, regulators, and shoppers.
europmc-pmc7479520:
Schürch and co-authors map how cell neighborhoods at the edge of colorectal tumors shape immunity. Anti-tumor defense needs ordered contact among immune cells. The team rebuilt the CODEX imaging method for stored tissue samples.

They profiled 140 tissue regions from 35 patients with advanced colorectal cancer. Each region was read for 56 protein markers at once. Nine distinct cellular neighborhoods recurred across patients. One pattern, PD-1+ CD4+ T cells inside a granulocyte zone, linked with longer survival in high-risk patients. Broken links between tumor and immune zones marked worse outcomes. Split T cell and macrophage zones did too. The study gives a frame for reading tumor control as a joint act of cells and places.
europmc-pmc7519420:
Muñoz-Price and co-authors study racial disparities in COVID-19 incidence and outcomes in Milwaukee. The cross-sectional study covered 2595 patients in the pandemic's first weeks. It controlled for age, sex, income status, and comorbidities.

Positive tests linked with Black race, male sex, and age 60 years or older. Black race and poverty both linked with hospitalization in the cohort. Only poverty linked with intensive care unit admission, though. The authors read the pattern as a social gradient at work. Infection risk and hospital need tracked race early on. Once patients reached intensive care, poverty was the marker that mattered. The study adds local proof to national disparity reports. It points to poverty relief as part of pandemic response in cities.
europmc-pmc7547220:
Holter and co-authors link complement activation to respiratory failure in COVID-19. The complement system is a core part of innate immunity. Its overactivation was suspected to harm the lungs.

Hospital patients were studied from admission through their stay. Several complement products were raised in blood throughout. Levels stayed high over a long period. The terminal complex sC5b-9 linked to respiratory failure. That link held as a clear signal in the data. The authors argue complement may drive lung harm. Blocking complement is proposed as a treatment route. The work gives early evidence from systemic blood measures in patients.
europmc-pmc7574920:
Dao Thi and co-authors develop a colorimetric RT-LAMP test and LAMP sequencing for SARS-CoV-2. Large-scale testing was needed to track virus spread. Symptom-only testing misses silent carriers of the virus.

Their method amplifies viral RNA at constant temperature. A color change signals a positive result by eye. Clinical samples were used to test the assay. Sensitivity and specificity were both excellent in testing. RNA detection needs only specific short DNA pieces. That makes the test easier to scale than antibody assays. Sequencing of LAMP products adds a check on results. The approach may support repeated testing of large groups in a population.
europmc-pmc7602120:
Mellor and co-authors outline the 2020 Five Domains Model for animal welfare assessment. The model has been updated over 25 years of use. Each update adds current verified science on welfare.

The five domains are nutrition and physical environment. Health, behavioral interactions and mental state complete the set. This update adds human-animal interactions into the structure.
