It gives guidance on judging human behavior effects. Handlers, owners, vets and researchers are all covered. Harm cases include harsh acts and poor prior contact. Help cases include calm company and favored foods. Training rewards and ending deprivation also count as gains. The fuller model should improve welfare checks in practice.
europmc-pmc7664620:
Wang and co-authors review how lactic acid in tumors weakens anti-cancer immunity. Cancer cells often burn sugar fast and release lactic acid. The acid builds up around the tumor and makes its surroundings sour. Once seen as mere waste, this acid is now known to shape tumor growth.

The authors report that lactic acid blocks immune cells that attack tumors. It slows their growth and can push them into less mature states. It also switches on cells that damp down immune attack. The review ends with ideas to turn this knowledge into stronger immune therapies for cancer patients.
europmc-pmc7689420:
Goedhart and Luijsterburg present a web app for making and sharing volcano plots. Volcano plots show effect size against statistical strength for thousands of genes or proteins. Only a few points get labels, so most data in such plots stays hidden. The app aims to open that data up.

The tool, VolcaNoseR, is free and runs online in a browser. Users can build a plot, probe each point, adjust labels, and share the result with its raw data. Data can load direct from online repositories. The authors say this reuse and openness will help others mine large genome and proteome screens.
europmc-pmc7762220:
Pinto and co-authors review 3D tumor spheroids as lab models for cancer drug tests. Most drug screens still grow cancer cells flat in two dimensions. Such cultures lack cell contacts and the true tumor setting. Most drugs that shine in flat culture then fail in patients. Spheroids grow cells in balls that mimic tumors more closely.

The review covers how to build spheroids and how to judge drug effects on them. It weighs their use for screening new candidates before costly animal work. Cases with nanomedicines show how the models expose drug resistance that flat tests miss. The authors frame spheroids as a cheaper, truer step in the preclinical chain.
europmc-pmc7767220:
Cabral-Pacheco and co-authors review matrix metalloproteinases and their inhibitors in human disease. These enzymes cut almost every part of the matrix that holds tissues together. That cutting serves growth, vessel forming, and repair. When enzyme levels go wrong, the matrix breaks down in abnormal ways.

A natural inhibitor family, the TIMPs, keeps these enzymes in check. The balance between the two sets steers cell growth, death, and vessel growth. When it tips, chronic disease, diabetes complications, nerve degeneration, and cancer can follow. The review details key pairs such as MMP-2 with TIMP-1. It closes with current plans for drugs that block these enzymes.
europmc-pmc7779020:
Chang and co-authors describe BRENDA in 2021, the main database for enzyme function and metabolism data. BRENDA began in 1987. In 2018 it became an ELIXIR Core Data Resource.

The database holds over 5 million data points. They cover about 90 000 enzymes from about 13 000 organisms. Curators drew them from about 157 000 primary papers. Text mining, data integration, and prediction tools add more content. Supplements cover disease data, sequences, structures, and kinetics. Pathway maps were fully revised for easier interactive use. A new 3D structure viewer was added. A tool called EnzymeDetector now merges BRENDA notes with genome databases to find enzymes.
europmc-pmc7861720:
Monson writes on the factors that shape occlusion, the meeting of the teeth. The paper was read before the National Dental Association in August 1921. It was reprinted in 1922 and carried in The Dental Register. Full denture work is his opening theme. He notes how often it ends in grief.

Technical skill, he argues, steadily removes that grief. Impressions and looks each get their craft. Yet deeper factors govern how false teeth meet and work. Bite balance decides comfort and function over years. The article presses dentists to weigh those factors early. It is a period voice for careful denture design.
europmc-pmc7916320:
Song and co-authors report a systematic review and meta-analysis of adult ADHD prevalence worldwide. Attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder was long viewed as a childhood condition. More adults are now known to carry it. Yet a current global estimate was missing. The team searched major databases for population studies of adults.

Both forms of adult ADHD grew less common with age. After adjusting for the world's age structure in 2020, persistent ADHD affected 2.58% of adults. Symptomatic ADHD, counted with or without a childhood start, affected 6.76%. Those rates mean about 139.84 million and 366.33 million adults in turn. The authors call for a clear shared strategy for diagnosis. They also urge larger studies of how the condition is spread across populations.
europmc-pmc7919320:
Zhang and co-authors present a review of single-cell RNA sequencing in cancer research. The method reads the gene activity of single cells in a complex tissue. It can expose differences between cells that bulk tests blur. It also finds new cell types and markers. The review explains the method's principles and its main uses in tumour work.

Tumours are mosaics, and the method maps that variety cell by cell. It can track how a tumour develops over time. Applied to immune cells in a tumour, it sorts their types and shows how they escape attack or resist drugs. It also reveals how tumour cells talk with their non-malignant neighbours. The authors expect the method to bring major gains to cancer research and care.
europmc-pmc7931820:
Bonfield and co-authors present a software paper on HTSlib, a library for reading and writing sequencing data. Files in formats such as SAM and VCF are the raw stock of genomics. Many tools must open, write, and index them fast. HTSlib grew out of the SAMtools code to give programs one robust way to do that work.

The library adds newer access routes and support for the compact CRAM format. Indexing, iteration, and threading have all improved. A basic read-write loop now runs 5 times faster than in the old release. Format conversion runs 13 times faster. The library has been downloaded more than 1 million times. An estimated 900 projects on GitHub use it directly. Bindings extend it to Perl, Python, Rust, and R. The authors present it as shared plumbing for the field.
europmc-pmc7963220:
White and co-authors report a preclinical study of the drug plitidepsin against SARS-CoV-2. Most antiviral hunts aim at the virus's own proteins. This drug aims at a host protein instead: eEF1A, part of the cell's protein-making machinery. The virus needs that machinery to copy itself. Hitting a host target may be harder for the virus to dodge.

In cells, the drug proved far more potent than remdesivir, the standard comparison drug. It did so with limited harm to the cells. Given before infection, it protected mice against the virus. The authors argue the drug merits trials as a treatment. Host-targeted drugs could also serve against future coronaviruses, they note. Three such viruses have reached humans in the past 20 years. The study widens the search beyond the virus itself.
europmc-pmc7979820:
Garcia-Martinez and co-authors present a review of epigenetic mechanisms in breast cancer therapy and resistance. Most breast cancers carry the estrogen receptor, and drugs against that path are the main treatment. Hormone therapy has worked since the 1940s. Yet resistance arises in many patients, and the disease returns. The review asks what part chemical marks on DNA and its packaging play in that failure.

Fresh studies show the mark landscape shifts as resistance forms. Factors that place or erase the marks help set the resistant state. Because the marks are reversible, they tempt drug designers. Blocking the mark machinery may restore the power of hormone drugs. The authors weigh which factors look most promising as targets. The review argues the epigenome is a core part of treatment response, not a sideshow.
europmc-pmc8036620:
McSweeney and co-authors consolidate what is known about cisplatin-induced acute kidney injury. Cisplatin is a potent chemotherapy, approved in 1978 and used against many cancers. Kidney damage is its dose-limiting harm. The injury can ease, yet signs linger years after treatment ends. No drug reliably prevents it. The authors blame the tangled map of causes.

The review walks through each mechanism in turn. Cellular uptake and efflux, apoptosis, and vascular injury all play roles. Oxidative stress, endoplasmic reticulum stress, and inflammation join them. For every mechanism, the authors list the drugs tested against it. They report what each trial or study found. Genetic modification studies close the survey. Some gene changes blunted the disease in models, hinting at future shields.
europmc-pmc8100220:
d'Enfert and co-authors review how Candida albicans turns from quiet tenant to invader. The fungus lives harmlessly in the mouth, gut, and genital tract of most people. Local bacteria, tissue barriers, and immune defenses keep it in check. Disturb that balance and it overgrows. The result ranges from mouth and vaginal infections to deadly bloodstream spread.

Three players drive the switch, and the review tracks them all. Fungal traits vary between strains, and some isolates hit harder than others. Host immunity differs by body site and by person. Gut, mouth, and vaginal bacteria shift with diet, drugs, and hormones. Each shift changes fungal growth and the immune reply to it. The stakes are plain: most women face vaginal candidiasis at least once. Invasive fungal disease kills over a million people a year worldwide. Tailored antifungal care is the authors' goal.
europmc-pmc8126720:
Basu and co-authors review how T helper cell subsets tip cancer immunotherapy toward success or failure. Helper cells can attack tumors directly in some settings. More often they prime killer T cells to do the work. Other helper subsets shield the tumor instead. The tumor milieu hosts this tug of war daily. Dendritic cells start the helpful arm by waking TH1 cells.

TH1 help then arms CD8 killers against the cancer. TH2 activity pulls the other way, calming the attack. TH9 and follicular helper cells add immune support. Regulatory T cells suppress the whole response by design. TH17 cells play both sides depending on context. Newer work shows TH1 cells can target neoantigens directly. Current therapies already reshape these balances in patients. The authors argue for designing with the balance in mind. Blocking escape routes starts with knowing the scale.
europmc-pmc8261820:
Yang and co-authors chart the signal pathways behind cytokine storm in COVID-19 and its treatment. Immune misfiring seems to drive much of the disease's harm. The cytokine storm floods the body with pro-inflammatory signals.

Storm patients often show lymphopenia and delayed type I interferon responses. Monocytes and macrophages lose their normal control too. High cytokine output tracks with poor prognosis. The review maps the pathways that feed the storm. It then sorts treatments aimed at those paths. Blocking the right signal at the right time is the shared goal. The right drug at the wrong phase could backfire.
europmc-pmc8262720:
Adasme and co-authors extend the PLIP interaction profiler to DNA and RNA targets. Protein structure data keep growing, and interaction analysis grows with them. PLIP detects and displays how ligands bind their targets.

Over 7% of Protein Data Bank structures include DNA or RNA. The 2021 release now reads those complexes too. It serves docking checks and study of new complexes alike. Output comes in formats ready for further work. Drugs that target DNA or RNA-binding proteins gain a tool. The update widens one profiler to most biomolecular targets. Interaction lists export cleanly for pipeline use.
europmc-pmc8369920:
Reed and co-authors give a broad review of type 2 diabetes, a metabolic disease now at pandemic scale. The disease rests on weak insulin secretion and weak insulin action. The review covers how common it is, what causes it, and how it harms the body.

Much of the focus falls on GLP-1, a gut hormone that boosts insulin release after meals. Natural GLP-1 fades fast, so long-lasting GLP-1 mimetics were built and now treat the disease well. The authors report that these drugs also ease some later complications and cause weight loss. Newer drugs hit two or three hormone receptors at once. The review closes with future treatment paths.
europmc-pmc8566220:
Mlcochova and co-authors study how the Delta variant of SARS-CoV-2 copies itself and dodges immunity. Delta was first found in Maharashtra in late 2020. It spread through India and outran the Kappa and Alpha lineages. Its speed raised two questions: growth and escape.

In lab tests, Delta was far less sensitive to antibodies from recovered patients and vaccine users. Its spike also resisted many lab-made antibodies. Delta copied itself faster than Alpha in airway models. Its spike sat in a mostly cleaved state, ready to fuse cells. That fusion was harder for antibodies to block. The authors tie these traits to Delta's rapid spread.
europmc-pmc8604720:
Choi and co-authors report interim results from a trial of variant mRNA vaccine boosters in healthy adults. Participants had two doses of mRNA-1273 about six months before. New virus variants raised doubts about how well the first shots still worked. The study tested the old vaccine and variant-tuned forms as a single booster.

Four booster groups held 20 people each. Antibody levels against the first virus form had waned by booster day. Levels against beta, gamma, and delta were low or not found. All boosters were safe and well tolerated. Each one raised antibody levels against the first virus form. The variant forms also raised levels against the variants they targeted.
europmc-pmc8700820:
Stojkov and co-authors review how the structure of hydrogels shapes their flow behavior, or rheology, across uses. Hydrogels serve many industries, from medicine to food. Their makeup can vary widely by recipe. That range yields gels with distinct strength and flow traits.

Knowing how structure drives flow is key to picking the right gel. The review links chemical structure to measured flow traits in detail. It describes common tests, such as time, temperature, and frequency sweeps. Results from those tests are reported for many gel types. The authors then cover the most common uses of hydrogels. Each use is tied back to the flow traits it needs.
europmc-pmc8789820:
Yoo and co-authors show how focused ultrasound excites cortical neurons through force-sensitive calcium channels. Ultrasound could one day steer deep brain activity without surgery or drugs. How it excites mammalian neurons was not clear. The team tested cultured mouse cortical neurons with sound pulses and channel blockers.

Excitation came mainly from a mechanical effect. Sound opened calcium-selective channels that sense force. Calcium then built up in steps and was amplified by other channels. That chain produced a burst of firing. Cavitation, heat, and cell contacts were not required. Blocking the key channels cut the response, and adding more raised it.
europmc-pmc8833520:
Van den Boogaard, Komninos, and Vermeij argue that not all chemotherapy damage is alike. Cancer survival keeps rising, for children and adults alike. Survivors, though, often face lasting side effects later in life. Many show signs of faster aging. Most chemotherapy drugs work by damaging DNA. The review asks how each kind of damage leads to harm.

Different drugs leave different lesions in DNA. Where a drug travels and how the body clears it also matter. So does the organ and cell type it reaches. The authors sort side effects seen in survivors by these factors. They build a framework linking drug class to organ harm. The goal is care that weighs cure against long-term cost.
europmc-pmc8891020:
Brown and co-authors show how ALS risk variants and TDP-43 loss combine to drain a vital synaptic gene. The gene is UNC13A, central to synapse function. Its variants raise risk of ALS and frontotemporal dementia. Both diseases feature TDP-43 leaving the cell nucleus. The team asked what TDP-43 loss does to UNC13A. Depleting TDP-43 triggered heavy cryptic exon inclusion. The faulty RNA was then destroyed. UNC13A protein fell as a result.

Two common variants sit where TDP-43 binds. Both variants strengthen the cryptic splicing. The effect showed in cultured cells. It also showed in patient brains and spinal cords. The authors frame a clear mechanism. Genetic risk magnifies the harm of TDP-43 loss. They offer the pathway as a drug target. It could serve a whole class of TDP-43 diseases.
europmc-pmc9008420:
Qi and co-authors build a silver-coated gel dressing that uses light and heat to fight wound infection. The base particle is polydopamine, a bio-inspired material. Plain versions convert light to heat weakly. Growing silver on the particle surface changed that. The team set the particles in a charged guar gum gel. The gel keeps particles from clumping. Its surface groups also grab bacteria on contact. Heat and capture then work as a team.

The tuned gel hit a heat conversion rate of 38.2%. That is more than double the plain particle rate. Tests in dishes showed strong bacteria killing. Tests in animals matched the dish results. Wounds healed faster under the dressing. The authors call the design a simple boost for this material class. No antibiotic drug is involved. That matters as drug resistance spreads.
europmc-pmc9019120:
Dempsey and Corr review how Lactobacillus bacteria may support gut health. These lactic acid producers are popular probiotics, and evidence links some strains to real benefits. The authors examine how the bacteria strengthen the gut barrier, fight infections, and calm inflammation. Effects vary by strain and by person, which makes studies hard to compare.

The review weighs what is known about the ways these effects arise. It also stresses the need for trials that pin down which strains help with which conditions. Used with care, the authors argue, Lactobacillus products remain a promising support for digestive health.
europmc-pmc9204620:
Ricciuti and co-authors link high tumor mutation burden to better outcomes of PD-L1 blockade in lung cancer. The study asks whether mutation count predicts benefit across all PD-L1 levels. Non-small cell lung cancer often responds unevenly to these immune drugs. A clear extra marker would help doctors choose treatment.

The cohort held 1,552 patients whose tumors had genomic profiling. Patients with high mutation burden had better response rates and survival after PD-1 or PD-L1 therapy. The edge held across every PD-L1 expression subgroup. High burden tumors also held more CD8-positive T cells and stronger immune gene signatures. The authors say mutation burden marks tumors already primed for immune attack.
europmc-pmc9225620:
Abka-Khajouei and co-authors review the structures, properties, and applications of alginates. Alginate is a hydrocolloid from brown algae and from some bacteria. It is built from two acids, mannuronic and guluronic, in varied patterns. Those patterns shape its physical and chemical traits.

Sodium alginate is the best-known member of the family and forms useful hydrogels. Uses span food, medicine, tissue engineering, wastewater treatment, and fuel. It is generally recognized as safe under good practice. The review details how monomer order affects gel strength and behavior. Sources range from kelp to soil bacteria. Readers get a full account of a versatile natural polymer and its many roles.
europmc-pmc9439720:
Byrska-Bishop and co-authors present high-coverage genome sequencing for the expanded 1000 Genomes Project cohort. The project is the largest open set of whole-genome data with no use limits. Its phase 3 release held 2,504 unrelated samples from 26 populations. Most of that data was low coverage.

The new resource covers 3,202 samples sequenced to a depth of 30X. It adds 602 complete parent-child trios. The team called single-letter variants and short insertions and deletions. Structural variants were built by merging methods through a machine learning model. Calls beat phase 3 on sensitivity and precision, most for rare variants. An improved reference panel for imputation came out of the work. That panel makes the new variants usable in association studies.
europmc-pmc9455620:
Yau and co-authors pool patient data to test residual cancer burden after chemotherapy in breast cancer. The RCB score grades cancer left after drug treatment before surgery. Single studies had tied it to outlook. Whether it held across subtypes and settings needed a bigger test.

The analysis merged data from 12 institutes and trials. It covered 5161 patients who had chemotherapy before surgery. Median follow-up ran to 56 months, with 1164 event-free survival events. Higher RCB scores meant worse event-free survival in every subtype. The link held after adjusting for age, grade, and stage factors. Hazard ratios per unit of score ranged from 1.52 to 2.09 in adjusted models. The authors back RCB as a broad prognosis tool.
europmc-pmc9556320:
Garvey and co-authors report two-year effects of semaglutide in the STEP 5 trial. The trial tested weekly semaglutide against placebo in adults with obesity or overweight plus a weight linked condition. No participant had diabetes. Both arms got behavior support as well.

A total of 304 participants were assigned, split evenly between arms. At week 104, the semaglutide group had lost far more weight than the placebo group. The gap between the arms was wide and held across the two years. Far more drug treated participants reached a loss of 5% or more. Gut side effects came more often with the drug than with placebo. Most such events were mild to moderate in grade. The authors call the weight loss substantial and sustained. The trial backs long term use for weight control.
europmc-pmc9825520:
Nassar and co-authors report the UCSC Genome Browser database in its 2023 update. The browser gathers omics data into one graphical viewer. It now enters its twenty-third year of service. Over a million users visit it each year worldwide.

Clinical data took center stage in this year's work. New tracks and ready track sets landed on the main human build. A single cell track group joined the browser as well. The virus sequence tree passed 12 million placed sequences. The GenArk archive grew past 2,500 assembly hubs. Users can request assemblies that are still missing. New chart displays widen how tracks can be drawn. A naming bridge eased showing custom annotations. Makers of new data got fresh tools for their tracks. The team also expanded chart types for repeat data.
fenton-s-quest-pg11720:
Braddon again: Fenton's Quest is M. E. Braddon's sensation novel, kept here in the uniform edition that lists forty-five of her novels in print. The chapter heads name the cast and the turns of the plot. John Saltram steps forward early. Then come Halcyon Days, a Sentence of Exile, a farewell, and a chapter called Missing. Jacob Nowell enters as the search goes on.

The middle of the book finds the lover near the Grange, in a garden where the chrysanthemums have withered. He tells himself he must put away all selfish, vengeful thoughts. If his rival loves his darling as he does, he will fall back into the shade of her life, glad to be her brother and friend. The scene states the book's knot: a love that must yield, and a quest that will not.
fitzgerald-flappers-and-philosophers-192:
F. Scott Fitzgerald published Flappers and Philosophers in 1920, riding the instant success of his first novel. The eight stories had mostly run in The Saturday Evening Post, which paid him handsomely. Together they form the flapper canon in its first collected form.

Bernice Bobs Her Hair turns a dull cousin's visit into a small war of popularity, ending with scissors. The Offshore Pirate sails a rich girl into a staged romance that turns real. Other tales cover icy debutantes, headstrong boys, and young people testing every rule their parents kept. Fitzgerald's dialogue sparkles, but regret already shadows the fun. The book defined the Jazz Age heroine for America.
fitzgerald-this-side-of-paradise-1920:
F. Scott Fitzgerald published This Side of Paradise in 1920, when he was twenty-three and fresh out of the army. The novel grew from his Princeton years and his courtship of Zelda Sayre. It sold out its first printing in days and made him the spokesman of his generation.

Amory Blaine, handsome and self-absorbed, drifts through prep school, Princeton, and the war, falling in and out of love and ambition. The book mixes prose, verse, and play script with youthful confidence. Amory ends poorer, sadder, and beginning to understand himself. Fitzgerald named a generation's restlessness here and invented the Jazz Age novel in the process.
frus-1861-d120:
Charles Faulkner, the outgoing American minister to France, wrote to Secretary of State Jeremiah Black on 19 March 1861. The letter is document 120 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

Faulkner wrote in the last days of the Buchanan order in Paris. Within weeks Seward would replace Black, and Dayton would replace Faulkner. The letter marks the old guard handing over the most delicate post in Europe as the Union split. Faulkner's Virginia roots made his loyalty a point of talk in that tense spring. Loyalty in that spring was a coin whose worth each man's acts would fix.
frus-1861-d20:
Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote to Henry Sanford on 26 March 1861. Sanford was the new American minister to Belgium, based in Brussels. The letter is document 20 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

Sanford was an eager, well connected envoy who made Brussels a listening post for the Union. Seward's March letter belongs to the first set of orders sent to Lincoln's new men abroad. It set the terms on which Sanford would watch Europe for the Union cause. Sanford later raised funds and arms for the Union on his own bold account.
frus-1861-d220:
Guidance for Mr. Marsh left Washington on 20 September 1861, signed by William H. Seward. The printed record keeps it as Document 220 in the President's message volume for 1861. The date falls in the first summer of the Civil War, when the Union fought to keep foreign powers from backing the South.

Outbound letters like this one told the envoy what line to take and what to report back. Its worth grows in context, as one link in a chain of letters that kept the peace with Europe. The State Department's Office of the Historian keeps the series, called Foreign Relations of the United States.
frus-1862-d120:
Secretary of State William H. Seward sent a dispatch to Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London on 4 August 1862. The printed record keeps it as Document 120 in the 1862 Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs volume. It belongs to the summer of 1862, the war's second year, when keeping Europe out of the war was a core task for Washington.

Outbound letters like this one told the envoy what line to take and what to report back. For students of the war, the value lies in the sequence: one dated step in a long exchange. The Foreign Relations series, kept by the State Department's Office of the Historian, preserves the full run.
frus-1862-d20:
Guidance for Charles Francis Adams left Washington on 17 February 1862, signed by William H. Seward. The printed record keeps it as Document 20 in the 1862 Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs volume. It belongs to the winter of the war's second year, when keeping Europe out of the war was a core task for Washington.

Outbound letters like this one told the envoy what line to take and what to report back. For students of the war, the value lies in the sequence: one dated step in a long exchange. Foreign Relations of the United States, the official record series, is where the full exchange can be traced.
frus-1862-d220:
William Stuart answered on 25 June 1862 with a letter to Secretary of State William H. Seward, printed as Document 220 in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. Stuart was acting head of the British legation during Lord Lyons's absence.

A stand-in envoy walks a fine line, firm for his government yet careful not to commit it too far. Stuart's letters show that care in formal, measured prose. His reply came as the Seven Days battles opened outside Richmond. News that soon reached Washington and sharpened every question between the two governments that summer. Cases under such notes were often small: one ship, one prisoner, one point of form.
frus-1862-d320:
William L. Dayton reported from Paris on 28 August 1862 in a letter printed as Document 320 of the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. It went to Secretary of State William H. Seward in Washington.

Dayton wrote on the first day of the second Bull Run battle, in a Paris still working from July's picture of the war. His report adds the French court's reading at the very moment the facts were changing across the ocean. Papers like this one, filed late in the volume, reward readers who follow dates rather than document order. French mills wanted Southern cotton, and French yards watched the Union blockade with care.
frus-1862-d420:
From the American legation in Madrid, Horace J. Perry wrote to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 25 May 1862. The dispatch is Document 420 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs.

Late May brought word of Union advances in Virginia and the West, and Perry's job was to make that news count in Spain. Spanish officials also had to weigh France's deepening grip on Mexico, next door to their own stake in the Americas. Reports of this kind gave the State Department its picture of Madrid's mood. They are worth reading as the ground-level half of a conversation whose other half is Seward's string of instructions.
frus-1862-d520:
Two days after Antietam, on 19 September 1862, Secretary of State William H. Seward addressed this instruction to James Shepherd Pike. It is Document 520 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the official record.

Seward wrote before the battle's full result was known in Washington, let alone its meaning abroad. His orders in that week kept to first principles: the Union would win, foreign interference was unwelcome, and neutral duties must be honored. Pike at The Hague would soon have better news to use, including Lincoln's emancipation order of 22 September. The dispatch catches the correspondence mid-turn, as the autumn's new facts began their slow journey into every legation's instructions.
frus-1862-d620:
Jacob S. Haldeman, the American minister at Stockholm, sent this report to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 10 December 1861. It is Document 620 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, opening the Swedish file.

Haldeman served the joint kingdom of Sweden and Norway, a poor, seafaring north whose people were then emigrating to America in growing numbers. His December report reached Washington in the Trent winter, when every court's attitude was being tallied. Sweden's sympathy for the Union was genuine and its weight small, a combination that made for pleasant, undemanding correspondence. The letter begins the volume's Scandinavian file, the far edge of the Department's European map.
frus-1862-d720:
On 6 November 1862, Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote to Friedrich Hassaurek, the American minister in Ecuador. The letter is document 720 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1862, the last paper in this part of the volume. It answers Hassaurek's dispatch of early October.

Seward's reply closed the Ecuador file for the year in the printed record. His outward letters set the brief for each post; for a far Pacific legation, they also carried the news of home that an envoy needed. This one shows the full span of the State Department's reach in 1862. It ran from the courts of Europe to a lone post high in the Andes.
frus-1863p1-d120:
William H. Seward sent this second letter of 16 March 1863 to Charles Francis Adams in London. Adams was the American minister there. The letter is document 120 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863.

The second sheet of the day took the next head of the brief in line. Seward's points for London were the war's points in Europe: fair dealing, the blockade's rights, and the warships in British yards. This letter holds its slice of that work. In the row of four it is a mid-piece, and its worth is in the row as much as in itself.
frus-1863p1-d20:
On 25 December 1862, Charles Francis Adams wrote to Secretary of State William H. Seward from London. A Christmas Day dispatch is a fair sign of how full the legation's plate was. The letter is document 20 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863.

Adams closed the year with reports on the ground he had held: Britain had not backed the South, and its government trod with care. His letters also tracked the press and the public mood, which Seward weighed with the cabinet's acts. This dispatch ends the 1862 run of the London file in the volume, a quiet cap to a year of strain.
frus-1863p1-d220:
To guide his minister in London, Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote these orders on 22 June 1863 to Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London. They stand as document 220 of the 1863 volume. The document comes from the Foreign Relations of the United States, the government's own published record of Civil War diplomacy.

Adams was told to deal chiefly with Lord John Russell, the foreign secretary. Seward's letters armed him with facts and wording for those meetings. Kept with the rest of the 1863 papers, it forms part of the fullest record of how the Union handled its most dangerous foreign relationship.
frus-1863p1-d320:
To Mr. Stuart of the British legation in Washington, Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote on 12 November 1862. The note is document 320 in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume. The letter is printed in Foreign Relations of the United States, the official series that publishes American diplomatic papers.

The questions reaching the British legation were the war's daily friction: stopped ships, seized cargoes, arrested men, and the rights of a neutral flag. Stuart's letters deal with that traffic. Set in its place in the volume, it helps readers trace how two governments talked their way past repeated crises.
frus-1863p1-d420:
Washington's business with Britain on 23 March 1863 included this note from Secretary of State William H. Seward to Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington. The paper is document 420 of the 1863 volume. The text is preserved in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume, which gathered the year's diplomatic mail for Congress and the public.

Notes on this route often dealt with single ships, single cargoes, or single men. Small cases mattered, because each one tested what neutrality would allow. Kept with the rest of the 1863 papers, it forms part of the fullest record of how the Union handled its most dangerous foreign relationship.
frus-1863p1-d520:
William H. Seward, Secretary of State sent an official note to Britain's minister in Washington, Lord Lyons on 20 May 1863. The letter sits in the published record of how the Lincoln government handled foreign affairs in the spring of 1863. The printed volume gathers the year's diplomatic mail so Congress and the public could see it.

A reader gets the feel of diplomacy done by hand: formal greetings, careful wording, and hard points pressed without open threats. Confederate warships built in British yards were a sore point all year. Washington pressed London to stop them, and letters like this carried that pressure. The volume's editors printed it without comment; its meaning comes from the company it keeps in the file.
frus-1863p1-d620:
William H. Seward, the Secretary of State sent an official note to William Stuart, the British chargé d'affaires in Washington on 16 September 1863. With Lyons away from Washington, Stuart kept the British side of the correspondence going through the autumn of 1863. It appears in Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the State Department volume printed with the President's annual message for 1863.

What the page shows is process, not drama. Claims, protests, and replies moved back and forth until small disputes stayed small. Single letters rarely settle anything here. Their worth is in the chain they form, which lets a reader watch a dispute rise, cool, and fade in real time. The volume's editors printed it without comment; its meaning comes from the company it keeps in the file.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d120: Stalin wrote to Roosevelt on November 12, 1943, and a second Stalin letter of the same date follows it in the volume. This one is Document 120 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. Two letters in a day from Moscow, as the president sailed, suggests urgent or divided business, though the record names no topic for either. Both are printed in the Foreign Relations series.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d20: T. V. Soong, China's Minister of Foreign Affairs, wrote to Harry Hopkins, the President's special assistant, on June 21, 1943. The message is Document 20 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. Hopkins was Roosevelt's closest aide, and foreign envoys often worked through him. The catalog's title carries no date; its older note supplies June 21. No topic is recorded, so the note's errand must be read in the printed Foreign Relations text.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d220:
Ambassador Laurence Steinhardt cabled Washington from Ankara on 14 November 1943, in telegram 1871, sent an hour after his previous report that day. It carries one hopeful signal from the Soviet ambassador in Ankara, Sergey Vinogradov, about Turkey's fears of Russia.

Vinogradov had told Foreign Minister Numan that if Turkey's worry was only about excessive Soviet demands in the Balkans, and not a general mistrust, a fair settlement should be easy to find. Numan answered that if Ankara could be sure Russia held no ambitions in the Balkans, the two countries could resume the cordial, close friendship they had shared for many years. The cable was repeated to Moscow.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d320:
The British Chiefs of Staff issued paper C.C.S. 408/1 at Cairo on 26 November 1943, answering the American proposal for a supreme commander over all operations against Germany. After careful study, they state at once that on military grounds they profoundly disagree.

Total war, they argue, is not a military affair alone. Nearly every big problem carries political, economic, and domestic weight. The commander would have to consult both governments on almost everything. He would become an extra link deciding only minor matters. The Foch parallel from the last war fails, since Foch never held so many fronts. They also attack the clause letting the Combined Chiefs reverse his orders, warning of troops marching on orders later countermanded in confusion.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d420:
John Jernegan, third secretary of the American embassy in Iran, wrote to Major John Henry at Tehran on 3 December 1943. Henry was General Hurley's aide. The letter sets down the main facts behind the Declaration on Iran, signed two days before, as far as Jernegan's knowledge ran. It is the fullest inside account of how that document came to be.

Prime Minister Soheily asked Eden and Dreyfus on 29 November for a joint statement covering Iran's help in the war, the treaty pledges of independence, and her economic needs. Hurley won British agreement, and Dreyfus supplied the draft, shortened from Jernegan's own. The Soviets hung back until Roosevelt made a strong personal request of Stalin on 1 December and Stalin consented. That night the draft was accepted with small changes, signed at the final session's end, and shown to Foreign Minister Saed, who initialed a copy and agreed to hold its release.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d520:
President Roosevelt wrote to Brendan Bracken, Britain's Minister of Information, on December 18, 1943. Bracken was one of Churchill's closest friends and ran Britain's wartime information and propaganda effort. The letter appears in the State Department's Cairo-Tehran conference volume.

A letter from an American president to a British cabinet minister outside the usual chain shows the personal web that bound the two governments. Bracken stood near the center of Churchill's circle, and Roosevelt knew the value of that friendship. For readers, the message is a reminder that the alliance was held together by personal ties as well as by treaties, staffs, and formal notes.
frus-1944-quebec-d120:
In telegram 780, sent the same evening as his personal appeal, Churchill forwarded Roosevelt the text of a War Cabinet message to Moscow. The British government had cabled the Soviet leadership about Warsaw on September 4, 1944. Churchill wanted the president to see exactly what London had said before the Quebec Conference.

The message told Moscow that British public opinion was deeply moved by Warsaw's suffering. It said people could not understand why no material help had reached the Poles, or why Soviet-held airfields were closed to American aircraft. If the Poles were overwhelmed within days, the shock would be incalculable. The refusal, London said, clashed with the spirit of Allied cooperation.
frus-1944-quebec-d20:
President Roosevelt replied to Prime Minister Churchill on August 8, 1944. The message appears in the State Department's Quebec 1944 volume, among the letters preparing the September conference.

Roosevelt answered from a Washington intoxicated by victory in France yet facing hard choices: how fast to press Germany, how to treat liberated France, and how to supply the final campaigns. His August letters to Churchill mixed command decisions with the politics of the alliance. For readers, this reply shows the President setting the terms on which the two leaders would meet at Quebec a month later.
frus-1944-quebec-d220:
Roosevelt's memorandum of September 20, 1944, is only a few lines long. Its substance is the map attached to it, reproduced in the volume. On that map the president drew lines and notations in red, blue, and green pencil, sketching his own idea for dividing Germany after the peace.

The editors call it, in Roosevelt's words, a very rough suggestion made by him, among others, for a subdivision of Germany. The map is probably the one he was working on with three colored pencils when Morgenthau called at noon on September 15. It shows the zones question being settled not only in conference papers but in the president's own hand.
frus-1945-50-intel-d120:
The National Intelligence Authority wrote to Attorney General Clark on 8 August 1946. The board addressed the cabinet officer who oversaw the FBI, in the middle of the Latin American dispute. The text comes from the Foreign Relations of the United States volume that looks back at American intelligence work from 1945 to 1950.

A letter from the whole authority carried the combined weight of State, War, and Navy. Sent to Clark, it told the Justice Department where the board stood on the division of foreign intelligence work. Readers have reached the ruling stage of the summer's fight. The papers that follow, Hoover's protests and Leahy 's direction, show the ruling being received. Few episodes in the volume display the 1946 system working as designed so completely.
frus-1945-50-intel-d20:
Secretary of War Robert Patterson and Secretary of the Navy Forrestal wrote jointly to Secretary of State Byrnes on 29 September 1945. Two cabinet officers signing one letter is itself a signal. The text comes from the Foreign Relations of the United States volume that looks back at American intelligence work from 1945 to 1950.

The military departments wrote together because the OSS order had pushed them into a shared corner. The War Department held the spy units, the Navy its own services. Both faced a State Department newly armed with analysts. A joint letter shows the two services settling their differences to face the civilians as one. Readers see coalition building at cabinet level, the necessary first step before the long negotiation over a central intelligence system could begin.
frus-1945-50-intel-d220:
A memorandum from the Director of Central Intelligence (Hillenkoetter) reached the National Intelligence Authority on 11 September 1947. The Office of the Historian kept it as document 220 in the Foreign Relations intelligence volume for 1945 to 1950. Lawmakers were close to passing the National Security Act, which would put central intelligence on a firm legal footing.

The value of the form is its speed: a page or two, a clear ask, and a name at the top to answer for it. The note's brevity hides its weight: men at this level did not write to each other for practice. Its worth lies in the trail it leaves: a dated, signed step in the long build-up of the CIA and the Council.
frus-1945-50-intel-d320:
On 17 July 1947 the 14th Meeting of the Intelligence Advisory Board sat, and the minutes of the session survive here. The Office of the Historian kept it as document 320 in the Foreign Relations intelligence volume for 1945 to 1950. Lawmakers were close to passing the National Security Act, which would put central intelligence on a firm legal footing.

The text is the meeting as the secretaries kept it, topic by topic, with the results marked as they were reached. For a reader now, the draw is the nearness: this is the meeting as its own staff chose to keep it. Pages like this one are the bricks of the story: plain, dated, and load-bearing.
frus-1945-50-intel-d420:
On 2 May 1950, W. Park Armstrong wrote again to Under Secretary of State James Webb. The memo is document 420 in the Foreign Relations volume on American intelligence from 1945 to 1950.

By the spring of 1950 the shape of American intelligence was still open to change. The State Department's share of that work depended on aides like Armstrong making their case in writing. His May memo is one more round in a long contest over who would speak for the facts abroad. Weeks later the Korean War began, and debates like this one turned at once into wartime tasks.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d120:
President Roosevelt pushed back on the Germany planners in this private memorandum of 29 September 1944. Writing to the Secretary of State, he questions the rush to settle the treatment of German industry. The paper is printed in the Malta and Yalta volume of Foreign Relations.

No good purpose, he says, would be served by sounding out British and Russian views just now. The European Advisory Commission, in such a case, sits on a tertiary level, not even a secondary one. The real nub is keeping Britain out of complete bankruptcy when the war ends. He also attacks a leak: somebody has told the press that Germany is to be made wholly agricultural, and, he insists, no one wants that.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d20: Churchill replied to Roosevelt on 16 November 1944, two days after the president's last letter. Document 20 in the Foreign Relations volume on Malta and Yalta preserves his side of the exchange, as published by the Office of the Historian. The November letters show both men turning from campaign season toward the practical questions of where and when the Big Three would meet.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d220:
Ten billion dollars, not six: the Treasury raised Moscow's bid in this memorandum to the President of 10 January 1945. “A $10 Billion Reconstruction Credit for the U. S. S. R.” is printed in the Malta and Yalta volume. It argues that Russia can pay, chiefly in goods America lacks.

The credit would buy reconstruction goods in the United States, at two percent interest over thirty-five years. Repayment would come mainly in strategic raw materials that are short at home. Russia's means are set out in three parts. She can sell those scarce materials. She can earn dollars through tourist trade, exports, and a favorable balance with the world. And she holds a gold stock put at two billion dollars, with yearly output in the hundreds of millions.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d320:
President Roosevelt and Prime Minister Churchill joined the Combined Chiefs of Staff at Malta on February 2, 1945, to review an interim report. Roosevelt praised how much the military talks had achieved in so short a time. The leaders then went through the report paragraph by paragraph.

One clause on basic pledges drew debate. General Marshall warned about the British wording. It put supplies for freed areas on the same level as battle needs, beyond what was required to stop sickness and unrest. That shift, he argued, would change the claim those supplies had on scarce shipping and gear. The record catches a president and a prime minister doing staff work, line by line.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d420:
Bohlen left only three words for one Yalta luncheon — no notes available — and this editorial note builds what it can around them. Times and guests come from the official trip log. Admiral Leahy's memoir supplies more: the talk centered on voting procedure in the assembly of the planned world body.

Churchill, Leahy writes, agreed orally to an arrangement at that lunch. The United States, Britain, and the Soviet republics would hold equal voting power in the assembly. A mark on Hiss's notes for the afternoon plenary confirms the subject was live that day. The note shows editors squeezing a key bargain out of a memoir's single paragraph.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d120:
Charles Bohlen confirmed Ambassador Harriman's place at Berlin in a telegram sent July 4, 1945, over Secretary Byrnes's signature. The message is document 120 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. Harriman had twice asked whether the President and the Secretary wanted him at the meeting, and had heard nothing since Stettinius resigned.

Both the President and Byrnes desire him present, Bohlen writes, and he should bring Edward Page with him. Washington also thinks Harriman should reach Berlin a day or two early to look over housing and arrangements for the civilian staff. Official instructions will follow. The short cable ended the ambassador's anxious wait and put his knowledge of the Russians at Truman's service.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d20:
Truman opened the Hopkins mission in this top secret message to Stalin of May 19, 1945. He was sure Stalin shared his sense of the difficulty of dealing, by exchange of messages, with the complicated questions they faced. Pending a possible meeting, he was sending Harry Hopkins with Ambassador Harriman to Moscow. They would discuss these matters personally with Stalin.

Hopkins would return immediately to Washington to report to the President in person. They planned to arrive in Moscow about May 26. Truman asked whether that time suited Stalin. The message, sent by Navy channels, revived Roosevelt's most trusted channel for the hardest errand of the spring.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d220:
The British Chiefs of Staff laid out the daily rhythm for the staff talks in a memorandum dated July 15, 1945. The paper, C.C.S. 880/9, is document 220 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. It was drawn up at Babelsberg as the delegations gathered.

Following past practice, each side's chiefs would hold their own meetings in the morning. The Combined Chiefs of Staff would meet together at 2:30 in the afternoon. The attached program runs four days. First come the Japanese situation and Pacific operations. Then come British participation and command questions. Next come basic objectives and other nations' roles. Last come the directive to the Southeast Asia commander, Russian participation, and the planning date for the war's end. An editor's note lists the subjects the Soviet delegation asked to add when Truman met Stalin.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d320:
Finland is the subject of a short memorandum written at Babelsberg on July 15, 1945, by Thompson, a secretary at the London embassy, for Assistant Secretary Dunn. Stalin, it recalls, had told Churchill on June 14 that he saw no reason to delay restoring diplomatic relations with Finland. Finland, Stalin said, was meeting the armistice terms.

The memo argues that the United States stands in a stronger position than its allies. America had never been at war with Finland, though it broke off relations in June 1944. Thompson urged that Washington resume ties as soon as it could do so without badly offending the Russians, and use the conference to clear the way.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d420:
President Truman's coal message to Churchill is transmitted in a Washington cable to Winant of June 24, 1945. The coal famine threatening Europe this coming winter, Truman writes, has impressed him with the urgency of the problem. He proposes directing the military authorities in Germany to exert every effort to raise German coal production.

All coal above minimum German needs, he urges, should go for export. Without immediate concentration on German coal, he warns, turmoil and unrest will strike the very areas of western Europe on which the continent's stability depends. Truman also proposes like pressure on France and Belgium to raise their own output, and a directive to his own commander.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d520:
Poland's claims and allied control collide in Dunn's memorandum to the Secretary, written at Babelsberg on July 15, 1945. At present, Dunn writes, Marshal Zhukov claims he has no control over the areas of eastern Germany which have been unilaterally placed under Polish administration. Those areas contain the mining resources of Upper Silesia and a large part of Germany's food surpluses.

Before any joint economic policy for Germany can be agreed, whether on reparations or on the Control Council's responsibilities, it is necessary to know what Germany those policies relate to. This government, Dunn states, approves in principle territorial adjustment for Poland's benefit, but opposes unilateral action in this as in other territorial settlements.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d620:
Edwin Pauley, the U.S. member of the Allied reparations body in Moscow, wired the Secretary of State on June 24, 1945. His top secret message is document 620 in volume one of the Foreign Relations papers on Potsdam. It links East European farm and oil goods to the war against Japan.

Pauley says the U.S. has in effect waived reparations claims on Rumania and Hungary, save for harm to U.S. property. Yet U.S. occupation forces in Germany are fed and fueled from America. Rumania, Hungary, and Austria hold surplus oil and farm goods that could supply them instead. If the Soviets, who expect some of those goods as reparations, passed them on as reverse lend-lease, two gains would follow. The war on Japan would be helped, and the net sum drawn from Germany would rise.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1020:
Soviet delegates circulated this proposal on the Königsberg area at Potsdam on July 22, 1945. It records approval of a Soviet request on East Prussia's future. Pending final settlement at the peace settlement, part of Germany's Baltic coast would pass to the Soviet Union.

The new Soviet western border would run from a point on the western shore of Danzig Bay. From there it passes eastward, north of Braunsberg and Goldap. It ends where the borders of Lithuania, Poland, and former East Prussia meet. The line would give the Soviet Union the northern part of East Prussia, with the city of Königsberg.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1120:
The Soviet team tabled this formal proposal on 18 July 1945, the second day of the Potsdam Conference. Early papers staked out each side's opening demands. Only later did the real trading begin, once all three teams had shown their first hands.

Moscow came to Germany set on gaining ground after the Soviet Union's vast losses in the war. Its dead ran into the tens of millions, a fact its envoys raised often. A proposal from the opening round shows the Soviet bid in its first, fullest form. Later papers can then be measured against it to see what the bargaining wore away.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1220:
Hurley wrote to the Secretary of State on 29 July 1945. His dispatches from China came often that summer. Each carried the state of a country split between a Nationalist government and communist armies, with Japan's defeat near and civil war looming behind it.

The secretary read China news beside the German bargaining. The two files met in Soviet intentions, which touched both. This cable is one piece of that dual picture. It shows an envoy at a hard post keeping his chief informed in the summit's last days. The crisis he reported would outlast the peace.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1320:
The United States team tabled this proposal on 20 July 1945. Formal papers were the currency of the summit: each one a claim in writing, offered for the other teams to take, amend, or refuse. This one came at the end of the first week.

By then the American stands on the chief questions were known, and drafting had turned to terms that might close. A proposal of this date belongs to that sharpening phase. It survives in the official record in the team's own words. Readers can weigh it against the final protocol to see what the week of trading did to it.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1420:
Herschel Johnson, the American minister in Sweden, wrote to the secretary of state on 6 July 1945. Johnson's post in Stockholm kept Washington in touch with a neutral capital close to the war's edge. It is printed in volume two of Foreign Relations of the United States, the official record of American diplomacy at Potsdam.

Neutral capitals were listening posts in 1945, full of envoys, rumors, and quiet feelers from all sides. A minister's letter from Stockholm in the week before Potsdam adds that northern view to the volume. Readers meet a lesser-known channel here: the reports that flowed in from the war's margins. It sometimes carried word of moves the main capitals had not yet seen. It widens the map before the summit papers begin.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d710a-120:
John McCloy, the Assistant Secretary of War, wrote to Secretary of State James Byrnes on July 27, 1945. McCloy was one of the War Department's most trusted hands. He dealt with occupation problems and the hard seams between war and peace. His letter reached Byrnes at Potsdam in the conference's final week.

Letters between the War and State chiefs show the two machines meshing. Armies would have to run much of what diplomats agreed. McCloy wrote with that burden in view. Readers get a senior soldier-administrator's voice, direct and practical. The exchange stands in the second Potsdam volume, among the papers that shaped the closing days.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d710a-20:
An extract from Joint Chiefs of Staff minutes of July 19, 1945, covers what war facts to give the Russians. It is an unnumbered item in volume two of the Foreign Relations papers on Potsdam. The subject had split the U.S. and British chiefs in the papers printed in volume one.

General Hull told the chiefs that Britain wanted facts passed to Moscow on a combined basis. That, he said, had not been the Joint Chiefs' policy. Two intelligence reports on Japan were in hand, one combined and one purely American. Hull doubted the British would agree to hand over the combined report itself. He thought the U.S. chiefs would be willing to give Moscow the American report instead. General Marshall guessed at a British motive beneath the dispute. London, he thought, cared more about facts on special projects than about operational intelligence.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d720:
Document 720 is Hurley's letter to the Secretary of State dated August 1, 1945. The Potsdam Conference adopted its final protocol that day. Hurley wrote from China, where the war against Japan still ran. His letter joined the closing run of the second Potsdam volume's China papers.

Last-day timing gives the letter a hinge quality. It looks back at the conference and ahead to what followed. Readers see an ambassador positioning his mission for the peace. The document reminds us that Potsdam's choices landed worldwide. Embassies everywhere had to live with them, starting at once.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d820:
Melbourne reported from Rumania on July 26, 1945, in document 820. The acting representative in Bucharest wrote to the Acting Secretary of State. His letters reach a near-daily rhythm in the volume's second week. This one joined the second Potsdam volume of the official record.

By late July, Melbourne's reports form a chronicle. Each adds a day's facts to a worsening file. Readers can watch a mission's position erode in real time. The document shows the worth of that persistence. Because he kept writing, the record of Rumania's turning is full. Silence would have served the other side.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d920:
Soviet delegates circulated this plan of reparations from Germany at the foreign ministers' meeting of July 23, 1945. It sets a total sum of 20 billion dollars for consideration. About half would come from one-time removals of German national wealth within two years of the surrender. The rest would come as yearly deliveries in kind over ten years.

The plan prices the removals by industry, from war and chemical plants to foreign investments and shares. Yearly goods would include coal, sugar, chemicals, cattle, cement, and timber. Prices rest on 1938 levels, with set markups. The exchange rate is fixed at 3.5 marks to the dollar.
frus-1952-54v13p2-d820:
Editorial Note 820 in the Indochina volume quotes two memoirs on the 194th National Security Council meeting. That session, on April 29, 1954, took up Indochina and the Geneva talks. President Eisenhower's account reports that Dien Bien Phu's area had shrunk to 1,500 yards across.

The garrison held 8,500 infantry and 1,200 artillery troops against 40,000 Viet Minh. An air strike was weighed once more. Eisenhower warned that solo wars across Asia would drain American strength. Richard Nixon's diary adds that Harold Stassen urged ground troops if needed. No strike was approved. The cable sits among the cease-fire feelers of that crowded spring.
frus-1955-57v20:
Arms control and atomic energy share Volume XX of the 1955–1957 set. A review of basic disarmament policy leads, with talks in the UN Disarmament Commission's subcommittee. Inspection and checking plans fill long runs.

Nuclear tests and fallout fears take the next block. Peaceful atomic uses and the birth of the International Atomic Energy Agency close the volume. Talk records with Gromyko show the gap in plain words. The papers hold both halves of the atom's story, the bid to curb it and the bid to share it. Fallout data drove the test debate in these pages.
frus-1961-63v20:
The Congo crisis fills Volume XX of the 1961–1963 set from first page to last. Lumumba's fall and the Gizenga regime lead, through August 1961. Katanga's secession then drives the record for two years.

Fighting in Katanga and the Kitona accord fill the second block. Peace bids run through 1962. The secession's collapse closes the crisis in January 1963. The Congo after the crisis takes a short final run. The files show a new state held together by UN arms, and a superpower contest fought through proxies and mining shares. Katanga's mines are the prize named in file after file here.
frus-1964-68v20:
Volume XX of the 1964-1968 series picks up the Arab-Israeli dispute after the 1967 war. It opens in the wake of UN Security Council Resolution 242, adopted on November 22, 1967. Its 376 documents run through 1968. They follow the UN mediation effort and the search for a settlement. They also cover arms supply, as France held back planes and Israel pressed Washington for aircraft.

A statement by the Historian frames the volume as a record of aims not met. By late 1968 the mediation had stalled and the arms balance had grown more tense. The papers show the Johnson team handing the dispute to its successors with no settlement in sight.
frus-1969-76v20:
Volume XX of Foreign Relations of the United States, 1969-1976, covers Southeast Asia outside Indochina, from 1969 to 1972. Thailand takes the first and longest chapter set. Regional affairs, the Philippines, and Indonesia follow. The Thai chapters deal with U.S. bases, aid, and the insurgency there. The Philippine chapters cover bases and ties with the Marcos government.

The Indonesia chapters follow ties with the Suharto government after the fall of Sukarno. Aid figures and force plans fill many pages. The records show Washington leaning on these states as the Vietnam war wound on. Each chapter weighs local politics against U.S. war needs.
frus-1977-80v20:
Volume XX of the 1977-1980 series covers Eastern Europe. A regional section opens the volume. A second treats Radio Free Europe, Radio Liberty, and the Voice of America. Country sections follow for Bulgaria, Czechoslovakia, East Germany, Hungary, Romania, and Yugoslavia. Romania and Yugoslavia again take the largest shares. The Hungary papers note progress on consular services for growing numbers of Americans.

The records show the Carter team testing its human rights policy in the East. Dissidents, exit visas, and trade terms recur throughout. Charter 77 falls in the Czechoslovakia span. The volume ends with Yugoslavia as Tito's era neared its close.
galsworthy-in-chancery-1920:
John Galsworthy continued his Forsyte family saga with In Chancery, published in 1920. The novel follows The Man of Property and the short piece Indian Summer of a Forsyte. Galsworthy tracked the rich, possessive Forsytes across decades of English change.

Soames Forsyte, divorced from Irene, wants an heir and pursues the young Annette Lamont. Irene, meanwhile, finds late love with Soames's cousin Jolyon, now head of the family's other branch. Old bitterness poisons every new happiness, and the war years hang over the younger generation. Galsworthy shows a proud family slowly learning that money cannot settle matters of the heart.
gao-gaoreports-b-295620:
The protest in file B-295620 reached GAO's ruling on February 18, 2005, with Spotless Janitorial Services, Inc., as the protester. The Department of Energy had rejected its bid for custodial work at the Forrestal Building and a nearby child care center in Washington. The bid, as modified, stated that it was proprietary and not to be disclosed publicly. The agency treated that bar as making the bid nonresponsive. GAO denied the protest. The rejection was proper on the bid's own terms.

A bidder may not condition a bid on secrecy the process does not allow. Snow removal formed part of the work sought under the electronic invitation.
gao-gaoreports-b-298020:
IPlus protested a Navy award for college program help in GAO decision B-298020, dated June 5, 2006. The winner was Dynamic Systems Technology. The program helps service staff seek school growth. The firm hit talks, marks, and the pick. It said talks were not even. Price chats with the winner were at stake.

GAO denied the protest. Price chats fixed slips that were clear on the face of the bid. Those chats were clear-ups, not talks. Other chats that may have been talks did the firm no harm. Past work of both lead and sub firms could count. Both sat in a guide and pupil plan for small firms.
gao-gaoreports-b-298720:
Midland Supply, Inc. protested a General Services Administration award to Danaher Tool Group. The buy covered socket wrench sets among 50 commercial hand tool items. Midland had supplied the sets to the government since 2001. GAO decided B-298720 and B-298720.2 on November 29, 2006.

Midland held the stronger technical score at a higher price. The agency picked the cheaper, lower-scored offer. GAO found the pick flawed in method. The file showed a raw match of point totals. No note showed a true trade-off of price against merit. A best-value pick needs that weighed call on record. GAO sustained the protest.
gao-gaoreports-b-299720:
Carson Helicopter Services protested an Army award to Croman Corporation. The contract covered aerial wildland fire suppression services. The work serves the Yakima Training Center in Washington. The craft must haul at least 1,000 gallons of water per trip. GAO ruled in B-299720 and B-299720.2 on July 30, 2007.

The award rested on the low-priced, fit bid. The winner's bid claimed its craft met the load bar. Yet facts in that same bid raised real doubt. A reviewer who knows helicopters should have caught the clash. The craft's load limits sat below the claim. The agency took the claim at face value. That review was flawed. GAO sustained the protests.
gao-gaoreports-b-299820:
PWC Logistics Services protested a Defense Logistics Agency award to Science Applications International Corporation. The contract covered supply and storage of chemicals and packaged fuel goods. Those goods serve military sites worldwide. GAO decided B-299820 and B-299820.3 on August 14, 2007.

The firm claimed a hidden test on environmental risk plans. GAO found all firms got the same facts in talks. Those facts in effect set the test for all alike. Talks on the firm's plan did occur as well. Its plan drew just a minor flaw mark. The panel also found real contrasts in plan quality. Those calls stood up on the record. GAO denied the protest.
gao-gaoreports-b-303920:
The Administrative Office of the United States Courts asked GAO to lift a clerk's liability in B-303920. The clerk was Clarence Maddox, of a federal district court in Florida. The plea hit improper payments for bottled water. GAO issued its ruling on March 21, 2006.

The sums broke into two groups. Relief came by force of law for 27 payments made before March 2003. Those sums came to $947.62 in total. The rest of the plea failed. For 11 payments that came to $485.60, GAO could not grant relief. The clerk thus stayed liable for that part. The split tracked the dates of the payments.
gao-gaoreports-b-307720:
Farm payments past set caps are ruled improper in this GAO opinion, B-307720, dated September 27, 2007. The Conservation Security Program pays farmers for green work on their land. The law sets a top sum per year for such pay. An April 2006 GAO report found the Agriculture Department paid past those caps in fiscal year 2004. A senator asked if the department had power to do so.

GAO held that it did not. The caps sit in 16 U.S.C. section 3838c. Pay past the cap lacks legal support. Each such payment counts as an improper payment. The opinion gives teeth to a report that first flagged the overpay.
gao-gaoreports-b-311420:
DAV Prime, Inc. saw its protest thrown out under GAO decision B-311420, dated May 1, 2008. The Forest Service sought field latrines for its crews. DAV Prime is a firm owned by a hurt veteran. It said the call had to be set aside for firms of its class. It said the agency missed its class goal and ran no market scan. The goal in view was 3 percent of yearly deals.

GAO dismissed the protest. The class law says a chief may set a deal aside. It does not say a chief must do so. A goal for a class is a hope, not a court-bound duty. No valid base for the fight was shown.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-420:
Electronic Government, GAO-05-420 of April 25, 2005, follows the cash for a set of web plans that no one fund feeds. The budget office backs plans to put state work on the web, per the President's plan. Most such plans hold no cash line of their own. They live on gifts of cash from the arms that share their use. That path can stall or skew a plan.

GAO was asked to check two years of that flow. For fiscal years 2003 and 2004, it asks if each arm gave the sum it vowed. It asks when each gift came. Late or short gifts leave the plans at risk, the tale shows.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-720:
In report GAO-05-720 (June 17, 2005), GAO reviewed the patent work of the U.S. Patent and Trademark Office. Applications had grown more complex and more numerous. Wait times had risen, and doubts had grown about patent quality. GAO checked progress on the office's strategic plan. It also checked efforts to hire and keep skilled examiners.

GAO found the office had fully or partly put in place all 23 steps meant to build skill and quality. Only 8 of 15 steps to cut wait times were fully or partly done. Lack of funds was the main reason given. A new fee law passed in December 2004 let the office revisit some steps. Hiring gains were real, but it was too soon to judge lasting success in keeping staff.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-820:
Postal rate data quality is reviewed in GAO-05-820, a report dated July 28, 2005. A 1999 study found room to improve the data behind mail rates. The Postal Service agreed to act. Doubts remained about what it had in fact done. Reform bills in Congress also turned on data quality. GAO listed the key steps the service took. It then weighed what reform laws would change.

GAO found the service changed its cost tracking for mail handled by staff. Staff costs are over three-quarters of all costs. It refreshed data on letter carriers, replacing 1980s figures. It gathered more data for sharper estimates, and fixed weak manuals. Two reform bills would create a stronger regulator with power over rate data. The service disputed GAO's call for structural reform. GAO held its ground, with a caveat on how reform is carried out.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-20:
Immigration benefit backlogs and the push to clear them are examined in GAO-06-20, dated November 21, 2005. Long waits burden immigrants, their families, and firms that sponsor them. The law told U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services to end the backlog. The agency set a goal: clear it by September 30, 2006, and decide each case within six months. GAO measured the backlog's size and the steps taken to end it. It also judged the odds of meeting the deadline and the quality checks meant to keep decisions sound.

Speed and quality pull in two directions. Rushing cases can breed errors and uneven rulings. GAO urged the agency to size its backlog the way the 2000 law defines it. Its new case system should soon let it count by the age of each case. GAO also urged the agency to spell out what gains it expects from heavy spending on new technology.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-520:
Specialty hospitals owned by doctors were said to push general hospitals to change. On April 7, 2006, report GAO-06-520 tested that claim. Specialty hospitals treat specific conditions or do specific surgery. Supporters say rivalry prompts efficiency and quality gains. Critics fear added services that duplicate what a town already has. Doctors' financial stakes in such hospitals also drew questions.

GAO surveyed about 600 general hospitals. Some faced specialty rivals and some did not. Replies came from 401 hospitals. GAO compared reported operational and clinical changes. Changes were largely unaffected by the presence of a rival, GAO found. Readers get survey evidence in a heated debate.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-620:
Computer security at the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation is assessed in GAO-06-620, a GAO report dated August 31, 2006. The corporation insures bank deposits and enforces banking laws. It relies heavily on computer systems to run its financial and mission work. GAO reviewed the systems as part of the audit of the calendar year 2005 financial statements.

GAO found that the corporation had fixed or eased 18 of 24 security weaknesses reported earlier. New steps included tighter limits on access to sensitive files. But GAO said controls were still not applied evenly across systems. Weak spots left key financial data at some risk. The report urges steady work to close the remaining gaps.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-720:
Oversight of the H-1B visa program is examined in GAO report GAO-06-720, released on June 22, 2006. The program lets United States employers hire highly skilled foreign workers for set periods. The Labor Department reviews employer applications and polices some program rules. Homeland Security and Justice also hold enforcement roles. GAO described how Labor carries out its part and how it works with the other agencies.

GAO found that Labor's authority is limited in scope by law. Its review of applications was timely, yet it lacked quality assurance controls. Some errors in employer filings could slip through as a result. GAO also saw room for Labor to share more information with Homeland Security. Better sharing, GAO said, would help catch employers who break the rules.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-920:
Headway on aerospace advice, and the gaps left, are measured in GAO report GAO-06-920, dated September 13, 2006. Flight, defense, and space work make aerospace key to U.S. wealth and strength. In 2001 Congress set up a commission on the industry's future. It gave its advice in 2002.

GAO picked advice on airspace, space policy, management, world issues, workforce, and research. It checked how far federal agencies had acted on each pick. It also named the hurdles that remain, such as an aging workforce and stiff world rivalry. The report shows which bold 2002 ideas had turned into action by 2006.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-1020:
Job help for veterans with service-linked disabilities is surveyed in GAO report GAO-07-1020, dated September 12, 2007. In 2005 the Departments of Labor and Veterans Affairs agreed to link their job services for these veterans. At the same time the veterans agency launched a Five-Track job program, with job coaches and job resource labs.

GAO tracked headway on the 2005 pact, and the snags in its way. It checked the state of the Five-Track rollout, and strain from newly home veterans. It weighed what coaches and labs do for those they serve. More planning, watch, and data work would lift the aid, GAO found.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-20:
The Pentagon now buys more in services than in major weapon systems. GAO judged how it manages that buying in GAO-07-20, a report dated November 9, 2006. Service contract duties rose from $82.3 billion in fiscal year 1996 to $141.2 billion in fiscal year 2005. GAO named the traits of sound service buying at two levels. It then tested the department's approach against those traits. Both big-picture strategy and single deals were in scope.

The department's approach was mostly reactive, GAO found. It lacked a clear view of where service dollars go. Its review system could not even say how many deals had been reviewed. The services had reviewed deals worth less than 3 percent of service dollars in fiscal year 2005. Day to day, staff focused on awarding contracts, not on results. GAO made six recommendations for a proactive approach. The department agreed with all of them.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-320:
Hospitals must report care quality scores, and gathering the data eats clinician time. GAO studied the workload in GAO-07-320, a report dated April 25, 2007. Eight hospitals with varied computer systems served as case studies. GAO traced their six-step reporting process. It asked how far computers ease the work. It also asked whether the health department pushes that shift.

All eight hospitals followed the same six steps, GAO found. Trained staff read each chart to pull the required values. More measures meant more staff hours. Computers helped staff find and read records. They could not automate the judgment calls. Notes sit in free text, and paper mixes with electronic files. Systems inside one hospital often cannot share data. The health department backed studies of the problem. But it had no step-by-step plan or deadlines. GAO asked it to publish both.
