gao-gaoreports-gao-07-520:
Restoring the Everglades will take at least 40 years, and GAO-07-520, dated May 31, 2007, reports slow, costly headway. The South Florida ecosystem spans about 18,000 square miles. A century of water control works harmed its health. A 2000 plan set out to repair it at a cost of $15.4 billion. Some 60 key projects form the Comprehensive Everglades Restoration Plan, run by federal, state, local, and tribal partners.

GAO charted which projects were done or under way. The biggest gains, it found, rest in projects not yet built. Project order had been set by cash on hand and build logic, not by the full criteria the law's authors wrote. Cost growth and delays compound the strain. Math models that steer the work get a review as well. GAO urged the partners to rank projects by gain, so early money buys the most nature back.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-620:
Special Operations Command buys its own gear with mixed results, and GAO-07-620, issued June 28, 2007, grades the shop. The command's duties swelled after the September 11 attacks. It now leads the U.S. fight against global terror networks. Its buying budget more than doubled in step, from $788 million in 2001 to about $1.91 billion in 2006. Congress asked GAO to review how it manages its programs.

Small buys shine in the record. The command does well when it adapts shelf goods and simple tech. Big builds that need fresh design, or that lean on the regular services, fare worse. GAO checked whether the program list fits the mission; it does. The strain sits in staff size and skill mix, and in tools to track many programs at once. Sound business cases before launch are the standing advice, above all for joint builds.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-920:
Using existing roads better is the theme of GAO-07-920, dated July 26, 2007. Traffic has outgrown the road network for decades. Building more lanes is the familiar answer. This report looks at squeezing more from the roads already built. GAO studied efforts in five states. It reviewed research and asked officials what works. Three forces hold back smarter use. Old designs cannot handle today's volumes. Fuel taxes charge the same in rush hour and at midnight. Project picking rarely weighs total social benefit.

Tools exist to ease the strain, the report finds. Signal timing and ramp metering smooth flows cheaply. Pricing can shift trips out of peak hours. Managed lanes reward carpools and buses. Local results vary with design and follow-through. GAO lays out strategies to spread the best methods. Federal guidance and funding rules shape local choices. The report gives Congress options short of new pavement.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-20:
Closure of a famed pathology institute is studied in GAO report GAO-08-20, dated November 9, 2007. The 2005 base closure round ordered the Armed Forces Institute of Pathology shut down. Its pathologists give expert diagnoses when other doctors are stuck. In 2006, they handled over 40,000 consultations. Almost half served the Defense Department, with the rest split between veterans' and civilian doctors.

The institute also teaches and does research. GAO reviewed plans to end, move, or contract out its services. It weighed the harm closure could do to military and civilian care. Lawmakers told the department to weigh this report in its plan. GAO offered three steps to soften the loss.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-320:
Foreign investment rules in 10 countries are described in GAO report GAO-08-320, dated February 28, 2008. GAO was asked how other nations guard national security in foreign takeovers, the concern behind the Exon-Florio amendment in the United States. The study updates a 1996 report and adds six countries, including China, India, and Russia.

Each country defines national security in its own way, so limits range from narrow defense-sector review to broad economic and cultural tests. Eight of the 10 countries use a formal review process, often led by an economic body with security input. Shared concerns include the defense industrial base, energy, and buyers that are state-owned firms or sovereign wealth funds. Several countries had lately tightened their rules after disputed deals.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-420:
Issued March 7, 2008, GAO report GAO-08-420 looks at the Internal Revenue Service's fiscal year 2008 modernization spending plan. Business Systems Modernization is a multibillion-dollar effort to replace the agency's aging tax systems. The plan asked for $235.8 million from the modernization account.

GAO found the plan met the conditions set in law, and the agency had acted on some past advice. Most milestones held up well: 13 of 14 due in 2007 landed within 10 percent of cost estimates. But one milestone for the Customer Account Data Engine ran 66 percent over its schedule with a 15 percent cost rise, and another slipped 153 percent on schedule. GAO recommended a dated plan for the technology staffing strategy. The acting commissioner agreed.
gardner-journey-earths-interior-1920:
Marshall B. Gardner gave the hollow earth claim its fullest 20th century form in this book of 1920. It is a revised and much grown version of his first work on the theme. Gardner was a keen lay reader of polar tales and reports.

He holds that a vast warm sea and land lie inside the earth, reached by polar holes. He points to mammoths found in ice and to gaps in the tales of Cook and Peary at the pole. His book is the last great brief for the scheme, writ with full zeal.
goenner-rothschild-lotterie-anlehen-1820:
Nikolaus Thaddaus Gonner, a Munich law scholar, wrote this study of a Rothschild loan in German in 1820. Its theme is the lottery loan of 20,800,000 gulden run with the banker Parish. The loan was one of the young house's first great state deals in the south German lands.

Gonner sets out the terms of the loan and the law that bears on each part of it. He writes as a lawyer of the time, for men who held or might hold a share. The dry work is a true first hand record of how the house did its state work.
govdocs-archive_org-Report-President-Sur:
On April 24, 2015, U.S. Attorney Preet Bharara's office in New York sent a short cover letter connected to a major disclosure. The letter transmitted a three-volume report on the President's Surveillance Program, released in a Freedom of Information case brought by the New York Times.

The file holds the letter alone, not the report that followed it. Even so, it marks the formal moment when records about warrantless government surveillance moved from secret files toward the public record. Such letters show the paperwork behind disclosure: who sent the material, when, and under what legal pressure it left the government's hands.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_afghanis:
America's war in Afghanistan lasted twenty years, from the autumn of 2001 to the summer of 2021. Afghanistan 20/20 tells that war through twenty documents. One briefing book page gathers the records that mark its main turning points.

Twenty well-chosen papers can carry a long war: the first decisions after September 11, the turn to Iraq, the surge, the peace talks, and the final exit. The format suits readers who want the primary record without reading a whole shelf of reports. Each document stands for a phase of the war. Together they show how a short mission became the longest war in American history.
harris-the-bomb-1920:
Frank Harris published The Bomb in New York in 1920, at his own press. The novel is a confession that never was: its narrator names himself Rudolph Schnaubelt, and states his claim on the first page. I threw the bomb which killed eight policemen and wounded sixty in Chicago in 1886, he says. Now he lies in Reichholz, in Bavaria, dying of consumption under a false name, in peace at last. The Haymarket bomb was history's most famous unsolved outrage of its age.

Harris builds a life around the claim: the anarchist circles of Chicago, the trial of men who denied the deed, and a fugitive's years of hiding. The book is fiction, yet written with a reporter's relish for the inside story. It reads as both thriller and argument, about labor, violence, and the state. Few novels of the period take so bold a mask.
history-of-friedrich-ii-of-prussia-volum:
Thomas Carlyle's twentieth volume holds Book Twenty: Friedrich is not to be overwhelmed, and the Seven-Years War gradually ends, April 1760 to February 1763. Three campaigns remain, Carlyle warns, but 1760 is the crisis that renders the others possible. Ill-luck has followed Friedrich like his shadow since Kunersdorf, and it does not yet leave him.

Berlin is raided, Liegnitz and Torgau are won at terrible cost, and survival replaces victory as Prussia's aim, while France is led with winged steps down her own road in Hanover. The death of the Tsarina Elizabeth in 1762, the miracle of the House of Brandenburg, finally saves him. Carlyle closes the war worn out, as his subject was.
hoffmann-tomcat-murr-1820:
Hoffmann's last novel, The Life and Opinions of the Tomcat Murr, appeared in German in 1820 and after. No English translation from the time survives in public domain, so the text here is the German original. Murr, a literate tomcat, writes his memoirs on scrap paper meant for a life of Kapellmeister Kreisler.

By a printer's error, the two lives come out mixed, page by page. The cat's smug tales of love and learning mock the earnest artist's sorrows below. Kreisler's story, in fragments, gives the pain behind the joke. Hoffmann built the first collage novel of modern times out of that mix. It is funny, sad, and far ahead of its age.
hopalong-cassidy-s-rustler-round-up-or-b:
Clarence Edward Mulford introduced Hopalong Cassidy in this first of the Bar-20 novels, published as Hopalong Cassidy's Rustler Round-Up, or Bar-20. Hopalong rides for the Bar-20 ranch outfit in the cattle country near the Mexican border, alongside foreman Buck Peters and the red-headed Red Connors. Rustlers are lifting Bar-20 stock, and the outfit answers with the round-up of the title: pursuit, gunplay, and rough justice across the range.

Mulford packed the book with cowboy speech, camp humor, and working detail of ropes, brands, and water holes. His Hopalong is gruffer than the clean-cut hero films later made of him. This opening volume built the series that carried the Bar-20 crew through dozens of westerns.
houdini-miracle-mongers-1920:
Harry Houdini, the famed escape artist, published Miracle Mongers and Their Methods in 1920. Houdini knew stage tricks from the inside, and he turned that knowledge on performers who claimed real marvels. Fire eaters, sword swallowers, and fake holy men all came under his eye.

Houdini explained how such acts were done, from swallowing swords to handling fire and poison without harm. He drew on old books, posters, and his own talks with performers. His subjects came from across Europe and America. The result is both a history of stage marvels and a sharp lesson. It shows how easily skill presented as magic can fool a crowd.
irenaeus-demonstration-of-the-apostolic-:
Irenaeus of Lyons made his name fighting Gnostic teachers, yet his Demonstration of the Apostolic Preaching shows a gentler side. Written as a summary of the faith for a friend, the work survives in an ancient Armenian translation. The English version by Robinson, published in 1920, presents that text.

The Greek and Latin originals were lost, so the Armenian copy carries the whole weight of the book. Irenaeus walks through creation, the fall, and Christ's work in clear, warm order. Pastor rather than polemicist, he focuses on the core of what Christians believe. The Demonstration balances his great refutation of heresies across the shelf. Readers meet a second-century bishop teaching the faith like a catechism, simply and with love.
jesuit-relations-thwaites-vol-20:
Montreal begins in the years covered by Volume 20, from 1898. Thwaites gathers Quebec reports from 1640 to 1642, a span of siege. The colony sorts itself out for sheer survival under attack.

The new post at Montreal rises as a bold thrust into Iroquois country. Priests bless its start and share its hunger and risk. Letters weigh faith against fear in a camp that may not last. The men who lived those birth pangs wrote them down here. Their trust in the cause never wavers across these pages. New France takes lasting shape under fire in this volume.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-aaron-ben-meir-:
Aaron ben Meir of Brest was a Lithuanian rabbi who died at Brest-Litovsk on November 3, 1777. Born there about the beginning of the eighteenth century, he came from the Katzenellenbogen-Padua family. His teacher was Eliezer ben Eliezer Kolir, a noted Pilpulist.

Aaron carried the Pilpul method of Talmud study to its extreme limits. His "Minḥat Aharon," printed in 1792, gives glosses on the treatise Sanhedrin. An appendix adds responsa and notes on Talmudic topics. Some of his responsa also appear in a work of 1836 by his grandson, Jacob Meir of Padua.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-aaron-berechiah:
Aaron Berechiah ben Moses ben Nehemiah of Modena was an Italian cabalist who died in 1639. He studied under Rabbi Hillel of Modena and Rabbi Menahem Azariah of Fano. At the request of the burial society at Mantua, he set up rites for them.

His "Ma'abar Yabboḳ" treats separation, purity, and holiness, with prayers for the sick and the dead and rules for their care. He also wrote morning prayers, a commentary on "Tiḳḳune ha-Zohar," and a large work on the Cabala in four volumes. Another book, "Magen Aharon," sums up the works of Luria.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-abaye-called-al:
Abaye was a Babylonian amora born about the close of the third century, who died in 339. His real name was Naḥmani, after his grandfather. Left an orphan early, he was adopted by his uncle, Rabbah bar Naḥmani, who nicknamed him Abaye, or Little Father. His teachers were Rabbah and Joseph bar Ḥama.

When Joseph died in 333, Abaye became president of the Academy of Pumbedita, and kept the post until his death. His debates with Raba shaped the dialectic method for legal tradition, and are known as the Debates of Abaye and Raba. In all but six cases, Raba's view won in the end. Abaye's own maxims urge mild speech and good will toward all.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-abel-maim-meado: Abel-maim, meaning meadow of the waters, was a tract in Upper Galilee. It is now known as Abil-el-Ḳamḥ, the entry says. The Syrians under Ben-hadad took it, as Second Chronicles, chapter 16, verse 4, records. In the matching list in First Kings, chapter 15, verse 20, the place stands as Abel-beth-maachah. That town was taken by the Assyrians in 732 B.C., a date the entry ties to Second Kings, chapter 15, verse 29.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-abina-called-al:
Abina, also called Abuna or Buna, was an amora of the third and fourth centuries, always cited with no added surname. Born in Babylonia, he was a disciple of Rab Huna I. Most of his learning, though, came from R. Jeremiah ben Abba. It is in Jeremiah's name that he most often passes on rulings, in both lands. In time he moved to Palestine, where Zeira and Jacob ben Aḥa became his friends.

One ruling of his fixes how the name of God is to be said. It is written in one form and read in another, he holds, on the ground of a verse in Exodus. He also faced down a heretic who mocked Israel's claim to be set apart among the nations. His answer came from Balaam's own words in Numbers. Israel, that verse says, shall not be reckoned among the nations at all.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-abraham-ben-mei: Abraham ben Meir ha-Kohen was a rabbi and hymn writer of the end of the eleventh century. He lived probably at Speyer. He was a colleague of Rashi, and the two men carried on a learned correspondence. In 1096 he composed an elegy, a kinah, on the persecutions of the Jews. He had seen those attacks with his own eyes, the entry notes. No other work or life detail is given for him.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-abrahamson-abra:
Abraham Abrahamson was a German medalist and master of the Prussian mint. Born at Potsdam in 1754, he died at Berlin on July 23, 1811. He learned engraving from his father, Jacob Abraham, and soon passed him in skill as an artist.

Chodowiecki's designs shaped his early work, but after four years in Europe's art centers he designed most of his own medals. Famous pieces mark the Peace of Teschen, the meeting at Tilsit in 1808, and Queen Louise's death in 1810. Two historic thalers mark Jewish emancipation in Westphalia and under Alexander I. His medal portraits cover Mendelssohn, Kant, and Lessing, among many others.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-accessories-720:
Accessories share guilt for a crime they did not do themselves. English and American law knows two kinds. One man urges or plans the act before it is done. He is as guilty as the chief doer. A second man hides the doer after the act. His guilt is less. The Bible treats this theme most fully for idol worship.

A man who lures others to false gods is called a seducer. Deuteronomy xiii. sets death by stoning for him. The try alone draws the penalty, even if no one was led astray. To hide such a man is also a sin, though it draws no court penalty. For other crimes the written law sets no fine for the helper before the fact. A late debate asks if a man who sends an agent to kill is liable. Shammai said yes, with death as the price.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-adler-hermann-8:
Hermann Adler was chief rabbi of the United Hebrew Congregations of the British empire. He was born in Hanover in May, 1839. He was the second son of Nathan Marcus Adler. He studied in London, then at Prague and Leipsic from 1860 to 1862. He took his doctor's degree at Leipsic in December, 1862. Prague's chief rabbi gave him his rabbinic diploma the next year.

In 1863 he became head of Jews' College in London. In 1864 he took the Bayswater Synagogue as well. As his father's age grew, he took on the heavy parts of the chief rabbi's work in 1879. His father died in 1890. In June, 1891, he was chosen to succeed him, with no votes against. His sway ran through the whole empire. He led the London court of Jewish law. He also worked for groups that guard children and house the poor.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-aguilar-avelar-: David Uzziel d'Aguilar was a friend of De Barrios. De Barrios praised him in the "Relacion de los Poetas." He is known for one piece of work. He translated the writings of Philo into Spanish. The manuscript of that translation seems to be lost. The entry gives no other facts about his life. He survives as a name in a poet's praise. His Philo is known only by report.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-aguilar-diego-d:
Diego d'Aguilar was also called Moses Lopez Pereira. He was a Marano who flourished in the eighteenth century. He was born probably in Spain. He died at London in 1759. In 1722 he moved from Lisbon to London. He then went on to Vienna. From 1725 to 1747 he held a monopoly. It covered all tobacco in Austria. He could set up factories and fix prices.

Empress Maria Theresa favored him strongly. She had him rebuild the palace at Schonbrunn. She made him a baron and privy councilor. He founded the Spanish or Turco-Jewish community in Vienna. He won relief for many oppressed fellow Jews. In 1742 he helped shield the Jews of Moravia from pillage. He also helped stop a plan for expulsion. The plan would have removed Jews from the whole empire. It was dropped in 1748 or 1749.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ajalon-1020:
Ajalon was a city in Palestine that gave its name to the Valley of Ajalon. Its site is the present Yalo, a small village in the hills. The El-Amarna tablets name it Aialuna and Ialuna. The Danites failed to conquer it, the book of Judges says. It stayed Canaanite until the Ephraimites subdued it.

Ajalon is listed with the land of Dan, yet Chronicles calls it a city of Benjamin. The Egyptian king Shishak names it among towns he took under Rehoboam. Rehoboam himself fortified the place. Later the Philistines seized it from King Ahaz. The entry warns readers not to mix it with Aijalon in Zebulun.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-alexander-the-g:
Alexander the Great was the famed conqueror of the East, who lived from 356 to 323 B.C. Bringing Greek culture into Syria and Egypt, he shaped Judaism more than any other non-Jew. Yet almost nothing joins him in person to Jewish history. After the siege of Tyre in 332 B.C. he marched through Palestine unopposed. Only Gaza resisted, and it was razed.

Josephus tells of a visit to Jerusalem, in a somewhat fantastic manner. The high priest Jaddua, warned in a dream, came out in purple and miter to meet him. Alexander said he had seen that figure in a dream in Macedonia. It had urged him to cross the sea and promised him Persia. He sacrificed in the Temple and was shown the Book of Daniel. He let the Jews live by their fathers' laws, free of tribute in the seventh year. Many scholars doubt the tale.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-altar-mizbeah-a:
Altar is the place of slaughter in the Hebrew Bible. The Hebrew word is mizbeah. Early altars in Genesis were heaps of stones. One law in Exodus favors an altar of earth. Stone altars were allowed if the stones stayed unhewn. Steps up to the altar were barred by that law.

The altar of the tabernacle gets a full account. It was acacia wood clad in bronze. It stood five cubits square and three cubits high. Horns rose at its four corners. A second altar burned incense and was clad in gold. The long entry runs on to the Temple altars. It ends with the altar as a sign of God's table.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-amon-king-of-ju:
Amon was a king of Judah, son of Manasseh. He took the throne at the age of twenty-two. His reign ran about 640 to 638 B.C. It lasted just two years in all. He went back to the idol rites of his father. Chronicles says he was worse than his father. His father had turned from his sins in time.

His own servants rose and killed him in his house. The people then slew those killers in turn. They set his young son Josiah on the throne. Sages call him the most sinful of Judah's bad kings. One tale says he burned the scrolls of the Law. His name was spared one grim list for Josiah's sake.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-antonio-dom-162:
Dom Antonio, prior of Crato, was a pretender to the throne of Portugal who died in 1595. He was the natural son of Dom Luis, brother of King Henry, and of a converted Jewess, Iolanthe. His father later made him legitimate.

Portugal's secret Jews hoped for his rise, the entry says, since he was unlikely to persecute his own mother's kin. When Henry died on January 31, 1580, Philip II of Spain claimed the crown and offered Antonio 40,000 ducats a year to step aside. Antonio refused, had himself proclaimed king, lost at Alcantara, and fled to exile. Philip then took cruel revenge on the Maranos.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-arbattis-1720: Arbattis is a place named in First Maccabees, chapter 5, verse 23, in connection with Galilee. From both districts Simon Maccabeus brought back captive Jews to Jerusalem. That is the sum of what this short entry reports. It adds one honest limit: the exact site of Arbattis has not been positively identified. No size, ruler, or later history is given, and the entry rests on the single Maccabean passage it cites.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-arroyo-isaac-be: Isaac ben Moses Arroyo lived in Salonica toward the end of the sixteenth century. Two books of his are named here. One, Makil Kohelet, meaning The Preacher Preaching, treats Ecclesiastes. The other, Tanhumot El, meaning Consolations of God, treats the Pentateuch. Both are described as philosophical expositions, printed at Salonica in 1597 and 1573. The entry gives no dates for the man himself and no further facts of his life.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-maacah-10220:
Maacah is untangled in the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia as a name shared by a kingdom and several Bible figures. First comes a small Aramean kingdom east of the Sea of Galilee. Its king hired his troops out to the Ammonites in their war against David. The city Abel of Beth-maachah likely took its name from this people.

The article then lists the persons who bear the name. One Maacah was a wife of David and daughter of Talmai, king of Geshur. Another was a king of Gath whose son Achish sheltered David's men. A third was wife of Rehoboam and mother of Abijah, removed as queen mother by her grandson Asa. Still more figures of the name appear across Genesis and Chronicles. The short entry works as a map for readers lost among many similar names in the history books.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-mayo-raphael-is:
Raphael Isaac ben Aaron Mayo was a Talmudical scholar of Smyrna who died in 1810. The Executive Committee of the Editorial Board and J. Brennsohn entered him in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Nearly all that the record keeps of him is his books. The books share a joke: each title plays on “ha-Yam,” the sea, which echoes his name. The catalogue of Steinschneider, the entry notes, spells him “Maggio” instead.

His chief work is “Shorashe ha-Yam,” Roots of the Sea. It is a commentary on the code of Maimonides, the Yad ha-Hazakah, printed in three volumes at Salonica between 1806 and 1815. Around it stand “Darke ha-Yam,” homilies and funeral sermons, and “Sefat ha-Yam,” legal decisions and responsa. There is also “Pe'at ha-Yam,” a commentary on the tractate Bezah with rules appended. It appeared in 1832, long after his death.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-menahem-b-aaron:
Menahem ben Aaron ibn Zerah was a Spanish codifier. Violence twice wrecked his life. Solomon Schechter and Louis Ginzberg profile him in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born at Estella, whither his father had fled from the French expulsion of 1306. In the massacre of 1328 his parents and four younger brothers were murdered. He was wounded and left for dead. A knight who had known his father saved him. He studied under Judah ben Asher. In 1361 he became rabbi of Alcala. In the civil war of 1368 he lost everything again.

At Toledo, Don Samuel Abravanel sheltered him. For that patron he wrote his code, the "Zedah la-Derek." The article stresses the book's oddity. It is a law book cut short for rich Jews. Such men moved among princes. They kept the commandments loosely. The book gives them the essentials. It stresses the laws such men were likeliest to break.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-meshullam-ben-s:
Meshullam ben Solomon, surnamed En Vidas, was a Hebrew poet who lived at the start of the thirteenth century. His Jewish Encyclopedia entry, by Richard Gottheil and Isaac Broydé, appeared in 1906. Jedaiah Bedersi counted him among the Provençal poets, but the article argues his native country was more likely Spain, near Gerona.

In the fight over philosophy, Meshullam stood with the Orthodox and aimed his attacks at Judah al-Ḥarizi, translator of Maimonides' Guide. He wrote several satirical poems against the Moreh Nebukim, later published by Steinschneider from manuscripts. Abraham Bedersi ranked him high among Hebrew poets, and the entry notes that most of his poems survive only in manuscript copies.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-miggo-10820:
Miggo is an Aramaic term of Talmudic logic, contracted from words meaning from within, for reasoning by analogy from one case to another. Isidore Singer and Jacob Zallel Lauterbach explain it in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Its Hebrew twin is mittok, and the article works through examples from the Talmud itself.

In one case, a man who would steal is presumed ready to swear falsely too, though the inference only runs from grave sins to light ones, never backward. In another, a ledge that counts as a wall for the festival booth counts as a wall for the Sabbath as well. A third argues from work allowed on a holiday for one's living to work allowed without that need.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-mohilewer-samue:
Samuel Mohilewer was born at Hluboka in the government of Wilna on April 25, 1824. He was the Russian rabbi who made Zionism his life's second career. Herman Rosenthal and Max Schloessinger recount his life in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. His father taught him secular subjects beside Hebrew. He stayed an advocate of European culture. Ordained at eighteen, he held five pulpits, ending at Byelostok.

In 1875 he spoke at the celebrations for Moses Montefiore's ninetieth birthday. There he declared openly for colonizing Palestine. After the pogroms of 1881 he escorted refugees as far as Lemberg. He urged that they be sent to the Holy Land instead. In 1882 he founded the first Ḥovevei Zion society in Warsaw. He carried the cause to Paris, winning support with the help of Zadoc Kahn and M. Erlanger.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-morocco-called-:
Morocco, called Al-Maghrib al-Aksa, the extreme west, in Arabic, receives a long country article in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Four writers share the work: Joseph Jacobs, Max Schloessinger, Gotthard Deutsch, and Budgett Meakin. The article traces Jewish life in the sultanate of northwestern Africa from ancient times onward.

It begins with traditions that Jewish settlers reached the region, once part of Roman Mauritania, before the Temple fell. The account moves through Roman rule, the Vandal years, and the persecution edict of Justinian in 534. It gives space to the Berber Jewish tribes and to Kahinah, the Berber Jewish leader who died resisting the Arab conquest in 703. For readers it preserves how Moroccan Jewish history was told a century ago.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-munk-immanuel-1:
Immanuel Munk was a German physiologist born at Posen on May 20, 1852, the younger brother of Hermann Munk. Isidore Singer and Frederick T. Haneman wrote his Jewish Encyclopedia entry. He studied medicine at Berlin, Breslau, and Strasburg, taking his diploma in 1873. He practised in Berlin and taught physiology at its university.

His essays deal with nutrition, assimilation, and the secretion of urine. From 1897 he edited the Zentralblatt für Physiologie. His textbook on the physiology of man and the mammals reached a fifth edition by 1899. With Uffelmann he wrote a handbook on the feeding of the healthy and the sick.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-napoleon-bonapa:
Napoleon Bonaparte appears in the Jewish Encyclopedia only where his career touched the Jews. The article, by the editorial committee and Joseph Jacobs, begins in 1806. In council he first called the Alsatian Jews a state within the state. A week later he declared against persecuting them, and suspended debts owed to Jews for a year.

That same decree summoned the Assembly of Notables, which led to the French Sanhedrin of 1807. Napoleon then organized French Jewry into consistories, aiming at assimilation. His greater gift was indirect: his armies broke feudal Europe and carried in legal equality. German Jews long named him a chief forerunner of their emancipation, and some took Schöntheil, Bonaparte translated, as a surname.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-nehama-judah-11:
Judah Nehama was a Turkish rabbi of Salonica. Isidore Singer and Meyer Kayserling wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born there in 1825 and died there in 1899. He served as rabbi in his native city. For years he helped lead the local Alliance committee.

Nehama wrote letters to Luzzatto, Rapoport, and Zunz. He also edited the journal El Lunar for a time. His Ladino world history for children appeared in 1861. He wrote a life of Dr. Albert Cohn in 1877. A Hebrew address honored his father's memory in 1888. His printed letters also preserve Salonica's Jewish history. They cover its printing houses as well as its people.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-numenius-11620:
Numenius was a Jewish envoy of Maccabean days. Richard Gottheil and Samuel Krauss wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was a son of Antiochus. With Antipater he traveled to Sparta and Rome. Jonathan Maccabeus sent them first on that errand.

Simon sent them again on the same mission. They brought back decrees whose text still survives. Josephus dates one such decree under Hyrcanus II. It doubtless belongs to those same embassies though. How far to trust the tale turns on Josephus. His quoted documents carry the whole weight here. In 139 B.C. Numenius went to Rome again. That year Rome expelled Jewish proselytizers, Valerius Maximus says. A Jewish mission of words was plainly active there.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ottolengo-josep:
Joseph Ottolengo was an Italian scholar of the fifteen hundreds. Isidore Singer and Umberto Cassuto wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was a German by birth and by speech. He came from Ettlingen to Cremona, in Italy. He died about the year 1570, the entry says.

At Cremona, Joseph ran a school for Jewish boys. He fell into a feud with Joshua dei Cantori there. He had some twenty Hebrew books printed at his own cost. They were printed at Riva di Trento, a town near by. The press there was set up by a cardinal of the church. The books came out from 1558 to 1562. Some men wrongly call him the author of a short work. That work was a brief of notes on Rashi, in fact. He was its editor, not its author, the piece says.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-parsi-joseph-11:
Joseph Parsi was a mathematician who worked near the end of the fifteenth century. Almost nothing else is known about his life. His entry was written by Isidore Singer and M. Seligsohn for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. The article is short because the record on him is thin.

Parsi left one work, an unpublished manual called Keli Faz. It showed how to build mathematical instruments. The scholar Steinschneider thought Parsi might be Joseph of Lisbon. That Joseph was a physician and astronomer at the Portuguese court. He advised King John to use the astrolabe at sea. He also sat on the panel that judged Columbus's plan. The article notes the name Parsi points to Persia instead.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-phinehas-b-hama:
Phinehas ben Hama was a Palestinian teacher of the fourth century. The Executive Committee and Jacob Zallel Lauterbach wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born, most likely, at Siknin. He studied under Jeremiah and Hilkiah there.

Phinehas also lived for a time in Babylonia. He defended the pure descent of its Jewish families. Only Palestine, he said, ranked above Babylonia in that honor. Many of his legal rulings were preserved by others. His sayings on life are still quoted. He called poverty in a house worse than fifty plagues.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-podiebrad-david: David Podiebrad was a Prague writer and record keeper. Isidore Singer and Alexander Kisch wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born in 1816 and died in 1882. For thirty years he served as secretary of Prague's burial society. He collected manuscripts on the Jews of Prague. His documents underlie Foges' book on the Josefstadt. That work appeared at Prague in 1870.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-poultry-12320:
Poultry in old Palestine is the subject of an article by the Editorial Board and I. M. Casanowicz. It appeared in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Keeping tame fowl became part of farm work late, they say. It began only after the return from Babylon. The dove was half tame by the time of Isaiah, though.

The fowls on the table of Nehemiah were likely pigeons. Small birds of other kinds may be meant as well. The quail is named as food in Exodus. Fatted fowl stood on the table of Solomon. The article sorts the birds of the Bible by name and use. It shows which were kept, which were hunted, and which were eaten.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ptolemy-i-surna:
Ptolemy the First, surnamed Soter, founded a line of kings in Egypt. Richard Gottheil and Samuel Krauss wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was satrap of Egypt from 322 to 307 B.C. He then ruled as king from 305 to 285. His house is called the Lagid house from his father. His father's name was Lagus, which means hare.

A rabbinic tale hangs on that name, the writers note. Greek translators shunned the word hare in two law verses. They did so, the tale says, out of tact for the king. New proof from stone records has been claimed of late. It would show that he hid his father's lowly name. The article weighs that claim against older accounts.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-races-of-the-ol:
Races named in the Old Testament are listed by Crawford Howell Toy and Joseph Jacobs. Their article appeared in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. The old Hebrews met peoples unlike them in many ways. Those peoples spoke other tongues and kept other customs. Their very forms struck the Hebrews as strange at first sight. In time the Hebrews learned to name them all.

One whole list of such names stands in Genesis. It is the tenth chapter of that book. The list reads like a survey of the known world. It runs from Mesopotamia to the Aegean isles. Tarshish and Abyssinia stand at its far edges. The article takes each name and asks which folk it meant.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-recording-angel:
The recording angel, in popular belief, writes down every person's deeds. Kaufmann Kohler and Judah David Eisenstein wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. Those deeds decide future reward or punishment. Rabbi Akiba gave the idea a vivid image.

The article quotes Akiba's picture of an open shop ledger. The dealer gives credit, and the hand keeps writing. Rabbi Shila said two angels follow each person as witnesses. At death, all deeds are listed with place and date. The dying person then endorses the statement himself. Prayers too are recorded in heaven, the writers say. Gabriel appears as the chief recording angel. The entry blends folklore, ethics, and Bible verses.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-rona-joseph-128:
Joseph Róna was a Hungarian sculptor born on February 1, 1861. Isidore Singer and Ludwig Venetianer wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He was born at Lovas Berény. His parents meant him for a mercantile career.

The article says he instead became a sculptor's pupil. He did menial studio work by day. At night he copied sculptures on his own. A state scholarship sent him to Vienna for study. In 1882 he entered Zumbusch's school as a royal stipendiary. In 1885 he won Berlin's Roman prize. His Saint Sebastian and Olympic Victory earned it. After Rome and Paris he settled in Budapest in 1886. His noted works include statues of Kossuth and Prince Eugene. A Pallas lexicon is the entry's cited source.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-rubin-solomon-1:
Solomon Rubin was a Galician Neo-Hebrew author born in Dolina on April 3, 1823. Herman Rosenthal and Peter Wiernik wrote his entry for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. He was trained for the rabbinate, but modern learning drew him away.

Rubin tried business for five years, then studied bookkeeping and languages at Lemberg. After army service he taught, then took a trade post at Galatz in Rumania. Evenings there went to the studies he loved most. In 1859 he returned to Galicia to head a boys' school at Bolechow. In Vienna he promised Smolenskin a full work each year for Ha-Shahar.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-samuel-ben-kalo:
Samuel ben Kalonymus he-Hasid of Speyer was a tosafist, poet, and philosopher of the twelfth century. Joseph Jacobs and M. Seligsohn wrote his entry for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. Some called him the Prophet, so Solomon Luria reports.

Samuel seems to have lived in both Spain and France during his life. The tosafot quote him, and RaSHBaM quotes him on a passage of Pesahim. He commented on the tractate Tamid, as Abraham b. David notes. His Shir ha-Yihud hymns God's unity in seven parts, one per weekday. Solomon Luria forbade its recitation, but other rabbis allowed it freely.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-satanow-isaac-h:
Herman Rosenthal and Julius Gottlieb wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia entry, published in 1906, on Isaac ha-Levi Satanow. He was a scholar and poet. Satanow was born at Satanow, in Poland, in 1733. He died in Berlin on December 25, 1805. As a young man he left Poland for the Prussian capital. There wealthy patrons found him work as a teacher.

The article paints Satanow as a bundle of contrasts. He dressed like a Polish Jew yet acted like a German. Orthodox in belief, he still favored Reform in practice. He mastered Jewish tradition yet thought freely as a philosopher. His Mishle Asaf mixes Bible style with modern fine writing. Critics could not decide how to judge it. Some took it for an ancient relic. Others called him a fraud who passed off new work as old.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-schuhl-moise-13:
Frederick T. Haneman and Isidore Singer wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia entry, published in 1906, on Moïse Schuhl. He was a French rabbi. Schuhl was born at Westhausen, in Alsace, on May 2, 1845. He studied at the lyceum at Strasburg. He then trained at the Rabbinical Seminary in Paris. He became rabbi at Saint-Etienne in 1870.

In 1888 Schuhl rose to chief rabbi of Vesoul. In 1896 he became chief rabbi of the consistory of Epinal. His books gather sayings from the Talmud and Midrash. That work appeared at Paris in 1878. He also wrote on the superstitions of modern Judaism. Another book answers Roman charges against the Jewish religion. His Nos Usages Religieux, on Jewish religious customs, came out in 1896.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-senator-herman-:
Herman Senator was a German clinician and medical writer born at Gnesen in 1834. Isidore Singer and Frederick T. Haneman wrote the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry on him. He took his medical degree at Berlin in 1857. A year later he began practice in that city.

Senator climbed Berlin's medical ranks step by step. He taught at the university, led wards at the Augusta Hospital, and joined the Charité. In 1888 his Charité unit grew into the university's third medical clinic, with him as director. From 1872 he also edited a leading medical journal. The entry records a long career spent joining bedside care with research and teaching.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-shebna-13520:
Shebna was chamberlain of the king's palace in ancient Judah, the Bible says. Emil G. Hirsch and Eduard König wrote the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry on him. He may match the steward Isaiah denounces in a sharp oracle. That office could also be held by others, like Jotham.

Isaiah scolds Shebna for carving himself a tomb high in the rock. The tomb stood near the royal graves on Mount Zion. The prophet's words hint Shebna was an upstart or foreigner. His doom would be exile to a broad, flat land. Shebna favored an alliance with Egypt against Assyria. He likely fell prisoner when Assyria invaded. The entry reads a proud official's fall through one prophet's warning.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-shurrabi-shelom:
Shelomo Salem Shurrabi was religious head of the Beni-Israel community of Bombay, India. Joseph Jacobs wrote the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry on him. He was born at Cochin late in the eighteenth century. A sea wreck changed his life around 1836.

Sailing to Bombay with his grandfather, Shurrabi was shipwrecked en route. A Beni-Israel soldier found him and got him work binding books. Shurrabi knew much Jewish lore and sang the service well. The new synagogue hired him as its reader. His pay was one hundred rupees a year. He taught the Beni-Israel their faith's traditions with care. Through his efforts new synagogues rose in four towns. He died at Bombay in 1856, a chief keeper of that community's faith.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-simeon-b-tarfon:
Simeon ben Tarfon was a tanna of the second generation of rabbinic teachers. Wilhelm Bacher and Jacob Zallel Lauterbach wrote the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry on him. Four of his readings of Scripture have been preserved. Each one works closely on a verse's exact wording.

One reading makes both oath taker and oath causer responsible. If perjury is proved, both share the blame, he held. Another finds a ban on enabling adultery in Exodus. A third reads a Deuteronomy word by its letter parts. You spied out and desecrated God's dwelling, he rendered it. A fourth explains why the Euphrates is called the great river. It borders Palestine, and nearness to greatness lends honor. The proverb he cites runs, approach the anointed and smell of ointment. The entry shows wordplay serving law.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-soborten-13820:
Soborten was a town in Bohemia with a very old Jewish community. Isidore Singer and H Galandauer wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. The community covered parts of three districts in all. Its synagogue had a tower with a clock. Two lamps in it bore the dates 1553 and 1654.

For a time, Dresden Jews used the cemetery at Soborten. Many stones mark graves of Jews driven from Prague. Some of those buried there had died as martyrs. Until 1848 the Jews were confined to a ghetto street. In 1883 the community won independence in its rabbinate. It then had about 150 Jewish residents in all.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-sonnenfeld-sigi:
Sigismund Sonnenfeld was a Hungarian journalist born at Vagujhely in 1847. Isidore Singer and Frederick T Haneman wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He was born there on October 1 of that year. He studied at Prague, Presburg, and the University of Budapest. He took his doctor's degree at Budapest in 1870.

That year he joined the staff of the Pester Lloyd. He served that paper until 1890 in Budapest. He also taught at the gymnasium of Budapest for years. In 1890 he moved to Paris to direct Hirsch institutions. He later directed the Jewish Colonization Association from Paris. He traveled for it to Argentina and to Rumania twice.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-steinthal-herma:
Hermann Steinthal was a German philologist and philosopher born at Gröbzig in 1823. Isidore Singer wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article about him in 1906. Steinthal was born on May 16 of that year. He studied philology and philosophy at the University of Berlin. He died at Berlin on March 14, 1899.

Steinthal was a pupil of Wilhelm von Humboldt and edited his language works in 1884. In 1860 he founded a journal of folk psychology and language science. He founded it with his brother-in-law Moritz Lazarus. The journal helped launch a new science of racial psychology. His own books treat the origin of language and its classes. He also wrote a history of language study among Greeks and Romans.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-tobiah-ben-elij:
Tobiah ben Elijah of Vienne was a French tosafist of the thirteenth century. A. Peiginsky wrote this article with the Executive Committee of the Editorial Board for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. He was a younger contemporary of Isaac of Dampierre. He may also have been Isaac's pupil. He attended Isaac's funeral in 1210.

Later writers praise Tobiah as a great teacher of law. His casuistic work fed many decisions quoted in his name. His pupil Abraham cites him often as an authority. The Tosafot and other collections quote him as well. He also wrote Bible commentary and religious poetry. His penitential poems entered a Burgundian prayer-book. Persecution of his fellow Jews inspired those verses.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-trinquetaille-h:
Trinquetaille, a suburb of Arles on the Rhone, held a weighty medieval Jewish community. Isidore Singer and S. Kahn wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. The lords of Baux received its Jews with favor. They lived in peace there until 1300. That year the town merged with Arles, and the communities united.

By 1349 Arles wanted the union dissolved again. Trinquetaille's Jews refused to share communal expenses, Arles claimed. The town bred noted scholars in its good centuries. Meir ben Isaac defended Alfasi against sharp attacks. Nathan ben Meir wrote on the Pentateuch and illegal seizures. Todros Todrosi, the translator, also lived there. Isaac Lattes mentions the town in his writings.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-uziel-14620:
Uziel was a Sephardic family name found in Spain by the fifteenth century. Gotthard Deutsch, Schulim Ochser, Richard Gottheil, and Isaac Broydé wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. Expulsion scattered the Uziels across North Africa and Italy. The Levant received branches of the family as well.

Hayyim Uziel wrote an ethical work in Judaeo-Spanish at Smyrna. Isaac b. Abraham Uziel was a physician and poet born at Fez. He taught at Amsterdam, where Manasseh ben Israel studied under him. Uneasy at lax observance, he founded the Neweh Shalom congregation. He became its rabbi in 1610 after Judah Vega died. His Hebrew grammar appeared in 1627 through a pupil. Jacob Uziel practiced medicine famously at Venice.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-weigert-karl-14:
Karl Weigert was a German pathologist. He was born at Münsterberg, in Silesia, on March 19, 1845. Isidore Singer and Frederick T. Haneman wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia entry, published in 1906. He died at Frankfort on August 5, 1904. He studied at Berlin, Vienna, and Breslau. He graduated in 1868 and served as a war surgeon.

Weigert assisted leading researchers at Breslau and Leipsic. He followed Cohnheim to Leipsic in 1878. In 1884 he became professor at the Senckenberg Stiftung. His fame rests on staining methods for bacteria. Those methods let scholars see germs under the microscope. His writings cover smallpox, kidney disease, and nerve tissue. The entry lists his chief works.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-worms-jules-150:
Jules Worms (1830-1898) was a French army doctor and hospital chief. Isidore Singer and Frederick T. Haneman wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Born in Paris, he took his degree at Strasburg in 1852. He then served at a war school in Paris.

He went to the Crimea as a surgeon in the war. Back in Paris he worked at the Gros-Caillou Hospital. From 1865 he served as surgeon at the Rothschild Hospital. He held that post for ten full years. He kept the health counts of Paris for a decade. In 1875 he rose to chief doctor of the Northern Railroad. His one named book treats the cutting out of growths. The entry is a plain list of posts well held.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-yom-tob-ben-isa:
Yom-Tob ben Isaac of Joigny was a scholar and poet slain at York. Joseph Jacobs and Meyer Kayserling wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He died there in March of the year 1190. He was a pupil of the famed Rabbi Tam.

The Jews of York fled to the fort from a wild mob. They held out for days with no hope of aid. At his word most of them chose death by their own hand. He is oft named with the word ha-Kodesh, the holy one. That word marks him as a martyr of the faith. He wrote notes on the Bible as well as hymns. One hymn is sung on the eve of Atonement still. One prayer of his has fourteen parts in verse form.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-zeisler-sigmund:
Sigmund Zeisler (born 1860) was an American lawyer of Chicago fame. Cyrus Adler and Frederick T. Haneman wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Born at Bielitz in Austria, he read at Vienna first. He then read law at a Chicago school in his new land.

He joined the Chicago bar and rose in that town fast. He served as aide to the defense in a famed case. That case was the anarchist case of 1886 and 1887. In 1893 he won the post of chief aide to the town. He quit that post in 1894 for poor health at the time. He toured Europe for some months to mend his health. Back home he went back to his own law work in town. He wrote for law books and reviews of the day as well.
journal-of-discourses-vol-20:
Fifty years of Mormonism mark Volume Twenty, published in 1880. The church counts its jubilee from a farmhouse start in 1830. A commonwealth in the mountains stands where six converts began.

Discourses look back over exodus, martyrdom, and the desert's hard bloom. Blessings are counted while the federal crusade still rages outside. Memory serves as armor in these proud, backward-looking Tabernacle talks. The Saints tell their own story as proof that God led them. Commemoration carries an edge here, since the fight is far from won in their eyes. Pride in the past arms the Saints for a grim present.
kafka-ein-landarzt-1920:
Ein Landarzt, published in 1920 by Kurt Wolff, is the story collection Kafka prepared in his lifetime, holding his short parables and tales. The title story, 'A Country Doctor', gives the book its center.

A doctor is summoned on a winter night to a boy whose wound holds a horror no medicine can answer. Around it stand 'Before the Law', the doorkeeper parable later set inside The Trial, and 'An Imperial Message', sent but never delivered. Each piece is a small machine of dread and logic. Together they are the purest dose of Kafka's short fiction.
keats-poems-1820:
John Keats published his third and last book of poems in 1820, less than a year before his death at twenty-five. The volume holds the great odes and story poems on which his fame now rests. Publishers issued it while Keats was already ill with tuberculosis.

The odes to a nightingale and on a Grecian urn ask how art and beauty survive death. Lamia tells of a serpent woman in rich, glittering verse. Isabella adapts Boccaccio, and The Eve of St. Agnes glows with color and romance. La Belle Dame sans Merci adds a chilling ballad. Few single volumes in English hold so much lasting poetry.
lalla-vakyani-grierson-barnett-1920:
Lal Ded, called Lalla, wandered Kashmir in the fourteenth century singing short sayings, vakhs, on the soul and God. George Grierson and Lionel Barnett edited and translated the Lalla-Vakyani for the Royal Asiatic Society in 1920. Their edition gives the Kashmiri text with translation, notes, and full tools for study.

Lalla, a Shaivite yogini, sings of the body as a worn cloth, of breath, of the name of Shiva, and of the self lost and found. Hindus and Muslims of Kashmir both claim her songs to this day. The editors add notes on yoga, on her language and meters, and a concordance and vocabulary. The book is the scholarly base for all work on her.
lawrence-lost-girl-1920:
The Lost Girl won Lawrence the James Tait Black prize and became one of his best-selling novels on its appearance in 1920. Its heroine, Alvina Houghton, is a music teacher in a drab Midlands mining town, suffocating under her father's respectability.

Alvina joins a troupe of Italian performers and follows one of them to Italy, escaping the life laid out for her. The novel is the first full statement of Lawrence's flight motif: salvation through escape to a wilder place. It is also warm, funny, and full of observed small-town life. The flight south would drive his later fiction again and again.
lawrence-new-poems-1920:
New Poems, published in 1920, gathers Lawrence's verse from the end of the war years, when his style was changing fast. The tight rhymes of his youth give way here to open, breathing free verse.

The collection holds 'Piano', his famous memory of childhood music breaking a grown man's composure. Other poems reach toward the elemental force he would soon praise in 'Snake' and the animal poems. Lawrence writes about men, women, and the gulf between them with new plainness. The book is a threshold: behind it, the Georgian poet; ahead, the prophet of the living body.
lawrence-women-in-love-1920:
D. H. Lawrence published Women in Love in 1920, his intense, visionary novel of modern relationships in England. The tale sets Ursula and Gudrun Brangwen with two very different men in the mining Midlands of wartime. It is the sequel, in spirit and in Ursula's story, to The Rainbow.

Ursula weds the school inspector Rupert Birkin, Lawrence's spokesman for a new, balanced union of equals. Gudrun takes up with Gerald Crich, the mine owner, in a bond of fascination, cruelty, and mutual ruin. Wrestling, dancing, a drowned sister, and a rabbit's scratch mark the couples' opposed paths toward love or death in snow. Gerald dies in the Alps at the close, while Birkin mourns both wife and friend in unresolved grief. The novel's psychology of power and desire still startles readers a century on.
letters-to-the-times-upon-war-and-neutra:
Thomas Erskine Holland collected his letters to The Times on war and neutrality. Longmans issued this third edition in London and New York in 1921. Holland held Oxford's Chichele chair in international law.

The letters span the years 1881 to 1920. A first chapter treats measures short of war for settling disputes. Friendly measures and a petition to America's president open it. Holland wrote as a scholar addressing the public through a newspaper. His letters trace international law through four decades of crises. Holland helped found the Institut de Droit International's work. Newspaper letters let scholars speak beyond the university walls.
lewis-main-street-1920:
Sinclair Lewis published Main Street in 1920, a novel about a young woman in a small Minnesota town. Carol Kennicott arrives in Gopher Prairie as a bride full of plans. She wants art, reform, and a finer life for the town. The town resists her at every step with gossip and smug habit.

Carol tries clubs, plays, and new buildings, and mostly fails. Her marriage to the kind but dull Dr. Kennicott strains under the fight. Lewis mocks small-town pride yet shows real affection for its people. The novel was a huge bestseller and sparked debate nationwide. It gave American speech a lasting name for dull conformity.
library-of-the-world-s-best-literature-a:
Volume Five continues the Warner anthology of ancient and modern literature. Editor Charles Dudley Warner worked with three associate editors on the series. University scholars, including an observatory director from California, advised on selections. The Connoisseur Edition presented the set as a permanent home library.

This volume gathers excerpts from honored authors across many lands and ages. Each selection stands as a sample of a writer the editors judged important. Busy readers could meet major works in manageable portions. The book remains useful as a guide to what the 1890s reading public valued most. The council mixed eastern professors with western scholars like Holden. Such names assured buyers the selections carried real academic weight.
lidzbarski-mandaische-liturgien-1920:
Lidzbarski followed his Book of John with Mandaische Liturgien in 1920, a German translation of Mandaean ritual texts. These are the prayers and directions used at baptism and at the mass for the dead. The Mandaeans are often called the last living Gnostic sect.

The liturgies name the rivers of light, the watchers at the soul's ascent, and the words spoken over the water. Priests still use versions of these rites in Iraq and in exile communities abroad. For scholars, the volume preserves the working prayer book of a faith that survived two thousand years. The texts are given with the care of a scholar who knew the rites were still alive.
lie-family-at-gilje-eastman-1920:
Samuel Coffin Eastman translated Jonas Lie's The Family at Gilje into English in 1920 for the Scandinavian Classics series. Lie set his novel on a Norwegian captain's farm in the 1840s. Captain Jaeger, his capable wife, and their children face straitened means with pride and invention.

The daughters' prospects, the sons' schooling, and one long-remembered ball fill the household year. Lie writes domestic life with humor, tenderness, and a seaman's eye for weather. The novel became Norway's beloved picture of its own recent past. Eastman's version served the American-Scandinavian Foundation's aim of carrying such classics west. Few family novels of the North are read with warmer feeling.
lindsay-voyage-to-arcturus-1920:
David Lindsay sent a bold soul to a far world in A Voyage to Arcturus, his strange novel of 1920. The world is Tormance, lit by a bright star. Each land holds a new creed. Each creed reshapes the flesh and mind of those who pass through.

The trek reads as a quest for truth through pain and change. Few tales are so odd or so stern. C. S. Lewis and J. R. R. Tolkien both felt its pull. It stays a cult peak of deep thought in tale form. Maskull, the bold guest from earth, bears fresh organs and creeds in each land. Each change strips a lie from his view of life and self.
lowie-primitive-society-1920:
Robert Lowie, another student of Boas, published Primitive Society in 1920 as a broad survey of how early peoples organize their lives. He drew on reports from North America, Africa, and the Pacific islands. The book became a standard college text in anthropology.

Lowie explains kinship, marriage, property, rank, and the rise of the state without ranking peoples on a ladder of progress. He argues that customs grow by borrowing and chance as much as by design. His clear, skeptical voice helped free the field from grand schemes of human progress. He writes with respect for the peoples described and little patience for easy theories.
maier-septimana-philosophica-1620:
Solomon and the Queen of Sheba trade riddles across a philosophical week in Maier's Septimana philosophica of 1620. The Latin work frames golden enigmas on every kind of nature as the royal pair's answers to each other. Alchemy, natural philosophy, and emblematic wisdom meet in the dialogue, question by question.

Maier, physician and Rosicrucian apologist, loved the riddle form, since it lets truth wear a mask. Each day of the week brings its theme, and each answer opens a small treatise in disguise. Readers meet here the playful, learned face of early modern alchemy, where a game between monarchs carries a whole view of nature.
malthus-principles-political-economy-182:
T. R. Malthus published his Principles of Political Economy in 1820 as a reply to Ricardo's school. The two men were friends and rivals in the young science of economics. Malthus doubts that supply always creates its own demand, the claim tied to Say's Law. Spending can fail, and goods can glut the market unsold.

His stress on effective demand, the will and means to buy, shapes the book. Landlords, workers, and savers each get weighed for their role in demand. Keynes later praised Malthus as the truer guide on slumps. The treatise is the great anti Ricardian work of its age. Its questions returned in the Great Depression.
mansfield-bliss-1920:
Katherine Mansfield, a New Zealand writer living in England, published Bliss and Other Stories in 1920. It was her second collection and the book that fixed her reputation. Mansfield wrote with a rare gift for the revealing moment, the small scene that changes everything.

The title story follows a happy wife whose perfect day cracks at a dinner party. Other stories visit a widow's memories, a child's first ball, and the cold routines of office life. Mansfield wastes nothing: a glance, a pear tree, a shaft of light carries the meaning. The collection helped define the modern short story in English.
mariner-an-account-of-the-natives-of-the:
William Mariner spent four years among the Tongans from 1806 to 1810, and John Martin edited his Account, published in 1820. Mariner was a ship's clerk seized when his vessel was taken, kept alive for his skills and adopted into chiefly life. Gods, taboo, burial rites, and war customs fill his singular record.

No European had lived so deep inside a Polynesian society so early, and the detail shows it. Mariner learned the language, fought in its wars, and mourned its dead. His account stands as the earliest intimate record of Polynesian life, still vivid after two centuries.
mayflower-compact-1620:
Aboard the Mayflower in November 1620, forty-one male passengers signed a short agreement before going ashore. The Pilgrims had landed outside the area covered by their patent, so their legal standing was unclear. They promised to form a civil body politic and obey laws made for the common good.

The compact is brief, only a few lines long, yet its idea carries weight. A community agrees to govern itself by consent, rather than by orders from a distant ruler. The settlers then founded Plymouth Colony on that basis. Later Americans prized the compact as an early seed of self-government.
merritt-metal-monster-1920:
A city of live metal waits in high hills in Abraham Merritt's novel The Metal Monster, from 1920. Men on a trek find cubes, spheres, and shapes that move as one mind. The shapes can form beasts, walls, and vast forms at will.

Awe turns to fear as the mind in the metal wakes. Merritt writes in lush, bright prose full of strange sights. The book is pulp awe at its peak. Its weird life form feels fresh and vast a full age later. Ruth, a brave guest on the trek, stands as the heart of the tale. Her nerve steadies the men when awe turns to blind fear.
millay-few-figs-1920:
Edna St. Vincent Millay published A Few Figs from Thistles in 1920, a slim book that made her the voice of young America. Millay was living in Greenwich Village, poor, brilliant, and famous among the bohemians. The title comes from a biblical phrase about gathering figs from thistles.

The poems are short, bright, and defiant. First Fig gives the era its motto: my candle burns at both ends. Millay writes about lovers taken lightly and freedom guarded fiercely, in strict forms handled with a wink. Older critics scolded the book's flippancy while young readers memorized it. A Few Figs from Thistles captures the flaming youth of the Jazz Age in verse.
much-ado-about-nothing-pg1520:
William Shakespeare's comedy opens in a street in Messina. The cast names Don Pedro, his brother Don John, and young Claudio. Benedick of Padua and Leonato's house fill out the scene. Hero and her sharp niece Beatrice stand at its heart.

A note warns this is an early Gutenberg file, lightly proofed. A cleaner text is offered as ebook 1519. Still, the play reads whole here, tricks and all. Villains slander Hero while friends plot to wed the wits. V1 praised its faked death, rescued bride, and the most joyful battle of the sexes ever staged.
nietzsche-antichrist-mencken-1920:
Friedrich Nietzsche wrote The Antichrist in 1888, near the end of his sane life. The English text here is H. L. Mencken's translation of 1920. Nietzsche attacks Christianity as a religion of pity and denial of life. He contrasts it with what he sees as noble, life-affirming values.

He re-reads the New Testament as a story of decline from Jesus to Paul and the church. The book is brief, harsh, and deliberately provocative. It states his revaluation of all values in its sharpest form. Mencken's version made it widely read in America. Readers still argue over its force and its fairness.
o-henry-memorial-award-prize-stories-of-:
Prize Stories of 1920 gathers that year's O. Henry Memorial Award tales, chosen by the Society of Arts and Sciences. Blanche Colton Williams again wrote the introduction. Williams taught English at Hunter College and story writing at Columbia. Maxwell Struthers Burt opens the contents with Each in His Generation.

Frances Noyes Hart's Contact and F. Scott Fitzgerald's The Camel's Back follow. Esther Forbes, Guy Gilpatric, and Alice Duer Miller all place here. Slow Poison is Miller's entry, and Footfalls closes the list from Wilbur Daniel Steele. A professor's used car and butterflies sit between graver tales. The volume maps the short story's range in one year.
oneill-emperor-jones-1920:
Eugene O'Neill published The Emperor Jones in 1920, his breakthrough play of a Pullman porter's rise and flight. A Black Pullman porter turned Caribbean emperor flees through the jungle, stripped of power by drums and ghosts. The play made O'Neill's name and brought expressionist method to the American stage.

Brutus Jones, who fled a chain gang to rule an island by fraud and a silver bullet, faces revolt. Through eight scenes of forest darkness he sheds his uniform, his boasts, and his mind to ancestral visions. The drums quicken like a heartbeat while Jones fires his revolver at ghosts and at last at himself in mind. Pursuers find him at dawn, killed by the silver bullet he had reserved for his own end in the forest. The play's power and its racial burdens are still argued wherever it is staged.
openalex-w1948094720:
Federico Costa, Albert Ko, and co-authors reviewed this disease worldwide. Their review appeared in PLoS Neglected Tropical Diseases in 2015. Leptospirosis is a bacterial disease passed from animals. It strikes rural farmers and urban slum dwellers hardest. No global counts of its illness and death existed.

The team reviewed studies and databases from many nations. Eighty studies from thirty-four countries met quality standards. Models adjusted the counts by age and sex. Some regions, such as Africa, lacked good studies. The estimates give the disease a firm global scale. Better numbers can end its neglected status, they argue.
openalex-w2016100220:
Sigbjorn Tveteras, Frank Asche, Marc Bellemare and colleagues built a world fish price index. Their paper appeared in PLoS ONE in 2012. Seafood feeds billions of people as a key protein source. Yet the UN food agency tracked other food prices, not seafood. Food prices had hit record highs in 2011.

The team filled the gap with the Fish Price Index. It uses trade data, which are easy to update. Seafood trade links local prices to world markets. The index proved steadier than other food price indices. It showed fewer sharp price spikes. Wild catch fish grew scarcer in recent years. Farmed fish growth roughly kept pace with demand. Regional prices sometimes moved in opposite ways.
openalex-w2251394420:
Soujanya Poria, Erik Cambria, and Alexander Gelbukh presented this paper at the EMNLP conference in 2015. Their new trick extracts text features from inside a deep convolutional neural network.

The network's inner layer activations become a compact fingerprint of each sentence. Those features join visual and audio features from the same clip. A multiple kernel learning classifier, suited to mixed data types, then judges sentiment. The combined system beat the prior state of the art by a wide margin. A faster decision-level fusion method is also offered, trading a little accuracy for parallel speed.
openalex-w2401282820:
Kaustubh Adhikari, Macarena Fuentes-Guajardo, Mirsha Quinto-Sánchez, and colleagues published this genome scan in Nature Communications in 2016. Working with the CANDELA cohort in Latin America, they hunted genes behind normal facial variation. Earlier European and East Asian studies agreed on almost nothing, one gene region apart.

Over six thousand volunteers had fourteen facial features scored from photographs, from chin shape to nose profile. Their genomes were scanned for matching DNA patterns. The scan confirmed the known PAX3 link to the nasal bridge point. It also implicated five further gene regions, mostly shaping the nose. All five genes were already known players in building the face during development, now tied to everyday differences among adults.
openalex-w2955714720:
Shiu Kumar, Alok Sharma, and Tatsuhiko Tsunoda published this study in Scientific Reports in 2019. It tackles brain wave classification for brain-computer interfaces, systems that let people control devices with their thoughts. Sorting brain waves correctly is the core challenge for such systems.

The authors build a predictor based on a long short-term memory network, a kind of artificial neural network that learns from sequences. They call their approach OPTICAL. A common older method extracts features from EEG signals, but the best frequency band differs from person to person. A poorly chosen band adds noise and lowers accuracy. Their network approach aims to classify brain waves with greater accuracy across users.

Jack Fu, F. Kyle Satterstrom, Minshi Peng, and colleagues hunted rare gene variants behind autism, in Nature Genetics in 2022. Their data covered more than one hundred fifty thousand people, including large autism cohorts.

Joint analysis linked seventy-one genes to autism at a strict evidence threshold, and many more at a looser one. Most of the signal came from new protein-breaking variants, with damaging missense changes and larger deletions adding more. The genes point to the cell types and brain pathways where autism risk acts. That map can guide both biology and future diagnosis.
openalex-w7204257220:

The mechanisms involve hormone mimicry, epigenetic changes, and the gut-brain axis through disturbed gut microbes, and mixtures of chemicals at low doses can reinforce each other. The authors call for closer monitoring and for more long-term studies, including in Latin America.

Maisa Niehues wrote a Portuguese-language umbrella review, in Brazil in 2026, on Crohn's disease in the era of advanced therapies. The widening drug arsenal has shifted the medical debate from relieving symptoms to changing the disease's natural history. Searching global biomedical sources, Ibero-American work, and current guidelines in 2026, the review prioritizes phase-three trials with endoscopic results, head-to-head comparisons, long-term extensions, and large cohorts.

The targets added over two decades, from tumor necrosis factor blockers through interleukin and trafficking inhibitors to Janus kinase inhibition. Clearly widened medical and endoscopic control, Niehues finds, with lasting power shown while treatment continues. Evidence of structural course change is more limited and uneven, and how early treatment starts and the strategy weigh heavily.

Vilmar da Silva Nascimento and Rozineide Iraci Pereira da Silva published a Portuguese-language literature review in Brazil in 2026 on occupational diseases among basic education teachers. The harms concentrated in three categories, they find: mental health problems, vocal disorders, and musculoskeletal changes. The most frequent were occupational stress, anxiety, burnout syndrome, dysphonia, vocal fatigue, and lower back pain, nearly always tied to work overload, pressure for results, absent institutional support, and intense voice use. Teaching's characteristics favor these illnesses, they conclude, demanding health promotion, prevention, and better working conditions.

Márcio Rubens de Oliveira and Allene Carvalho Lage released a Portuguese-language study in Brazil in 2026 on Mães da Resistência, Mothers of Resistance. An organization in Pernambuco whose maternal activism confronts LGBTphobia. LGBTphobia rests on cis-heteronormative pillars and shows up as prejudice and violence against people who defy hegemonic demands on sexual orientation and gender identity. Part of a nationally funded research project, the study used epistemology and an extended case method, hearing the organization's president on its school methods.

Those methods matter, the meanings gathered show, as tools of struggle, welcome, and knowledge building that strengthen families and support LGBTQI+ people in Pernambuco. Maternal activism turns private grief and fear into public, school resistance on behalf of other families' children too.
openalex-w7212054920:
Vitoria Cristina Lopes leads a team reading the health files of women with endometriosis, a chronic disease of the womb lining. The disease strikes women in their fertile years and cuts deep into life quality. The team checked files from a private clinic in Cascavel, Parana. The records ran from 2022 to 2025 and numbered just over two hundred. They tracked gut signs, mood signs, and bowel function.

Gut signs were near universal in the group. Bloating, constipation, and pain on passing stool led the list. Two in three women had both anxiety and low mood at once. The pattern, the authors argue, ties gut change, chronic pain, and mind in one knot. Endometriosis, in their view, has many faces at once. Care for it must cross fields, not sit in one clinic room.
openalex-w7212249820:
Julio Cesar de Faria Maciel leads a team on fake drugs, and on the drug expert who stands in their path. Fake pills can fail to cure, or can harm and kill. The team ran a full search of past work from 2020 to 2025, plus laws and state guides. Five studies made the final cut. The lens joins law, track-and-trace tools, and the daily work of the pharmacist.

Laws and trace tools form the base of the fight, they find. Yet the parts do not link up well, and watch is thin in spots. The pharmacist stands out as a key guard. That expert checks where a drug came from, spots flaws, and guides the public. The authors call for a joined-up push: law, tech, and the drug counter as one line of care.
openalex-w7213417220:
Andréa Silva do Nascimento reports on distance extension courses used inside a face-to-face chemistry teaching degree. The setting is the Federal Institute in Duque de Caxias, Rio de Janeiro. Other assessment routes were allowed, so the online course was a choice, not a compulsion. Seminars and process-based assessment completed the design. The aim was to deepen future teachers' reading on inclusion and rights.
openalex-w7213878420:
Lucas Vilela Franco and Liliane Vieira Martins Leal study payroll loans and older people's debt in Brazil. Payroll credit is thus presented as a byproduct of socioeconomic insecurity, dressed in the language of access.
openalex-w7216363420:
Maria Auxiliadora Coelho Pinto wrote a 2026 historical article on the Magüta, also called Ticuna, Indigenous people of the Upper Solimões region in Amazonas, Brazil. She asks what colonization and Christianity did to their traditional religiosity and way of life. Her qualitative approach follows the passage from an autonomous Indigenous worldview to imposed foreign doctrine.

Before Portuguese and Spanish contact, she finds, Magüta religion was woven with their gods and taught unity, sharing, and respect for nature. The forced arrival of Christianity broke apart that social organization, causing severe cultural losses and harming their education and family life. Religious colonization split the people's identity and original values of fraternity, she concludes, replacing their sovereignty over their own culture with forced integration and weakening the people's structure. The article speaks to its title's theme, a truly Indigenous church, by first bringing back what was displaced.

Arithmetic is shaped by culture yet held by a stable mental architecture. And philosophy of logic now finds both extreme psychologism and its opposite overstated. They refine necessity as indexed to the operation that produces it, propose five sources of it, and derive testable predictions, including a clinical dissociation doctors could check.

Sidália Marques da Silva, Flávia Marques de Almeida, and Paulo Victor da Costa Campos reviewed preventive pediatric dentistry in a 2026 article: the strategies that keep children's mouths healthy before disease starts. Their narrative review draws on health databases, books, and official documents about children's oral health.

parry-voyage-northwest-passage-1819-20:
William Edward Parry sailed in 1819 with the ships Hecla and Griper to find a North-West Passage through the Canadian Arctic. His Journal of the voyage appeared in 1821. Parry got farther west than any European before him.

The ships wintered at Melville Island, where the crew staged plays, ran a school, and printed a playbill in the ice. Parry describes Inuit meetings, Arctic wildlife, and the strange light of the polar night. His success won a prize for crossing a key line of longitude. The journal became the model for a generation of Arctic exploration accounts.
pigou-economics-welfare-1920:
Arthur Pigou taught economics at Cambridge and shaped the study of how markets affect public welfare. His 1920 book The Economics of Welfare asks when private bargains help society and when they harm it. It became the founding text of welfare economics.

Pigou shows how a factory can gain while its smoke quietly costs neighbors their health and clean air.
