That shift improves access and lets it work alongside other R packages for activity and overlap analysis. Unlike rivals, Rosario can analyse overlap among many identities at once, from individuals to whole communities. The authors say this gives a fuller view of temporal niches. They present standardisation in R as key to the method's continued use in ecology.
pmc-13282920:
Picking the right family donor for a half-matched transplant is the dilemma in Mahtab Mashayekhi's 2026 leukemia cohort work. Such transplants can cure patients who lack a fully matched donor. The best donor age, sex, and family link remain uncertain.

Records covered 159 adults treated from 2015 to 2022 with one drug protocol. Most donors were siblings, then parents, then offspring. Survival and relapse were tracked for three years with adjusted models. Patterns differed between myeloid and lymphoid leukemia types. Offspring donors showed weaker results in some groups. The study helps centers weigh donor choice when several relatives can donate.
pmc-13283220:
Spin waves and lattice vibrations merge into hybrid particles inside a layered magnet, Qili Li's tunneling experiments reveal in 2026. Such mixed waves are called magnon polarons and link magnetism with sound-like motion. Clear proof in metal magnets had been scarce before this work.

Crystals of Fe3GeTe2 were probed with a scanning tunneling microscope at very low temperature. Energy spectra showed spin and lattice bands merging at crossing points. Strong coupling lifted rules that normally block spin wave signals in metals. That lifted rule is a hallmark sign of the mixed waves. The result gives a test bed for tuning spin-lattice effects in thin materials. Future devices may use such hybrids.
pmc-13283920:
Breathing failure tied to severe obesity anchors a 2026 clinical case from Sajedeh Zarghi and colleagues. Obesity hypoventilation syndrome leaves carbon dioxide high and oxygen low in blood. Late recognition can bring long intensive care stays and organ strain.

Hidden malnutrition can worsen outcomes even in patients with excess body fat. The case frames obesity itself as a chronic inflammatory, whole-body disease. Linked harms span heart disease, diabetes, fatty liver, stroke, and sleep apnea. Early team-based care is presented as the way to cut harm and cost. Nutrition support teams play a named role in that early response.
pmc-13284120:
Peng Yu and colleagues tested in 2026 how blocking vision changes leg mechanics in athletes after knee ligament surgery. Athletes who have had an anterior cruciate ligament rebuild often lean harder on sight because joint position sense is blunted. Twenty such athletes and twenty healthy athletes each performed a sharp ninety-degree cutting move with eyes open and with strobe glasses that disrupt vision, while cameras and force plates recorded the body.

Under visual disruption, the rebuilt group landed with greater inward knee collapse and more inward ankle roll, plus a stronger hip extension push and weaker knee extension push. Healthy athletes showed no clear change between the two visual conditions. The authors warn that sight disruption exposes risky movement patterns in the rebuilt group that may raise re-injury risk.
pmc-13284420:
Yin Mo and co-authors share a research update, published in 2026, from the ADVANCE-ID trial network on drug-resistant bacterial and fungal infections. The update gathers highlights from the network newsletter for March to April 2026. It shows how new trial results can guide policy and daily care in varied health settings.

One large trial in rural township hospitals in China cut antibiotic use for chest infections sharply with a digital stewardship program, with no rise in hospital return within 30 days. A trial in England and Wales, by contrast, found procalcitonin-guided rules did not cut early antibiotic starts, though deaths were lower in that arm. The contrast stresses that local setting and delivery shape whether stewardship works.
pmc-13285020:
Emma Bergstedt and Ann-Charlotte Nedlund trace health policy stories in Sweden in a 2026 study covering 1992 to 2024. Governments worldwide urge use of best evidence in health choices, yet real policy is shaped by politics and rival ideas. The team read 132 Swedish government documents and sorted the stories that frame problems and fixes.

Four periods emerged, each ruled by a distinct story about health care ills, fixes, and the role of evidence. Stories also set who counts as part of the problem, what values drive action, and how change should work. The authors show that evidence use is never neutral, since the ruling story decides what proof matters.
pmc-13285320:
A 50-day-old boy with chlamydial lung infection and a blocked, collapsed lung lobe is the subject of a 2026 case report by Yuan Huang and colleagues. Chlamydia trachomatis passes from mother to baby and usually causes a milder lung pattern in infants. A mucus plug blocking a bronchus, with lobe collapse, is rarely seen.

The full-term baby had coughed for fifteen days. Scans showed pneumonia and collapse in the left upper lobe. Sputum testing found the germ, and fluid from a scope wash backed the call with targeted gene sequencing. Care paired erythromycin with scope clearing of the plug. The baby recovered fully, with no return over two months of checks.
pmc-13285420: Mariam F. Farid and co-authors issue a correction, dated 2026, to a cat study of a cell-free spinal cord treatment for multiple sclerosis. The notice states that control images were reused from a sister study by the same team without clear notice. The authors say reuse kept the studies comparable and cut animal use, in line with welfare rules that favor fewer animals and kinder handling.
pmc-13285920:
Yanbin Chang and co-authors report a family case of Townes-Brocks syndrome in a 2026 case report centered on cup-shaped ears. The rare inherited disorder usually mixes ear, thumb, and bowel defects, but its signs vary a great deal. Here a seven-year-old boy came in only for cosmetic repair of folded ears on both sides, with clean hearing and kidney checks.

A three-generation family tree showed the same ear shape in the boy's father and grandfather, pointing to dominant inheritance. Gene tests found the same damaging change in the SALL1 gene in boy and father, which confirmed the syndrome. Both had ear surgery with good early cosmetic results. The case warns that a family ear shape alone can hide the syndrome, so history taking, gene checks, and long-term watch belong in care.
pmc-13286520:
Esma Cinar, Demet Sengul, and Ilker Sengul stack imaging clues to judge uncertain thyroid lumps in a 2026 retrospective study. Needle samples sort most thyroid nodules cleanly, but the middle categories leave surgeons guessing between watchfulness and removal. Six years of records supplied 838 nodules from 716 patients, scored by size, blood-flow patterns, guideline risk tiers, and stiffness readings from an elasticity scan.

Uncertain-category nodules ran larger than plainly benign ones on average. Richer blood flow inside and around a nodule, higher guideline risk tiers, and the stiffest elasticity grades all clustered in the uncertain groups. Cancer confirmed under the microscope also came more often from those groups. Age and nodule position, by contrast, predicted nothing. Layering the measures together, the authors argue, sharpens the call on which uncertain lumps merit surgery.
pmc-13286920:
Ying Shen and colleagues follow self-care ability in 209 spinal cord injury patients from just before hospital discharge through their first year at home. The 2026 study, based at a hospital in northern China, measured self-care at five time points plus mental health knowledge and perceived social support at the start. Self-care prevents complications and supports life back in the community.

Average self-care peaked one month after discharge, then slid gradually. Modeling found three paths: about a third of patients declined from a low start, two fifths held steady at a middle level, and the rest improved from a high base. Sex, education, mental health literacy, and social support predicted the path. Early gains can fade, the authors warn, so support should follow the trajectory.
pmc-13287020:
Zengrong Ye and co-authors compare five ways of drying a medicinal rhubarb relative from China's high plateau, measuring which method best preserves its looks and chemistry. The 2026 study weighs physical traits such as color and rehydration alongside the plant's active compounds, using metabolite profiling to track hundreds of chemicals through drying. The root serves as both a traditional drug and a functional food.

Vacuum freeze drying best protected appearance and the widest set of key metabolites. Microwave drying kept the most of the headline drug compounds, the free anthraquinones. A combined score across all quality dimensions crowned a different method, labeled SG. Flavonoids, phenolic acids, and amino acids formed the core of the chemical differences between methods.
pmc-13287220:
Desmond Darko Asiedu and colleagues searched the maize genome in 2026 for regions that protect stalks against Fusarium rot, a soil-borne disease that cuts yields worldwide. They crossed 180 lines from an Austrian flint landrace with a tester line and scored disease after deliberate infection at two sites over two years.

Resistance and related traits such as height and flowering time were moderately to strongly heritable. Two regions together explained about a fifth of inherited variation in disease severity, and nearby genes fit known defence roles. Because many small effects shape resistance, the authors suggest selecting on the whole genome may serve breeding programmes better than single markers.
pmc-13287420:
Yohei Takenobu and colleagues present in 2026 a patient whose abnormal blood vessel link at the neck level of the spine caused damage far away in the brainstem, copying a vomiting-centre syndrome. Detailed vessel imaging traced drainage upward from a fistula at the sixth neck vertebra.

Merged three-dimensional scans showed a sharp narrowing where the draining vein passes a skull fissure. The team reads that pinch as a bottleneck that pushed blood into the medulla. Blocking the fistula with a catheter cured the problem on scans and in symptoms. A literature review covers similar remote cases and common diagnostic traps. The authors favour catheter treatment when anatomy suits it.
pmc-13287620:
Ahmed Sobhy and colleagues modelled power supply options in 2026 for Ras El-Hekma, a large coastal project in Egypt with peak demand of 28.8 megawatts and yearly use near 100.46 gigawatt-hours. Six mixes of wind, solar, grid, and storage were simulated over twenty years, both tied to the grid and standalone.

A grid-linked wind setup of 15 megawatts came out cheapest in their runs. Costs and savings figures are given in the study, with green sources covering 68.6% of supply. Carbon emissions fell by 60.45% against a grid-only base. Wind speed and finance terms swayed results most. The authors present the case as a model for other coastal mega-projects.
pmc-13287820:
Mahmood Alawainati and colleagues measure diabetic retinopathy in Bahraini primary care in a 2026 cross-sectional study. Retinopathy is eye damage from diabetes that can lead to blindness if missed. The team invited adults with diabetes at clinics across all primary health centers in Bahrain during late 2025. A specialist checked each patient's retina with a camera that needs no dilating drops.

The study included 594 patients, most with type 2 diabetes and a median age of 61 years. Retinopathy appeared in 88 patients, or about 15 percent, and most cases were the milder non-proliferative form. Longer time with diabetes, high blood pressure, and poor blood sugar control each raised the odds. A simple foot sensation test linked to nerve damage also predicted eye disease. The authors press for yearly eye screening and tighter risk control in primary care.
pmc-13288620:
Alexander J Auty and colleagues probe how oxygen content changes light-driven charge behavior in printed graphene films, in 2026. The films are made from graphene aerosol-gel inks rather than perfect flat flakes. Ultrafast laser pulses let the team watch excited charges appear and fade across visible and near-infrared light. Films differed in how much oxygen sat inside the carbon lattice.

Higher oxygen content lined up with more long-lived trapped electronic states after the light pulse. Computer calculations point to oxygen atoms swapped into the lattice as the likely trap sites. Film shape, particle makeup, and carbon bond quality all tracked with the transient signals. Pristine graphene films, studied earlier by the group, behaved differently from these printed gels. The authors frame oxygen as a tuning knob for printed graphene electronics. Adjusting it could tailor films for sensors or light-based devices.
pmc-13288720:
Ziyu Wang and colleagues ask whether caffeine genuinely speeds swimmers in a 2026 systematic review and multilevel meta-analysis. Five databases yielded thirteen randomized placebo-controlled crossover trials in competitive swimmers, contributing 28 performance effects from 144 men and 48 women, pooled with three-level models that handle several results per study.

Caffeine improved performance by a moderate margin, worth about 1.71 percent on race times when effects were expressed as percentage change in their supplementary analysis. Blood lactate after racing also ran higher on caffeine. Bigger doses, at or above six milligrams per kilogram of body weight, looked more helpful than smaller ones, while stroke, distance, form, and athlete level showed no clear splits. Variation between studies stayed substantial.
pmc-13288920:
Andrea N Loes and colleagues compare flu vaccine types against a newly changed H1N1 strain in a 2026 study. The 2023/2024 vaccine updated its H1N1 part to match a new virus clade. Yet the vaccine trended weaker against that very clade than against its parent. The team measured antibody strength in blood from people who got either egg-grown or recombinant protein vaccine. Test viruses covered 58 H1N1 strains from that season.

Egg vaccine recipients showed a smaller antibody boost against the new clade. Recombinant vaccine recipients did not show that gap. The likely cause sits in the egg production seed strain, which had reverted a key surface mutation. That single change, named K142R, made egg-grown vaccine antigen differ from the target virus. The authors warn that production method can quietly reshape which strains a vaccine covers best. Their findings matter for yearly strain selection and manufacturing choices.
pmc-13289020:
Kelsey Hegarty and colleagues build a scale for coercive control in Australia. Their 2026 study deals with partner abuse of women. Past scales miss how abuse acts as a whole. The new scale is called C-CAS. It was built from older scales and expert views.

Data came from 854 adult women. Five survivors and eight experts gave feedback. The scale split into four parts. Mind control formed the largest part. Sex and birth coercion formed one part. Severe control and tech threats formed two more. Scores held up well in tests. Fear rose with more severe patterns. More checks in new groups are still needed.
pmc-13289220:
Geonhui Min and coauthors published a 2026 nationwide cohort study from Korea on bronchiectasis in people with systemic lupus erythematosus, often shortened to SLE. Bronchiectasis means lasting widening of the airways. They used National Health Insurance Service data and matched adults with SLE to controls by age, sex, and coverage.

Follow-up ran for a median of 12.8 years after a one-year lag from enrollment. New bronchiectasis appeared more often in the SLE group, at 374.8 versus 236.2 cases per 100 000 person-years in controls. Age over 40 and asthma raised risk further, while obesity linked to lower risk in the models. People with SLE who developed bronchiectasis also had more deaths, emergency visits, and hospital care, showing a real added burden.
pmc-13289320:
Yuxi Chen and coauthors report a 2026 mouse and lab study linking gut fungi to Pneumocystis pneumonia. Pneumocystis is a fungus that causes severe lung infection in people with weak immunity, now more often in patients without HIV. Gut fungi help tune immunity in distant organs, yet their role in this lung disease was unknown until now.

Mice infected with Pneumocystis murina had gut fungal sampling over five weeks, plus blood chemical profiling. Gut fungal makeup shifted from week three, matching peak lung fungal load, even though variety counts held steady. Two opportunistic fungi became more common, and blood chemistry shifted in amino acid and energy pathways. Wiping out gut fungi with fluconazole worsened lung burden, and transplant tests in germ-free mice probed cause directly.
pmc-13290120:
Plain knee X-rays may reveal joint damage normally seen only on MRI, with help from deep learning, in a 2026 study by Tariq Alkhatatbeh and colleagues. They used the Osteoarthritis Initiative database to train a model for knees with early or no radiographic disease.

The multi-task network learned from 8,260 knees belonging to 4,130 participants, grading osteoarthritis severity across all knees while predicting MRI-defined cartilage and meniscus damage in the mildest group. Severity grading agreed strongly with reference grades. In 2,561 early knees with MRI labels, discrimination for cartilage and meniscal damage was moderate rather than strong. The authors suggest the model could help flag patients who would benefit from earlier MRI, while stressing that referral decisions must rest on the full clinical picture.
pmc-13290820:
When spine and hip bone scores disagree, the gap itself forecasts death in older women but not men, Rıdvan Erten and Mehmet Poyrazer report in a cohort study from 2026. Spine density in older adults can be inflated by degeneration, so the team tested whether the spine-hip T-score difference carries risk information beyond either site alone.

The prospective analysis covered 6,364 U.S. adults aged 50 and over from five NHANES cycles, followed a median 9.3 years with 1,155 deaths. Each unit of spine-minus-hip difference raised women's mortality hazard by about a quarter, while the men's estimate stayed small and borderline. In both sexes the hip score alone predicted death best, and spine score alone lost meaning in women after adjustment. Erten and Poyrazer recommend reading the two sites together, especially in women.
pmc-13291420:
Medical students grow in trusted tasks during emergency training. Anne Marie Griebie leads a 2026 study of clerkship ratings. Such tasks are called Entrustable Professional Activities, or EPAs. Schools must know if growth curves follow learning theory.

The group held 481 students at one Minnesota school. Each did a four-week emergency rotation. Raters gave over seven thousand task ratings in total. Most task curves rose with the expected slowing shape. Five tasks broke that pattern and need a look. Six raters on six rounds gave solid score reliability. The data back the rating system’s design. Odd tasks may need better rater guidance.
pmc-13291720:
Betsabé Hernández-Santos and co-authors report a 2026 food science study on adding melon peel flour to extruded snacks made from soy protein and maize starch. They varied barrel temperature, feed moisture, the protein-to-starch ratio, and the peel flour content. A central composite design with response surface methods guided the experiment.

Feed moisture proved the strongest factor, lowering the energy used and the expansion while raising density and hardness. More melon peel also made the snacks denser and firmer because of its dietary fibre. The models fit most measured properties well, and the team concludes that melon peel flour can work in extruded snacks. The work gives food makers a route for turning a discarded by-product into a fibre-rich ingredient.
pmc-13292320:
Akinori Miyashita and co-authors revisit a 2026 number with outsized influence: how much the APOE e4 gene variant raises Alzheimer's risk in Japanese people. Early reports put the risk for e4 homozygotes versus e3 homozygotes above twentyfold, with one odds ratio of 33.1 in the older literature. Their fresh meta-analysis pooled published Japanese case-control studies found through PubMed and Web of Science under PRISMA rules. The pooled risk for e4 homozygotes landed at roughly 12 to 15 times the e3 homozygote risk. That range matches estimates in Caucasian populations rather than exceeding them. The authors argue population-specific figures should rest on the full, independent evidence base, not a handful of early small samples.
pmc-13292520:
Stefanie Rosner and co-authors watch a 2026 group of heart failure patients through a single COVID-19 telecoaching module, checking whether knowledge and habits stuck. The 419 patients already belonged to a telemonitoring and coaching program. Questionnaires ran just before the April 2020 coaching, three weeks after, and again eight months later.

Patients recalled more protective measures after coaching, rising from 2.1 items on average to 2.5 at both follow-ups. The authors credit the module cautiously, noting public campaigns were teaching the same lessons.
pmc-13293420:
Chiara De Poli and colleagues evaluate, in a 2026 study, how a co-designed information aid for people with dementia and family carers was put into practice in North-East England. Information needs in dementia often go unmet, despite policy stress on choice and control.

Interviews over time with a service manager and practitioners, plus a group talk with the design team, fed the review. Staff offered the leaflet often, though in varied ways, and some local tweaks appeared. The aid fit well into routine work and was welcomed by staff, who saw it as meeting a real need. Nine context levels and eight drivers helped explain how rollout went.
pmc-13293720:
Zhi-xiao Li and co-authors review, in a 2026 paper, how parvalbumin neurons, a key class of calming nerve cells, go wrong in depression. These cells keep the balance between excitation and inhibition in the brain, a balance known to break down in low mood.

Changes span gene control, chemical marks on DNA, and transmitter and receptor faults in these cells. Circuit problems center on the prefrontal cortex, hippocampus, and amygdala, regions tied to mood and memory. Drugs, growth factors, and brain stimulation that restore these cells show promise in early work. The review gathers molecular and circuit proof for future studies.
pmc-13293820:
Blanca Gonzalez-Sánchez and co-authors survey, in a 2026 study, loneliness and leisure life among older adults who study at a university program in Extremadura, Spain, and live outside care homes. Loneliness is cast as one of the greatest challenges of later life.

A total of 89 students at the University of Extremadura for Older Adults filled the ESTE II loneliness scale, which also covers social support, technology use, and participation. Overall loneliness was low, and no measured factor split scores clearly. Moderate links appeared with widowhood, having many children, and lacking social or cultural leisure. Staying active may help hold loneliness down.
pmc-13293920:
Adrián Idoate-Bayón and coauthors compare cooking skill and diet in a 2026 cross-sectional study of 592 Spanish adults, with 287 living with type 1 diabetes and 305 healthy controls. An 18-item scale measured culinary competence, covering skills like reading labels and adapting recipes. Models adjusted for social background factors.

Patients scored higher on competence than controls, notably on health-focused skills. In the diabetes group, stronger skill meant less use of convenience and pre-prepared foods. Among controls, skill mainly meant fewer heavy sauces and cooking methods. Two skill groups emerged, and the expert group ate fewer ultra-processed foods at every income level.
pmc-13294220:
Kinga Skieresz-Szewczyk and Hanna Jackowiak trace tongue hardening in goose embryos in a 2026 tissue staining study. Cornification builds the tough surface layer from structural proteins plus the enzyme transglutaminase-1. Two tongue coverings, one with dead surface nuclei and one without, were followed from day 9 to day 25 of incubation across early, transformation, and prehatching stages.

Protein signals began early, then surged as layers split and a temporary periderm formed. By prehatching both coverings had a cornified layer, yet only some protein patterns matched adult birds. Hardening thus starts about two thirds through development, and final maturation still lags behind hatching.
pmc-13294420:
Khaled El Ghonemy Said, Nada Mohammed Aggour, and Ahmed Ibrahim Basiony test drug injection into the cornea for stubborn fungal eye infection in a 2026 prospective series. Fungal keratitis causes 30–40% of cases in developing countries in the cited range and resists drops often. Twenty-one eyes that failed at least two weeks of surface therapy got voriconazole shots around the ulcer, with scan-guided depth checks.

Patients averaged 57.19 years, mostly rural men with plant injury histories. Aspergillus led isolates at 52.4% in the reported share. Vision improved sharply by 3 months, and 19 patients, or 90.5%, healed fully. Direct delivery rescues cases that drops cannot reach.
pmc-13294820:
Kaitlynn E. Ellis and colleagues ask whether the number of caregivers at home shapes child brains and behavior beyond what money explains, in a 2026 study. Income and schooling are the usual stand-ins for a child's setting, yet they miss daily facts like watchfulness and support. The team compared 7,890 nine- and ten-year-olds in one- or two-caregiver homes, holding income, schooling, age, and sex steady.

Two-caregiver homes had higher income and schooling, as expected. Even with those held equal, home structure tracked with acting-out behavior and attention problems. Brain scans showed small, wide-spread size gaps that held up under added checks. Overall brain size linked part of the pattern. The authors stress that the effects were modest and ask which daily habits matter most.
pmc-13295520:
Ru-Ping Li, Fu-Shan Xue, and Yi Cheng raise questions about a hip fracture trial in a 2026 commentary. The trial under discussion tested a fascia iliaca nerve block before spinal anaesthesia in older adults having hip joint replacement. It reported less positioning pain, faster spinal placement, and longer pain relief, but weaker leg muscles afterwards.

The commenters welcome the effort yet list gaps that blur how much credit the block deserves. Missing detail on the wider pain plan, unclear importance of the pain gain, and uncounted time for the extra block all feature. Clarifying such points, they argue, would strengthen future trials of regional blocks in this frail group.
pmc-13295820:
Guo Wu and colleagues read gene activity behind stress behaviour in sea cucumbers in a 2026 study. The brainless animals answer threats by fleeing, clinging tight, or playing dead. Which pattern appears depends on the stress met, from dead tank-mates to cleaning water jets on farms.

Immune cells from stressed animals were profiled to trace the molecular switches behind each response. Comparing patterns across stress types separated shared alarm genes from response-specific ones. The work deepens understanding of how animals without a central brain still mount varied, fitting defences, and it may help farms cut stress losses in a valuable crop.
pmc-13295920:
Esias Ka Nanbe Bedingar and colleagues study, in 2026, paying vaccination workers by mobile money in Chad. Irregular cash allowances can sap motivation, so the team compare provinces that switched to digital payment with those that did not.

Surveys of 1,510 workers and dozens of interviews found higher motivation and job satisfaction where mobile payment was used. Workers praised prompt, reliable payment and said it cut money worries, letting them focus on the campaign. Barriers remained for remote staff with weak connectivity or low digital skills, pointing to training needs as such schemes expand.
pmc-13296220:
Elisée Mbombo and a large clinical team present, in 2026, four cases of previously healthy children with invasive disease from methicillin-sensitive Staphylococcus aureus. Such spreading infections are rarely reported in children in sub-Saharan Africa, yet they kill often when found late.

All four children had skin lesions and fever, with illness spreading across several body systems. Blood tests guided antibiotic choices, and long hospital stays with intensive care and source control ended in good outcomes. The authors urge suspicion when feverish infants show skin lesions with tender joints, since early aggressive care drives survival.
pmc-13296420:
Matteo De Simone and co-authors argue, in 2026, that the name chronic subdural hematoma misleads doctors about what the condition really is. Tissue evidence shows no natural subdural space exists, and the bleeding instead starts inside a fragile layer of the brain's outer membrane.

On their account the lump is a living, self-feeding problem: weak new vessels leak, clots dissolve too fast and fluid keeps seeping in, so recurrence reflects biology, not failed surgery. That view supports artery-blocking procedures and drugs aimed at vessel growth and clot breakdown. The authors urge new terms and team-based, mechanism-led care.
pmc-13296620:
SeungHwan Lee and colleagues test a DNA-derived compound against ulcerative colitis in mice, in a 2026 study. The compound, called PDRN, calms inflammation through a specific cell receptor. Colitis was triggered with a chemical in drinking water for seven days, and treated mice received daily injections.

Treated mice kept more body and colon weight, showed less tissue damage, and scored lower on a disease activity index. Inflammatory signals fell while a growth factor linked to tissue repair rose. Blocking the receptor with another drug erased the benefits, supporting the proposed pathway. The work is early animal evidence, pointing to signalling routes that future bowel-disease treatments might target.
pmc-13297920:
Monia Cecati and Arianna Vignini present a 2026 special issue on natural compounds used with standard cancer treatment. Their editorial frames resistance, tumour diversity, and treatment toxicity as reasons to study plant and other natural products as helpers rather than replacements. Contributions range from laboratory experiments to broad reviews.

Examples surveyed include fermented noni extract strengthening chemotherapy effects, saponins acting on growth signals in lung and breast cancer models, and juglone or D-limonene driving oxidative stress in colorectal models. Reviews cover curcumin, tyrosine kinase inhibitors from plants, herbal approaches in breast cancer, and luteolin in inflammation-linked bowel disease. The editors present multi-target action as the shared thread.
pmc-13298520:
Juanmei Chen and others train a deep learning model to separate thyroid lymphoma from Hashimoto's thyroiditis on ultrasound, in a 2026 retrospective study. The two states look alike in scans, which makes preoperative judgement hard. Images from 290 patients at one Chinese hospital fed a model combining grey-scale and colour Doppler views.

Their frequency-adaptive network beat the best of three ultrasound physicians on balanced accuracy in the internal test set. Performance dropped in a small external set from another hospital, though ranking ability stayed moderate. Heat maps showed attention on lesion texture and border zones. The authors call the tool promising decision support, pending larger multicentre checking.
pmc-13299220:
Most links between circular RNAs and disease are guesses awaiting lab proof, and Chang-Chun Liu with co-authors built a predictor to rank the guesses in a 2026 computational paper. Their system, STRCDA, fuses biological similarity data, smooths it with network diffusion, and learns sparse graph embeddings before scoring candidate pairs.

Tested on the CircR2Disease collection under cross-validation, the method reached an AUC of 0.9771 and a precision-recall score of 0.9826. Strikingly, independent experimental evidence already backs 18 of its top 20 predicted associations. The authors present the tool as a way to spend laboratory effort where confirmation is most likely.
pmc-13299520:
Marco Fabbri and Monica Martoni model how momentary boredom damages sleep through phone habits, in a 2026 survey study. Bedtime procrastination is known to harm sleep quality and shift timing, and boredom can push people toward problematic smartphone use as a coping response. An online survey of 259 adults measured boredom, phone addiction, bedtime delay, and sleep outcomes.

All variables correlated positively with each other. Boredom predicted poor sleep quality and daytime sleepiness directly, plus phone addiction and bedtime procrastination indirectly. Sleep timing shifted through the bedtime delay path. The authors identify several intervention targets for improving sleep and daytime functioning in bored phone users.
pmc-13300520:
J Van Koll and a large co-author team test a simple electrocardiogram trick for checking resynchronization during left bundle branch pacing, in a 2026 paper. When pacing leaves the back wall of the left ventricle lagging, an extra lead may still be needed, so a non-invasive marker of that delay would help. Across 106 paired recordings, a timing measure taken from the steepest downslope in V8 tracked the directly measured left ventricular delay very closely, with correlations above nine tenths in several pacing modes. Rival measures from V6 or from R-wave peak times correlated far more weakly. The authors present the V8 measure as a reliable stand-in for posterolateral delay and a basis for future guidance studies.
pmc-13300720:
U Skrzypczynska-Banasik and co-authors test whether a day of twelve-lead Holter monitoring can sharpen diagnosis of congenital long QT syndrome, in a 2026 study. The inherited condition raises sudden death risk, yet a resting tracing misses about a quarter of gene carriers because the QT interval drifts over time. The team recorded eighteen genetically confirmed patients and seventeen healthy controls, analyzing beat to beat corrected QT values across the day.

Minimum, mean, and maximum corrected QT values all ran higher in patients than controls. Patients spent a small but real share of beats above the 480 millisecond mark, while controls almost never crossed their lower threshold. No healthy participant reached the extreme values seen in the patient group. Measurement was harder in patients because their tracings vary, and fewer beats could be scored reliably. Even so, the authors judge round-the-clock monitoring a useful diagnostic aid.
pmc-13301320:
Lead in a mother's blood, more than her anemia, shadowed her toddler's development in Suriname, Anisma R. Gokoel and colleagues report in a 2026 cohort study. The Caribbean consortium cohort enrolled 755 pregnant women and assessed 644 children aged ten to twenty-six months with the Bayley scales. Mercury from artisanal gold mining framed the exposure setting.

Anemia touched 34 percent of mothers yet showed no independent tie to cognitive, language, motor, or social-emotional scores, though iron itself went unmeasured. Lead gave the steadiest signal, predicting lower scores across domains, while mercury's links ran weaker. Selenium seemed to soften some metal effects. The authors warn against causal claims from this cross-sectional snapshot.
pmc-13301620:
Alfredo Cruz-Gregorio and co-authors expose heart muscle cells to the food whitener titanium dioxide in a 2026 cell study. The additive, labeled E171, is eaten widely and roughly forty percent of it is nanoparticle sized, small enough to cross into the blood. Working with H9c2 cardiomyoblasts, the team measured loose intracellular iron, reactive oxygen species, and the cell's glutathione shield, then imaged mitochondria by electron microscopy and tested their breathing capacity directly.

Their mitochondria looked damaged, with thinned internal folds, and respiration testing showed weakened oxidative phosphorylation and a lower maximal capacity. Quercetin, an antioxidant and iron chelator, failed to fully rescue the breathing defect at the dose tried. The authors propose iron driven oxidative injury as the mechanism linking a common food additive to cardiac cell harm.
pmc-13301720:
A Smagulova and co-authors ablate rhythm problems in pregnant patients without X ray exposure in a 2026 prospective study. Radiation free navigation matters in pregnancy, yet drug therapy carries fetal questions. A team enrolled 116 women, averaging about twenty-five years old and twenty-three weeks pregnant: forty-seven received zero fluoroscopy ablation with three dimensional mapping, and sixty-nine were managed with antiarrhythmic drugs.

Ablation succeeded in every case, with one complication, a leg vein thrombosis. The arrhythmias were supraventricular tachycardia and premature beats in both groups, and risk scores matched. Pregnancy courses stayed smooth on both paths: preeclampsia and blood flow problems appeared at like rates. Term delivery exceeded ninety-five percent in each group, and birth weights and Apgar scores were normal. Across twenty-four months, no deaths occurred and no rhythm problem returned. The authors call the procedure a safe answer when drugs fail or frighten.
pmc-13302320:
T Kamakura and colleagues examine, in a 2026 study, lasting effects of pulsed field ablation on the large vein that drains the upper body into the heart. That vein, the superior vena cava, sits close to the right upper lung vein, a routine ablation target. Earlier reports noted the vein's signals slowing or blocking right after treatment.

Among 407 patients treated with three different systems, eighteen returned for a second procedure and had the vein remapped. A new low-voltage patch had appeared in the vein in fourteen of them right after the first ablation. Months later the change persisted in just over half of those cases, especially where the two veins lay closest together. In one patient the patch formed part of a new rhythm circuit.
pmc-13303620:
Danial Mirzaee, Seyed Amir Malekpour, and Ata Kalirad propose a 2026 statistical method for estimating total population size from mark and recapture data. Counts of marked animals seen again underpin work in ecology, conservation, and disease study, but common formulas lean on rough approximations.

Their exact hypergeometric posterior method turns the two-sample likelihood into exact chances for each possible whole-number population size. Closed-form math yields quick summaries and exact credible ranges, with a sensible upper cap for sparse data. Repeated sampling rounds can be merged for sharper estimates. Extensions handle lost marks and uneven catch chances between groups.
pmc-13303820:
Hyun-Jung Kwon and co-authors look, in a 2026 retrospective study, for features that predict failure of a nerve block used for neck-root pain. The stellate ganglion block offers a safer alternative to spinal injections, but responders vary. Records of patients treated with the ultrasound-guided block were sorted by whether pain halved within three months.

Narrowing of the nerve exit caused by bony overgrowth, rather than a slipped disc, also cut the odds substantially. Success rates fell step by step as risk factors accumulated, from nearly ninety-five percent with none to about forty percent with both.
pmc-13304220:
Chukwuka Elendu and co-authors write a 2026 letter on liver shrinkage during immune drug hepatitis, responding to a fatal case report. Checkpoint drugs help liver cancer patients, but immune attack on the liver can turn deadly even when blood enzyme rises stay small.

In scarred livers, few working cells remain to leak enzymes, so standard blood tests can badly understate true damage. Fast liver shrinkage on scans may warn of failure sooner than enzyme grades suggest. The letter urges teams to weigh scans, symptoms, and specialist input together rather than trusting enzyme numbers alone in patients with cirrhosis.
pmc-13304320:
Bailiang Zhuang heads a 2026 study using ultrasound to improve frozen sand molds for cleaner metal casting. Frozen molds avoid polluting resin binders, but uneven moisture during mixing leaves weak wet and dry patches.

An ultrasound-assisted mixing platform spread water evenly through tiny liquid bridges between chromite sand grains. Ice then grew fine and even, weaving a linked sand-ice web that resisted frost swelling and cracks. Pulling and crushing strengths of the frozen forms rose markedly. The method could speed adoption of digital frozen sand casting in aerospace and machine building while cutting pollution.
pmc-13304420:
Shenchen Liu leads a 2026 design study of disk-shaped triboelectric generators, which turn rubbing motion into electric charge. Top-scoring designs often sit on steep slopes, so small building errors can wreck their output.

Nearly two thousand simulations trained a stand-in model that splits performance into charge transfer and capacitance parts. Thousands of design points were then sorted into charge-led, mixed, and capacitance-led zones. Mixed-zone designs kept most of their output under a set size error, while peak designs could lose nearly all of theirs. An open web tool helps builders pick sturdy designs before cutting parts.
pmc-13305320:
Christopher E. Potts leads a 2026 case report on immune brain inflammation with no detectable antibodies in an older adult. Such seronegative cases are hard to prove, especially when the first signs look like mental illness.

The patient suffered repeated bouts of confusion, lost speech, and psychosis, while brain scans and spinal fluid tests stayed unremarkable. Steroid treatment had helped greatly in a past episode, and immune therapy was started again with psychiatry input. The case argues for keeping immune causes in mind when thinking and behavior collapse quickly without another explanation.
pmc-13306020:
Călin Muntean followed 921 students through their first university year in a 2026 study of meal timing and weight change. Students aged 18 to 24 had body mass index measured at entry and again after one academic year.

Meal frequency, choice of main meal, breakfast habits and late eating were tested against index change and against large gains above +1 kg/m2. Average change was slightly downward at −0.45 ± 1.07 kg/m2 in the reported summary, yet individual paths varied widely. Adjusted models singled out timing habits linked to gain, supporting attention to daily eating rhythm during the move to university life.
pmc-13307020:
Nasrin Moshfeghi Far spun layered mats from two biodegradable polymers for food wrapping in a 2026 study. Cellulose acetate and polylactic acid layers were stacked by solution blow spinning in single and mixed orders while keeping high porosity.

Heat and infrared checks showed layers barely mixed at the molecular level, joining mainly by contact and void filling in reported results. Microscopy showed cellulose mats as open connected webs and polylactic mats as clearer fibre layers. Polylactic layers were stiffer and stronger, while cellulose layers bent more easily, and stacks failed at interfaces under pull.
pmc-13307420:
Hyungtai Kim and Mun-Taek Choi present in 2026 a robot learning design for long indoor jobs that mix driving, picking, and handling hinged objects. Standard learning gets few rewards on such long chains. The hand off between steps can also leave the robot in a pose where the next step cannot start.

Their design breaks each job into steps and adds a safe path plan as a step by step guide inside the reward. It also swaps fixed target points for a feasible region found from arm geometry. In the ManiSkill-HAB simulator, success and learning speed beat the baseline on all six steps tested, and the gain grew along the full chain.
pmc-13307920:
Joshua Nmezi reports in 2026 the anaesthetic care of a man aged 45 years with severe bipolar disorder who needed gallbladder surgery by keyhole method. The man took lithium twice a day and olanzapine at night, yet adherence was poor and no pre surgery mind health review took place.

Lithium was paused for 24 hours before surgery, while the night drug was kept on as planned for that day. Blood tests showed low lithium, skewed salts, and raised white cells before the operation began. During surgery his heart rhythm and blood pressure wavered, and he woke agitated, then faced sickness and delirium. Joint planning by surgery, anaesthesia, and mind health teams could cut such risks.
pmc-13308720:
Megan Hauptman and co-authors present in 2026 a rare case of leukaemia cutis that arose at an old biopsy site and gave away a fresh case of acute myeloid leukaemia. The patient, a man aged 69 years, had no known blood disease when a sore, fast growing thigh lump drew care.

Sub types that roam outside marrow, such as M4 and M5, carry the top risk for skin spread in this account. Whether rogue cells sat at the site before the cut stays unknown, so cause cannot be claimed with sureness. New lumps at scar sites merit fast biopsy.
pmc-13308820:
Eric Kibagendi Osoro and co-authors screen in 2026 farm chemicals for mosquito larva killers that jam a juvenile hormone binding protein in malaria vectors. They sifted 2874 compounds in a computer flow, docked the best to the target, and ran energy, likeness, hazard, and motion checks.

Fifteen leads bound as tightly as the known partner lodged in the target, by the energy scores in this screen. Two leads stood out for snug fit and steady grip in motion runs over time. In live larva tests those two killed half the group at 37.75 and 33.49 parts per million in the doses used. Both merit wider field and safety checks.
pmc-13308920:
Eryn Patin and co-authors report in 2026 face restoration with resilient hyaluronic acid filler in a woman with morphea plus Parry-Romberg syndrome, two linked ills that waste one side of the face. The woman, aged 38 years, had stable disease after a year of methotrexate and sought a low cut fix for lost volume.

Filler was placed at the lower eyelid, the nose to mouth fold, and the chin, where tissue had sunk most. Gains in symmetry came without sparking fresh swelling, a key worry in immune linked skin disease. The resilient form is built to stir less immune reaction than older fillers. Long watch must still prove how safe and lasting the fix stays.
pmc-13309020:
Guillermo Pérez Castro and co-authors build in 2026 finer models of free riding speed for bike traffic simulators, which now miss how slope, bends, crossings, and wind bend a rider pace. They coded three new models in SUMO and raced them against built in rivals on tracks from 57 commuters in Sweden and Germany.

All three new models beat the old ones at copying true speed traces from the field runs in both lands. A power based physics model came closest of all to the speeds riders truly held on each stretch. Skipping context blew up errors on hills and bends most of all. Town planners gain a sharper tool for testing bike ways.
pmc-13310620:
Qichang Tong and colleagues build a question-answering system in 2026 that mines printed experiments on microbial enzyme production, a field too large for manual reading. Machine learning filters first picked about eleven thousand high-quality articles from a major library. A large language model then pulled entities and links under a formal ontology, forming a knowledge graph.

The graph held over twelve thousand entities and nearly thirty-six thousand links, pulled with about 0.78 accuracy. On top of it the team built MEPAM, a search-backed assistant for enzyme questions. Tested against a leading general model, MEPAM scored 0.86 accuracy against 0.52 and nearly wiped out made-up facts. A cellulase case study mapped expression hosts, culture settings, and substrate likes end to end. Trusted, source-backed answers could speed enzyme building for factories and farming.
pmc-13310920:
Georgios Theotokatos and co-authors study employment in the United States after spinal cord injury in a 2026 survey. Injury curbs function, life quality, and job chances. The team used a global survey set to find traits and barriers that shape employment for United States adults with such injury.

Data covered 167 people, and about two thirds held jobs. Adults aged 30 to 39 years, with more schooling and a live in partner, had higher job odds. Short time since injury and disability payments linked to lower odds. Unemployed people named poor transport most often, plus fear of losing benefits and blocked workplaces. Policy and rehab shifts may widen access.
pmc-13311220:
Roxane Abdel Gawad and colleagues outline a 2026 lab study that loads diosmin, a plant flavonoid, onto silver nanoparticles to help ligament stem cells form bone. Diosmin dissolves poorly in water, which limits its use.

The particles were made by a green method and tuned with a Box-Behnken design that varied silver, diosmin, and heat levels. Human ligament stem cells were then tested for survival and bone-forming activity using stains, enzyme tests, and gene checks. The tuned particles kept cells alive and raised bone markers. The approach could aid repair of teeth and jaw bone in future work.
pmc-13311420:
Luis Herrera and colleagues report a 2026 ultrasound study of how the heel fat pad changes with age. The fat pad cushions the heel bone during walking, and earlier work tracked mainly its thickness. The team instead examined 140 symptom-free volunteers aged 18 to 89, grouped into three age bands, and scored tissue brightness, internal structure, fibrous band integrity, and blood flow alongside thickness.

The structural measures shifted clearly with age, showing progressive breakdown and loss of the pad's chambered organization, especially in its deep layer and fibrous partitions. Thickness, by contrast, changed less and less consistently, and no meaningful internal blood flow signal appeared. The authors argue that qualitative ultrasound scoring catches age-related wear in this tissue more reliably than thickness alone, which could sharpen assessment of aging feet even before symptoms appear.
pmc-13311620:
James William Smithy and co-authors in 2026 analyze a multi-center series on checkpoint drug treatment after cell therapy failure in advanced melanoma. No standard path exists once tumor-infiltrating lymphocyte therapy stops working.

Fourteen centers pooled records of patients who got checkpoint drugs both before and after the cell therapy. Among 133 patients whose response could be judged, 11 percent responded to the later checkpoint treatment in this series, with three full responses. Survival was estimated with standard time-to-event methods. The modest response rate frames what doctors can expect when they retry this drug class after cell therapy.
pmc-13311820:
Lewis Murugu and co-authors in 2026 give a protocol for preparing and analyzing microscope images of LFA-1, a sticking protein, at T-cell contact zones. The method uses total internal reflection fluorescence microscopy.

The workflow pairs ImageJ macros for background removal and cell outlining with R scripts that find the ring-shaped cluster center, crop around it, and measure brightness by radius. T cells form these contacts with target cells or with coated glass that mimics them. A shared, flexible routine helps labs compare how the adhesion ring forms and changes, a key step in how T cells lock onto targets.
pmc-13311920:

The program ran in 50 VA centers from December 2022 to September 2025 and covered 167,505 veterans with artery disease. Each site worked with American Heart Association advisors to name local blocks and install fixes, including health coaches for some patients. Among 88,778 veterans starting above goal, 32.9 percent reached LDL under 70 within the follow-up in this report. The model shows system fixes can move a stubborn measure.
pmc-13312020:
Zhenggong Wang and colleagues present a 2026 case report and literature review on bronchial Dieulafoy disease, a rare defect in which an artery under the bronchial lining grows abnormally wide. The condition is uncommon but dangerous, because the vessel can burst and cause sudden, heavy coughing of blood that is hard to trace.

Their patient, a 54-year-old man, had coughed blood on and off for two years. Bronchoscopy showed a nodule in the right upper lung with an abnormal vessel pattern, and doctors sealed the diseased bronchial artery by embolization. He had no further bleeding during follow-up. The authors also review how the disease is found and treated, and note open questions about its cause, timing, and long-term care.
pmc-13312820:
Yajing Han and co-authors review, in a 2026 article, two decades of progress in making chiral triarylmethanes, molecules built from three aromatic rings on one carbon center. Their three-dimensional shapes, tunable electronics, and friendly chemistry make them valuable scaffolds for dyes, materials, and medicines, but building them in a single handedness proved a stubborn catalytic puzzle.

For each, the authors compare catalyst systems, how the stereochemistry is controlled, the handedness purity and yields achieved, and the prospects for scaling up. They close by naming the field's remaining challenges and the directions most likely to pay off. The survey serves as a reference both for inventing new routes to these molecules and for designing triarylmethanes built for a specific job.
pmc-13313920:
Shuji Suzuki and colleagues measure, in a 2026 study, how desmopressin affects bleeding time in anesthetized dogs. The drug is used to support clotting because it raises factor VIII and von Willebrand factor, but its behavior in dogs under general anesthesia was undefined. Controls averaged 128.2 seconds, while the highest dose group, at 1.8 micrograms per kilogram, averaged just 47.2 seconds in the reported medians, with the two higher doses significantly beating control. The authors offer the data as groundwork for using the drug to steady surgical patients at bleeding risk.
pmc-13314320:
Gasbjerg and colleagues tested in 2026 whether phase-contrast MRI, a scan that measures blood flow without contrast dye, gives repeatable readings of splanchnic flow, the circulation serving the gut and liver. Reliable flow measures matter for patients with gut vessel disease, yet methods are scarce. Repeat readings within a session varied by about 7 to 22 percent for the main gut artery, the celiac trunk, and the portal vein, while the liver artery varied more. A glucose drink lifted flow in the gut artery by close to 90 percent and in the portal vein by about two thirds, changes the method detected. The other two vessels showed no shift. The authors judge the technique reproducible and fit for tracking meal responses.
pmc-13314420:
Ping Yuan and colleagues ask whether blood hemoglobin levels foretell death in older patients with swallowing trouble, in work published in 2026. Hemoglobin is a known outlook marker in many diseases, but its worth in old people with dysphagia was not clear.

The team re-analyzed a public Japanese cohort of 253 patients from January 2014 to January 2017, with a median age of 83 years, per the report, 154 of them women. Hemoglobin was taken within 7 days before feeding support began and split into three bands. Each rise of 1 gram per deciliter tied to lower death risk, with an adjusted ratio of 0.83 kept mid-sentence here as reported. Middle and high bands fared far better than the lowest band. The simple blood test may help flag frail patients early.
pmc-13314920:

The team studied 94 people, of whom 45 carried brain amyloid, as counted in the report, with paired PET and MRI scans. They read three water-motion metrics in 98 brain regions, covering true diffusion, flow-linked spread, and the flow share. A learning model picked which metrics best foretold amyloid state, and scores were also set against thinking tests. If water motion mirrors protein load, a plain MRI could flag poor clearance without costly PET scans.
pmc-13315520:
Vishala Parmasad and colleagues test, in a 2026 multi-center study, whether teaching plus feedback can retire a low-value habit: culturing urine before surgery in patients without urinary symptoms. Guidelines advise against it across neurosurgery, orthopedics, and vascular surgery, yet the practice persists, driving cost and antibiotic exposure. Orthopedic surgery improved most dramatically, dropping from 18.7 percent to 7.4 percent over the same comparison, while the other specialties moved less. pmc-13316020:
Mondeep Gayan and a large team compare in 2026 two ways to teach spinal injury handling skills to undergraduate medical students in India, using a standardized patient versus a video demonstration. Fast trauma care in the golden hour can cut deaths by 20 to 50 percent, so early training matters.

Acted patients allow hands-on practice and build communication skill, but they are scarce, while video is easy and reliable to deliver. The prospective comparison study weighs skill gains under each method within a competency-based curriculum. The result can guide schools that must train many students with few live simulated patients.
pmc-13316220:
Ingrid J. Hickman and colleagues ran a national needs survey in 2026 on implementation science skills in the clinical trial workforce of Australia and New Zealand. Moving trial results into routine care stays patchy, and building worker skill in putting evidence into practice could fix translation much earlier in the pipeline.

An online survey with rating scales and open answers, spread through trial networks, drew 353 responses across regions and professions, including consumers. It measured familiarity with implementation methods, interest in training, and barriers and preferred ways to get support, to guide future workforce programs.
pmc-13317220:
Satyendra Pratap Singh and co-authors uncover, in a 2026 study, how a crop fungus launches its asexual spores into the air, solving a puzzle in orchard disease spread. These spores were thought to travel only in splashing water, yet disease jumped long distances without the sexual stage ever being seen in Israel.

As air dries, the glue around spores hardens off and wind carries them, farther at higher wind speeds. The humidity burst and dry release pattern held across related tree pathogens, reshaping how growers should time protection.
pmc-13318720:
Qiuyu Jin and colleagues offer a 2026 bibliometric analysis of cognitive behavioural therapy for chronic pain. Few such maps of the field existed. The team charted two decades of publications, from 2005 to 2024. Sources were the Web of Science and PubMed trial records.

They found 1,070 papers from 67 countries and 1,584 institutions. The United States contributed 59.16 percent of publications and led citations. The University of Washington was the most productive institution. Frequent keywords included depression, sleep, anxiety, and quality of life. Hotspots now centre on digital delivery of therapy. Managing linked conditions and tailoring treatment to specific groups also draw attention. The authors frame the map as a roadmap for future trials.
pmc-13318920:
Karina Medina-Jiménez and colleagues present a 2026 study of a prebiotic-based biostimulant, FoliarBlend, on rice growth and yield. The variety was Kitaake, grown under controlled conditions from germination to seed production. Automated imaging tracked seedlings, and manual checks followed plants to day 82. Later, treated plants grew taller with fewer leaves and tillers. They produced more panicles, more biomass above and below ground, and ultimately more grain. Photosystem efficiency and chlorophyll content improved from day 49 onwards. The authors see promise for sustainable rice production.
pmc-13319420:
Jian Liu and co-authors give a broad review of epilepsy in a 2026 article on causes, body changes, and care. The seizure illness affects more than 50 million people worldwide and adds to early death and long term hardship. Near one third of patients still have seizures despite drug care, which shows how much remains unclear about how seizures start.

Gene faults, faulty cell signals, swelling in brain tissue, energy strain, and shifts in cell control are traced as paths that leave brain circuits prone to fire too much. Care now spans exact gene tests, surgery, implanted devices, diet plans, and timed dosing. New gene and immune based methods aim to change the illness itself, not just calm seizures.
pmc-13320420:
Pham Thanh Hieu and Nguyen Kieu Linh present a benchmark data set built from world trade records in a 2026 data article. Trade webs settle into balance states that math models frame as inequality puzzles, yet test sets for solver tools were scarce. A pipeline turns product level trade files into clean puzzle cases with known trade flows as ground truth.

Source files cover yearly flows among lands for 2017 to 2024 at fine product detail. Steps filter live flows, group products into five sectors, pick lead trade lands, and tune a cost and price rule to match real flows. Cases ship in two sizes with feasible sets, tuned rules, flow tables, and check scores, plus solver test results and build scripts for reuse.
pmc-13320520:
Anqi Lin and colleagues offer a 2026 perspective on germs that live inside bowel tumours. Bowel cancer ranks among the most common cancers and a leading cause of cancer death. Those inner groups differ from germs in nearby healthy tissue and vary from place to place within a tumour. The authors set out the makeup of these groups, how they may help tumours grow or resist care, and how they might open new treatment paths. Their dual role, as both driver and possible target, frames the discussion.
pmc-13322620:
Minesh Kapadia, Lorraine V Kalia, and Suneil K Kalia write a 2026 letter on electrical stimulation and protein clearance in Parkinson's disease. The letter discusses a study by Bechkos and others where direct current stimulation cut clump build-up in cultured neurons and improved cell survival. The writers note that this matches and extends their own group's finding that high frequency stimulation aids clearance. Comparing stimulation styles may shape future disease slowing therapy.
pmc-13322920:
Yujia Wu and co-authors review Chinese herbal formulas for Hashimoto's thyroiditis through the thyroid-gut axis, in a 2026 article. Standard hormone replacement fixes low thyroid hormone but does not reverse the autoimmune attack itself, which leaves room for other approaches.

Searching databases for work from 2015 to 2025, the team kept eight studies of eligible formulas. Their framework sorts action into four nodes: gut barrier repair, microbe reshaping, immune balance and hormone recovery, alone or in combination. Most evidence came from varied animal studies and stayed correlative, with safety reporting uneven. The authors call for randomised clinical trials, causal microbe tests and standard outcome measures before firm claims can be made.
pmc-13323020:
Mina Xu and co-authors trace a shift from virtual pregnancy models to digital twin obstetrics, in a 2026 review. Static checks at set visits miss how pregnancy changes over time, so newer models simulate mother, placenta and fetus as one changing system.

Digital twins extend that idea with live, multi-type data that keep a patient-specific model updated. Inputs include clinical profiles, imaging and radiomics, multi-omics and wearable signals, joined through machine learning. Uses centre on preeclampsia, gestational diabetes, preterm birth, growth restriction and placental failure. The authors weigh promise against proof, noting that personal prediction tools still need strong trials before routine obstetric use.
pmc-13323720:
Younghwan Lee and co-authors tested whether a peptide drawn from human telomerase can slow Alzheimer disease in mice. Their 2026 paper studies GV1001, a 16-amino-acid peptide from the catalytic part of telomerase reverse transcriptase, which had already improved memory with proven safety in a phase II trial in patients. Sequencing showed the peptide pushed microglia toward migratory and phagocytic states, and pulldown work identified bradykinin receptor 1 as its binding target, acting through an mTORC2-dependent route. The authors present GV1001 as a promising disease-modifying candidate, with its mechanism now mapped in microglia.
pmc-13324220:
Clara Fernandez-Cordón and Ignacio Amat-Santos review valve alignment strategies in transcatheter aortic valve replacement, published in 2026. Younger patients now receive these valves more often. Aligning the new valve's posts with the native seams thus matters for lifetime care.

Good commissural alignment eases later coronary access. It also cuts obstruction risk and enables leaflet work in repeat procedures. Flow and durability may improve as well. The authors summarise clinical impact, success rates and limits. They set coronary alignment against commissural alignment as rival targets. Step-by-step techniques for the latest valve systems close the review, for teams weighing present access against future re-intervention.
pmc-13325420:
Dinara Turebekova and colleagues review links between blood markers and life quality in long COVID in a 2026 systematic review. Lasting symptoms drag down daily life, but the biology behind the loss is murky.

Searches of PubMed, Web of Science, and Scopus gathered controlled studies, yielding ten papers with 1,078 patients and 768 healthy controls. Life quality fell hardest in physical function, energy, daily activity, and breathing comfort. Inflammation and vessel markers such as CRP, IL-6, and D-dimer were measured most often. Few studies tied markers to life quality directly, though inflammation and vessel dysfunction signals recurred. The authors call for uniform tools so future studies can compare cleanly.
pmc-13325720:
Adel S. Alagl and Marwa Madi test antibacterial hydroxyapatite coatings on titanium in a 2026 lab study. Bacterial films on dental implants drive peri-implantitis, a leading cause of implant failure.

Discs of grade 2 titanium were coated by sputtering plus hot water treatment or left bare. After 24 hours with Staphylococcus aureus, Escherichia coli, or both, coated discs cut colony counts by 97.9 to 99.7 percent across all setups. Surface type alone explained 74.1 percent of the difference in bacterial survival. The coat hit the Gram-positive species harder than the Gram-negative one. Mouth-like conditions still need testing before clinic use.
pmc-13326120:
Alexander C. Razavi and Roger S. Blumenthal argue that timing is everything in lowering LDL cholesterol. About half of adults sit at or above 100 mg/dL, and roughly 1 in 250 to 300 carry levels at or above 190 mg/dL consistent with familial hypercholesterolemia.

They highlight adults who gain most from statin therapy and LDL control. These include those with premature family history, high-risk ancestry, high polygenic risk, chronic inflammatory disease, high lipoprotein(a) or swelling markers, persistently high triglycerides, cardiometabolic syndrome, or markedly high LDL or apolipoprotein B. The message is to act early, not to wait for disease.
pmc-13327020:
Fan Yang and team traced knee osteoarthritis burden in China and where it heads next. Their 2026 study used Global Burden of Disease 2021 data. It ran age-period-cohort and ARIMA trend models on new cases and years lived with disability from 1990 to 2021, with forecasts for the next fifteen years. Knee joint wear leads as a cause of disability, hitting women and older adults hardest.

New cases and disability rose a lot over three decades, most among women, with a clear rise by age. The trend model sees a slow fall in new cases and disability after 2021, which may mirror health reforms and guard steps. The team stresses the rising health load. pmc-13327520:

pmc-13334720:

pmc-13336420:

pmc-13336620:

pmc-13336920:

pmc-13337020:

pmc-13339620:
