Suren Kanayan reports a 2026 low-cost safety project in a Phnom Penh tertiary hospital in Cambodia. Safety problems in low-resource hospitals often go unreported, so fixes arrive late and harm repeats. The project set out to make reporting routine without new technology.

A one-page checklist went to four departments, covering emergency and intensive care, maternity, outpatients and children's wards. Weekly reviews, feedback and department champions kept the system moving through small Plan-Do-Study-Act cycles. Within three months, written standard procedures rose from none to ten, the report states. Resistance to extra work and uneven submissions were handled by simplifying forms and coaching, with a hospital quality committee watching progress.
pmc-13405120:
Lydia S Massae and co-authors explore why vacuum-assisted birth is rarely used at a Tanzanian tertiary hospital, in a 2026 qualitative study. A vacuum cup can deliver a baby safely when labour stalls, sparing some mothers a caesarean. Underuse of the method remains a concern across similar settings.

Twelve clinicians with relevant experience gave in-depth interviews, analysed for recurring themes. Barriers fell into organisational and individual groups. Equipment was scarce or unreliable, and poor teamwork slowed decisions about using the device. Individual barriers, including confidence and training gaps among clinicians, complete the picture the authors draw. Their findings aim to guide training and equipment plans that could revive the technique.
pmc-13405620:
Kely Catarine Matteucci and a large team show how malaria infection rewires energy use in immune cells, in 2026 mouse work. The tumour necrosis factor, TNF, both fights the parasite and causes sickness behaviour such as inactivity and appetite loss. The chain linking those effects was traced in Plasmodium chabaudi infection.

TNF proved necessary for switching on nitric oxide production, stabilising the HIF-1alpha factor and raising glucose uptake in monocytes. Mice lacking parts of that chain showed weaker glucose burning, higher parasite counts and greater tolerance of disease. Liver and spleen took up more glucose under TNF signalling in the reported experiments. The pathway is presented as central to host defence.
pmc-13407720:
Dirk Linke and co-authors chart, in 2026, German hip and knee replacement volumes and project them to 2035. Using federal statistics and hospital quality reports from 2015 to 2024, they tracked first-time and revision operations, patient ages, hospital stays, and how many hospitals still offer the procedures.

First-time operations grew steadily, adding roughly five thousand cases a year for each joint, while revision volumes stayed flat. Patients skewed older over time, with shrinking shares under fifty. Projections show total first-time volume nearly stable to 2035, but hips rising by about eleven thousand cases while knees fall by a similar amount, and revisions climbing, especially past age seventy-five. Hospital stays shortened each year, and hospital numbers fell sharply, signalling centralisation the authors say planning must confront.
pmc-13408820:
Yiwang Chen and team rebuilt the long-term evolution of drug-resistant tuberculosis across China from over 18,000 bacterial genomes. Their 2026 work takes on a gap: antibiotics have treated tuberculosis for over 80 years, yet population-level dynamics of resistance under drug pressure had been poorly mapped. Spatial and temporal patterns matter for control plans.

Resistance mutations to varied drugs arose time and again, forming hundreds to over a thousand small resistant clades, mostly arising in the past two decades. Once set, clades spread mainly within provinces, but could widen with human movement and bacterial fitness. Genomic and CRISPRi data flagged mutations tied to resistance rise and spread. The work highlights migration and bacterial adaptation as shapers of local drug-resistant tuberculosis epidemics.
pmc-13410920:
Ahad Bakhtiari and colleagues explore in 2026 fresh ways to pay for health care for migrants and refugees in Iran. Money is tight, authority is split across many bodies, and displacement has lasted for years. Afghan migrants form the main group affected, with mixed legal and insurance status.

The team combined a literature sweep, national document review, and interviews with 44 people from agencies, insurers, charities, and migrant communities. Fifteen experts also mapped who influences whom in a network analysis. Stakeholders were rated by interest, money-raising power, and policy sway. Findings point to underused funding routes that link existing pots of money more tightly, rather than building parallel systems for displaced people.
pmc-13411120:
Elaheh Dadashi and colleagues examined frailty, health literacy, and pill-taking habits among 210 older adults in Tabriz in 2026. Frailty leaves older people more open to falls, illness, and hospital stays. The team used standard scales to test whether understanding health information lines up with staying strong and taking medicines as directed.

About 42 percent of the group met frailty criteria, while nearly all reported high medicine adherence and about half showed adequate health literacy. Stronger health literacy looked protective against frailty, which points clinics toward plain-language teaching as a practical frailty defense.
pmc-13411320:
Beatriz Bartulic Machado and co-authors assess in 2026 how Brazil's data protection law reshaped research involving human participants. Personal databases have grown fast with digital tools, and the law, plus a 2024 health council resolution, set new guardrails. Document analysis compared the rules before and after the change.

Consent and privacy duties now carry legal weight beyond ethics custom. Researchers must justify data use, protect identities, and respect participants' rights under enforceable rules. Gains in protection come with real operational strain for study teams. The authors weigh that tension: health and science need data, while each person keeps a claim on their own information. Clear procedures, they argue, let both goods stand.
pmc-13412420:
Meng-Hsing Ho and co-authors compare two follow-up chemotherapy regimens after stomach cancer surgery in a 2026 nationwide Taiwan cohort study. Both XELOX, a two-drug pairing, and TS-1, a single-drug option, are guideline choices after D2 gastrectomy, yet direct comparisons in stage III disease were scarce. Insurance and cancer registry records identified patients treated from 2010 to 2019, and matching balanced the groups for fair comparison.

In 490 matched pairs, TS-1 patients survived longer and progressed less overall, with three-year survival near 65 percent versus about 57 percent on XELOX in this dataset. The advantage concentrated in stage IIIA disease, while stages IIIB and IIIC showed no clear difference. The authors label the finding hypothesis-generating and ask for a randomized trial.
pmc-13413520:
Yingwu Shi and co-authors track in 2026 how a friendly bacterium settles inside cotton plants and primes them against Verticillium wilt, a devastating soil fungus. The biocontrol strain, Bacillus velezensis BHZ-29, was tagged with antibiotic resistance so its travels could be followed without changing its behaviour. Pot trials then measured where it colonized, which defence enzymes it stirred, and how well it protected several cotton varieties.

The strain took up stable residence in roots, stems, and leaves, with roots as its stronghold. Treated plants fired up five defence and antioxidant enzymes, gained vitamin C, and suffered less cell damage when the wilt fungus attacked alongside. Greenhouse checks confirmed broad, steady protection across varieties, backing the strain as a green alternative to chemical sprays.
pmc-13413720:
Takashi Nagai and colleagues look in 2026 at whether bone drugs called SERMs lose their punch as women age, using real-world Japanese clinic data. These estrogen-like drugs are a staple for postmenopausal osteoporosis, yet routine practice rarely tests age effects. Records covered women treated for one year between 2017 and 2021, split into three age bands, with density measured at spine and hip and bone turnover tracked in blood and urine.

Spine density rose significantly in every age band across the year of therapy. Hip density improved significantly only in the youngest band, women aged fifty to sixty-four, and gains there were smaller overall. Once baseline density and kidney function were accounted for, age itself predicted nothing at either site. Lower starting density forecast bigger relative gains, the authors note.
pmc-13414720:
Hae-Yeon Cho and colleagues ask whether methyl gallate can soften the side effects of the antibiotic tylosin in weaned piglets, in a 2026 trial. Forty piglets were assigned to salt solution, tylosin, methyl gallate, or both compounds, each drug at 10 milligrams per kilogram. Blood, weight, and gut bacteria were tracked after one injection.

Growth and feed measures stayed similar across groups. Tylosin lowered Lactobacillus counts and shifted immune signals, a pattern suggesting brief gut disturbance. Methyl gallate raised several cytokines linked to adaptive immunity. Given together, the plant compound partly eased the gut bacteria changes, though one major bacterial group stayed unchanged.
pmc-13415020:
Anna Giorgio and colleagues review two decades of work on attaching peptides to gold and platinum cancer drugs, publishing in 2026. Metal drugs kill cancer cells well yet often harm healthy tissue and meet resistance. Peptides, short protein chains, can steer a metal complex toward tumors and change how cells take it up.

Platinum pairs in the common form mostly keep their DNA attack, with peptides improving delivery rather than potency. A higher oxidation form acts as a prodrug, switched on inside cells. Gold pairs target sulfur or selenium sites in proteins instead. Success depends on balancing peptide delivery against the metal's own chemistry, the review concludes.
pmc-13415320:
Şerife Yılmaz Gürbüz, Oğuzhan Yağdı, and Erhan Başar examine two tricky patterns in hepatitis B blood testing, reporting in 2026 from Karabuk. Their records spanned 2021 to 2025. One puzzle is a lone core antibody result, the other a weak surface antigen signal close to the cutoff.

Among 17,356 people screened, 506 showed the lone core antibody pattern, and about three percent of them carried viral DNA. That pattern grew commoner after age fifty. For weak surface antigen signals, a threshold near three times the cutoff caught every DNA positive case in 213 checked specimens. Every specimen below that range tested DNA negative, which could spare needless follow-up testing.
pmc-13415520:
Rongcen Zhao and colleagues recycle spent indium tin oxide, the coating used on display glass, through electrochemistry in 2026. Spent material is the main secondary source of scarce indium. Their method makes the spent oxide the anode in a water based cell, where charge excitation multiplies surface oxygen vacancies.

Weakened metal oxygen bonds release indium and tin ions into the liquid. The ions migrate to the cathode and form a high purity indium tin alloy, separated from impurities by their differing electrical behavior. At hundred ampere scale, current efficiency reached about 71 percent with modest energy use. The electrolyte can be reused, cutting wastewater sharply.
pmc-13415720:
Vanessa Gipson leads a large team testing the RALE score, a numbered grading of lung clouding on chest X-rays, in acute respiratory failure in 2026. Portable films from 814 critically ill adults, 4,259 images in total, were scored by trained clinicians blinded to clinical details. Patient groups ranged from ARDS to heart failure lung edema and airway protection cases.

Scores rose in steps from no airspace disease to limited to diffuse involvement. A cutoff score of seven caught 96 percent of cases with any airspace disease. Scores overlapped heavily among ARDS, heart edema, and lung scarring flare groups, since films look alike. Poor X-ray penetration inflated scores and wrecked accuracy.
pmc-13417720:
Antonello and colleagues reported in 2026 a hard-to-diagnose fever case at a public hospital in southern Brazil. A man in his sixties had high fever for over three weeks and severe leg muscle pain that limited walking. Tests for infection and cancer found no cause, meeting the formal idea of fever of unknown origin.

Blood tests showed many white cells, very high ferritin, a protein linked to inflammation, and strong inflammation markers. That pattern pointed to a body-wide inflammatory disease rather than infection. Rheumatology specialists supported adult-onset Still disease, a rare inflammatory disorder, using standard criteria. A low steroid dose helped partly, and a higher dose ended the fever and muscle pain quickly. The authors stress structured reasoning and careful reading of lab patterns where advanced tests are scarce.
pmc-13418420:
Alice Lacan and colleagues tested diffusion models in 2026 for creating synthetic gene-expression data to ease small-sample problems in precision medicine. RNA data sets often hold too few samples for deep learning, and earlier synthetic generators leaned on variational autoencoders and adversarial networks.

Diffusion models trained on landmark genes predicted better on cancer and tissue reference data, and methods that rebuild the full transcriptome lifted diffusion, autoencoder, and adversarial models alike. Researchers gain a strong new synthetic-data option for training models where patient samples stay scarce. The work matters where gene data are precious and every sample counts.
pmc-13418520:
Roberto C French and co-authors capture brain activity and connectivity together while people watch a social film, in a 2026 neuroscience study. Viewers judged awkwardness, a cue to detecting social blunders and reading minds. Earlier work usually measured local activity or connections separately, and rarely tracked their change over time during natural scenes.

Sensorimotor activity rose with awkwardness ratings, while default network activity fell. Dynamic connections, especially involving the frontoparietal control network, explained extra variation beyond activity alone. Social judgement thus draws on both local firing and shifting network teamwork, the authors conclude, and methods should track both at once.
pmc-13419020:
Ashwag Al Dhuhaibat and colleagues review what is known about the money side of medical scribes in United States outpatient clinics. Scribes take over note writing so doctors can spend more time with patients, yet reports on cost and output gains have been mixed. The team searched nine databases for work from January 2010 to September 2024 on scribe effects in clinic care.

Screening 1,945 records left 20 studies that fit the review, spanning before-and-after designs, cohort work, two randomized trials, and simulations. Only 13 of the 20 studies tried a return-on-investment count, and just 6 of those counted full costs like pay, training, and staff turnover. Gains in doctor output appeared often, but uneven study designs limit firm claims. Clinic managers get a clear map of what the proof does and does not show.
pmc-13419220:
Ayse Bilicioglu Gunes and Serife Zeybekoglu Yesil probe how missing answers and drifting question difficulty distort the matching of scores across test forms. Large testing programs use several forms of the same test, and scores must mean the same thing on each. Their computer simulation built the setting of two unequal groups linked by shared anchor questions.

Each run placed 2,000 test takers on a form, with 500 repeats for each of 25 condition mixes. The mixes varied how many answers went missing, why they went missing, and how far question difficulty drifted. A standard linking method then tried to recover fair score matches under each mix. The results show which mixes testing programs can shrug off and which ones bend scores enough to matter.
pmc-13419320:
Elizabeth Sanseau and colleagues argue that medical simulation should be treated as an implementation strategy, not just as a teaching tool. Simulation already trains clinicians and probes hospitals for hidden safety flaws before new units open. Implementation science, the field that studies how good practices spread, has its own models that simulation rarely uses.

The authors map simulation work onto three known frameworks that guide change in health systems. They also set a research agenda where the two fields meet and share methods. Framing practice runs as change tools could help hospitals roll out new care routines with fewer surprises. The piece gives simulation leaders and change specialists a shared language for joint projects.
pmc-13421320:
Shir Maimon and colleagues recorded place cells in 2026 from bats flying tunnels up to 200 meters long. Their work revealed a coding split between hippocampal areas CA3 and CA1 that small arenas had hidden. Both areas hold place cells, yet why two consecutive stages would code space identically was a puzzle.

CA1 neurons fired densely across many place fields, while CA3 neurons fired ultrasparsely with mostly single fields, though field sizes matched across environments from 6 to 200 meters. The paper shows a sparse-to-dense transformation that speeds learning of new maps, with trajectory history shaping place cells over 100 meters in complex routes.
pmc-13421920:
Kadriyan and colleagues examined in 2026 whether handwash stations in health education institutions help students follow World Health Organization handwashing models. Knowledge alone often fails to change behavior, so they also watched the facilities themselves.

The single-center study surveyed 273 preclinical medical students and inspected the washing stations. Nearly all students showed high awareness of hand hygiene, and most reported high compliance. Awareness by itself did not predict how often students used the stations. Station use, however, was strongly tied to actual compliance with the hygiene rules the team measured during the same survey period across the institution's teaching sites. Observers judged the main washing infrastructure sufficient but found the supporting facilities, such as supplies around the sinks, substandard.
pmc-13422120: Correction: Saygin and colleagues correct their 2017 paper on CD55, a surface protein marking self-renewing, drug-resistant cells in endometrioid tumors of the ovary and uterus. Two figure errors are fixed. In one panel, a blot image for a related protein was copied from the wrong film; in another, a control blot was accidentally duplicated from a different figure. The notice shows the original and corrected figures and states that conclusions and legends are unchanged. Corrected versions now appear online; the errors survive only in print and older downloads.
pmc-13424320:
Caroline Aguilera Stewart leads a thirteen-author study of what skin stretching does to fibroblasts, the dermal cells that support epidermal stem cells during tissue expansion surgery. Surgeons routinely stretch skin to grow extra tissue for reconstruction, and coordination between the skin's two layers is essential, yet the support-cell side of the response was unmapped.

Gene profiling of stretched skin showed fibroblasts waking from rest, dividing again, making less collagen, and switching on matrix-reshaping genes, in a programme resembling embryonic skin. Because embryonic versions of these cells are classic feeders for growing skin grafts, the team tested the state directly: low-collagen cells boosted epidermal stem cell self-renewal. The findings inform expansion protocols and graft production.
pmc-13424420:
Yoshihiro Kishida and eleven colleagues compare scope-only removal with full surgery for early colorectal cancers carrying high-risk features. Their patients were aged eighty or more. Guidelines favour surgery for such cancers, but frailty often argues otherwise. Records from 2008 to 2021 covered fifty-nine patients, twenty-three treated by endoscopy alone and thirty-six by surgery.

Tumour features and complication rates were similar in the two groups, near 7–8%, with one surgery-related death. Over roughly five years of follow-up, no cancer recurred and no patient died of the disease in either group. Five-year survival reached 90% after endoscopy and 81% after surgery, a non-significant gap. Poor nutrition scores marked the patients at risk, especially in the scope-only group.
pmc-13424520:
Gil Genuth, Peter Stavrou, and Lukas D Iselin compare heel tendon surgery with and without a bioinductive collagen scaffold. The scaffold is a patch meant to coax healing. It was tested for insertional Achilles tendinopathy with Haglund deformity. Their retrospective study covers thirty consecutive patients treated by one surgeon between 2021 and 2024, fifteen with the scaffold added to the standard repair and fifteen without.

Patients reported function and pain scores before surgery and at six, twelve, and eighteen months, and MRI scans were taken at the start and at one year. Return-to-sport timing and complications were also recorded. Meaningful change thresholds were set in advance for the scores: five to eight points for function, eight to ten for pain interference. The comparison can therefore judge whether the patch earns its cost.
pmc-13424620:
Alana Darcher leads an eighteen-author team releasing SUMMER, a dataset of single-neuron recordings from twenty-nine epilepsy patients who watched a complete commercial film, 500 Days of Summer, during monitoring. Electrodes already implanted for care captured 2,286 neurons across the amygdala, hippocampus, and neighbouring memory regions during the film's full eighty-three minutes.

Frame-by-frame annotations label characters, locations, camera cuts, and the lead character's speech throughout. The package includes spike times, average waveforms, patient details, and electrode positions in a standard format, plus quality metrics and demonstrations that single neurons tune to film features. Decoding analyses even predict scenes from population activity. The authors offer the set as ready-made ground for machine learning.
pmc-13424820:
Laaraj and colleagues measured in 2026 how place and ripeness change the fruit of the carob tree, a drought-tolerant Mediterranean species valued for food and health products. They sampled three hundred trees at three sites in central Morocco across seven growth stages. Tests covered pod size and color, sugars, and health-linked compounds such as polyphenols, flavonoids, and tannins.

Both site and ripeness strongly shaped the fruit, and the two factors interacted. Pods grew about fivefold in length across development, reaching over twenty-one centimeters at late stages in the best site. Health-linked compounds peaked earlier, at mid-ripeness stages, with phenolics topping out at stage two. A summary analysis captured about eighty-four percent of all variation and grouped samples clearly by stage and site. The findings help growers pick harvest timing and origin for food, drug, and supplement uses.
pmc-13424920:
Duffy and colleagues tested in 2026 whether community health workers in rural Guatemala could manage high blood pressure safely with a phone app that guides each step of care. Blood pressure is a leading killer, and poor countries carry the heaviest load with the fewest doctors. The app, built on World Health Organization guidance, advised on drug dose changes, lifestyle counseling, and when to consult a physician.

Thirty-two patients were followed monthly for six months. The workers' prescribing matched the supervising doctors' judgment in almost ninety-nine of a hundred cases. Top-number blood pressure fell by about seven and a half points on average, and control rates rose. Eleven app errors occurred across more than two hundred visits, none harming a patient. The authors call the model ready for larger trials.
pmc-13425620:
The European Food Safety Authority (EFSA) set out in 2026 the working plan for rewriting its guidance on how plant protection products are tested for risk to land-dwelling wildlife. Three new guidance documents are in scope: one for insects and other arthropods besides bees, one for organisms living in soil, and one for wild land plants. The protocol was drafted by the authority's risk assessment working group and its plant products panel.

For each document, the mandate was turned into an assessment question with sub-questions on exposure, hazard, and risk. The plan states how much new data each sub-question merits. The focus is the first assessment tier, the screening level used before deeper studies. A formal protocol, though not required, was judged worthwhile given the task's complexity.
pmc-13426020:
Theurich and colleagues published a 2026 study on when Brent geese leave for their breeding grounds. These geese stage each spring in the Wadden Sea before flying north. Leaving on the right wind can save energy and boost breeding success. The team tracked 43 tagged geese across seven spring seasons.

Departure odds rose by about a fifth for each extra unit of tailwind. Rising air pressure also made departures more likely on a given day. Damp air, by contrast, held birds back from leaving the staging site. Early in the season, geese picked their winds with great care. By early June, urgency grew and birds left on poorer winds. Weather records were matched hour by hour to each bird's position.
pmc-13426120:
Hu and colleagues tested in 2026 a metaverse rehab platform built for people who have survived colorectal cancer. The virtual platform combines exercise training, diet guidance, mental health teaching, and habit management in one place. Cancer survivors and family members at a partner hospital used the platform, then rated it with two standard usability surveys and took part in structured interviews.

Hu included data from 18 participants with an average age of 47 years. The overall usability score was 65, which sits near the middle range for such tools, and survey scores did not differ by sex, age, or schooling. Learnability, how easy the system is to pick up, scored lowest, while the quality of interaction scored highest. Interviewees liked the rich content and ease of access but said the controls still felt awkward to run.
pmc-13426320:
Alipour and colleagues published a 2026 study testing a suspected diet link to breast cancer. Advanced glycation end products form when food browns at high heat. Some past work tied these compounds to higher breast cancer risk. The team ran a careful case-control study across several centers in Iran.

The study compared 44 patients with 42 healthy controls of like age. Diet intake of the compounds matched between the two groups overall. Blood and tissue levels of the compounds also showed no real gap. Patients did report far less physical activity than the control group. The authors say their null result argues against a diet-compound link here. Larger studies that follow women over time could still revisit the question.
pmc-13426720:
Coelho and colleagues report a 2026 case of a 36-year-old motorcyclist with a severe vertical shear pelvic injury. The front joint of his pelvis had sprung apart by forty-two millimeters. After temporary external fixation, surgeons used a W-shaped double plate at the front, shaped to the bone. It allowed long screws to grip deep into the front column of the pelvis.

Back screws through the skin into the sacroiliac joint completed the repair. The patient bore full weight at two weeks, earlier than advised, and could squat fully without pain by four weeks. At twelve months, X-rays showed stable alignment with no implant failure and no re-widening of the joint. Bone bridging was incomplete, yet function was excellent. The authors argue reinforced double plating suits very unstable front pelvic injuries.
pmc-13426920:
Cardaras and colleagues published a 2026 study on software that reads bar charts in papers. Bar charts hold key trial results, yet their data sit locked in pictures. Review teams copying numbers by hand waste hours and risk slips. The team built a four-step pipeline that pulls numbers out automatically.

The pipeline sorts chart parts, reads labels, and rebuilds values from the axes. On 28 charts from eye-disease trials, it spotted most chart types correctly. About four in five rebuilt values landed within five percent of hand-checked truth. Most errors traced to misread digits or fuzzy bar edges in scans. The proof-of-concept tool could speed up large evidence reviews greatly. Hand checks used a semi-automated labeling tool as reference standard.
pmc-13427220:
Li and colleagues report a light-driven method that chops lignin and upgrades the pieces in a single pot. Lignin is the tough polymer binding plant cell walls. The method skips the usual separate depolymerization and refining steps. Their cadmium zinc sulfide photocatalyst couples lignin fragments directly with alcohols. The products are unsymmetric aromatic diols, molecules with two alcohol groups on a ring.

The catalyst's light-generated holes create radicals. Its electrons rescue over-oxidized intermediates. Together they steer the chemistry toward cross-coupling, instead of the unwanted self-coupling of identical fragments. Applied to real lignin rather than model compounds, the protocol delivered the aromatic diol products at up to 10 percent by weight in monomer yield. The authors note the diols feed directly into thermoplastic polyurethanes and other functional materials. That gives the one-pot route practical value for biomass use.
pmc-13427320:
Navez and co-authors reviewed whether adding stem cells or their secreted vesicles to machine-perfused donor kidneys, organs kept alive on pumps before transplant, can repair preservation damage and improve graft outcomes. Following standard review guidelines, they searched three databases for experiments in animal or discarded human kidneys.

Nine studies qualified, and seven entered the meta-analysis comparing treated and untreated perfused kidneys. Several studies reported lower inflammatory signals, including interleukin-6, interleukin-1 beta, and the injury marker NGAL, after cell or vesicle treatment. The pooled analysis, however, found no significant benefit for creatinine clearance, urine output, or NGAL levels across studies. Stem cell retention in the organs was limited, mechanisms remain poorly understood, and only one study checked function after actual transplantation, so the authors call for standardized transplant-based trials.
pmc-13427620:
Setoguchi and Hennessy mapped in 2026 the two-way relationship between climate change and medications. In one direction, extreme heat, storms, and broken supply chains threaten drug stability, access, and safety, from mail-order insulin spoiling in heat to an IV fluid shortage after a hurricane. In the other, making, using, and discarding medicines adds to health care's carbon output, feeding the warming that creates those threats.

The authors note that equally effective drug options can differ widely in carbon cost, so cutting needless prescribing and choosing lower-carbon equivalents are levers clinicians and pharmacists already hold. Warnings about heat and drugs still rest largely on mechanism and case reports. The authors call for studies linking weather exposure data to drug outcomes, with confounding by illness and multiple medicines as the central hurdles. Where greener choices already match guidelines, they urge action now, backed by formulary and guideline reform.
pmc-13428120:
Oriana Awwad and colleagues checked whether an Arabic version of a 23-question heart failure survey measures quality of life soundly in Arabic-speaking patients. The Kansas City questionnaire asks about symptoms, daily limits, and social life in people whose hearts pump weakly.

The study enrolled 331 patients at two centres in Jordan and tested the survey's consistency, stability over time, and structure. Scores held together very well, with a consistency measure of 0.937 on a scale where one is perfect, and repeat answers stayed steady. Patients who were married, active, and faithful to their medication reported better quality of life. Awwad concludes the Arabic survey is fit for clinic and research use across the region.
pmc-13429120:
Manting Hao and colleagues review, in a 2026 paper, tiny probes that both image rheumatoid arthritis and treat it in the same package. Such theranostic particles home to inflamed joints, light up disease activity on scans, release therapy on cue, and report back on the response. Rheumatoid arthritis varies a lot between patients, which makes that feedback loop attractive. The review follows the field from joint targeting through imaging to drug delivery and monitoring.

Therapies riding these particles include anti-inflammatory drugs, immune modulators, and light-based treatments. The authors draw a line between truly integrated systems and simple carriers with a dye attached. Translation to patients lags far behind animal work. Safety over time, body distribution, repeat dosing, factory consistency, and regulatory paths all remain open problems, and the review names them without flinching.
pmc-13429220:
Leo Lui and co-authors test, in a 2026 Hong Kong study, a one-step cleaning product for surfaces around patients carrying a resistant staph germ. MRSA spreads partly through bedside surfaces that staff touch all day. Over six months in medical, surgical, and bone wards, each patient's surroundings were split in half. One half got the classic two-step clean, detergent then bleach solution, while the other half got a combined detergent-disinfectant in a single pass.

Both methods cut MRSA detection sharply, from about 69 percent of samples to the low teens. Cleanliness test failures also plunged under both. The one-step method saved about six minutes and about ten wipes per patient. Scaled to public hospitals citywide, the authors project savings above six million Hong Kong dollars a year. Equal cleaning power with less time and waste is the selling point.
pmc-13430820:
Neetha Harisha and co-authors tested in 2026 whether values from dental cone beam scans can flag low bone strength, and how those values line up with heel sound tests and blood markers. Bone thinning raises risks for the skeleton and for dental work. The cross-check study enrolled 86 adults older than forty.

Heel sound scores split the group into normal and low-bone sets. Scan values for both hard outer bone and spongy inner bone ran far higher in the normal set. The two scan measures tracked heel scores closely, and both tracked blood levels of vitamin D as well. Shape-based scan measures fared poorly by contrast. A graded scan index of the jaw cortex moved the other way, as worse grades went with lower heel scores.
pmc-13432020:
Macarena Siri and co-authors probed in 2026 how two fiber types blend to give E. coli biofilms their strength, treating the slimy mat as a tunable layered stuff. Biofilms of this gut germ rest on a shared matrix built from stiff amyloid threads and a changed plant-like fiber, held in water. The stiff threads lend firmness, while the plant-like fiber lends cohesion.

The team grew mats from strains that make both fibers, one fiber, or blends at set ratios. Poking tests, fine scopes, and cold 3D imaging showed mat stiffness tracks both the mix and the layout of the fibers. The plant-like fiber swells, yet stiff threads cage that swell where they touch. The wild strain blends the pair at a tiny scale into a hybrid stuff whose traits beat what each part gives alone. The authors see a route to grown living goods.
pmc-13432820:
Bo Yan and co-authors reviewed in 2026 the tiny bubbles that E. coli germs shed from their outer skin, and how those bubbles spread harm, drug proofing, and talks with hosts. The bubbles are balls of skin stuffed with proteins, wall sugars, and gene scraps. Drug-proof and fierce strains of this gut germ pose a rising threat to public health.

The review maps how bubbles form, what they carry, and the jobs they do in illness. Bubbles can ferry drug-proof traits to kin germs and tune how host immune cells react. The authors also weigh fresh uses: bubble-based vaccines, bubble couriers for drug loads, and bubble strikes on tumors. A firm grasp of bubble traits, they argue, can seed new ways to spot, block, and treat infections.
pmc-13433320:
Saman Abbaspoor, Ayman Aljishi, and Kari L Hoffman recorded cell crowds in 2026 in the deep memory hub of free-moving macaques. The monkeys called back item chains from that day, the day before, or weeks past. How fresh learning reshapes old traces without wiping them stays a core puzzle. Sleep replays help firm new traces in many species.

Crowds tuned to old chains drifted less, linked more thickly, and replayed harder in sleep than crowds tuned to fresh chains. Old and mid-age crowds paired into joint teams that held from task to sleep, a tie fresh pairs lacked. In the hub, two cell layers grew more prone to team up as the memory aged. The authors read swift sorting and firming at work.
pmc-13433620:

pmc-13467420:

pmc-13478320:

Emily Lau and nine colleagues measured in 2026 social drivers of death anxiety in advanced cancer outpatients receiving comfort care. Death anxiety is common, but its risk factors in specialised comfort-care settings were little known.

Among 203 clinic patients, 46.3 percent reported moderate to severe death anxiety. Greater anxiety tracked lower household income and living alone, but not time since advanced diagnosis, time since first comfort-care visit, or nearness to death. The authors call for research into whether targeted counselling and comfort-care support can ease distress tied to economic disadvantage and solitary living.
pmc-13479820:
Lili Xu and coauthors published a 2026 review and meta-analysis of anxiety and depression in idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis, a scarring lung disease that worsens over time. Low mood and worry are common in this group, yet reported rates vary wildly between studies. Four data banks were searched from their start to late October 2025 under standard reporting guidelines.

Two screeners worked on their own, pulled out rate figures, and rated study quality. Pooled numbers give a world average for each illness, while checks of study gaps hunt for what drives the spread, such as region, test tool, or how sick patients were. The authors mean the pooled numbers to support routine mental health screening in fibrosis clinics and to size future treatment trials.
pmc-13483120:
Christine Sevilla-Dedieu and co-authors present a 2026 phone survey on whether a taste for risk predicts healthy habits among French adults. The random sample held 2,666 people insured by the national health system. Each gave social and health details plus a thirty-item score of risk appetite across life domains, and the team modelled three habits: regular sport, not smoking, and a normal weight range.

Just under three in five played sport often, near seven in ten did not smoke, and about three in five sat in the normal weight band. Risk scores linked firmly to each habit, yet the direction flipped by habit. A bold streak may feed sport while fighting weight control, for instance. Health-minded people thus show no single pattern; each habit trades risk off in its own way, which prevention drives should respect.
pmc-13483420:
Pan Jiang and co-authors share a 2026 case report on a jaw joint problem where scans and motion told different parts of the story. A 22-year-old woman arrived with three months of clicking in both jaw joints and pain on the left. Standard criteria and MRI both pointed to discs slipping forward, then snapping back on opening.

Her first splint, built to hold the jaw forward, made the left side worse, so the team stopped it. A computerised jaw tracker then mapped her motion, drawing a figure-eight path with poor overlap between repeats. Forward travel on the left ran near three to four millimetres against ten to eleven on the right. A pivot splint followed; short checks showed easier motion, lighter symptoms, and a better disc position on repeat scan. One case proves little, the authors note, yet motion data sharpens judgement when still images mislead.
pmc-13483620:
Julia Michelin and co-authors train deep learning models to spot dental problems from video rather than still photographs. Their 2026 validation study recorded 708 videos with a toothbrush fitted with a tiny mouth camera. Thousands of extracted frames were labeled by two dental experts for findings such as decay, fillings, plaque, and staining, plus tooth type.

The findings model reached strong overall precision, performing best on amalgam fillings and decay. A separate tooth-type model scored even higher, with molars and premolars identified most reliably. Performance held up despite no fixed filming routine for users. Embedding such checks into a daily brushing device could support remote monitoring and earlier care, especially where dentists are scarce.
pmc-13483720:
Stephani Edwina Lucia builds a live imaging window into the pancreas to watch pancreatic cancer blood vessels change over time. Published in 2026, the study implants tumor cells and a viewing window in mice, labels vessel walls with a fluorescent marker, and tracks glowing red blood cells for flow. Repeated viewing of the same regions follows growth of this highly lethal cancer.

Time-lapse viewing caught vessels sprouting, being pruned away, widening, and collapsing as tumors progressed. Flow varied sharply from vessel to vessel, with some channels losing flow abruptly while neighbors flickered or partly recovered. Vessel-targeting drugs have repeatedly failed in this cancer despite strong growth signals. Watching supply lines evolve at cell level may reveal when and where such drugs could actually help.
pmc-13484320: Walid Nabgan and co-authors are named on a 2026 journal notice concerning a catalysis article about reforming and cracking microplastic waste dissolved in phenol. The notice is an expression of concern only, recording that the editor flagged unresolved questions about accountability for the work on July 23, 2026. Related publications show a broader pattern that casts doubt on reliability. The authors offered an explanation that neither settled nor confirmed the concerns. Readers should treat the flagged findings as unverified while the journal process continues.
pmc-13486020:
Carlotta Keiko Vedolin and others track lives and death among Italian adults with Addison disease, a rare failure of the adrenal glands, over many decades. In 2026, the study gathers 1,826 patients seen at thirty hormone units from 1947 to 2024 and compares their mortality with an age- and sex-matched Italian group. Causes range from self-attacking disease to genetic, cancer-related, vessel, and surgery forms.

Overall mortality ran about a third higher than in the general group, but the average hid sharp gaps. Three quarters of patients, including those with common self-attacking forms, had lives close to normal. Three smaller groups faced roughly fivefold risk: type 1 self-attacking polyendocrine syndrome, genetic forms, and cancer-related disease. The authors insist that each cause must be judged separately rather than lumped together.
pmc-13486120:
Cong Chen connects a little-known antibody-factory protein to how severe pancreatic inflammation becomes. Published in 2026, the study profiles blood immune cells from mild and severe pancreatitis patients across disease stages with single-cell sequencing. B cell programs tied to antibody production grow more prominent late in severe disease, with the protein MZB1 standing out.

Mouse experiments test cause directly, since animals lacking MZB1 suffer worse pancreatic inflammation. Missing MZB1 also cuts IgA antibody output and weakens the intestinal barrier, letting gut-driven inflammation feed back into the crisis. Supporting the MZB1 to IgA to barrier chain may therefore calm severe pancreatitis from an unexpected direction, beyond the innate immune targets that dominate current thinking. Humoral immunity earns a seat at the severity table.
pmc-13486420:
Nevin Belder builds a gene signature that flags which ulcerative colitis patients are sliding toward colon cancer. Published in 2026, the single-author analysis mines transcript data from colitis and cancer cohorts separately, hunting changes that repeat across both. A cell-state program called epithelial-mesenchymal transition keeps surfacing among switched-up genes.

Twenty-four shared candidate genes narrowed to fourteen that run high in colitis-linked precancer compared with quiet colitis, each separating the states strongly. Machine learning distilled a seven-gene panel whose combined score climbs stepwise from quiet disease through precancer to cancer. Long-standing colitis carries real cancer risk, yet colonoscopy alone cannot see molecular momentum. A tissue score that rises along the danger path could focus surveillance on the patients who need it most.
pmc-13486720:
Vladimír Ivančík and others compare facial expressions with felt emotions during social interaction in schizophrenia, autism, and neurotypical adults. In 2026, the study uses automated facial analysis during same-form interaction with thirty-eight people with schizophrenia, sixteen autistic adults, and thirty-nine neurotypical adults. Blunted affect, or reduced outward emotion, appears in both medical groups but may mean different things.

People with schizophrenia showed more neutral faces and lower valence and arousal than neurotypical adults, while autistic adults showed typical facial expressions yet found lower positive feelings. The split matters for finding and treatment, since schizophrenia often warrants antipsychotic medication while autism alone does not. Doctors get evidence that outward levels and inner experience can diverge in opposite directions.
pmc-13487920:
Asal Kamani Fard and Mohammad Paydar study women's walking and well-being in six middle-income neighborhoods of Santiago, Chile, in a 2026 survey. Walking is a main way women get around, yet fear and poor street conditions can discourage it. The team used questionnaires with both closed and open questions, plus maps and street audits to record the built setting.

Women named insecurity as the chief barrier, tied to crime, weak lighting, and unsafe streets. Walking habits were linked with how well women felt, though the design cannot show cause. Income, work, social ties, and street quality all played a part. The authors urge safer, better lit, and more welcoming streets.
pmc-13488120:
Bochu Liu and co-authors map online fresh food ordering across Shanghai neighborhoods in a 2026 cross-sectional study. Delivery apps may ease shopping where stores are scarce, yet use may still favor richer areas. Citywide order records for green groceries, supermarkets, and fruit were linked to over eleven thousand small areas, with local income, age mix, car ownership, and nearby food shops recorded for each area.

Orders clustered in better-off neighborhoods, and rates ran lower where shares of older, younger, or low-income residents were higher. Areas with more nearby supermarkets and grocery stores ordered less online across all food types. Car-free areas ordered more, which hints delivery helps when travel is hard, though gaps remain.
pmc-13488220:
Heng Xiao and Yanbin Ren survey human papillomavirus infection among women in southern Hebei, China, in a 2026 study from Handan Central Hospital. Cervical samples from more than forty-one thousand patients and health-check visitors between 2022 and 2025 were typed for twenty-three virus strains, split into high-risk types tied to cancer and low-risk types. Rates were compared across age groups and cervical disease levels.

About twenty-four percent of samples tested positive overall. Types 52, 16, and 58 were the most common, and high-risk types dominated the findings. Infection peaked in women under twenty and rose again after sixty. Rates ran much higher in women with precancerous changes or cervical cancer than in the general group. The authors offer the data for screening and vaccine planning.
pmc-13488720:
Ösken and team screened nutritional health in 113 patients with Sjögren disease, an autoimmune condition best known for dry eyes and mouth but able to attack organs throughout the body. Their 2026 study split patients into 26 with such organ involvement and 87 without, scoring nutrition with two blood-based indexes that combine albumin, cholesterol, and immune cell counts.

Patients with organ involvement showed worse nutrition on both indexes, with higher risk scores and lower protective values than the comparison group. They also carried certain autoantibodies, anti-Ro and anti-Ro-52, more often in this sample. The nutrition scores correlated with a standard disease activity index the clinicians recorded. Average age was about fifty-six, and nearly ninety-five percent of patients were women. Ösken recommends both cheap, routine-lab scores for flagging malnutrition risk in rheumatology clinics.
pmc-13490420:
Yeh and team scanned the brains of 24 younger and 27 older adults while they judged picture sequences showing sports actions in sensible or scrambled order. Following motion sequences underpins daily skills like driving, and aging may change the strategy used. Their 2026 imaging study varied sequence order across three conditions and recorded both coherence ratings and brain activity for each quartet of pictures.

Younger adults' ratings tracked the true ordering faithfully across the conditions presented in the scanner. Older adults were less sensitive to ordered sequences yet still rated them above randomized ones. Their brains leaned harder on left frontal regions and on default-mode areas, the network tied to internal knowledge, especially for scrambled sequences. Yeh reads this as a shift from bottom-up watching toward top-down guessing, not simple sensory decline.
pmc-13491720:
Xiangyu Guo and four colleagues ask in 2026 whether blood chemistry profiles can sharpen genetic predictions of feed efficiency in pigs. Feed conversion ratio, the feed needed per unit of growth, is costly to measure head-on, so breeders predict breeding values from DNA. The team tested whether adding metabolite profiles from magnetic resonance spectroscopy sharpened those predictions in Duroc pigs.

The herd held 8,174 pigs, with males at a test station providing feed records and females checked through their offspring. Adding the chemistry data lifted prediction accuracy by only about two percent. Pairing the trait with daily gain added a gain of the same small size. Neither gain reached statistical significance. The authors blame one-time sampling and suggest better sampling designs could let chemistry data contribute more.
pmc-13491820:
Hui Jiang and four colleagues test in 2026 whether music tempo can sharpen self-control in men recovering from drug addiction, and whether psychological resilience changes the answer. Forty-four men, split into high and low resilience groups by questionnaire, performed a reaction task where drug pictures meant withholding a response. Brain waves were recorded under fast, medium, and slow music plus silence.

High-resilience men responded faster overall. Brain signals showed low-resilience men spending more effort on early conflict detection, while high-resilience men allocated resources more efficiently at a later stage. Under slow music the high-resilience group showed a clear boost in conflict monitoring that vanished at fast tempo. The authors argue that music-based rehabilitation should be tuned to each patient's psychological profile rather than applied uniformly.
pmc-13492020:
Huiling Zhou and six colleagues build in 2026 a deep learning system that flags likely cyberbullying perpetrators among Chinese university students, a group that is hard to spot because offenders are rare. Only fifty-four of 660 surveyed students admitted perpetrating, so ordinary algorithms drowned in the majority class. The team answered with two-stage training plus a weighted penalty that forces attention onto the rare offenders.

The model recovered ninety-two percent of true perpetrators, far ahead of standard methods such as random forests. Explanation analysis ranked screen time, negative emotions, weak school connectedness, online disinhibition, violent media exposure, and deviant friends as the strongest predictors. School connectedness appeared to buffer several risks at once, which the authors say gives prevention programs a concrete lever.
pmc-13494620:
Mia R. Zolna and others update contraceptive use and unfulfilled preferences among United States women aged fifteen to forty-nine in 2022 to 2023. In 2026, the secondary analysis uses the National Survey of Family Growth, covering 5,586 respondents, after policy changes and the pandemic disrupted reproductive health access. The study asks who uses which methods and who cannot get their preferred method because of cost.

Fifty-seven percent used contraception, most often pills, condoms, permanent methods, withdrawal, and intrauterine devices, with over a fifth using multiple methods. Thirteen percent of users picked another method and thirty-one percent of nonusers wanted to start one absent cost worries. Unmet preference ran higher among sexual minority users and younger or unmarried nonusers. Equitable, affordable access remains unfinished.
pmc-13495220:
Congcong Liu and colleagues evaluate, in a 2026 study from China, a leadership course for intensive care nurses. Nurse leadership shapes care quality, yet courses aimed at bedside nurses, rather than managers, are rare in China. Thirty-five nurses from two teaching hospitals took part, with about half given the course and half serving as the comparison group.

The course ran eight sessions on team building, planning, emotional skill, communication, and leading change. Afterward the trained group scored higher on leadership scales covering organization, planning, and people skills, and also on confidence and intensive care competence. Interviews with nine nurses added three themes: a wider grasp of what leadership means, shifts in their own thinking and habits, and hurdles plus hopes for future rounds. The authors urge nurse managers to spread such training more widely.
pmc-13495420:
Diego F Wyszynski reviews, in a 2026 article, pregnancy in systemic lupus erythematosus, a long-term autoimmune disease that mostly strikes women in their childbearing years. Lupus and pregnancy strain each other: the disease raises the odds of baby loss, early birth, blood pressure crisis, clots, and small babies, above all when kidneys are involved. Pregnancy can also stir the disease back to life.

Better watching and care have cut complications, yet risk stays above that of other mothers, and foreseeing flares or bad outcomes remains hard. Placental failure and immune attack are the suspected engines. Some lupus drugs can harm a fetus, which forces careful drug choice. The best odds come when conception waits for a quiet stretch of disease, with close joint care by several specialties and pregnancy-safe treatment holding the disease down.
pmc-13495520:
Lucas M Seuren and colleagues ask, in a 2026 interview study, why family doctors in Ontario take up, keep using, or drop a virtual team support line called SCOPE. The phone service links primary care doctors with hospital and community help for complex patients. The team interviewed twenty primary care doctors, three internists, and six project staff over video calls.

Seven themes shaped use. Doctors weighed a health system they saw as broken, plain awareness that the line existed, and whether its services matched their needs. A tool that felt useful and easy won a first try; habit and the effort of change then decided whether use stuck. Feeling heard by the service kept doctors coming back. The authors say such lines help only when doctors feel backed, grasp the gains, and get time to learn the new way of working.
pmc-13499920:
Divya Deodhar and colleagues compare in 2026 bloodstream infections caused by Candida auris, a hardy drug-resistant yeast, with infections from other Candida species at a university hospital in Muscat, Oman. Yeast in the blood is life-threatening and increasingly healthcare-linked. Their retrospective review covered all adults with such infections over five years, from January 2018 to December 2022, comparing risk links, outcomes, and drug susceptibility between groups.

Of 160 patients, 58 carried the resistant species while 102 carried other Candida types. Prior colonisation with Candida species was the strongest link to the resistant infection, raising odds several-fold in the reported ratios, and recent healthcare contact within ninety days also linked strongly. The authors suggest one drug family, echinocandins, as an early empirical choice when these warning links are present, while local susceptibility patterns are confirmed.
pmc-13500420:
Abigail Hui En Chan and colleagues assess in 2026 drug resistance in a gut worm of livestock that can also infect people, sampled in Thailand. Benzimidazole dewormers are heavily used, and resistant worms had been found at high levels locally. Working with 60 adult Trichostrongylus colubriformis worms from Sukhothai and Satun provinces, the team read resistance directly from a tubulin gene, a standard marker. A mitochondrial gene mapped diversity and population structure.

Strong resistance was present, with the mixed genotype carrying one resistant and one sensitive copy forming most worms. Genetic diversity ran high, while Thai worms differed sharply from those in other countries, hinting at limited gene flow across borders. That isolation cuts both ways, since local control measures could likely contain resistance spread, provided watching of this zoonotic worm continues.
pmc-13500720:
Zhiheng Tai and four co-authors report a 2026 study of a titanium composite made by laser directed energy deposition, a form of metal 3D printing. They built samples from the alloy Ti6Al4V, which is strong and light but wears poorly, and tried to grow hard titanium nitride particles inside it during printing. One route deposited the metal under a nitrogen-argon mix, while a second route remelted the surface under pure nitrogen. Dry sliding wear tests ran at room temperature and at 300 degrees Celsius.

The remelted samples grew larger, more densely spread nitride particles. Their friction was somewhat higher, yet wear volume fell by about 44.8 percent at room temperature and 78.8 percent at the higher temperature compared with the plain alloy. The directly deposited samples, with sparser and smaller particles, improved much less.
pmc-13500820:
Lilla Otrokocsi leads a five-author team with a 2026 mouse study of whether vaccines given in pregnancy affect how the offspring act. Pregnant mice received the COVID-19 mRNA vaccine BNT162b2, a flu vaccine, or a control, and pups were tested at four and eight weeks of age. Blood and fetal brain tissue were checked for immune markers: cytokines, the P2X7 receptor, BDNF, and fat oxidation damage. A comparison group received poly(I:C), which mimics viral infection.

The COVID vaccine raised two maternal cytokines modestly without inflaming the fetal brain. Some mild, age- and sex-linked changes in how pups acted appeared, but no consistent autism-like pattern emerged at either age. The flu vaccine caused smaller, passing effects, while poly(I:C) triggered strong inflammation and lasting changes. The authors conclude that prenatal COVID vaccination showed no widespread harm to brain development in this model.
pmc-13501620:
Derya Demirtaş Esmer leads a nine-author team reporting a 2026 study of whether low muscle mass blunts chemotherapy response in advanced ovarian cancer. The retrospective study covered 52 overweight or obese women with stage III to IV epithelial ovarian cancer treated between 2019 and 2022 with platinum and taxane chemotherapy before interval surgery. Muscle mass was measured on baseline CT scans at the third lumbar vertebra. Women were split into low and high muscle mass groups at the cohort median, and those combining obesity with low muscle were flagged.

That combined group responded worst: response rates were 46.7 percent against 62.2 percent for the others, and disease control rates were 80 percent against 100 percent. Body mass index alone and low muscle mass alone showed no significant effect. Median disease-free survival after surgery was 19.3 months. The authors propose muscle assessment as a risk marker, while noting overall survival data were immature.
pmc-13501820:
Ming Zhou leads a five-author team with a 2026 study of whether the choice of anti-seizure drug changes survival in low-grade glioma, where epilepsy strikes most patients. The team combined lenses: machine learning over 105 targets of ten anti-seizure drugs, molecular docking, a past-records patient cohort, and cell experiments. A thirteen-gene signature predicted prognosis. One sodium channel gene, SCN9A, emerged as a hazard factor, while two glutamate receptor genes, GRIN2C and GRIN3A, acted as protectors.

Three drugs, carbamazepine, oxcarbazepine, and lacosamide, were predicted to extend survival by blocking the hazard gene's product. Phenobarbital pointed the other way, shortening survival by suppressing the two protective genes. The cohort check supported those directions, and bench tests agreed: blocking SCN9A curbed malignant cell behaviour, while suppressing the protective pair enhanced it. The authors offer the work as guidance for drug choice.
pmc-13502820:
Longping Chen and others compare two traction methods for hard bile duct cannulation when a periampullary diverticulum distorts anatomy. In 2026, the single-center look-back study covers 193 patients undergoing endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography, with propensity matching producing sixty patients per group: clip-assisted versus clip plus rubber band-assisted cannulation.

Success reached 96.7 percent with clip plus rubber band versus 73.3 percent with clip alone, in about half the time, with far fewer rescue methods such as double-guidewire or transpancreatic sphincterotomy. Adverse events were comparable and all resolved conservatively, with no serious events. The merged method offers a safe, faster route through distorted papillary anatomy.
pmc-13503820:
Xiaoyu Xue leads a team showing how a genome-guard complex tags proteins with SUMO, a small modifier, in a 2026 study. Most tagging enzymes work alone, but the Nse2 enzyme only works as part of the larger Smc5/6 complex. How the other parts of the complex help was unclear.

Tests in yeast showed that DNA boosts the complex's tagging action by pulling enzyme and target close. Four partner parts use their grip on DNA to support that boost. Parts that bind ATP, the cell fuel, help the complex latch onto DNA and change shape for the task. The findings frame Smc5/6 as a joint tagging machine switched on by DNA and fuel together.
pmc-13503920:
Alejandro Santos-Mayo leads a team that built an AI model which predicts brain wave responses to words and pictures, in a 2026 paper. Brain waves read from the scalp, called EEG, show how the brain reacts to meaning and feeling. Most AI work decodes those waves; far less work runs the other way.

Their model, Concept2Brain, turns a picture or text into a rich trait vector with a public vision-language tool, then maps that vector into a brain wave space. The fake responses it makes closely match real ones recorded from people. The model is offered as a free web service, so labs can build open EEG data sets for any concept or image. The authors see it as a step toward modeling brain activity with AI.
pmc-13505120:
Desmond Maada Kangbai and others evaluate Sierra Leone's COVID-19 vaccination program and its role in introducing human papillomavirus vaccination. In 2026, the post-introduction review draws on eighty-four set talks across six districts plus a desk review, adapting the World Health Organization review tool. Sierra Leone launched COVID-19 vaccination in March 2021 and reached 73.2 percent full coverage among ages twelve and older by December 2022.

By October 2023, full coverage reached an estimated 86.7 percent, with over eighty-four percent of doses delivered through surge campaigns. Lessons included bringing adult vaccination closer to clients, retooling current infrastructure, engaging community leaders, strengthening electronic tracking, and integrating giving platforms. HPV uptake exceeded targets, with 119 percent of aimed girls vaccinated, mostly in schools, though surge giving strained staff and disrupted some routine immunization.
pmc-13505420:
Yi He and colleagues built a structural model of apolipoprotein A-II, the second most common protein carried on HDL, the particles that move cholesterol out of tissues. The protein grips lipids more tightly than its better-known partner APOA1, yet its shape on the particle was unsettled. The team combined computer modelling with targeted mutations to test how the chain folds.

Their model wraps the protein's paired chains as a double hairpin belt around disc-shaped HDL. Most charged building blocks sit in the hairpin loop, and internal bridges plus ring stacking hold the fold steady. Two strong lipid-binding stretches appear in each half of the pair, and the hairpin seems built to meet partner proteins. Chemical crosslinking found sixteen links between parts of the chain, and fifteen of them fit the belt model. The result gives lipid researchers a picture for explaining how APOA2 shapes HDL behaviour.
pmc-13506120:
Tony Tannoury and co-authors report outcomes for the longest front-of-neck fusions in their series, spanning four or five levels, drawn from 1,428 cervical fusion patients treated between 2009 and 2021. Twenty-seven patients met the study rules and had at least two years of follow-up. The graft material was the patient's own hip bone, fixed with a front plate and screws.

Function and pain improved markedly: average disability grade dropped by more than half, and neck and arm pain scores fell with clear statistical strength. Neck alignment also improved on imaging, and every patient achieved solid fusion. Swallowing trouble was the commonest early problem, affecting about thirty percent, but it faded to a small share by late follow-up. Three patients developed wear at a neighbouring segment. The authors conclude the extended operation gives excellent results for multi-level cord compression when patients are chosen well.
pmc-13507020:
Anna Piotrowska and colleagues report 2026 mouse tests of cenicriviroc, a drug that blocks two chemokine receptors tied to nerve pain. Mice had a chronic squeeze injury to the sciatic nerve, a standard model of nerve pain. Twice-daily doses were compared with morphine over sixteen days, and spinal tissue was checked for pain-related signals.

On day three, pain relief matched morphine, and on days eight and sixteen the new drug worked better. Mice given cenicriviroc before morphine also lost less response to morphine over time. Spinal readings showed lower pain-driving signals and higher calming ones at key points. Dual blockade may offer a fresh route for nerve pain care.
pmc-13508220:
Yuanyuan Yin and four co-authors pilot a seminar-case teaching model for postgraduate students in orthodontics, the field of teeth straightening, in 2026 work. Chinese training in this field leans on lectures and apprenticeships, which can leave reasoning skills underbuilt. Their model mixes seminar debate with real case work. Sixty-four students from 27 dental schools joined a summer program and were split into six small groups. Each group, led by a seasoned teacher, worked through three complex cases.

Surveys before and after showed strong approval of the model. More than four fifths of students rated it better than traditional teaching. Large majorities reported gains in diagnosis, treatment planning, and clinical reasoning. Most felt ready to apply what they learned in clinic. Gains varied oddly with experience, dipping for the middle group. The authors present the model as a workable upgrade for specialist training.
pmc-13508520:
Li Ye, Maoting Chen, Qianling Wei, and Yue Wang study whether starting tube feeding within a day of heart surgery helps young children recover, in 2026 work. Feeding timing after congenital heart repair is disputed. Records covered 246 children aged one month to three years operated between 2021 and 2023. The early group, 128 children, began feeding within twenty-four hours. Infection rates, nutrition blood levels, and time in intensive care and hospital were compared.

Early feeding came with far fewer hospital infections, about fifteen percent against twenty-seven percent. Surgical wound infections also ran lower in the early group. Blood nutrition markers a week after surgery were higher with early feeding. Those children left intensive care sooner and went home days earlier on average. Adjusted models named delayed feeding an independent risk factor for hospital infection. The authors back starting feeds within a day when the child's state allows.
pmc-13509320:
Walid Atiki, Najia Ameur, Atika Zidouh, Abdelmoula Elouardi, and Latifa Tahri present a 2026 field survey of drug resistance in bacteria taken from broiler farms in the Rabat-Salé-Kénitra region of Morocco. The group sampled manure, drinking troughs, farm soil, more distant fields, and well water across 13 farms. In total they collected 543 samples between late 2023 and spring 2025.

Escherichia coli turned up in about a third of samples and Salmonella in about a quarter. Roughly six in ten isolates of each kind resisted drugs from three or more classes. Resistance was most common in manure, troughs, and farm soil. Resistant bacteria also appeared in nearby soil and well water. The authors say the pattern calls for tighter farm hygiene and joint human and animal health monitoring.
pmc-13510020:
Jiang and co-authors optimise the finger bones of a biomimetic robot hand. Their 2026 paper tackles a design tension: compact hands lose versatility. With total finger length fixed, the team asks how to split it among the phalanges. Designs were scored three ways. The criteria were grasp capability in a shared workspace, kinematic dexterity from the Jacobian matrix, and key-press range for typing-like strikes.

A full grid search produced distinct optima per criterion, and Pareto analysis found 117 non-dominated designs balancing the three. Key-press range proved the most sensitive objective, varying by about a quarter across designs. A hierarchical strategy that privileged key-pressing while balancing the rest yielded a recommended compromise. Built and tested, it achieved a 98.8 percent keystroke success rate over 1,000 cross-row strikes without wrist movement. Grasp and dexterity validation remains future work.
pmc-13510820:
Nakao and colleagues tested in 2026 a body composition measure, intracellular water scaled by height squared, as a partner to the standard skeletal muscle index. Both come from bioelectrical impedance analysis, a method that sends a weak current through the body. The standard index can mislead when fluid balance is off, since extra water outside cells inflates it. The team studied 477 hospital patients and split results by sex, weight class, and hydration level.

Nakao found the water-based measure tracked body mass index more strongly than the muscle index in both men and women. The two measures agreed closely in men but only weakly in women. In men, their agreement grew sharply as body mass rose, while hydration status shifted the pattern further. The authors argue the water measure reflects true cell volume and adds useful context beside the standard index in sick patients.
pmc-13511720:
Hazal Su Bıçakcı Yeşilkaya and five co-authors design a system that reads emotion and stress from wearable brain and heart sensors, in 2026 work. Results travel over future 6G health networks. A deep learning model with an attention step sorts brain wave recordings into three emotion classes, while an image-style network sorts heart signal traces into three stress states. Radio performance was simulated inside a virtual hospital at two frequency bands.

On standard datasets, the brain wave model sorted emotions with accuracy above ninety percent. The heart model scored lower, with a clear drop from validation to held-out testing. Simulated radio links showed short signal smearing and wide usable bandwidth at both bands, better at the higher one. The authors present the frame as a workable base for personal health monitoring over next-generation networks.
pmc-13512820:
Togzhan Serbatyrova, Gulnar Shalgumbayeva, Assel Tukinova, Gulnara Sarsebayeva, and Laura Danyarova run a case-control study of gestational diabetes in Kazakhstan, where evidence from Central Asia remains thin, in 2026 work. The condition, diabetes first appearing in pregnancy, is rising worldwide and harms mothers and babies. The team compared women with the condition against women with normal glucose tolerance to find tied factors and outcomes.

Obesity before pregnancy and schooling level each held an independent link to gestational diabetes after other factors were counted. Women with the condition faced more high blood pressure problems, more cesarean deliveries, and more oversized babies than the comparison group. The authors say tackling obesity before pregnancy could cut both the condition and its fallout. They call for larger multi-center studies to guide maternal health policy in the region.
pmc-13514320:
Canonico and co-authors looked to kombucha, a fermented tea, as a source of yeasts for new plant-based drinks. Their 2026 study pulled yeast strains from the tea and named each type by its genes. They found fifty-two distinct strains in all. One type, Brettanomyces anomalus, was by far the most common in the mix. The team then put the yeasts through lab tests that mimic the gut.

More than eight in ten yeasts lived through the fake gut tests. Many also stuck to each other and held back two germs that can cause illness. Two strains of one yeast and one strain of a third stood out as the best picks. Mixed pools of these yeasts made drinks with good lab scores and good taste marks. A strain from a wild source also helped brew a kombucha with no bacteria at all.
pmc-13514820:
Lule and colleagues studied in 2026 whether chronotype, a person's natural tilt toward morning or evening activity, links to hidden belly fat and blood fat risk. They enrolled 282 adults with no known chronic disease and no regular medicines at one centre. Each person filled in standard questionnaires on morningness and sleep quality, and the team computed combined risk indices from body measures and blood tests.

Lule found that greater morningness went with lower scores on both a visceral fat index and a blood fat risk index, even after accounting for sleep quality and other factors. Sleep quality itself showed no independent link to either index. Hints that the link ran stronger in women did not survive stricter statistical correction. The link also faded in the subgroup with strictly normal blood sugar. The authors say late chronotype may flag early risk even when sleep feels fine.
pmc-13517320:
Mark Godley and five colleagues review how chronic energy shortage reshapes athletes' bodies in a 2026 article. When training burns more than food replaces, the leftover energy for basic body functions falls short, a state called relative energy deficiency in sport. The authors gathered eighty-five studies since 2000 and sorted the effects across four compartments: bone density, muscle mass, fat stores, and body water.

The patterns differ by sport and sex. Endurance and leanness-focused disciplines carry the highest risk, with up to three-fifths of athletes affected in some estimates. Bone thins, hormones falter, and fat and muscle shift in ways that screening tools can misread. Godley's team appraises what current nutrition and screening advice rests on and where it wobbles. Their synthesis aims at care teams who must spot underfueling early, before performance problems become lasting damage.
pmc-13517420:
Qiaobo Lei and five colleagues feed laying hens a prickly-ash leaf extract in a 2026 trial. Plant additives are sought as antibiotic-free ways to keep layers productive, and the leaves of Zanthoxylum armatum 'Jiuyeqing', a green prickly ash from southwest China, carry antioxidant compounds. Diets with several extract levels ran for eight weeks, and the team tracked laying, egg quality, antioxidant defences, gut structure, and liver chemistry.

Six grams per kilogram of feed gave the best overall response. Hens laid more eggs with deeper-coloured yolks, and their antioxidant protection strengthened. Immune-linked measures shifted as well. Gut structure responded unevenly along its length, a reminder that plant extracts rarely act uniformly. Liver metabolite profiles moved in step with the dose. Lei's team proposes the leaves, often an underused farm by-product, as a feed resource that lifts both output and the value of the crop itself.
pmc-13518820:
Jiejun Luo and six colleagues pin down in 2026 a sea-level rise rate beyond which tidal wetlands worldwide start vanishing fast. Salt marshes and mangroves drown as seas climb, yet proving the link at global scale had been difficult. The team merged several remote sensing sources covering two decades.

Loss sped up in a nonlinear way as relative sea-level rise increased. Past about 9 millimeters per year, the chance of accelerated loss topped 92 percent and the loss rate rose eightfold. Marshes shrank gradually before that point, while mangroves held steady until the threshold, then fell quickly. Edge erosion showed a slightly lower threshold, giving managers a concrete warning benchmark.
pmc-13519020:
Ipsita Kumar Sen and seven colleagues synthesize glowing carbon dots capped with heparin in 2026 and test how they mingle with human blood proteins. Carbon dots are tiny, low-toxicity light emitters suited to cell imaging, and heparin, a blood-thinning sugar chain, served as both cap and stabilizer. Glucose supplied the carbon.

The dots averaged 2.5 nanometers across with a strong negative surface charge. Fluorescence tests showed firm binding to both serum albumin and methemoglobin. Against lung cancer cells in culture the capped dots were slightly more toxic than bare dots, with a half-kill dose near 176 micrograms per milliliter. Red blood cell damage was negligible at high dose, supporting blood compatibility.
pmc-13519420:
Alka Modi Asat and colleagues surveyed homes in Mandsaur city, India, to learn what residents know and do about dengue prevention. Published in 2026, the cross-sectional study visited 1,061 households in seven high-risk areas during the monsoon months of July through September 2025. Surveyors asked one adult per home about dengue knowledge and habits, then inspected water containers for mosquito larvae.

Knowledge sat at a middling level while reported habits scored better, yet larvae turned up in 195 homes, nearly one in five. Standing water, low income, and poor water storage each predicted larvae strongly. After the survey, the team gave one-to-one advice and live demos on emptying, cleaning, and covering containers.
