Prior biological knowledge greatly helps researchers make sense of such data. Causal networks built from relationships curated out of the literature are especially suited to the task.

Those networks let the software propose mechanistic hypotheses: which upstream regulators could explain an observed pattern of gene changes. Such hypotheses guide follow-up experiments instead of leaving teams with raw lists. The paper explains the reasoning behind a widely used commercial analysis platform.
pmc-4424520:
Agarwal, Mulgund, Hamada, and their co-authors gave a global view of male infertility in 2015. Infertility affects a large share of couples worldwide. Men are the sole cause in a notable fraction of cases and contribute to about half of all cases overall.

The authors stress that global figures hide wide differences between regions. Causes, access to testing, and cultural attitudes vary a great deal around the world. Male factors have often been under-studied compared with female factors. A clear worldwide picture helps clinics and policy makers give male infertility the attention and services it has lacked.
pmc-6084020:
Arnold Mitnitski, Alexander Mogilner, and Kenneth Rockwood developed a frailty index approach in this 2001 paper. Judging health in older people needs more than a list of diseases. The authors define an index as the share of health deficits a person has gathered.

Deficits include symptoms, signs, limits in daily tasks, and abnormal test results. The index behaves like a state measure, rising with age and predicting death and care needs. It works even when the exact deficit list changes between studies. The idea became a foundation of frailty research and is still widely used in geriatric medicine.
pmc-8262720:
Melissa Adasme and co-authors reported in 2021 an expanded version of PLIP, a tool that profiles the interactions between a small molecule and its target. As protein structure data pile up, understanding exactly how a drug-like molecule grips its target grows more important for design. PLIP automatically detects those contacts and draws them in clear visualizations.

The 2021 update widened the profiler beyond proteins, so it can also analyze molecules binding to DNA and RNA. The authors describe the new scope and the formats the tool produces for further work. Interaction profiles help medicinal chemists see which contacts hold a drug in place, and which changes might make it grip harder.
pound-hugh-selwyn-mauberley-1920:
Ezra Pound published Hugh Selwyn Mauberley in 1920, just after the First World War wrecked the London literary world he had conquered. The work is a sequence of eighteen short poems. Pound later treated it as a farewell to that world before he left England for Paris and Italy.

The sequence sketches Mauberley, a fastidious minor poet out of step with his age, and the age itself. War dead, profiteers, and faded aesthetes pass in cool, ironic quatrains. Pound mourns a civilization that chose commerce over art, in verse of lapidary control. Mauberley is his masterpiece of the postwar reckoning and one of the central poems of modernism.
pound-instigations-1920:
Instigations, published in 1920, gathers Pound's essays and provocations from the years when he was modernism's loudest advocate in London. The critic here is a provocateur: praising, attacking, and clearing space for new work.

The volume includes his long appreciation of Henry James, pieces on the French critic Remy de Gourmont, and his 'Art' manifestoes. Pound argues that criticism should test work against the best that exists, anywhere, in any age. His judgments are swift, learned, and often unfair, but never dull. The book shows how modern taste was fought into being, one essay at a time.
punch-or-the-london-charivari-volume-158:
Punch for March 17, 1920, volume 158, opens with Charivaria, short jokes on a German prince, a boxer's wedding, and Scotland's drink habits. Two years into peace, the London weekly still draws its humor from princes, promoters, and the prime minister.

Prince Albert Joachim, the column notes, only gave the signal when a French officer was attacked at the Hotel Adlon, which earns him a mocking pat on the head. Promoter C. B. Cochran drops plans to stage-manage the Carpentier wedding. Scotland will not go dry on purpose, a new lever can stop a bus, and Lloyd George studies handwriting yet misses the writing on the wall.

Volume 158 of Punch, dated March 24, 1920, leads with Charivaria, brief jokes on a failed rising in Berlin, cheap sermons, and Sunday golf in Wales. The Kapp revolt in Germany had just collapsed, and the column treats it with open scorn.

No one knows how near the Kapp counter-stroke came to success, and a kind word from a British critic might, in jest, have saved it. A film star fails to be run down by a taxi on purpose. A vicar protests at sermons sold for five shillings each. A robin nests in an old bully beef tin at Caterham.

Punch for March 3, 1920, volume 158, begins with Charivaria, a page of short jokes on dance halls, tanks, taxi fares, and a lost corkscrew. Postwar London supplies most of the targets, with the ex-Kaiser kept in view at the edge.

An escaped patient is caught in a West End dance hall because his waltzing was too perfect to be sane. A new tank of thirty tons can cross a brick without crushing it. Taxi fares may rise by half while the small first charge ends. An election crowd at Paisley mourns a lost corkscrew. A shoplifting society lady is freed for the sake of her two poodles.
punch-or-the-london-charivari-volume-159:
Dated August 11, 1920, this Punch, volume 159, opens with Charivaria, short jokes on Ireland, wet weather, and a famous hall in Manchester. Ireland's troubles dominate the news that summer, and the column returns to them again and again.

Keeping Dr. Mannix off Irish shores, the column argues, matters less than the government landing firmly on Ireland itself. Belfast shooting is blamed, in jest, for the wet summer. Manchester buys the Free Trade Hall for ninety thousand pounds and may search its basement for lost Liberal principles. Gold moved from the Bank of Ireland for safety faces, the column warns, a worse risk in a certain minister's hands.

Punch, volume 159, for August 18, 1920, leads with Charivaria, quick jokes on grouse shooting, Cork, army huts, and the Daily Mail's huge sales. Ireland again fills much of the page, handled with the column's usual dry edge.

The grouse season opens with a newly rich shooter sending two gamekeepers to hospital. A few hours in Cork, a reporter warns, would show a civil war near, which the column defines in its own way. An Irish council buys an army hut for a nursery. A paper asks who invented railways. A reader's count of the Daily Mail's daily sale is offered as wet-day sport for holiday crowds.

For August 25, 1920, Punch in volume 159 starts with Charivaria, brief jokes on calm advice, prize gooseberries, Scots and drink, and a riot in Londonderry. Lord Rothermere's call to mind one's own business opens the page.

That advice, the column notes, was printed by a rival paper back in August 1914. Gooseberries no bigger than bantams' eggs win a show prize, which looks like a fall from the giants of ten years before. A Whitehall messenger seen running was only acting for the films, Churchill is said to enjoy fine health apart from writer's cramp, and a lighthouse is offered for sale in The Times.

Punch dated August 4, 1920, volume 159, opens with Charivaria, a set of short jokes built almost wholly on high rail fares. Rain in Britain, drought abroad, and the price of a ticket to the coast give the column one theme, worked from many angles.

Drought grips India and East Africa while rain pours down at home. A rich art buyer gives up Old Masters to save for a rail ticket. A man bound for the south coast asks what happens if fares fall while he travels, and Scots in England may need a fund to get them home before prices rise again.

December 1, 1920 brings volume 159 of Punch and a Charivaria column of short jokes on early lambs, a refused life story, and advice for grooms. Winter had barely begun, yet the page already pokes at spring signs and Christmas-season books.

Lambs appear in Dorset, though the Poet Laureate will not rush to greet them. A golden eagle in Lincolnshire prompts a question the column refuses to answer. A West Ham library board declines to buy Margot Asquith's life story. Baden-Powell advises men to study a bride's tread before marriage. A Scotsman knocked down in New York revives on water. He asks how often he must fall to earn something stronger.

Punch for December 15, 1920, volume 159, opens with Charivaria, short jokes on Christmas travel rules, Chaplin, and a long-serving royal guard. The festive season shapes the page, from rail tickets to a rugby match at the universities.

No cheap Christmas rail tickets will be sold for trips under one hundred miles, so some travelers must go farther than they planned. Charlie Chaplin is reported amusing in private life, which the column treats as a shock. A Scotland Yard man has watched the King for twenty years without the King once acting in a doubtful way, and Austria's striking officials draw envy.

Volume 159 of Punch for December 22, 1920, leads with Charivaria, brief jokes for the week before Christmas: meteors, singing prizes, frozen ices, and rats. Cold weather and coal prices run through the page like a refrain.

December meteors shine in unusual numbers, and readers are told to write to their member of Parliament about it. Lloyd George's first prize, for singing, dates from a simpler age. An old Londoner recalls a Christmas so cold that ices froze in a Soho dining room. A flightless bird at the Zoo suits a rich sportsman's estate, and the year's rat drive ends with the rats planning a protest report.

Punch dated December 8, 1920 opens with Charivaria, short jokes on President Wilson's dress, Chaplin's plans, and a strange marriage case in Kentucky. The column moves from Paris peace circles to American courts in a few short lines.

Lord Riddell recalls that Wilson's trousers and boots fell short of his smart look above the table. Rumors link Chaplin's planned retirement to an offer to enter British politics. Two million Chinese pigtails reach America for use in soup straining, and a Kentucky judge must rule whether a man may wed his divorced wife's mother.

For July 14, 1920, Punch in volume 159 leads with Charivaria, quick jokes on the ex-Kaiser's trial, coal fights, and peace talks staged like sports fixtures. A war in Asia Minor and a film star's wish to carry off part of England round out the page.

The ex-Kaiser will reach his trial, in jest, through the Channel Tunnel. One coal war blurs into the next, and the government still has open dates for peace talks, billed like away matches. A huge new blast furnace opens at Ebbw Vale, the Turks ask the Allies to stop only the Greek half of the fighting, and Mary Pickford is offered Ireland as a souvenir.

Punch for July 21, 1920, volume 159, begins with Charivaria, brief jokes on the Spa Conference, wet weather, and members' pay. Peace talks dragged on that summer, and the column treats the delegates as men growing old in the job.

The Spa talks may yield a peace to end peace itself, and the delegates may soon need pensions. Rain soaks Britain and blame is passed around. Members of Parliament warn they may strike for higher pay, which the column fears will be settled far too fast. Food officials say the way to cheap meat is not to buy it, a plan the column sums up in one sour line.

Volume 159 of Punch for July 7, 1920 opens with a comic story called "Timon," about a lost dog with strong views on the post. The narrator cannot quite describe the small greenish dog, missing part of one ear, yet knows his habits in full detail.

Timon guards the gate at Bellevue and sorts each postman's load at sight. Cheques, invites, and requests for autographs pass in peace. Bills, tax demands, tracts, and rejected work bring a growl and a chase that sends the postman over a four-foot gate. Local postmen, the narrator claims, could win the sprint and hurdles at any games held nearby.

Punch dated November 10, 1920, volume 159, leads with Charivaria, short jokes on the American election, music taste, and a Scottish golf club flooded with new members. Armistice week that year still found room for small, dry comedy.

With America's vote over, Irish-Americans who joined election gangs are urged to go home. A peer says he would trust a crossing-sweeper's ear for music over a public school man's. The golf club mystery is solved: a caddy refused a sixpenny tip, and the news leaked. A Hallowe'en haggis arrived ten minutes late after losing a fight with a dog.

For October 13, 1920, Punch in volume 159 starts with Charivaria, quick jokes on a Russian envoy's hard name, miners at quoits, and standing room in the Tube. Autumn leaves and coal pay disputes mark the season on the page.

Mr. Riazanov, the new Russian envoy in Grosvenor Street, has a name readers will say wrong nine times in ten. Two miners play quoits for a hundred pounds while seeking a two-shilling rise. Asked where England stands, the column answers that in the Tube most of it stands on the writer's feet. A Welsh collier up for tax says he earns eleven pounds a week and wants every penny.

Punch for September 22, 1920, volume 159, opens with Charivaria, brief jokes on strikes, boxing, golf, and crowds on the Matterhorn. A miners' leader, a promoter tired of broken contracts, and an American golf champion share the page.

Strike while the iron is hot, says a business man, though the miners' chief cares less about the heat. A Midlands strike stalls when its leader loses his notes and forgets the grievance. Promoter C. B. Cochran quits boxing over broken deals, an American champion invents a new putter, and so many climbers crowd the Matterhorn that its top may need bracing.
russell-bolshevism-1920:
In 1920 Russell traveled to Soviet Russia with a Labour delegation and came home to write this report. The Practice and Theory of Bolshevism, published that year, is a rare thing: a sympathetic visitor's clear-eyed refusal to convert.

Russell admired the revolution's energy and its leaders' ability, and he met Lenin. But he found the regime's methods appalling: secret police, crushed dissent, and a dogma that licensed any cruelty. He predicted much of what followed with grim accuracy. The book split him from the British left and still reads as a model of honest political travel writing.
sandburg-smoke-and-steel-1920:
Carl Sandburg published Smoke and Steel in 1920, his third book of poems. Sandburg, the son of Swedish immigrants, had worked as a laborer, soldier, and Chicago newspaper reporter. He wrote about the industrial Midwest from inside knowledge of its mills and rail yards.

The poems honor furnaces, freight trains, and the workers who tend them. Sandburg's long free-verse lines stack images of smoke, pig iron, and prairie wheat. He also remembers war dead and praises ordinary people's endurance. The book carries forward the work of his Chicago Poems with a wider national sweep. It remains the great book of American industry in verse.
sanger-woman-and-new-race-1920: The opening of this record holds no page of the book itself. What survives at the front is the standard wrapper Google Books placed on its public-domain scans. The notice explains that the volume was copied from a library shelf copy whose copyright had expired. The record is Margaret Sanger's Woman and the New Race, dated 1920 in the record's title. Beyond the wrapper, nothing of Sanger's text is visible in this record, so her arguments cannot be described from it.
santayana-character-opinion-us-1920:
Character and Opinion in the United States, published in 1920, gathers lectures the Spanish-born Santayana gave on the American mind. No outsider has written about America with this mixture of affection, amusement, and cool distance.

He describes the genteel tradition, the inherited idealism of American culture, beset by the skyscraper world of business and sport. Emerson, James, and Harvard itself pass under his gaze. His image of the American as a man divided, his will in the present and his intellect in a colonial mansion, is still quoted. The book remains a penetrating portrait by a resident alien.
schlick-space-time-physics-1920:
Space and Time in Contemporary Physics, published in English in 1920 in Henry L. Brose's translation, is Moritz Schlick's introduction to relativity for philosophers. Schlick, founder of the Vienna Circle, was the thinker best placed to explain what Einstein meant.

He leads readers from Newton through special relativity to the general theory's curved geometry, always asking what the physics assumes and what it proves. The treatment is lucid, brief, and philosophically exact. The book became the Vienna Circle's founding statement on physics. It still serves as a model of how philosophy should receive a scientific revolution.
schrenck-notzing-phenomena-materialisati:
Albert von Schrenck-Notzing put seers in a lab in Phenomena of Materialisation, his report of 1920. Schrenck-Notzing was a healer in Munich with a zeal for strict tests. His seers wore sewn suits, sat in lit cages, and were held by the hands. Yet, he claims, a strange stuff crept from them and took shapes like limbs and veils.

He calls the stuff ectoplasm and prints plates by the score. Peers cried fraud in case past case. His book is the high mark of that strange line of tests. Its claims still row.
seaborn-symzonia-1820:
Captain Adam Seaborn is the pen name on this sea tale of 1820, the first novel of the hollow earth. No one knows for sure who wrote it, though Symmes and his kin are oft named. The tale takes Symmes's polar holes as its map and sails straight in.

The ship's crew pass through the north hole and find a mild inner world, named Symzonia. Its folk are fair, wise, and strange, with crafts and laws of their own. The book set the form for a long line of tales of worlds hid inside our own.
shelley-prometheus-unbound-1820:
Percy Bysshe Shelley wrote Prometheus Unbound in Italy and published it in 1820. He took the Greek Titan Prometheus, chained by Zeus for giving fire to mankind, as his hero. Greek legend left Prometheus bound forever; Shelley set out to free him.

In Shelley's lyrical drama, Prometheus endures centuries of torture without cursing his enemy. When hatred finally leaves his heart, the tyrant Jupiter falls and a new age of love begins. Spirits, Earth, and the Moon sing the change in soaring choruses. The play is less a stage work than a vision of human liberation. It stands as the purest statement of Romantic optimism.
slave-narratives-a-folk-history-of-slave: Volume VII of the Slave Narratives holds the Kentucky accounts, drawn from talks with former slaves. The typed records were made by the Federal Writers' Project of the Works Progress Administration for Kentucky, and the set was put together at Washington in 1941. Nine names appear as those who spoke: Dan Bogie, George Henderson, Harriet Mason, Bert Mayfield, Will Oats, Belle Robinson, Edd Shirley, and Wes Woods among them.
splendor-solis-alchemical-treatises-of-s: Splendor Solis bears the date A.D. 1582 on its title page. The opening leaves form a library scan wrapper. A Cornell University Library book plate stands first. The Given Foundation Book Fund supplied it. The plate honors John La Porte Given of the class of 1896. A date-due slip follows with faint stamps. The Cornell note names its own library as holder of the first copy. It states no known bar on the book's use in the United States.
spr-proceedings-vol30-1919-1920:
Volume thirty binds parts seventy five through seventy eight and an appendix, for 1919 and 1920. Peace returns, and the Society for Psychical Research counts its losses and its files. The postwar sittings with mediums draw crowds of the bereaved. Cross references and proxy sitters guard the reports as before.

Telepathy experiments resume their peacetime forms and scoring. Apparition cases from the war years receive their checked write ups. The volume bridges the archive from war into a new decade. Its records fed the famous postwar books on survival. Volume thirty closes the society's first forty years in print. The debate it serves ran on to 1930.
state-of-the-union-addresses-pg5020:
Zachary Taylor gives one yearly address, dated December 4, 1849, in a set parted by three stars. Sixty years have passed, Taylor opens, since this government was set up, and Congress meets again to make laws for an empire of freemen. The evil foretellings of old prophets who swore the free forms would fall are now recalled only to be laughed at.

The United States at this hour show the world the most stable and lasting government on earth, Taylor holds, the fruit of the labor of those gone before. On Congress will rest the future keeping of the free system and its handing down whole to those who come after. Peace holds with all nations, and the year has blessed the land with rich fruits, though a dread sickness for a time ravaged wide parts before its hand was stayed.
stoddard-rising-tide-color-1920:
Lothrop Stoddard published The Rising Tide of Color Against White World-Supremacy in 1920. Stoddard, a Harvard-trained writer, surveyed the world after the First World War and warned his white readers that their global rule was ending. The book's title gave its whole argument in one image.

Stoddard treated the growth and revolt of colonized peoples in Asia and Africa as a single threat to white supremacy. He urged unity among white nations and strict immigration bars at home. The book sold widely and shaped restrictionist debate in the United States. Scholars cite it as a key primary source on white-supremacist ideology and the fears behind immigration restriction.
suppressed-gospels-vol-2-1820:
Volume 2 of The Suppressed Gospels and Epistles, in William Wake's translation, appeared in this edition in 1820. The volume centers on the Protevangelion, an early account of the birth and youth of Mary. Wake, an archbishop of Canterbury, had translated early Christian writings outside the New Testament.

The Protevangelion tells of Mary's parents, her childhood in the Temple, and the birth of Jesus with added wonders. Such texts shaped art and folk belief for centuries, though churches left them out of scripture. Reading them shows what early Christians wanted to know about the holy family's hidden years. The volume belongs to a nine-volume set of these disputed writings.
suppressed-gospels-vol-3-1820:
Volume 3 of The Suppressed Gospels and Epistles, translated by William Wake, appeared in 1820. Its main text is the Infancy of Jesus Christ, an early gospel about the childhood of Jesus. The canonical gospels say almost nothing about those years, and this text filled the gap with wonders.

Stories show the child Jesus giving life to clay birds, striking playmates, and working miracles in Egypt. Medieval readers loved these tales, and they fed plays, poems, and paintings. Church leaders judged the book unreliable and left it outside scripture. The volume preserves a vivid record of how popular faith pictured the young Jesus.
suppressed-gospels-vol-4-1820:
Volume 4 of The Suppressed Gospels and Epistles, in William Wake's translation, appeared in 1820. Its named text is the Gospel of Nicodemus, an early account of the trial, death, and descent of Christ. Nicodemus appears in John's gospel as a secret follower who came to Jesus by night.

The text expands Pilate's court, the wonders at the crucifixion, and Christ's descent to free the dead. A second part tells of Joseph of Arimathea and his imprisonment and release. Medieval drama drew heavily on these scenes. The volume shows how early and medieval Christians enlarged the Passion story far beyond the four gospels in their Bible.
suppressed-gospels-vol-5-1820:
Volume 5 of The Suppressed Gospels and Epistles, translated by William Wake, appeared in this edition in 1820. The set gathered early Christian writings that stood outside the New Testament. Wake, archbishop of Canterbury, had made these translations to let readers judge the texts for themselves.

Writings in this middle volume continue the set's mix of gospels, acts, and letters linked to apostles and early teachers. Some claim missing details of Christ's life, while others teach or warn the young churches. Scholars value the set for showing the wide range of early Christian writing. General readers get stories and teachings that nearly entered scripture but did not.
suppressed-gospels-vol-6-1820:
Volume 6 of The Suppressed Gospels and Epistles, in William Wake's translation, appeared in 1820. Its named figure is Clement, an early leader of the church in Rome. Writings linked to Clement were among the most respected texts outside the New Testament.

Letters and teachings in the volume deal with order in the church, good conduct, and the duties of bishops and members. Clement's name carried weight because tradition placed him close to the apostles themselves. Readers can see how the early church settled questions of authority and morals. The volume helps explain why some texts were treasured for centuries even though they never became part of the Bible.
suppressed-gospels-vol-7-1820:
Volume 7 of The Suppressed Gospels and Epistles, translated by William Wake, appeared in this edition in 1820. The nine-volume set reprinted Wake's translations of early Christian writings left outside the New Testament. By this volume the set has moved deep into letters and acts linked to the first generations of the church.

Texts here preserve teachings, travels, and trials ascribed to apostles and their followers, with much added legend. Some passages agree with scripture, while others add marvels the churches rejected. The set lets readers compare accepted and disputed writings side by side. That contrast is the value of the volume: it shows the border of the Bible being drawn in real time.
suppressed-gospels-vol-8-1820:
Volume 8 of The Suppressed Gospels and Epistles, in William Wake's translation, appeared in 1820, near the end of the nine-volume set. Wake's project gave English readers the early Christian writings that churches had read, debated, and finally set aside. Volume 8 continues that disputed library.

Gospels, acts, and letters in the volume claim apostolic roots, yet carry stories and teachings found nowhere in scripture. Some fed medieval devotion, art, and feast days for a thousand years. Others survive only in fragments and old lists. Together they show how much early Christian writing the canon left behind, and why scholars still mine these texts for the beliefs of the first churches.
tales-and-novels-of-j-de-la-fontaine-vol:
The Devil in Hell and Neighbor Peter's Mare pair up in the twentieth volume of La Fontaine's Tales and Novels. Both tales play on bargains and fears, one infernal and one rustic.

The Devil in Hell opens with a warning: he is surely wrong who loves and fears, and does not flee when beauty first appears. The poet swears off burning his fingers in that flame again. Then he brings a charmer by way of proof. Her beauty stung even a hermit. With her, the sin excepted, a very pleasant intercourse was kept. The joke lands where the title points, in a hell where a woman proves more than a match for its devils. Neighbor Peter's Mare returns the volume to village horse-dealing and its cheats.
tawney-acquisitive-society-1920:
R. H. Tawney published The Acquisitive Society in 1920, a classic of ethical socialism. Tawney argues that modern society honors acquisition over function. Property that serves no work, he claims, has weak moral title. Rights should attach to service rendered, not to mere ownership.

He calls for industry organized as a profession, with standards and public purpose. The book grew from his wartime and postwar lectures and essays. Its prose is lucid, grave, and quietly angry. Tawney influenced the Labour Party's moral outlook for a generation. Later editions kept it in print for students. It remains a model of social criticism grounded in ethics rather than envy.
the-brochure-series-of-architectural-ill:
The Brochure Series of Architectural Illustration, Volume I, Number 11, for November 1895, shows The Country Houses of Normandy. A plate at the front shows the Ferme la Vallauine. The houses chosen, the piece says, are of different types and dates. They were built for men of different stations, and of different materials. All stand in Normandy, in northern France, and all outside the towns.

The piece then notes a strong French bent: houses are built in compact groups. Detached houses with free space on all sides are the exception, even in the country. It quotes Louis H. Gibson, from his book Beautiful Houses, to the same effect. In this the French taste splits from the American, where open space round a house is a chief draw. So these houses, it warns, are not to be taken as typical of French building at large.
the-great-round-world-and-what-is-going-: The issue of March 25, 1897 is No. 20 of The Great Round World and What Is Going On in It, a weekly newspaper for boys and girls. Only front matter is present here. It gives the masthead and two notices. One tells booksellers and newsdealers that they may supply any book named in the paper. They may take subscriptions at club rates, for a commission. The other offers school and college text-books at wholesale prices. They are sold at the publisher's new store at 3 and 5 West 18th Street, New York.
the-history-of-don-quixote-volume-2-part:
Volume 2, Part 20 of Don Quixote comes from Cervantes, in Ormsby's English rendering. Chapter six tells of what took place between Don Quixote and his niece and housekeeper, called one of the most important chapters in the whole history. The opening runs two household talks in parallel.

While Sancho Panza and his wife, Teresa Cascajo, hold their conversation, Don Quixote's niece and housekeeper are not idle at home. The women guard the knight against a fresh sally, while Sancho weighs the venture at his own hearth. Cervantes builds the next expedition out of talk at two kitchen tables.
the-mirror-of-literature-amusement-and-i:
Saturday, September 13, 1828, brings the Mirror's No. 331, which proposes a pilgrimage to Stratford-upon-Avon. Any reader who thinks all beyond Hyde Park a desert is urged to reform at Shakespeare's birthplace. The article quotes Sterne on wanting a companion for the road, then prefers a garrulous old guide. Its destination here is Charlecote Hall, one of the Shakespearean relics on the Avon's banks four miles from Stratford.

Sir Thomas Lucy built Charlecote in the first year of Elizabeth's reign. A quoted lampoon calls Lucy a parliament member and justice of the peace, at home a poor scarecrow and at London an ass. The joke points at the old deer-stealing legend linking Lucy with the young Shakespeare. The hall thus enters the magazine as scenery and evidence at once. Readers are sent touring with theatre memories in their pockets, measuring a justice's mansion against a poaching story.

Only the supplement sheet closing Volume 12 of the Mirror is present for this record, so no single article appears here. The sheet reprints the volume's contents promise: original essays, historical narratives, biographical memoirs, sketches of society, topographical descriptions, novels and tales, and anecdotes. It then opens an editorial address announcing that the sheet completes the twelfth volume. Six years, the editors note, have filled twelve volumes, or sessions, without a recess. They hope, as members of the republic of letters, to be re-elected by their numerous constituents.

Volume 20, No. 562, dated August 18, 1832, opens with the falls of the Genesee River in North America. The river's name comes from an Indian phrase for pleasant valley, which the writers find fitting. Its falls lack Niagara's scale, they concede, but make up for it in beauty.

Rising on the high table-land of western Pennsylvania, the Genesee runs through New York State to Lake Ontario at Port Genesee, below Rochester. Falls of 96 feet stand six miles from its mouth, with falls of 75 feet a mile higher. Boats could travel nearly seventy miles above them before meeting two more falls. A long footnote on how cataracts form, drawn from Maltebrun's geography, follows.
the-theater-1720: The Theatre, a 1720 periodical essay set signed Sir John Falstaffe, was reprinted in 1948 as the first number of the Augustan Reprint Society's fourth series, with an introduction by John Loftis. This record shows the reprint's editorial pages only: the society's general and advisory editors, from Michigan, Yale, Columbia, and other universities, and the Ann Arbor printer. Loftis's introduction and the 1720 essays themselves do not appear in the pages present. What survives is the scholarly frame built around an eighteenth-century theatre paper.
tob-0020:
Legends of Jesus as a child fill the Infancy Gospel of Thomas, a work the early church never took into its canon. The boy forms sparrows from river clay and breathes them alive before startled playmates. His powers amaze the village, and sometimes they frighten it.

The child's temper proves as miraculous as his gifts: those who cross him wither or fall. Teachers fare no better against his strange knowledge. The stories are vivid, unruly, and very human in their curiosity about a holy childhood. The evidence notes no public-domain text is attached to this entry yet. The tales survive because believers loved them.
tob-0120:
Few forgeries have done more harm than the Protocols of the Learned Elders of Zion. The text claims to record a Jewish plan for world domination. In fact it was fabricated in the orbit of the Tsar's secret police, the Okhrana, stitched together from older satire and fiction.

Newspapers and courts exposed the fraud within two decades of its spread, yet the lie kept traveling. It fed pogroms, Nazi propaganda, and hate movements that still quote it. This library keeps the text as evidence: a case study in how a fake document can poison a century. It is presented as a debunked forgery, never as fact.
tob-10020:
William Walker Atkinson, a New Thought writer, published under the pen name Yogi Ramacharaka for books on Eastern-style spiritual teaching. In Mystic Christianity he turns that lens on Jesus, reading the Master's life and sayings as an inner teaching rather than mainly a matter of church doctrine. The work first appeared in the early 1900s.

Miracles and parables become lessons about the growth of the soul. Atkinson blends ideas from Eastern and Western religion into one system, arguing that hidden meaning lies beneath familiar Gospel stories. Readers get an early American attempt to join Christian devotion to a wider, comparative spirituality popular in his period.
tob-10220:
Bertrand Russell published The Problems of Philosophy in 1912 as a short introduction for general readers. He begins with a familiar object: the table in front of us. How do we know it is real, and what exactly do we know when we look at it or touch it?

From appearance and reality, Russell moves through matter, knowledge by acquaintance and description, universals, and truth and falsehood. He is candid that philosophy often raises questions it cannot finally settle. Readers get a clear demonstration of why the big questions matter anyway, and a model of thinking slowly and precisely about things common sense takes for granted.
tob-10920:
Albert Pike published Morals and Dogma in 1871 as lectures on the thirty-two degrees of the Ancient and Accepted Scottish Rite of Freemasonry. Each degree receives a chapter drawing morals from ancient symbols, comparative religion, and philosophy. The volume is massive, dense, and endlessly digressive by design.

Pike ranges from Egyptian and Greek mysteries to Kabbalah and medieval chivalry, reading Masonic ritual as a school of ethics and toleration. Few members have read it whole, yet it remains the most famous and most misunderstood book in American Masonry, quoted and misquoted by admirers and conspiracy writers alike. Patient readers find a nineteenth-century moral philosophy in ritual dress.
tob-4020:
John Locke's Essay Concerning Human Understanding opens, in volume one, with an attack on innate ideas in Book One. Book Two builds his alternative: the mind begins as a blank slate, and all knowledge flows from sensation and reflection. Ideas, simple and complex, are tracked to their sources in experience.

Substance, identity, power, and association all receive patient analysis in Locke's plain, methodical prose. The two books lay the foundation of British empiricism and quietly declare thought's independence from scholastic authority. For readers tracing how modern philosophy and liberal politics share a root, Locke's first volume, modest in tone and radical in effect, is essential ground.
tob-4120:
John Parker's 1897 translation gathers the works credited to Dionysius the Areopagite, a writer of about the fifth or sixth century who took the name of Paul's Athenian convert. The Celestial Hierarchy ranks the angels in nine orders. The Divine Names weighs what names like Good and Being can say of God.

The Mystical Theology, shortest and boldest, says God lies beyond all names, in darkness beyond light. No writer did more to shape Christian mysticism, East and West, for a thousand years. Checked from the 1919 edition, Parker's volume gives the fountainhead in full Victorian dress.
turner-frontier-american-history-1920:
Frederick Jackson Turner first set out his famous frontier thesis in an essay read to fellow historians in Chicago in 1893. His 1920 book gathers that essay with later papers on the same theme. Turner argued that free land on the western edge of settlement shaped American life more than any law or leader.

He claimed the frontier bred self-reliance, fresh starts, and a rough form of equal standing among settlers. He also warned that the census of 1890 had declared the frontier line closed, so a first great chapter of national life had ended. Few ideas have guided American history writing so long, or drawn so much debate.
two-centuries-of-costume-in-america-volu: Alice Morse Earle's Two Centuries of Costume in America, volume one, covers 1620 to 1820 and is dated 1903. A long quotation from George Wither, dated 1625, praises the honest stationer who serves God and the public before his own profit. The contents open with the apparel of the Puritan and Pilgrim fathers, then dress of the New England mothers. Only the title page, motto, and start of the contents are present here, so the costume chapters themselves do not appear.
un-doc-address-to-the-united-nations-gen:
Chile's president, Michelle Bachelet, addressed the United Nations General Assembly on 20 September 2006. She spoke as the first woman elected to lead her country. Chile had come through hard years of dictatorship. Growth had lifted millions out of poverty in the sixteen years before she spoke.

She backs world law and a strong United Nations. Rich states should open their markets to goods from the South. Chile funds cheap drugs for the poor through a small levy on plane tickets. She faults the 2005 Summit for silence on disarmament. Chile serves with the peace mission in Haiti. She also marks thirty years since a former Chilean minister was murdered in Washington.

Venezuela's president, Hugo Chávez, addressed the United Nations General Assembly on 20 September 2006. He spoke the day after the president of the United States. He held up a book by Noam Chomsky and urged the hall to read it. The talk made world headlines within hours.

He calls the American president the Devil and says the rostrum still smells of sulphur. He charges the United States with seeking world rule through war. He lists Iraq, Lebanon, and Palestine as proof. Venezuela offers four fixes for the United Nations. The Security Council should grow, the veto should end, and the Secretary-General should gain strength. He also presses Venezuela's bid for a Council seat.

President John F. Kennedy of the United States addressed the United Nations General Assembly on 20 September 1963, his last speech to the body. A treaty banning nuclear tests in air, space, and sea had just been signed. Near one hundred states had joined it. The Cuban crisis of the year before had eased.

He calls the test ban a first small step, not peace itself. More steps should follow: guard posts against surprise attack, curbs on the spread of nuclear arms, a ban on weapons in space. He floats a bold thought. Why should the first trip to the moon be a race? The two rivals could send a joint crew instead. He closes with world health, hunger, and rights.

Sri Lanka's president, Mahinda Rajapaksa, addressed the United Nations General Assembly on 20 September 2006. His country had fought the LTTE rebels for over twenty years. A truce had broken down and attacks had grown again. He had won office the year before on a pledge to seek an honourable peace.

He calls terror a curse tied to drugs, guns, and dirty money. He lists rebel crimes: suicide bombs, massacres, child soldiers, whole villages driven out. His government still offers talks and a political fix through new basic-law plans. Force alone, he says, cannot end the war. He reports strong growth and thanks the world for help after the tsunami.
un-ga-res-20: Judges of the new International Court of Justice needed a pension plan, and Resolution 20 of the General Assembly took up the task on 6 February 1946. The Assembly directs the Secretary-General to draft the plan with the court's registrar. It covers judges, the registrar, and court staff, and it was due back before the second part of the first session.
un-ga-res-50-220:
Guatemala's human rights mission had its mandate stretched in Resolution 50/220, passed in April 1996. The Mission for the Verification of Human Rights in Guatemala had been set up in 1994 to check that both sides kept their pledges. A September 1995 vote had stretched its term by six months, to 18 March 1996. The Assembly now had the mission chief's third and fourth reports before it.

Those reports weigh how the state of Guatemala and the rebel URNG kept their word under the rights deal. Their findings and counsel are taken note of in full. The vote keeps the mission in place as talks moved toward the firm peace signed at the end of 1996.
un-ga-res-a-69-20:
The question of Palestine returns, as it does each year, in Resolution A/69/20, from the General Assembly's sixty-ninth session. The text recalls the long chain: partition in 1947, the refugee vote of 1948, and the rights votes of 1974 and 1975. It had read the yearly report of the Palestinian rights committee. The joint recognition of 1993, between Israel and the Palestine Liberation Organization, is recalled as well.

Full heed of the deals struck by the two sides is demanded. The Assembly backs a full, just, and lasting peace for the conflict. Its terms rest on past UN votes and on the frame of the Madrid talks of 1991, with the rule of land for peace at their heart.
un-ga-res-address-to-the-united-nations-:
Michelle Bachelet, president of Chile, addressed the United Nations General Assembly on September 20, 2006. She had taken office that year as Chile's first woman president. Her speech came during the yearly general debate, when heads of state set out their world views in turn.

Bachelet pressed the case for social justice at home and across the globe. She spoke of fair growth, strong public services, and respect for human rights. She also backed reform of the UN itself. The address shows a new Latin American leader claiming a place on the world stage.

Hugo Chávez, president of Venezuela, addressed the United Nations General Assembly on September 20, 2006, one day after George W. Bush spoke in the same hall. Chávez opened by saying the podium still smelled of sulfur, a jab at Bush, whom he called the devil. The line drew laughs, gasps, and headlines worldwide.

Beyond the theater, the speech attacks United States power and the Iraq war. It calls for a rebuilt UN, seated away from American soil, and for a fairer world order. The address endures as the most quoted act of defiance ever staged in that hall.

John F. Kennedy returned to the United Nations General Assembly on September 20, 1963, for the last major foreign speech of his life. Two months later he was dead in Dallas. Weeks before this address, the United States, Britain, and the Soviet Union had signed a treaty banning nuclear tests in air and space.

Kennedy hailed the test ban as a first step away from nuclear fear. He urged further curbs on arms and joint work in space, even a shared trip to the Moon. The speech captures a brief thaw in the Cold War, in the speaker's own hopeful terms.

Mahinda Rajapaksa, president of Sri Lanka, addressed the United Nations General Assembly on September 20, 2006. He spoke as his government's war with the Tamil Tiger rebels was heating up again after a failed truce. Within three years that war would end in a bloody final offensive.

Rajapaksa defended his government's fight against the Tigers, whom he called terrorists. He asked the world to back states facing armed separatist groups. He also spoke on poverty and fair trade. Read today, the speech is the public case he made abroad while the war at home grew harsher.
un-ga-res-united-nations-general-assembl: At the twenty-third plenary meeting on 6 February 1946, the General Assembly adopted Resolution 20. It is a short order about pensions at the International Court of Justice. The Assembly wanted fair and sound pensions for the Court's judges, registrar, and staff. It told the Secretary-General to draw up a pension plan, working with the Court's registrar. He was to bring it to the second part of the first session.

General Assembly Resolution 50/220, adopted on 3 April 1996, renewed the Guatemala verification mission until 31 December 1996. The Assembly took note of the mission director's third and fourth reports. It voiced concern at weak carrying-out of the Comprehensive Agreement on Human Rights during 1995. There had been little action on the mission's advice.

At the same time it welcomed the new Guatemalan president's pledge to fight impunity and keep the peace process going. It welcomed the restart of talks aimed at an early final peace. Both parties were called on to act on the reports' advice and back the mission fully. They were called on to take steps to end civilian suffering and build trust.

Resolution 69/20 of the General Assembly is the annual mandate renewal for the Committee on the Exercise of the Inalienable Rights of the Palestinian People. The Assembly thanks the Committee for its work. It asks it to keep promoting Palestinian self-determination, and an end to the occupation that began in 1967 on a two-State basis. It authorizes it to adjust its program of work as events require. It also asks the United Nations Conference on Trade and Development to report on the economic costs of the occupation.
un-sc-res-1020:
United Nations Security Council Resolution 1020 deals with Liberia during its civil war in the 1990s. The Council adopted it on 10 November 1995. A cease-fire and a new Council of State had just raised hopes for peace. West African troops, called ECOMOG, were already on the ground.

The text reshapes the work of the United Nations Observer Mission in Liberia, called UNOMIL. Its observers would check cease-fire claims, watch disarmament, and help fighters leave the war. They would also support aid work and watch the planned elections. The Council capped the observer team at 160 and demanded respect for all peace staff.
un-sc-res-120:
Soviet troops were crushing Hungary's uprising when the Council met in November 1956. On 4 November 1956 it noted the grave situation made by Soviet military force. Hungarians, it said, were trying to reassert their rights. The permanent members could not agree, so the Council could not act on its own. That deadlock shaped the remedy the text chose.

The Council called an emergency special session of the General Assembly. It used the Uniting for Peace procedure of 1950. The Assembly would make fitting recommendations on Hungary. The move is a classic case of the Council passing a crisis to the wider membership. It could not, in the end, stop the Soviet crackdown.
un-sc-res-1220: Adopting Resolution 1220 on 12 January 1999, the Council acted on Sierra Leone. Fighting had worsened sharply, and the rebel advance on the capital put the peace effort at risk. The Council extends the United Nations Observer Mission in Sierra Leone, called UNOMSIL, until 13 March 1999. Most of its military observers will pull back to Conakry for safety. A small team stays ready to return once conditions allow. The Secretary-General must report by 5 March 1999 with ideas for the mission's future.
un-sc-res-1320: Entry number 1320 in the Council's official sequence is a resolution the catalog dates to 2000. Council texts of this kind carry weight under the UN Charter, since the Council holds the main duty for peace and security. The entry gives the decision in full, as transcribed on English Wikisource from the records of the United Nations. It sits in this library among other public records in the DECLASSIFIED group.
un-sc-res-1420: Bosnia's peacekeeping arrangements hit a legal snag at the end of June 2002. On 30 June 2002 the Security Council kept its earlier Bosnia provisions in force a little longer. The measures in resolution 1357 would now run until 3 July 2002. The Council acted under Chapter VII of the Charter. The text is two short paragraphs. The three-day bridge covered a dispute over the new International Criminal Court. A fuller settlement of the issue followed within days.
un-sc-res-1520:
The observer force on the Golan Heights was renewed in the settled form of those years on 22 December 2003. The force, called UNDOF, watches the cease-fire line between Israel and Syria. A report from the Secretary-General, dated 9 December 2003, was before the Council. Resolution 1520 was adopted unanimously.

The Council called on the parties to carry out Resolution 338 of 1973 at once. That text demanded a cease-fire and peace talks after the October war. UNDOF's mandate was renewed for six months, until 30 June 2004. At the end of that period, the Secretary-General had to report on developments in the area. His report also had to cover the steps taken to put Resolution 338 into effect. Renewals like this one had kept UNDOF on the Golan, term after term, for three decades.
un-sc-res-1620:
Sierra Leone's peacekeeping era closed into an integrated office on 31 August 2005. UNAMSIL had helped the country recover from conflict, the Council said. The Secretary-General's report of 26 April and its July addendum advised a follow-on office. Sierra Leone's president wrote on 21 June asking for the same. The office would back governance, conflict prevention, and the 2007 elections.

The Council asked the Secretary-General to establish the United Nations Integrated Office in Sierra Leone, UNIOSIL, from 1 January 2006. It would run for an initial twelve months. The government's primary duty for the country's peace and growth was underlined. The office had to be fully integrated, with one United Nations team speaking with a single voice. Planning for the Special Court's security after UNAMSIL left had to continue. The Secretary-General would keep the Council informed of the office's work. The handover marked the shift from peacekeeping to peacebuilding.
un-sc-res-1720:
Western Sahara's referendum mission rolled into another term in the autumn of 2006. On 31 October 2006 the Security Council extended MINURSO until 30 April 2007. The Secretary-General had reported on the dispute that month. The Council restated its support for him and his envoy. It again promised help toward a settlement both sides could accept. That settlement had to allow self-determination for the territory's people.

The parties had to respect the military agreements behind the ceasefire. Member states were asked to fund family visits for divided Sahrawi families. The Secretary-General owed a report before the term ended. His staff also had to enforce the United Nations' zero-tolerance rules in the mission. The political deadlock survived the renewal.
un-sc-res-1820:
Resolution 1820, adopted in June 2008, named sexual violence in war as a threat to world peace itself. Reports from Congo and other conflicts described rape used as a weapon against whole communities. The Council moved the issue from the margins to its main agenda.

The text demands that armies and armed groups stop all such attacks, orders peace missions to protect women and girls, and presses for soldiers who commit these crimes to face punishment. It built on Resolution 1325's earlier promises with harder language. Advocates still cite it as the turning point in how the UN treats wartime rape.
un-sc-res-1920:
Western Sahara's peace process gained another year of support in 2010. On 30 April 2010 the Security Council extended MINURSO until 30 April 2011. The parties had held small informal talks to prepare a fifth round of negotiations. The Council welcomed that commitment. It backed the Secretary-General and his envoy in their push for a settlement. Realism and compromise, it said, were essential.

Both sides had to respect the military agreements behind the ceasefire in full. They had to show political will and talk in good faith. The goal stayed a solution that lets the territory's people decide their future. The Council also called for trust-building steps, including family visits. The mandate renewal kept observers along the berm for another year.
un-sc-res-20:
Atomic energy control was the Council's subject in March 1947. The Atomic Energy Commission had sent its first report that winter. On 10 March 1947 the Council laid down a caution. Any agreement a member showed to parts of the report was only preliminary. Final acceptance of any part depended on taking the whole control plan. That rule stopped states from picking only the clauses they liked.

The Council sent the record of its debate back to the commission. It urged the commission to press on with all speed. Every phase of international atomic control needed study. Concrete proposals for a treaty were the goal. A second report was due before the next General Assembly session. The plan behind the report later failed amid Cold War distrust.
un-sc-res-220: In the sequence of Security Council decisions, Resolution 220 is the entry catalogued for 1966 in this library. Council texts of this kind carry weight under the UN Charter, since the Council holds the main duty for peace and security. The entry gives the decision in full, as transcribed on English Wikisource from the records of the United Nations.
un-sc-res-320: Bearing number 320, this resolution of the Security Council is dated 1968 in the catalog. Formal decisions of this sort guide UN staff, peacekeeping forces, and governments in the years that follow. What is preserved is the exact formal wording, transcribed on English Wikisource from the official record of the Council. Its place here reflects the library's aim of keeping primary records readable.
un-sc-res-420: Readers meet Resolution 420 here as a Security Council record, catalogued with a date of 1977. Such texts can call for cease-fires, set up missions, impose duties, or settle points of UN procedure and membership. Its value lies in the primary wording: the decision as adopted, kept through the Wikisource transcription of the record. No summary replaces it; the record itself is the content of the entry.
un-sc-res-520: The official series of Council decisions runs through Resolution 520, catalogued here for 1982. A resolution may address a conflict, a court vacancy, a new member, or the running of the United Nations itself. Anyone studying UN practice can read the decision itself here, in the Wikisource transcription of the official record. The catalog places it in the DECLASSIFIED group of official public records.
un-sc-res-620:
Chemical weapons use in the Gulf war drew a firmer Security Council line on 26 August 1988. Three missions sent by the Secretary-General had reported in July and August. Their findings showed continued use of chemical weapons in the Iran-Iraq conflict. Such use against Iranians had become more intense and more frequent, the missions found. Talks in Geneva on a full ban on chemical weapons were under way.

The Council condemned resolutely the use of chemical weapons in breach of the Geneva Protocol of 1925. It noted that the use defied its own resolution 612 (1988) of May. It encouraged the Secretary-General to investigate at once any claim by a member state of possible use of chemical, biological, or toxin weapons. He was to check the facts and report the results. The Council vowed to intensify its efforts to end all such use.
un-sc-res-720: The Council took formal action on the Secretary-General's post in Resolution 720, adopted unanimously at a closed meeting on 21 November 1991. The sitting chief's term was ending that year. The Council had weighed who should lead the United Nations next. It recommends to the General Assembly that Boutros Boutros-Ghali be appointed Secretary-General. His term would run from 1 January 1992 to 31 December 1996. The Assembly confirmed the choice, and the Egyptian diplomat became the sixth person to hold the post.
un-sc-res-united-nations-security-counci:
Liberia's peace process is reshaped in Resolution 1020, adopted on 10 November 1995. The Liberian sides had restored a ceasefire, installed a new Council of State, and agreed on a timetable running to elections. The UN Observer Mission in Liberia, UNOMIL, worked with the West African force ECOMOG. Ceasefire breaches and slow troop separation still caused worry.

The Council rewrites UNOMIL's mandate. The mission is to support ECOWAS and the transitional government. It is to probe reported ceasefire breaches and watch disarmament and the arms embargo. It is to help run assembly sites and fighter demobilization. It is also to back aid work and report on human rights abuses. It is to observe the planned legislative and presidential elections. Its military observers are capped at 160. States are urged to fund ECOMOG and the UN Trust Fund for Liberia, and the arms embargo is recalled.

Resolution 120 was adopted on 4 November 1956, as Soviet troops were crushing an uprising in Hungary. Ten members voted in favor and only the Soviet Union voted against. Because the permanent members were split, the Council admitted it could not carry out its main duty of guarding world peace in this crisis.

Rather than drop the matter, the Council sent it to the full membership. It called an emergency special session of the General Assembly under the 1950 Uniting for Peace procedure, which lets the Assembly step in when the Council is deadlocked. That session was asked to recommend what should be done about Hungary.

Resolution 1220, adopted by the Security Council on 12 January 1999, keeps Sierra Leone's observer mission alive while fighting worsens. The Council voices concern at the recent deterioration and backs efforts to restore lasting peace. It extends the mandate of the UN Observer Mission in Sierra Leone, UNOMSIL, until 13 March 1999. It notes the Secretary-General's plan to reduce the military observers, keep a small team in Conakry, Guinea, and send them back when conditions allow. It asks for a further report with recommendations by 5 March 1999.

What began as a small observer team on the Ethiopia-Eritrea border becomes a full peacekeeping force in this text of 15 September 2000. The mission, UNMEE, had been created weeks earlier, after the June ceasefire ended the border war. Now it needed soldiers, not just observers.

The Council authorized up to 4,200 troops, including up to 220 military observers, to serve until 15 March 2001. Their job was to watch the ceasefire, check that both sides kept their security pledges, and confirm that Ethiopian troops left ground taken after February 1999. The Council also pushed both countries toward mine clearing, aid access, and a final peace deal without delay.

Three days of cover for Balkan rules came out of a court fight in 2002. On 30 June, the Council adopted Resolution 1420 without dissent. It acted under Chapter VII. Nine days before, Resolution 1418 had kept the rules of Resolution 1357 alive to 30 June. That deadline had now arrived. The Council's next step on Bosnia was still not ready.

The text keeps Resolution 1357 in force to 3 July 2002. It stays seized of the matter as well. The scramble had a clear cause. A fight raged over the new world criminal court and shield for peacekeepers. The Council settled that fight in July with Resolution 1422.

Resolution 1520 is a routine UN Security Council renewal of the Golan Heights observer force, adopted unanimously on 22 December 2003. The United Nations Disengagement Observer Force has patrolled the separation zone between Israel and Syria since 1974, and the Secretary-General's December report described its continued work.

The resolution calls on the parties to implement Resolution 338, the 1973 ceasefire and peace-talks order, immediately, and renews the observer force's mandate for six months, until 30 June 2004. It asks the Secretary-General to report at the end of that period on developments and on steps toward carrying out Resolution 338. These twice-yearly renewals kept a quiet border under watch.

Sierra Leone's next step after peacekeeping is set out in Resolution 1620, adopted on 31 August 2005. The UN Mission in Sierra Leone, UNAMSIL, was set to leave at the end of 2005 after helping the country recover from war. Sierra Leone's president joined the Secretary-General in asking for a UN office that would stay on and help hold the peace.

The Council asks for a United Nations Integrated Office in Sierra Leone, UNIOSIL, for twelve months from 1 January 2006. Its tasks cover building state offices, planning a human rights action plan, readying fair elections in 2007, fighting corruption, and strengthening courts, police, and the security sector. It must also track cross-border troubles such as small arms flows and work with the Special Court for Sierra Leone.

One index gives this text the year 2003. The page's own facts say 2006. It cites the chief's report of 16 October 2006. Past votes from that spring are named too. The topic is Western Sahara, the desert land claimed by Morocco. A UN team, MINURSO, guards a truce there. A vote on the land's fate has been pledged since 1991.

MINURSO's term grew to 30 April 2007. The Council asked for a fresh report before that date. States were urged to fund goodwill steps. The chief ask was visits between kin split by the war. One more clause told the force to hold fast to the UN's zero-tolerance rule on sexual abuse by its staff.

Sexual violence in war is the subject of this 2008 follow-up to the landmark text on women, peace, and security. Rape and other sexual violence, it notes, are used as tactics of war to humiliate, dominate, and displace communities. Such acts can count as war crimes, crimes against humanity, or acts of genocide.

All parties to armed conflicts are demanded to stop all sexual violence against civilians at once. Parties must train troops on the ban, enforce discipline and command responsibility, debunk myths that fuel such violence, and screen forces for past abuses. Peacekeepers are to be trained to prevent and respond to sexual violence, and the Secretary-General is asked to report on where such violence is used as a weapon of war.

Talks on Western Sahara had run in fits and starts for years. Four rounds of formal talks were done by 2010. Loose talks in Austria and the United States had kept hope warm. A new envoy, Christopher Ross, toured the area. Resolution 1920 passed on 30 April 2010. The chief's report of 6 April lay on the table.

MINURSO, the UN team there, gained a year, to 30 April 2011. Both sides had to honor the truce pacts in full. Small, loose talks would pave a fifth round. Real will to deal was called for, on a base of give and take. Family visits, by land as well as air, won warm words. States were asked to fund such steps. The text is firm that the old standstill could not last for good.

How to cage the atom was the young UN's gravest task. Its Atomic Energy Commission sent a first report on the last day of 1946. The plan sketched world checks on the new force. Resolution 20 passed with no dissent on 10 March 1947. The Council had read the report with care.

No part of the plan bound a state on its own. Each vote of yes was a first step, not a last word. The full plan had to be taken as one whole. The record of the talks went back to the team. It was urged to press on with all speed. A draft treaty on world control was the goal. A second report was due before the Assembly next sat. Hope still ran high that the bomb could be ruled by law.

Cyprus still needed its United Nations peacekeeping force in the spring of 1966. The Secretary-General reported that the force was still required to keep the peace on the island. The government of Cyprus agreed it should stay beyond 26 March 1966. The island's basic problem, though, remained unsolved. Resolution 220 was adopted unanimously on 16 March 1966.

The Council reaffirmed all its Cyprus resolutions, back to Resolution 186 of 1964. It urged everyone involved to show the utmost restraint. The force was extended for three more months, ending on 26 June 1966. The Council stated its firm hope that real progress toward a settlement would come within that period. Short renewals like this one kept the peacekeepers in place while the search for a settlement went on.

Sanctions against Southern Rhodesia were being broken openly by 1972. Several states still traded with the illegal regime despite the mandatory embargo. The United States had reported that it authorized imports of Rhodesian chrome ore and other minerals. Resolution 320 was adopted on 29 September 1972.

The Council reaffirmed that the sanctions would stay fully in force. They would last until the goals of Resolution 253 of 1968 were met. All states were called on to apply the sanctions in full. The United States was urged to cooperate with the United Nations on enforcement. South Africa and Portugal were condemned for refusing to cooperate. The Council's sanctions committee was told to study stronger action as a matter of urgency.

The Golan Heights observer force received six more months on 30 November 1977, under Resolution 420. The force watches the separation of Israeli and Syrian forces. The Council noted the efforts made toward a durable and just peace in the Middle East. It also noted the urgent need to press on with those efforts. Tension in the area still prevailed.

The parties were called on to carry out Resolution 338 of 1973 at once. That text had demanded a cease-fire and peace talks after the October war. The observer force's mandate was renewed for another period of six months, until 31 May 1978. At the end of that time, the Secretary-General had to report on developments. His report also had to cover the measures taken to carry out Resolution 338.

Lebanon's president-elect was murdered in September 1982, during Israel's invasion of the country. Bashir Gemayel, named in the text, had been elected to lead Lebanon. Days after his death, Israeli forces moved into Beirut in breach of the cease-fire. Resolution 520 was adopted on 17 September 1982.

The Council condemned the murder of the president-elect. It also condemned every effort to block, by violence, the return of a strong and stable government in Lebanon. Its resolutions on Lebanon from earlier in 1982 were reaffirmed in full. The Israeli incursions into Beirut were condemned. Israel was told to return its forces at once to the positions held before 15 September. The Council also backed the United Nations observers stationed around Beirut. Lebanon's sovereignty was to be respected, under the authority of its own army.

Resolution 620, adopted on 26 August 1988, returns to chemical weapons in the Iran-Iraq war with harder evidence. Three missions sent by the Secretary-General that summer had confirmed continued poison gas use, and gas attacks on Iranians had grown fiercer and more often. The Council said it was deeply dismayed and worried about future use.

The Council condemned resolutely the use of chemical weapons in defiance of the 1925 Geneva Protocol and of its own demand that spring. It encouraged the Secretary-General to investigate new allegations from any member state quickly, with expert help. It also backed the Geneva disarmament talks then negotiating a total ban on developing, producing, and stockpiling chemical weapons, work that produced the 1993 Chemical Weapons Convention.

Choosing a Secretary-General is among the Council's gravest tasks. In 1991 the members met behind closed doors to pick a successor to Javier Pérez de Cuéllar. Resolution 720 was adopted unanimously at that closed meeting on 21 November 1991. The question was the recommendation for the UN's top job.

The Council put forward Boutros Boutros-Ghali of Egypt. His proposed term ran from 1 January 1992 to 31 December 1996. The General Assembly accepted the choice. Boutros-Ghali became the first African and first Arab to lead the UN. His tenure covered Somalia, Rwanda, and Bosnia. This one-line recommendation set all of that in motion.
vinogradoff-outlines-historical-jurispru:
Vinogradoff began his Outlines of Historical Jurisprudence with a first volume in 1920. The Oxford jurist, born in Russia and formed by several legal traditions, planned a survey of law's whole history. The Outlines were to be his synthesis, the fruit of a lifetime spent comparing legal systems.

Volume 1 begins with the ancient world: law born of custom, kingship, and the needs of early states. He moves from the Near East through Greece to the Rome of the emperors, tracing how legal ideas travel and change. Vinogradoff writes as a comparatist, always asking what one system's solution teaches about another's. The wide-ranging survey opens his grand design with characteristic calm. Few scholars of any age could have attempted the whole history of law in two volumes and carried it off.
wallas-human-nature-politics-1920:
Graham Wallas founded political psychology with Human Nature in Politics, first issued in 1908. The text here is the third edition of 1920, from Project Gutenberg. Older political thought pictured voters as reasoning machines, weighing each claim. Wallas, a Fabian socialist and teacher, found that picture false to life.

Impulse, habit, party symbols, and crowd feeling move real politics, he argues. Statesmen work with human nature as it is, not as theory wishes. His chapters urge honest study of how opinions actually form. The book opened a field that now studies campaigns and media. Its calm tone hides its radical break. Politicians ignore it at their cost.
wegener-entstehung-kontinente-1920:
Alfred Wegener, a German weather scientist, argued that continents slowly drift across the globe. His book The Origin of Continents and Oceans, shown here in German, first appeared in 1915 and grew in later editions. The 1920 text states his case in full.

Wegener points to matching coastlines, matching fossils, and matching rock layers on lands now split by oceans. South America and Africa, he says, were once joined. Most geologists mocked him, since he could not name the force that moves continents. Plate tectonics later proved the drift itself was real. Later finds on the ocean floor at last gave drift its engine.
wharton-age-of-innocence-1920:
Edith Wharton published The Age of Innocence in 1920, her novel of 1870s New York and its rigid codes. The tale tells Newland Archer's doomed love for the Countess Olenska inside that shuttered, tribal world. It won the Pulitzer Prize in 1921, the first awarded to a woman for a novel in America.

Archer, engaged to May Welland, is shaken by her cousin Ellen, returned from a scandalous marriage in Europe alone. Ellen's freedom exposes the cruelty and fear beneath his tribe's polished manners, dinners, and opera boxes in old New York. Archer chooses duty, weds May, and lives a respectable life haunted by the road not taken with Ellen. Decades later, in Paris, he sits below her window and sends his son up alone at dusk. Wharton's archaeology of her parents' world is tender, ironic, and quietly devastating in its close.
whitbourne-discovery-newfoundland-1620:
Richard Whitbourne, a Devon sea captain, wrote A Discovery of New-found-land in 1620 to promote English settlement there. He knew the island from years of fishing voyages. His tract praises the colony's wealth in cod, timber, and safe harbors for ships.

Whitbourne also reports a famous sight. He describes a mermaid that swam up to his boat and looked at the crew. That account became the classic English colonial mermaid story. The wonder sits atop a practical sales pitch for Newfoundland. Whitbourne hoped marvels and profit together would draw settlers and backers across the Atlantic.
whitehead-concept-nature-1920:
Alfred North Whitehead published The Concept of Nature in 1920, based on his Tarner Lectures at Cambridge. Whitehead asks what we mean by nature in modern science. He argues that nature is a process of events, not a set of static objects. Sense awareness, he says, shows passage and relation first of all.

He rejects the split between nature as sensed and nature as cause of sense. Points, moments, and objects are abstractions from the flow of events. The book laid groundwork for his later process philosophy. It also influenced modern philosophy of science. Readers meet Whitehead's key ideas here in compact form.
williams-kora-in-hell-1920:
Kora in Hell, published in 1920, is Williams's book of improvisations: short prose pieces written fast, day by day, during the war years. Kora is Persephone, the maiden carried to the underworld, and hell here is the modern world at war.

Each improvisation leaps from image to image, a doctor's day, a patient's face, spring fought out of winter, with commentaries that explain and argue with the text. Williams was testing how far spontaneity could carry meaning. The result is uneven, electric, and very personal. It is the first sounding of the American grain he would explore for decades.
young-journal-of-discourses-vol20:
With Volume XX in 1880, the Journal of Discourses entered its fourth decade of printed sermons. Liverpool still printed the set, and shorthand reporters still caught the words as they were spoken in Utah. Speakers include senior apostles and other elders, preaching to a church now led from the Twelve after Young's death.

Two decades of volumes behind it give this one a settled, archival feel for any reader. The talks instruct, correct, and encourage in the familiar pulpit voice of the movement at work. Volume XX adds a round number to the running doctrinal record of nineteenth-century Mormonism, with six volumes yet to come.
